08001.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

08005.text: Arapahoe County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the heat and drought claims are what stand out. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 1.09, so insurers paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre for 2026, down 10 percent from 2016, against a 2022 census land value of $2,773 per acre. Solar is the only large new use on the books, at 150.7 MW operating.

08009.text: Baca County is mostly dryland, and the dry side is where the pressure shows. Heat and drought made up 40 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.15, so claims have run past premium over the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre in 2026, up 40.9 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $123 per acre in 2023, and all of the county's irrigation water comes from groundwater.

08011.text: Bent County is mostly irrigated ground: 81 percent of harvested cropland, with irrigated rent at $178 per acre against $18 for dryland. The loss record is the story here. Crop insurance has paid out $68.4 million on closed years since 1989, and irrigation failure is the largest cause at 58 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.63, and 11 of 19 crop years paid more than the premium. The census puts land and buildings at $1,087 per acre in 2022, up 57.5 percent from 2017. Drought weeks in severe or worse conditions ran 483 of 1,357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, with 53 in the worst year, 2013.

08013.text: Most of the cropland here is irrigated, 75 percent by the 2022 census, and the water is surface supply, not groundwater. The notable thing is the heat and drought claims. They went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2000-2009, then 9 percent in 2010-2019 and 15 percent in 2020-2025. Hail is still the biggest single cause at 43 percent. The loss ratio over the full run is 0.71, and it was 0.69 over the last ten closed crop years. Irrigated rent is $96 per acre for 2026 against $49 non-irrigated for 2025, and the 2022 land and buildings value is $18,310 per acre. Only 73 CRP acres are left, and none expire through 2029.

08015.text:
Chaffee County is mostly irrigated ground. The census put 88 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, and the irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $61 per acre against $30 for non-irrigated ground. Most of the water comes from surface sources, with none from groundwater in 2015.

The drought weeks are the part to watch. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse went from 212 weeks across 2000-2025 overall, and 28 of those weeks fell in 2021-2025 alone. The worst single year was 2002, with 43 weeks.

Heat is not the story here. July nightly lows averaged 44.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 44.3 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F.

08017.text: Cheyenne County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what drives its claims. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out $294.8 million over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.12. Corn yields have trended down 3.1 bushels per acre a year since 2008, and the worst year was 2022 at 37.7. Non-irrigated rent has held at $32 per acre, while irrigated ground rents for $170, and wind is the one large use of the land, with 498.4 MW operating.

08029.text: Delta County is mostly irrigated ground: 93 percent of the harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from groundwater. The rent tells the story. Non-irrigated ground rents for $16 per acre, down 45 percent from 2014 to 2024, while irrigated ground goes for $120 per acre in 2026. Losses here come mostly from freeze and frost, which caused 71 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 0 percent in 1989-1999 to 1 percent in 2020-2025, so that is not where the money has gone. Land and buildings were valued at $7,364 per acre in 2022, up 53 percent from 2017.

08031.text: Denver County is a small corner of the state, and the notable thing here is the heat and drought claims. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 51 percent in 2000-2009 to 77 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 2000-2025 is 0.73, so the premiums have covered most of the claims. Land value is high next to what the ground can make: $122,408 per acre in the 2022 census, after rising 92.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. The county has 0 CRP acres and 6.8 MW of operating solar, with no wind.

08033.text: Dolores County's most telling number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities paid out $6.5 million across 1989-2025, and heat and drought accounted for 68 percent of that. The share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 82 percent in 2010-2019, and was 64 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 1.22, so claims paid out more than premiums came in. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which leaves most of the ground dependent on rain. Land and buildings were valued at $3,270 per acre in the 2022 census, up 83.4 percent from 2017, and 31.9 percent of the cropland base sits in CRP.

08035.text: Douglas County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 13 percent irrigated in 2022, and the census put land and buildings at $12,290 per acre. That value rose 82.2 percent from 2017 to 2022, which is well ahead of the $14 per acre non-irrigated cash rent reported for 2012. The bigger story for the ground is CRP, which covered 3136 acres in 2025, or 38.3 percent of the cropland base, and none of it comes up for expiration in fiscal years 2027-2029. Drought has been a steady presence: 179 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2002 the worst at 38 weeks. The July nightly low averaged 55.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 54.3 F normal.

08039.text: Elbert County is a dryland county where the cash rent has climbed fast. Non-irrigated ground rents at $28 per acre in 2026, up 50 percent since 2016. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: a loss ratio of 0.87 across the closed years 1989-2025, with heat and drought behind 70 percent of the claims in 2020-2025, up from 23 percent in 1989-1999. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 48.5 percent of the cropland base sits in CRP. The 2002 drought left 37 weeks in severe drought or worse, the worst year in the record.

08041.text: Most of El Paso County's cropland is not irrigated by the usual measure, but the county is in CRP heavily: 28184 acres, 78.2 percent of the cropland base, and none of those contracts expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. The land itself has moved fast. Census value was $2,688 per acre in 2022, and it rose 91 percent from 2017 to 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent was $7 per acre in 2024, down 50.4 percent from 2013. Irrigated cash rent was $80 per acre in 2017. Irrigation is 44 percent of harvested cropland, and 91 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 53 percent of closed crop insurance indemnities from 1993-2023.

08045.text: Garfield County is mostly irrigated ground, with 89 percent of harvested cropland under water, and none of that water comes from wells. Irrigated cash rent was $68 per acre in 2025, while non-irrigated rent was $31 per acre in 2020 and has risen 14.8 percent since 2009. Census land and buildings were valued at $3,654 per acre in 2022, up 52.3 percent from 2017. The drought record stands out: 376 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2021 the worst year at 51 weeks. July nightly lows averaged 54.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 53 F. There is no CRP ground here, and 45.3 MW of solar is operating with no wind.

08057.text: Jackson County is mostly irrigated, with 88 percent of harvested cropland under pivots or other systems, and none of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rented for $100 per acre in 2023, while non-irrigated rent was $14 per acre in 2024, down 14.7 percent from 2013. Land and buildings were valued at $2,216 per acre in 2022, and that value was up 67.5 percent from 2017 to 2022. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 183 of 1357 from 2000-2025, with 2002 and 2012 each at 37 weeks. The July nightly low is 43.4 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 43 F.

08061.text: Kiowa County is a dryland county, and the drought history is what stands out. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 69 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and the share was 33 percent in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2010-2019. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $29 per acre in 2026, up 7.4 percent from 2016. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.04, so claims have paid out more than premiums overall.

08067.text: Most of La Plata County's cropland is watered by ditch and pump, with 95 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the irrigated rent of $82 per acre is the number that matters here. Non-irrigated ground rents for $24 per acre, which tells you how much the water is worth. The crop insurance record leans hard on dry years. Heat and drought went from 57 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over closed crop years 1990-2025 is 1.41, meaning claims have paid out more than premiums came in. The July nightly low has warmed a little, from 51.7 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 52.7 F over 2017-2026.

08069.text: Most of Larimer County's cropland is irrigated, 74 percent of it, and the irrigation water comes from surface sources rather than wells. That shapes everything else here. Irrigated cash rent is $195 per acre, and non-irrigated ground rents for $29, so the two kinds of ground are very different things to rent. Heat and drought claims are a small part of the crop insurance record, but they went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the full closed period is 0.86, and it was 0.68 over 2016-2025. Hail is the largest cause of loss at 38 percent. Irrigated ground is where most of the money is, and it is worth knowing which kind of ground you are looking at.

08071.text: Most of the ground in Las Animas County is in grass, not crops. CRP covers 156,062 acres, or 88.3 percent of the cropland base, and none of those contracts expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. The irrigated ground is where the rent gap shows: $122 per acre irrigated against $6 for non-irrigated, with 57 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in the 2022 census. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 29 percent of the $3.3 million paid over 1989-2023, and its share went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. The census puts land and buildings at $1,005 per acre in 2022.

08073.text: Heat and drought is the story in Lincoln County. It caused 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2020-2025, and it accounts for 64 percent of all crop insurance payouts since 1989. The county's loss ratio is 0.96 over the closed years, with 11 of 29 crop years paying out more than premium. Most of the ground is in CRP, 249248 acres in 2025, which is 49.3 percent of the cropland base. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, and census land value was $900 per acre in 2022.

08075.text: Logan County is a dryland county with a large irrigated share, and the rent gap between the two shows it. Irrigated ground rents for $234 per acre in 2026, against $36 for non-irrigated, and irrigated rent was 3.58 times the dryland rent in 2010 and 6.41 times in 2026. Heat and drought made up 9 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 55 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are where the claims have been. Irrigation failure has paid out only $1.8 million across all closed years. Wind is the big energy presence here, with 999.1 MW operating and nothing proposed.

08081.text: Moffat County is an irrigated place by the numbers, with 46 percent of harvested cropland watered, and it's the irrigated ground that rents for real money at $90 per acre in 2023 against $20 for dryland. The thing I'd look at first is heat and drought, which made up 4 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2010-2019. Insurance has paid out $547,823 on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.35, so the claims have been modest against the premiums. Land values jumped 95.2 percent from 2017 to 2022, well above the $20 dryland rent, and CRP holds 27 percent of the cropland base, with 161 acres of it expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

08083.text: Montezuma County is mostly irrigated ground, 86 percent of harvested cropland by the 2022 census, and the water comes from surface supply, not wells. The number that stands out is the crop insurance loss ratio: 1.09 over closed crop years 1990-2025, and 1.23 over 2016-2025, so claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought is the largest cause of those claims at 37 percent. Non-irrigated rent was $24 per acre in 2025 and irrigated rent was $135 per acre in 2026, and the 2022 census put land and buildings at $1,736 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate.

08085.text: Most of Montrose County's cropland is irrigated, 91 percent in the 2022 census, and its irrigation water comes from surface sources, not wells. Irrigated cash rent was $138 per acre in 2026, while the census puts land and buildings at $5,909 per acre. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 1.13 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, and the county spent 85 weeks in severe drought or worse across 2021-2025.

08095.text: Phillips County is mostly dryland, but the irrigated ground is where the money is: irrigated rent is $257 per acre against $48 for non-irrigated, and 37 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all of it from groundwater. Heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims, at 58 percent of indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 2016-2025 was 1.03, so claims paid out more than premiums over those ten years. Non-irrigated rent is up 43.9 percent since 2016, to $48 per acre.

08099.text: Prowers is an irrigated county on paper and a dryland one in the rent. Irrigated ground rents for $154 per acre, and non-irrigated goes for $34. Groundwater supplies 29 percent of the irrigation water, and the county's corn has averaged 159.3 bushels per acre since 2008, with 2011 bottoming out at 128.4. The bigger story is claims. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years, the loss ratio was 1.09, so insurers have paid out more than they took in. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 79 in 2021-2025, and the 2013 peak was 53 weeks in one year.

08103.text: Rio Blanco is mostly an irrigated county. Eighty percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and the water comes from surface sources, not wells. Irrigated ground rents for $86 per acre in 2026, while non-irrigated ground goes for $12. Land and buildings were valued at $1,911 per acre in 2022, up 39.2 percent from 2017. The drought line is the one to watch: 353 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 64 of those weeks came in 2021-2025. July nights are also running warmer, with the average low at 55.7 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.7 F.

08109.text: Saguache County's cropland is mostly irrigated, at 90 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and most of that water comes from groundwater, 30 percent in 2015. The biggest reason claims get paid here is irrigation failure, which accounts for 48 percent of indemnities over the closed years. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums collected in 11 of the 23 closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.03. Irrigated cash rent is $189 per acre for 2026, and non-irrigated ground was $20 per acre in 2020. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 10 percent in 2020-2025.

08113.text: San Miguel County's cropland is mostly irrigated, two-thirds of harvested acres in the 2022 census, and the irrigation water is all surface supply. The bigger story in the claims is heat and drought, which made up 69 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1990-2025, and drought weeks have been frequent, with 341 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated cash rent was $14 per acre in 2026, and the 2022 census put land and buildings at $2,179 per acre, up 46.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low has edged up from the 1991-2020 normal of 51.8 F to 52.7 F in 2017-2026.

08115.text: Sedgwick County is a dryland county with a small irrigated base, and the gap between the two is large. Irrigated ground rented for $178 per acre in 2026 against $45 for non-irrigated, and irrigated rent was 5.03 times non-irrigated in 2012 and has been falling since. Heat and drought is the main cause of claims, with 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 79 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the county paid out $90.7 million, and 9 of 27 closed crop years paid more than the premium.

08121.text: Washington County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is where the county stands out. Crop insurance has paid out more than it collected in premium over the closed years 1989-2025, with a loss ratio of 0.94 and 10 of 34 crop years paying more than premium. Over 2016-2025 the ratio is 1.09. Heat and drought claims went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $40 per acre, up 41.1 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents at $214 per acre.

08123.text: Weld County is an irrigated county first. Irrigation covers 64 percent of harvested cropland, and the irrigated rent of $202 per acre is 8.08 times the non-irrigated rent of $25, up from 3.92 times in 2009. Most of the water comes from surface sources, with groundwater only 7 percent. The clearest change in the claims record is heat and drought, which went from 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. The 2002 drought was the worst year for drought weeks, with 37 of them.

08125.text: Yuma County is an irrigated county in a dry-land setting. Irrigated cash rent is $290 per acre against $45 for non-irrigated ground, and the gap has widened, from 4.68 times the non-irrigated rent in 2009 to 6.44 times in 2026. Irrigation covers 52 percent of harvested cropland, and all of its water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025. The insurance loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 0.87, and the county has 273588 CRP acres, 44.4 percent of the cropland base.

17001.text: Adams County is a rainfed county where the weather and the insurance claims tell the story. Heat and drought was 18 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 41 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 39 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.28, so the premiums have covered most of the claims that were paid. Non-irrigated cash rent is $238 per acre in 2026, up 36 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $8,631 per acre in 2022, and the 2022 rent was 2.06 percent of that. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has 13912 CRP acres, with 1955 of them expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

17003.text: Most of the ground in Alexander County is dryland, and the notable thing here is the water side. Every gallon of irrigation water comes from groundwater, and the county's irrigated cash rent in 2024 was $200 per acre against $189 for non-irrigated ground in 2025. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years are costing more claims than they used to. Excess moisture and flood still make up 86 percent of all indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio of 0.73 means claims have run ahead of premium over the full record. Non-irrigated rent rose 47.7 percent from 2014 to 2025.

17007.text: Boone County is mostly dryland, and the drought record is what stands out. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims from 1989 through 2025 at 40 percent. Its share went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2010-2019 and 28 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims come in waves rather than steadily. Non-irrigated cash rent is $267 per acre in 2026, up 7.7 percent since 2016. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.38, well under the 0.59 for the full record.

17009.text: Brown County is a dryland county with a wet-year problem more than a dry-year one. Excess moisture and flood is the biggest cause of claims at 28 percent, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.75, with 5 of 22 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 32 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $233 per acre for 2026, up 25.9 percent since 2016. The census land value was $6,571 per acre in 2022.

17013.text: The thing that stands out in Calhoun County is water, and too much of it. Excess moisture and flood account for 40 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the closed crop years have paid out $42.3 million, with the loss ratio at 0.84 and five of 19 years paying more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2010-2019, then 27 percent in 2020-2025, so it has grown into a real share but has not been the main story. Non-irrigated cash rent is $201 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,497 per acre in 2022. The county has 9015 CRP acres, which is 15.9 percent of the cropland base.

17015.text: Carroll County is a rainfed county with one notable pressure: heat and drought claims. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, and they remain the largest single cause over the full record. Corn yields have a trend of 3.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a worst year of 157.9 bushels in 2012 against a median of 204.6. Non-irrigated cash rent is $290 per acre in 2026, up 15.1 percent since 2016. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain.

17021.text: Christian County's most notable figure is the drop in heat and drought claims. They made up 45 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 47 percent in 2010-2019, and only 9 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.4, and only 1 of 28 closed crop years paid out more than the premiums that came in. Non-irrigated rent is $332 per acre for 2026, up 29.7 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $10,960 per acre in 2022, up 26.9 percent from 2017. The county's worst drought week count came in 2000, with 16 weeks.

17023.text: Clark County's heat and drought story is mostly a 2010s story. Heat and drought made up 37 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, then 70 percent in 2010-2019, before falling back to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record the county has paid out $86.0 million, and it has paid more than premium in 3 of 28 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $248 per acre in 2026, up 35.5 percent since 2016. Census land value in 2022 was $7,770 per acre, so rent was 2.93 percent of that.

17025.text: Clay County's heat and drought claims stand out. They were 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, rose to 69 percent in 2010-2019, and came down to 22 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.88, and the ten crop years from 2016 through 2025 was 0.51, so the payouts have been lighter lately. None of the cropland is irrigated, so the county depends on rain. Non-irrigated rent was $197 per acre in 2025, up 32.2 percent since 2014. CRP takes 8.3 percent of the cropland base, and 4556 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

17027.text: Clinton County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the water that does get used is 88 percent groundwater, so the bet on rain is the whole bet. Heat and drought has paid out 51 percent of the county's crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent was $218 per acre in 2023, up 47.3 percent from 2013. Land and buildings were valued at $9,036 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated. Heat and drought has been the main claim, and that is worth knowing before you set the rent.

17029.text: Coles County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here lives or dies by rain. Heat and drought made up 53 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 72 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Since 1989, the county has paid out $82.6 million in closed crop years, with heat and drought at 57 percent of that. Two of the 27 closed crop years paid out more than the premium, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.13. The 2025 season had 12 weeks in severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $286 per acre.

17031.text: Cook County is a crop insurance story more than a weather story. Excess moisture and flood have caused the largest share of claims since 1989, at 52 percent. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 1.13, and for the last ten closed crop years it is 1.34, meaning claims have run ahead of premiums. Heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 71 percent in 2020-2025, so the recent claims have leaned hard toward dry years. Cash rent is $136 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $18,054 per acre, so the rent is a small slice of what the ground is worth.

17033.text: Crawford County's heat and drought story has changed hands over the years. Heat and drought made up 43 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 24 percent in 2000-2009, rose to 65 percent in 2010-2019, and was 10 percent in 2020-2025. The closed-year loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.74, and 4 of 26 crop years paid out more than premium. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and that water is all groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $200 per acre in 2026, and CRP covers 5.6 percent of the cropland base, with 3266 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

17035.text: Cumberland County is a dryland county with a loss record that stands out. Heat and drought has driven 60 percent of the $69.5 million paid in crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the closed-year loss ratio is 0.75, with 1 of 22 crop years paying out more than premium. The 2010-2019 stretch was the bad one, at 71 percent of indemnities from heat and drought, against 16 percent for 2020-2025. The rent is $211 per acre, up 16.6 percent since 2016, and the land is valued at $8,894 per acre by the census. Solar is operating at 273.6 MW, and CRP covers 10.6 percent of the cropland base.

17037.text: DeKalb County is a non-irrigated county, with none of its harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, so the rain that falls is the crop's water. That makes the insurance history worth a look. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of indemnities at 31 percent, while heat and drought went from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025. Crop years paid out more than premium in 5 of 26 closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.45 across 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $318 per acre in 2025.

17039.text: De Witt County's heat-and-drought claims have moved around a lot. They were 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 62 percent again in 2010-2019, with a low of 17 percent in 2000-2009 and 22 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the county paid $44.1 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.37, but the last ten closed years was 0.13. Cash rent is $301 per acre this year, up 13.6 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $11,261 per acre in 2022, and rent that year was 2.63 percent of that value.

17041.text: Douglas County is a dryland county with no irrigated ground at all, so every bushel depends on rain. The yield trend is up 4.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but 2012 was 99.4 bushels against a median of 208.6. Heat and drought made up 52 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 80 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 19 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.52, and only 2 of 28 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated rent is $313 per acre, up 13 percent since 2016.

17043.text: DuPage is a county where heat and drought have become the main reason claims get paid. Their share of indemnities went from 13 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, with a 44 percent share in 2000-2009 in between, and the 2020-2025 figure is the most recent one. Only 24 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the average July low is 64.7 F against a 63.5 F normal for 1991-2020. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.76, and over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.77. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2024 was $150 per acre.

17045.text: Edgar County's cropland is all non-irrigated, and the crop has taken its hits from weather. Heat and drought made up 81 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-2025's heaviest stretch, 2010-2019, down to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.12, so the county paid out little against premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $275 per acre for 2026, up 1.9 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $10,162 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators estimated themselves, and rent was 2.76 percent of it.

17047.text: Edwards County is a county where the water problem has been too much rain, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 47 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the closed crop years show a loss ratio of 0.69, with only 3 of 22 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $156 per acre, up 24.8 percent from 2016. The county has 3204 CRP acres, which is 3.2 percent of the cropland base, and no solar or wind operating.

17049.text: Effingham County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here lives or dies on rain. The county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.78, but the last ten closed crop years was 0.33, which means claims have been light lately. Heat and drought made up 79 percent of claims in 2010-2019 and 44 percent in 2020-2025, so the big dry years still drive the picture. Non-irrigated cash rent is $199 per acre in 2026, up 32.7 percent from 2016. CRP covers 12914 acres, and 2591 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

17051.text: Fayette County's heat and drought story is the one to start with. Heat and drought made up 22 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 47 percent in 2020-2025. Nothing here is irrigated, and the county has had 19 weeks of severe drought across 2000-2025, with 8 of them in 2012. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.78, and 6 of 31 crop years paid out more than the premium. Cash rent is $192 per acre for 2026, up 31.5 percent since 2016.

17053.text: Ford County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the weather record is the story here. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 61 percent of the insurance payouts from 1989-2025, and their share went from 69 percent in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025. The county's ten closed crop years from 2016-2025 show a loss ratio of 0.19, so claims have been light lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $294 per acre, up 23.5 percent from 2016.

17057.text: Fulton County's biggest story in these numbers is water, and it's excess water more than dry weather. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 40 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years are part of the picture too. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.3, which means claims ran well under premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $263 per acre, up 28.9 percent from 2016.

17059.text: Gallatin County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the cash rent reflects that. Non-irrigated ground rents for $155 per acre in 2026, and that rent is down 3.1 percent from 2016. Only 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigated ground rented for $188 per acre in 2025, a ratio of 1.15 that was 1.19 back in 2009. Crop insurance indemnities came mostly from excess moisture and flood, which accounted for 47 percent of the $129.9 million paid across 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025.

17061.text: Greene County's notable number is how little of its insurance money has come from heat and drought lately. Heat and drought went from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025, though the share was 35 percent in 2010-2019, so it has swung around a lot. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause over the whole record at 35 percent. The loss ratio of 0.52 says claims have run well under premiums across 1989-2025, and only 3 of 26 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated rent is $280 per acre in 2026.

17065.text: Hamilton County has no irrigated harvested cropland in the 2022 census, so every acre here is dryland, and the claims history shows it. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of indemnities at 47 percent, and the county has paid out more than premium in 5 of 27 closed crop years, for a loss ratio of 0.74. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 23 percent in 2020-2025. The non-irrigated cash rent was $138 per acre in 2025.

17067.text: Hancock County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid $117.2 million since 1989 on closed crop years, and heat and drought went from 15 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, with 36 percent in 2010-2019 in between. The loss ratio over all closed years is 0.51, but over 2016-2025 it is 0.23. Non-irrigated cash rent is $284 per acre for 2026, up 29.1 percent from 2016. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, so most of this county's corn rides on rain.

17069.text: Hardin County's notable number is its losses from wet weather, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 54 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county's loss ratio over those years was 1.07, meaning claims paid out more than premiums collected. No cropland is irrigated, so every acre here depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent was $100 per acre in 2020, up 20.5 percent from 2009. Heat and drought claims went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2010-2019, then dropped to 25 percent in 2020-2025.

17071.text: Henderson County's biggest story in the numbers is wet ground, not dry. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims, at 47 percent of indemnities since 1989, and only 3 of 28 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is climbing. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $292 per acre, up 36.4 percent since 2016. The county's own July nightly lows are not a clear trend.

17075.text: Iroquois County is mostly dryland, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and its weather story runs through heat and drought claims. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025 at 40 percent, and its share went from 58 percent in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025. Still, the loss ratio of 0.63 over the closed years is well under 1, and the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.25. The county has 300.8 MW of operating wind and a small 2 MW solar site. Non-irrigated cash rent was $205 per acre in 2022, and the census land value was $8,638 per acre.

17077.text: Jackson County is mostly dryland, and the heat-and-drought side of its claims has been growing. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for the largest share over the full record at 49 percent. Crop insurance has paid out more than premium over the full span, with a loss ratio of 0.74, but the ten most recent closed years came in lower at 0.51. Non-irrigated cash rent is $172 per acre for 2026, up 27.4 percent since 2016. The census land value of $5,094 per acre is well above that rent, and only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

17079.text: Heat and drought drove the claims in Jasper County, but the pattern has shifted. Heat and drought made up 46 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, then 70 percent in 2010-2019, and only 17 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.29, well under the 0.73 for the full record, with 3 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $195 per acre in 2026, up 29.1 percent since 2016.

17081.text: Jefferson County is a wet-year county more than a dry-year one. Flooding and excess moisture are the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 43 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.82, with 6 of 24 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 33 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2010-2019 before falling back to 29 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $136 per acre, up 20.4 percent from 2016, and the census value of land and buildings is $4,940 per acre. Solar is at 2 MW with 155 MW proposed, and no wind.

17083.text: Jersey County is a dryland county, and the insurance record is where that shows up most. Heat and drought made up 52 percent of the $47.2 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989, and its share went from 27 percent in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2010-2019 before falling to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025, the loss ratio is 0.6, but the last ten closed years ran at 0.32, so the payouts have been lighter lately. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $221 per acre, down 7.9 percent from 2016.

17085.text: Jo Daviess County is a dryland county. Not a single harvested acre is irrigated, so every bushel here depends on what the sky does. The heat and drought share of insurance claims went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 26 percent in 2020-2025. The county also paid out $121.4 million in indemnities on closed crop years, against a loss ratio of 0.76, so claims have run well ahead of premium over time. The 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.36, which is a lighter stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $255 per acre for 2026, up 18.6 percent from 2016.

17087.text: Johnson County's notable number is water, and it is wet more than dry. Excess moisture and flood account for 58 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.95, with 4 of 13 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 39 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. The county has no irrigated acres, and the July nightly low has warmed 0.51 F per decade since 1976. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2025 is $129 per acre, up 61.3 percent since 2014.

17089.text: Kane County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the water problem here has been too much of it more than too little. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims, at 33 percent, and the county's loss ratio is 0.58 over 1989-2025, with 5 of 24 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, so that side is growing. Non-irrigated cash rent is $274 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $12,276 per acre in 2022.

17091.text: Kankakee County is notable for how little of its cropland is irrigated and for how much of its loss history comes from too much water rather than too little. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, and 93 percent of that irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Excess moisture and flood were the largest cause of indemnities at 44 percent, and the loss ratio of 0.65 over 1989-2025 means claims ran below premiums on the whole. Heat and drought went from 53 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025.

17093.text: Kendall County is a dryland county with one thing that stands out: heat and drought has been the biggest cause of insurance payouts, though its share has come down. It went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.4, so premiums have mostly covered claims. Non-irrigated cash rent is $297 per acre for 2026, up 25.3 percent since 2016, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings was $11,745 per acre. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and CRP acres are small at 396.

17095.text: Knox County's heat and drought claims stand out more than its rent does. Heat and drought was 16 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 43 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 23 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record the county has paid $61.0 million in indemnities, and the loss ratio is 0.31, so claims have run well under premium over time. Non-irrigated cash rent is $296 per acre for 2026, up 30.4 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $8,642 per acre in 2022, and the 2022 rent was 3.07 percent of that value.

17097.text: Lake County's biggest story is wet weather, not heat. Excess moisture and flood took 42 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.87. Heat and drought claims were 3 percent in 1989-1999 and 41 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has grown a lot in recent years. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $125 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $15,913 per acre.

17101.text: Lawrence County is mostly dryland, and its rent has climbed hard. Non-irrigated cash rent is $219 per acre in 2026, up 52.1 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground is $305 per acre in 2025, but that premium has been narrowing: irrigated rent was 1.46 times non-irrigated in 2009 and was 1.37 times in 2025. Flood and excess moisture drove 49 percent of the $91.6 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025, while heat and drought went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.28.

17103.text: Lee County's heat and drought claims stand out. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 40 percent in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 20 percent in 2000-2009. The loss ratio is 0.48 over 1989-2025, and 6 of 32 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $283 per acre, up 19.4 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $10,639 per acre, so rent is a small share of that. Most of the ground here relies on groundwater, which supplies 89 percent of irrigation water.

17105.text: Heat and drought are the story in Livingston County. They caused 68 percent of the $293.9 million in crop insurance indemnities paid for closed crop years 1989-2025, and their share went from 73 percent in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025. The county's 2025 drought was its worst, with 12 weeks in severe drought or worse, and 19 such weeks came in 2021-2025 alone. Corn yields have trended up 3.7 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 197.2 bushels and a worst year at 83.3 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent was $278 per acre in 2023, and the census put land and buildings at $10,108 per acre in 2022.

17107.text: Logan County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather risk shows up in the claims. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, at 36 percent of $155.5 million paid. Its share went from 40 percent in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025, but 45 percent in 2010-2019 shows how lumpy those dry years are. Non-irrigated cash rent is $326 per acre for 2026, up 11.3 percent from 2016. The 2022 census put land and buildings at $11,349 per acre, and the county has 656 MW of wind operating.

17109.text: Heat and drought have been the biggest cause of crop insurance claims in McDonough County, taking 33 percent of the $86.8 million paid out since 1989. Their share went from 12 percent in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2010-2019, then fell back to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio was 0.23, so claims have run well under premiums lately, though three of the 29 closed years still paid out more than was collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $293 per acre for 2026.

17113.text: McLean County is dryland ground, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census and all of its irrigation water from groundwater where any is used. Heat and drought took the largest share of indemnities across 1989-2025, at 66 percent of $180.2 million paid, and its share swung hard by period, from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025 with 77 percent in 2010-2019 in between. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 was 0.43, but over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 it was 0.11, so recent years have paid out far less against premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $326 per acre for 2026, up 19.9 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $7,074 per acre.

17115.text: Macon County's cropland is all rain-fed, and the one thing that stands out is how the heat and drought claims have moved. Heat and drought made up 47 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 11 percent in 2020-2025. The worst year on record is 2012, when the median corn yield of 212.1 bushels per acre dropped to 102.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $347 per acre, up 27.1 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $6,339 per acre. Corn yields have trended up 4.5 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2025.

17117.text: Macoupin is a dryland county where the crop insurance record tells the story. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims over 1989-2025, at 34 percent. Its share went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2010-2019, then came back to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.84, and five of 31 years paid out more than the premium, so the ground has been hard on the insurance company. Cash rent is $245 per acre for 2026, up 7.5 percent since 2016, and corn yield has trended up 4.4 bushels per acre a year. The census puts land and buildings at $8,862 per acre.

17119.text: Madison County's cropland is mostly non-irrigated, and the rent for that ground is $249 per acre in 2026, up 37.6 percent from 2016. Heat and drought is the biggest cause of insurance claims here, at 46 percent of indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2010-2019. The county's loss ratio is 0.72 over the closed crop years, with 4 of 27 years paying out more than premium. Over the last ten closed crop years the ratio is 0.28, so the recent record is much lighter than the long one.

17121.text: Heat and drought is the main thing to watch in Marion County. It was 23 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 35 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the whole closed run is 0.92, and 6 of 27 crop years paid out more than premium. Over the last ten closed crop years it has been 0.57. Non-irrigated cash rent is $172 per acre in 2026, up 15.4 percent from 2016. The county has 13190 CRP acres, and 3400 of them expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

17123.text: Marshall County is mostly rain-fed ground, with 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the heat and drought claims are the thing to look at. Heat and drought was 46 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 21 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.47, but over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.22, so the ground has paid back well in recent years. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $293 per acre, up 26.8 percent from 2016. Against the census land value of $10,448 per acre, that rent is 2.48 percent, a thin return for an owner.

17125.text: Mason County is a non-irrigated county in practice, and the heat and drought numbers are where I'd look first. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's 93 drought weeks since 2000 include 25 in 2005 alone. The corn yield trend is up 4.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the worst year, 2012, was 110.2 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $257 per acre in 2026, up 17.4 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $8,722 per acre in 2022, and 22,091 acres are in CRP.

17127.text: Massac County's heat-and-drought story has changed direction. Heat and drought made up 39 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 42 percent in 2010-2019, and 17 percent in 2020-2025. The county's bigger insurance problem has been too much water, which caused 57 percent of the $28.9 million paid since 1989. The loss ratio is 0.59 over the full record, and 0.57 over the last ten closed crop years, so the county has paid back less than the premiums it collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $121 per acre in 2025, down 18.2 percent since 2014. Irrigated ground rents for $203 per acre, but only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

17129.text: Menard County is a dryland county. Irrigated ground is rare here, and the irrigated rent figure rests on a thin base, so I'd lean on the non-irrigated numbers. Non-irrigated cash rent is $288 per acre for 2026, up 11.2 percent from 2016. The county's median corn yield over 2008-2025 is 209.3 bushels per acre, and the worst year, 2012, was 97.4. Heat and drought claims were 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 52 percent in 2010-2019, then dropped to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $62.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.59. Land and buildings were valued at $9,257 per acre in 2022.

17131.text: Mercer County is mostly dryland, and its loss history is worth a close look. Insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 0.42 across the closed years 1989-2025, and the 2016-2025 stretch alone is 0.22 with $1.15 paid per $100 of insured value. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, so that is the cause to watch. Cash rent on non-irrigated ground was $273 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $9,250 per acre in 2022. The county's corn yield trend has been climbing 4.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2023.

17135.text: Heat and drought is the story in Montgomery County. It was 28 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 54 percent in 2010-2019, then 22 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 19 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 2012 and 2000 tied for the worst year at 8 weeks. None of the cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. Over closed crop years 1989-2025 the loss ratio was 0.65, and indemnities paid out more than premium in 3 of 30 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $291 per acre in 2026, up 5.8 percent since 2016.

17137.text: Morgan County is mostly dryland ground, and the thing that stands out is how heat and drought has come and gone in the claims. Heat and drought was 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 13 percent in 2000-2009, jumped to 43 percent in 2010-2019, then came back down to 17 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full stretch of closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.55, and the county paid out more than premium in 3 of 26 crop years, so the claims have been real. The non-irrigated cash rent is $281 per acre for 2026, up 17.1 percent from 2016, and the county's corn yield trend since 2008 is 3.8 bushels per acre a year.

17139.text: Moultrie County is a non-irrigated county, with none of its harvested cropland under irrigation in the 2022 census, so every bushel here depends on the rain that comes. The loss history shows it. Heat and drought made up 55 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 15 percent in 2000-2009, then rose to 68 percent in 2010-2019 before dropping to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Insurers paid out more than premium in 3 of 26 closed crop years, and the 2012 corn crop was 115.1 bushels per acre. Non-irrigated cash rent is $337 per acre for 2026, up 29.6 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings census value was $11,597 per acre in 2022.

17141.text: Heat and drought is the main cause of crop claims in Ogle County, and its share has climbed. It was 34 percent of indemnities over 1989-1999 and 44 percent over 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.48, which means claims have run well under premiums overall, though 5 of 32 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Corn yields trend up 3.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 192.3 and a worst year of 142.9 in 2012. Non-irrigated rent is $282 per acre for 2026, up 16.5 percent since 2016.

17143.text: Peoria County's most notable number is the heat and drought record on the claims side. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2000-2009, and it was still 27 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 28 weeks of severe drought in 2005 alone, and the closed crop years paid out $50.0 million over the whole stretch against a loss ratio of 0.34. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground lives on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $253 per acre in 2026, up 14.5 percent from 2016.

17147.text: Piatt County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $73.8 million since 1989, and heat and drought drove 50 percent of that in 1989-1999 but 66 percent in 2010-2019 before dropping to 11 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.13, so claims have run well under premium lately. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2025 is $320 per acre, up 5.6 percent since 2014, and 2025 was the worst drought year at 16 weeks.

17149.text: Pike County is mostly dryland, with 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather shows up in the claims more than anywhere. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities at 40 percent, and its share went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 43 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.72, but the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.29, so recent years have paid far less than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $219 per acre in 2026, up 15.9 percent since 2016.

17151.text: Pope County is a dry-ground county that has mostly had too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 53 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.69 across all closed years and 0.7 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 39 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $92 per acre for 2025, down 10.7 percent from 2013. The county has 7286 acres in CRP, 20.4 percent of the cropland base, and 1568 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

17153.text: Pulaski County is mostly dryland ground, with only 6 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent you see is mostly for ground that depends on rain. Heat and drought was 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 38 percent in 2010-2019, and 31 percent in 2020-2025, so it has been a regular part of the claims here. Excess moisture and flood is the largest single cause at 54 percent over 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $152 per acre for 2026, up 16.9 percent from 2016. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.56, so the policies have paid out less than the premiums in those years.

17155.text: Putnam County is mostly dryland, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census, so the rain has to come on time. Heat and drought made up 52 percent of the crop insurance payouts from 1989 to 2025, and the share was 53 percent in 1989-1999 and 55 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio was 0.56 over those closed years, and it paid out more than premium in 3 of 20 crop years. The 2016-2025 ratio was 0.37, which is easier on the books. Non-irrigated cash rent is $246 per acre for 2026, up 2.5 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $9,797 per acre in 2022, up 17 percent from 2017.

17157.text: Randolph County's bigger story is wet weather, not dry. Floods and excess moisture account for 48 percent of the $84.5 million in crop insurance paid since 1989, and the county has paid out more than it collected in premiums in only 2 of 23 closed crop years. Still, heat and drought claims have climbed, from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025. July nights are warming, averaging 69 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $166 per acre in 2026, up 43.1 percent from 2016, and none of the harvested cropland is irrigated.

17161.text: Rock Island County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Insurers paid out $39.0 million on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and excess moisture and flood caused the largest share at 35 percent. The loss ratio is 0.41 for the full run, and four of the 23 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $228 per acre, and the county has no solar or wind operating.

17163.text: St. Clair County's heat and drought story has changed over time. Heat and drought made up 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 62 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 35 percent in 2020-2025. The county's worst year for corn was 2012 at 58.6 bushels per acre, and it had 11 weeks of severe drought or worse that year. Non-irrigated cash rent is $243 per acre, up 44.6 percent since 2016. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.65, and the county has 37.2 MW of solar operating with 155 MW proposed.

17165.text: Saline County is dryland ground, with no irrigation on any harvested cropland, so the weather and the insurance record matter most here. Heat and drought made up 53 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019, down to 29 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2012 drought cut corn to 50 bushels per acre, with 15 weeks of severe drought that year. Across 1989-2025 the county's loss ratio is 0.62, and insurance paid out more than premium in 4 of 23 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre for 2026, up 26.1 percent since 2016.

17167.text: Sangamon County's corn has been carrying more of its own weather than the rent suggests. Crop insurance paid out $156.5 million on closed years from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio is 0.49 overall, with 3 of 27 crop years paying out more than premium. The worst single year was 2012, at 131.3 bushels per acre against a median of 210.9. Heat and drought went from 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio was 0.23. Non-irrigated cash rent is $334 per acre, up 11 percent since 2016.

17169.text: Schuyler County is mostly dryland, with 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the bigger story is heat and drought in the claims record. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 33 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.7 across the closed years since 1989, and five of 22 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $249 per acre, up 26.4 percent from 2016. Census land value was $6,519 per acre in 2022, so rent ran 3.33 percent of that value, which is worth keeping in mind when you look at the ground.

17171.text: Scott County's cropland is mostly dryland, but the notable thing here is flood, not drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 46 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it collected in 4 of 20 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 36 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $273 per acre for 2026, up 24.1 percent since 2016, and the census land value is $8,195 per acre. The corn yield trend is up 3.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, against a median of 188.2 bushels.

17173.text: Shelby County is a dryland county, and its insurance history is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $144.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 65 percent of that. The sharewas 61 percent in 1989-1999 and 31 percent in 2020-2025, but the 2010-2019 stretch hit 73 percent, so the path has been up and down. The loss ratio over the full span is 0.62, though it was 0.22 over the last ten closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $255 per acre for 2026, up 34.9 percent since 2016.

17175.text: Stark County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. The heat and drought share of crop insurance indemnities went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 16 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.37, and insurance has paid more than premium in 3 of 27 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $292 per acre for 2026, up 22.2 percent since 2016. The worst corn year in the published record was 2012 at 148.4 bushels per acre.

17177.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Stephenson County. It made up 62 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019, the largest share in the run of periods, and 34 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought went from 18 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.49, and 3 of 27 closed crop years paid out more than premium. None of the cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 is $251 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $9,230 per acre.

17181.text: Union County's notable story is the claims. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still lead the full record at 52 percent. The loss ratio over the closed years is 0.89, and five of the 18 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $86 per acre for 2026, down 27.3 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $5,116 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 14.7 percent of the cropland base.

17183.text: Vermilion County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop lives or dies on rain. That is why the drought numbers matter most here. Heat and drought made up 67 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 24 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $267 per acre for 2026, up 14.6 percent from 2016. The insurance loss ratio over the full closed period is 0.52, and it was 0.22 over 2016-2025, so the payouts have been lighter lately. Wind is the big non-farm use, with 315 MW operating.

17187.text: Warren County is a dryland county. Not one acre of harvested cropland is irrigated, so every bushel here depends on what the sky does. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance payouts, at 28 percent of $65.4 million in indemnities since 1989. Its share went from 6 percent in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2000-2009 and 37 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The crop insurance loss ratio is 0.38 over the full record, but only 4 of 35 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is $281 per acre, up 13.3 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $10,349 per acre.

17189.text: Washington County is mostly dryland, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so the rain that falls in July and August is what the crop lives on. Heat and drought has been the biggest cause of insurance claims since 1989, at 54 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 24 percent in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2010-2019 before dropping to 40 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.75, and the 2016-2025 stretch is 0.36, so the recent years have paid out well under what was collected in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $190 per acre for 2026, up 29.3 percent since 2016, and the county's own estimate of land and buildings was $8,068 per acre in 2022.

17191.text: Wayne County's notable number is how little the drought claims carry. Heat and drought was 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 45 percent in 2010-2019, then 17 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 56 percent of the $292.5 million paid across closed years. The county's loss ratio over the whole period is 0.77, and 8 of 31 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $176 per acre in 2026, up 28.5 percent since 2016. Every bit of its irrigation water comes from groundwater, and there is no wind or solar operating.

17197.text: Will County's loss record stands out first. Crop insurance paid out $95.5 million over the closed years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio was 0.64, with 6 of 31 crop years paying out more than the premium. Excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 43 percent. Heat and drought went from 47 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 47 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is back where it started after dropping to 30 percent in 2010-2019. Corn has averaged 177.8 bushels per acre, with a worst year at 126 in 2012, and the fitted yield trend is up 3 bushels per acre a year. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $231 per acre.

17199.text: Williamson County is mostly dryland, and the main thing to watch is the water that comes too fast rather than the water that doesn't come. Excess moisture and flood make up 51 percent of the $54.5 million in indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 0.83, with 4 of 19 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 50 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $101 per acre for 2026, up 18.1 percent since 2016. The census land value of $4,701 per acre was set in 2022.

17201.text: Winnebago County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn yield trend and the drought claims tell the real story here. Heat and drought went from 26 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 45 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.59, and six of the 25 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. The corn yield trend over 2008-2025 is up 3.3 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 187.6 bushels and a worst year at 99.6 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $264 per acre, up 30 percent since 2016.

17203.text: Woodford County's notable number is the heat-and-drought pattern in claims. Heat and drought was 50 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 68 percent in 2010-2019, and 23 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has swung a lot from one stretch to the next. Yields trend up 3.4 bushels per acre a year on the published years 2008-2025, with a median of 206 bushels and a worst year of 102.5 in 2012. Non-irrigated rent is $290 per acre in 2025, and the 2022 census value of $10,987 per acre is the operators' own estimate.

18001.text: Adams County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Flood and excess moisture caused 43 percent of indemnities since 1989, and only 5 of 23 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Over the last ten closed years the loss ratio was 0.32, so the recent stretch has been calmer than the long run. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 29 percent in 2020-2025, which is worth watching. Non-irrigated cash rent is $235 per acre in 2026, up 23.7 percent since 2016, and census land and buildings were $10,771 per acre in 2022.

18003.text: What stands out in Allen County is the insurance side. Indemnities have paid out $70.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.58, with 5 of 22 crop years paying more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are doing more of the damage now. Non-irrigated cash rent is $219 per acre for 2026, and the census value of the land and buildings was $7,803 per acre in 2022, a 2.43 percent rent-to-value ratio. Not much of the ground is irrigated, so the rent is for dryland that depends on rain.

18005.text: Bartholomew County is mostly dryland ground, and its heat and drought history is the part to look at. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 95 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 60 percent of insurance indemnities in 2010-2019, then fell to 28 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.65, with 7 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Since 2016 the ratio has been 0.26. Non-irrigated cash rent is $224 per acre, up 21.1 percent since 2016, and irrigated rent is $258. Census land and buildings value is $6,180 per acre, down 7.6 percent from 2017 to 2022.

18009.text: Blackford County's loss history is shaped more by wet years than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 42 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and insurers have paid out more than premium in 4 of the 21 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025, which is the figure to watch if dry years keep coming. The county's corn trend is 3.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and non-irrigated rent is $246 per acre in 2026.

18011.text: Boone County's corn ground has never been irrigated, and the crop has taken its losses mostly from dry years and bad years of the weather, not from one steady drift. Heat and drought claims went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2010-2019, then came down to 22 percent in 2020-2025. The worst year in the record was 2012, when the median yield fell to 91.6 bushels per acre. Over the closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.63, and 4 of 29 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $264 per acre for 2026, and census land value is $9,472 per acre. The county has 787 CRP acres and no solar or wind operating.

18015.text: What stands out in Carroll County is how often heat and drought have been the cause of crop insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 59 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2000-2009, then back up to 57 percent in 2010-2019 and 41 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over all closed crop years is 0.44, and three of 28 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $275 per acre for 2026, up 10.9 percent since 2016.

18017.text: Cass County's most notable number is the heat and drought claims. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 60 percent in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2000-2009, then back up to 46 percent in 2020-2025. Claims have paid out more than premium in only 2 of 26 closed crop years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.22, so the record is mixed rather than a steady pattern of losses. Non-irrigated rent is $237 per acre for 2026, up 5.3 percent since 2016. Cass County has 3271 acres in CRP, and 469 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029, which is worth watching if you rent ground in the county.

18019.text: Clark County's heat and drought claims have eased, even as the nights run warmer. Heat and drought was 59 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 33 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.64 across the closed crop years 1989-2025, and insurers paid out more than premium in only 4 of 19 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre for 2026, up 20 percent since 2016. Corn yields are trending up 3.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, with a 2012 low of 69.9 bushels per acre.

18021.text: Clay County's crop insurance record is the first thing I'd look at. Indemnities have run ahead of premium in this county: the loss ratio is 0.72 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 4 of 22 crop years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2000-2009 and 55 percent in 2010-2019, then 19 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather that costs this ground has changed over time. Excess moisture and flood is the largest single cause at 42 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $218 per acre in 2026, and the county has no irrigated cropland to speak of.

18023.text: Clinton County is a dryland county that has done well on rent and on land value. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 was $298 per acre, up 30.7 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $9,492 per acre, and that value rose 32.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. Heat and drought was 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 34 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.38, with 3 of 28 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Excess moisture and flood, not drought, is the largest cause of losses here.

18025.text: Crawford County's heat-and-drought claims have been climbing. Heat and drought made up 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2020-2025, and that is the big thing to watch here. The county's loss ratio over all closed crop years is 0.73, so claims have run ahead of premiums over time, though the last ten years sit lower at 0.52. None of the cropland is irrigated, so the ground is only as good as the rain it gets. Non-irrigated cash rent was $115 per acre in 2025.

18027.text: Daviess County's most notable number is the loss ratio: 0.65 over the 1989-2025 closed crop years, with crop years paying out more than premium in 5 of 27. The ratio over the last ten closed years is much lower at 0.32, and the largest single cause of claims is excess moisture and flood at 41 percent. Heat and drought went from 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $255 per acre in 2026, up 34.2 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground is 4 percent of harvested cropland.

18029.text: Dearborn County's cropland is mostly dryland, with just 1 percent irrigated in 2022, and the bigger story here is wet weather. Excess moisture and flood made up 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch was 0.76. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $147 per acre. Heat and drought share of claims went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, so it has been a steady part of the picture rather than a rising one. The county corn yield trend since 2008 is up 3.7 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 160.6 bushels.

18031.text: Decatur County is dryland all the way through: none of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so every bushel here rides on rain. That makes the drought record the first thing to look at. Heat and drought claims were 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 57 percent in 2010-2019, then 34 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yield trends up 4.5 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2025, with a median of 184.8 and a worst year of 86.1 in 2012. Insurance has paid out $79.4 million on closed years, and the loss ratio is 0.59. Non-irrigated cash rent is $235 per acre, up 29.1 percent since 2016.

18035.text: Delaware County's rent has climbed without much help from water. Non-irrigated cash rent is $240 per acre in 2026, up 21.2 percent from 2016, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 37 percent. Corn yields have trended up 3.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 169.5 bushels. The insurance loss ratio is 0.54 across closed crop years 1989-2025, but only 0.27 over 2016-2025.

18037.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

18041.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Fayette County. It has been the largest cause of crop insurance claims since 1989, at 67 percent of the $30.1 million paid, and its share went from 53 percent in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 75 percent in 2010-2019. The county has paid out more than it took in premium in 3 of 19 closed crop years, and the 2012 drought brought the corn yield down to 74.9 bushels per acre. Non-irrigated cash rent is $255 per acre for 2026, up 40.9 percent since 2016. Corn yield has trended up 3.8 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the risk in the ground is still dry years.

18043.text: Floyd County's biggest story is heat and drought claims. They made up 59 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio for those closed crop years was 0.59. Not one acre of the cropland is irrigated, so the ground is leaning on rain. The county's cash rent for non-irrigated ground in 2024 was $92 per acre, and the census put land and buildings at $9,135 per acre in 2022, which was up 67.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. Heat and drought held at 54 percent of the claims in 1989-1999 and 55 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has not moved much.

18045.text: Fountain County is mostly dryland ground, and the crop insurance record is where the story is. Heat and drought made up 55 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 57 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 37 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid $66.3 million in closed crop years, and only 1 of 30 years paid out more than premium.
