Non-irrigated cash rent is $265 per acre in 2026, up 17.8 percent since 2016, and census land value was $8,277 per acre in 2022.

18047.text: Franklin County's story is in the claims. Heat and drought made up 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019, and that share fell to 36 percent in 2020-2025. Across all the closed crop years since 1989, the county has paid out $38.7 million, and it paid more than premium in 4 of 19 years. The median corn yield for 2008-2025 is 180.8 bushels per acre, but the worst year, 2012, was 89.1. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $177 per acre, up 15.7 percent since 2016.

18049.text: Fulton County's most notable number is heat and drought, which was behind 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 41 percent in 2020-2025. The county also had 20 weeks of severe drought in 2000, the worst year in the record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $208 per acre in 2026, up 9.5 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents at $302 per acre. Corn yields have trended up 2.7 bushels per acre a year since 2008, though 2012 was 127.1 bushels per acre. The county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.42 over 1989-2025, and only 0.17 over 2016-2025.

18051.text: Gibson County is a dryland-rent county with a wet-year insurance history. Most of the cropland is non-irrigated, and cash rent for that ground is $216 per acre in 2026, up 14.3 percent since 2016. The notable piece is the claims record: excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of indemnities at 53 percent, while heat and drought went from 19 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2010-2019 before falling back to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Groundwater is the only irrigation source, and irrigation failure has paid just $55,620 across all closed years. The 2022 census value of $7,732 per acre is the operators' own estimate, and the land value rose 19.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

18053.text: Grant County's biggest mark in these numbers is the insurance record. Crop insurance paid out $70.1 million on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio is 0.48, so claims have run well under premiums overall. The last ten closed years are lighter still, at 0.15. Heat and drought claims went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, the same share at both ends, so that rise is not a clear trend to act on. The county is not irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $195 per acre in 2026, unchanged from 2016.

18055.text: Greene County's biggest story in the numbers is water and wet springs, not heat. Groundwater supplies all of the irrigation water here, and the largest cause of crop insurance claims since 1989 is excess moisture and flood, at 65 percent. Heat and drought went from 29 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025, and excess moisture is the bigger worry. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $197 per acre, up 45.9 percent from 2016. The county's corn yield trend has risen 3.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 166 bushels per acre. Insurance has paid out $99.7 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.76.

18057.text: Hamilton County's cropland is mostly non-irrigated, and it has been a reliable place to grow corn. The median county corn yield from 2008 to 2025 was 174.1 bushels per acre, and the trend over those years is up 3.2 bushels per acre a year. The worst year in that run was 2012, at 121.9 bushels. Crop insurance has paid out less than premiums over the long run, with a loss ratio of 0.57 across closed crop years from 1989 to 2025. Excess moisture and flood, not heat, is the largest cause of claims at 38 percent. Heat and drought went from 56 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $239 per acre, up 16.6 percent since 2014.

18059.text: Hancock County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims, and it made up 52 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 42 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.65 across the closed years, and only 3 of 26 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $240 per acre in 2026, up 11.6 percent since 2016. The corn yield trend is 3.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 179.3 bushels per acre.

18061.text: Harrison County's ground has been getting more expensive to rent, and the rent figure is the first thing to look at. Non-irrigated cash rent is $170 per acre for 2026, and it was up 73.5 percent from 2016. The bigger story in the insurance record is heat and drought, which made up 65 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 52 percent in 2020-2025. Across 1989-2025 the county's loss ratio was 0.55, and only 2 of 22 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Corn yields have a trend of 3.7 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the 2012 year was 52.2.

18063.text: Hendricks County is a dryland county, and the water record is what stands out here. None of the cropland is irrigated, so every bushel depends on rain. Heat and drought made up 13 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 1 percent in 2000-2009, 25 percent in 2010-2019, and 23 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks were rare, 24 of 1357 since 2000, but 2012 alone logged 11. The median corn yield over 2008-2025 is 183.4 bushels per acre, with 2012 at 58.3. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $260 per acre, up 28.7 percent since 2016. Insurance has paid out more than it took in across the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.89.

18065.text: Henry County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much of the insurance paid out here has come from heat and drought. Heat and drought was 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 53 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still the largest cause at 45 percent over the full record. Corn yields have a steady upward trend, 3.2 bushels per acre a year, but 2012 fell to 92.4. Non-irrigated rent is $203 per acre, up 1.5 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $8,606 per acre in 2022, which puts rent near 2.44 percent of that value.

18067.text: Howard County's cropland is entirely dryland, and the notable thing in the insurance record is that wet years, not dry ones, have driven most of the claims. Excess moisture and flood account for 35 percent of indemnities since 1989, and only 1 of 22 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, a small move. Non-irrigated cash rent is $255 per acre for 2026, up 13.3 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $5,875 per acre in 2022.

18069.text: Huntington County's heat and drought claims have been climbing. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 27 percent in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 26 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2021-2025 alone. Excess moisture and flood, not drought, is still the largest cause of claims, at 32 percent over 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $200 per acre for 2026, and the county has only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated. The crop insurance loss ratio over those years is 0.61, and six of the 26 closed crop years paid out more than the premium brought in.

18071.text: Jackson County's notable number is water, or the lack of it, at least in the ground we'd call dry. Excess moisture and flood account for 64 percent of the indemnities paid here since 1989, and the county has paid out more than premium in only 6 of 27 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 46 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $196 per acre in 2026, up 19.5 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings census value is $6,958 per acre for 2022. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the acres here depend on rain.

18073.text: Jasper County's most notable number is the rise in heat and drought claims. They were 53 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 24 percent in 2010-2019, and came back to 52 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed years the loss ratio is 0.6, and excess moisture and flood, not heat, has been the largest cause at 49 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $235 per acre in 2026, up 12.4 percent since 2016. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the $277 irrigated rent is mostly a number for a small slice of ground. The county has 329.8 MW of solar and 200.1 MW of wind operating now.

18075.text: Jay County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much of the insurance money now goes to heat and drought. That share was 38 percent over 1989-1999 and reached 50 percent over 2020-2025, while flood and excess moisture still lead the all-time list at 43 percent. The loss ratio over the full record is 0.63, and six of the 27 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $217 per acre in 2026, up 20.6 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $10,478 per acre in 2022, a value that rose 38.1 percent from 2017 to 2022.

18077.text: The thing that stands out in Jefferson County is water, and it's too much of it, not too little. Excess moisture and flood took 58 percent of the indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the county's loss ratio over that stretch was 0.82, with 6 of 22 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 67 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre for 2026.

18079.text: Jennings County is notable for how little of its trouble comes from dry weather. Excess moisture and flood account for 53 percent of indemnities since 1989, and heat and drought went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out more than premium over the whole closed record, with a loss ratio of 0.73, and 6 of 26 crop years paid more than was collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $209 per acre in 2026, up 26.7 percent since 2016, and the county's land and buildings were valued at $6,620 per acre in 2022.

18081.text: Johnson County is a non-irrigated county with no irrigation water taken from anywhere but the ground, and the corn record shows why growers watch dry years closely. The worst year was 2012 at 58.1 bushels per acre, against a median of 171.9. Heat and drought claims were 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 43 percent in 2010-2019, then 28 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out more than premium in 4 of 22 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.79 over the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $228 per acre and was up 30.3 percent from 2016.

18083.text: Knox County's most notable number is in the insurance record: crop insurance has paid out $139.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.56, which means indemnities have run below premium overall. Six of 29 crop years paid out more than the premium, though, and excess moisture and flood account for 56 percent of those claims. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $229 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground rents for $239, with only 12 percent of harvested cropland irrigated.

18085.text: Kosciusko County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often the insurance claims come from heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 31 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.55, but for 2016-2025 it is 0.24, so the big payouts came in earlier years. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $219 per acre, and the census land value for 2022 was $8,605 per acre. CRP is 2.1 percent of cropland, with 1297 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

18087.text: LaGrange County is mostly non-irrigated ground, with irrigation on 30 percent of harvested cropland, and the gap between irrigated and non-irrigated rent has been narrowing: 1.99 times in 2009 against 1.72 in 2026. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.59, and only 5 of 23 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $159 per acre in 2026, up 13.6 percent since 2016. Census land value is $14,455 per acre, up 56.3 percent from 2017 to 2022.

18089.text: Heat and drought claims are the thing to watch in Lake County. Their share of indemnities went from 29 percent in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out more than premium in only 4 of 23 closed crop years. Most of the loss over the whole record came from excess moisture and flood, at 54 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $186 per acre for 2026, up 6.3 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings census value was $7,916 per acre in 2022. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has 1063 CRP acres.

18091.text: Heat and drought is the thing to watch in LaPorte County. It caused 30 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 45 percent in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 21 percent in 2010-2019. Corn yields have trended up 2 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 154.2 and a worst year in 2012 at 122.3. Non-irrigated cash rent is $200 per acre in 2026, up 19 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $290. Only 32 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

18093.text: Lawrence County is a rain-and-flood county more than a heat county. Excess moisture and flood make up 57 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in only 3 of the 19 closed crop years in that span, so the loss ratio over the whole period is 0.66. Heat and drought claims went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $179 per acre for 2026, up 19.3 percent since 2016, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Land and buildings were valued at $5,474 per acre in the 2022 census, up 47.3 percent from 2017.

18095.text: Madison County is a rent story more than a weather story right now. Non-irrigated cash rent is $245 per acre for 2026, and it has gone up 23.7 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims are the part to watch: they went from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause of claims over the whole record, at 43 percent. Crop insurance has paid out $63.1 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.49, with 4 of 26 closed crop years paying more than premium.

18097.text: Marion County is a county where the land and the rain matter more than the rent. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019, down to 35 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 record is 1.06, so claims have run past premiums. Cash rent is $185 per acre for non-irrigated ground, but the census put the land and buildings at $11,101 per acre in 2022. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the July nightly low has climbed to 65.9 F over 2017-2026 against a 64.6 F normal.

18099.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Marshall County. It was 44 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.32, so the claims have been coming in but the premiums have covered them. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and that water is 87 percent groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $219 per acre in 2026, up 32.7 percent since 2016, while irrigated rent is $210. Census land and buildings value was $7,190 per acre in 2022.

18101.text: Martin County is a rain-and-flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 44 percent, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in only 3 of 19 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.65 across 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $190 per acre, up 46.2 percent since 2016, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. CRP holds 1535 acres, with 264 expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

18103.text: Heat and drought is the story in Miami County. Its share of indemnities went from 39 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid $40.8 million in claims across closed crop years 1989-2025. Corn yields here have trended up 3 bushels per acre a year on the published years 2008-2025, with a median of 172.9 bushels per acre. Non-irrigated cash rent is $218 per acre for 2026, up 10.7 percent since 2016. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. The 2000 drought ran 20 weeks in severe territory, and 2021-2025 logged 25 more weeks.

18105.text: Monroe County is a dryland corn county where wet years cost more than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.72. Heat and drought claims were 34 percent in 1989-1999 and 56 percent in 2010-2019, which is the number to watch. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground carries whatever rain it gets. Non-irrigated rent is $149 per acre, up 41.9 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $6,514 per acre in 2022, a number the operators gave themselves, and that value fell 0.8 percent from 2017 to 2022.

18107.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Montgomery County. It was 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 6 percent in 2000-2009, then 62 percent in 2010-2019 and 41 percent in 2020-2025. The worst year was 2012, when the median corn yield fell to 104.5 bushels per acre against a county median of 197.9. Indemnities total $86.3 million since 1989, and the loss ratio over the closed crop years is 0.46. Non-irrigated cash rent is $287 per acre for 2026.

18109.text: Morgan County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the crop insurance record is where the weather shows up. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims over 1989-2025, at 35 percent. Its share went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2010-2019, then 28 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have paid $56.4 million against a 0.62 loss ratio, with 3 of 22 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $190 per acre, up 2.7 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $7,642 per acre in 2022.

18111.text: Newton County is mostly dryland corn and soybean ground, and the notable thing is how little of it gets water from anywhere but the sky. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Crop insurance has paid out $78.2 million since 1989, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 48 percent. Heat and drought went from 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years have been carrying more of the claims lately. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $235 per acre, up 14.1 percent from 2016. The 2008-2025 yield trend is up 2.8 bushels per acre a year, with a worst year of 110.9 in 2015.

18113.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Noble County. It was 33 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 44 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2020-2025 stretch is the largest share in the record. The county's corn yield trend is 4.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the worst year, 2012, was 105.7 bushels per acre against a median of 169.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $190 per acre for 2026, up 26.7 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $9,064 per acre in 2022, after a 41.8 percent rise from 2017 to 2022.

18115.text: Ohio County is a dry-land county with no irrigation, and heat and drought has been the biggest cause of crop insurance claims here, though the share has moved around. Heat and drought was 49 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 41 percent in 2000-2009, 50 percent in 2010-2019, and 33 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.71, and over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.47, so claims have run lighter lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $90 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $6,126 per acre in 2022, up 40.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nights have been warming, with the average low at 67.5 F over 2017-2026 against a 65.2 F normal for 1991-2020.

18117.text: Heat and drought used to drive most of the crop insurance claims in Orange County, and that has eased. It was 57 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 69 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The county has no irrigated cropland, so rain is the whole game here. Insurance paid out $27.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and only 2 of 18 crop years paid more than the premium. The 2012 corn crop was 30.1 bushels per acre against a 177.2 median. Non-irrigated cash rent is $209 per acre, up 49.3 percent since 2016.

18119.text: Owen County is a rainfed county that has mostly lost its crops to too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the $43.4 million in crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the closed crop years since 1989 show a loss ratio of 0.85. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2010-2019, then fell back to 19 percent in 2020-2025. The ten most recent closed years run a much lower loss ratio of 0.48. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $162 per acre, and the corn yield trend since 2008 is up 4 bushels per acre a year.

18121.text: Parke County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the notable thing here is wet springs more than dry summers. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 37 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 0.62, with only 5 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years are getting more of the weight. Non-irrigated cash rent is $197 per acre for 2026, up 9.4 percent since 2016, and the census land value is $7,262 per acre.

18123.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Perry County. It made up 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 56 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 53 percent in 2020-2025. Since 1989 the county has paid out $14.3 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio of 0.56 says the premiums have covered most of that. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land. Non-irrigated cash rent is $127 per acre, and the census puts the land and buildings at $5,209 per acre, which is an operator estimate.

18125.text: Pike County's most notable number is flood, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 52 percent of the insurance payouts since 1989, and the closed crop years have paid out $63.6 million against premium, with the loss ratio at 0.72. Three of the 22 closed crop years paid more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 39 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 0 weeks in severe drought since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $194 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings for 2022 is $5,920 per acre.

18127.text: Porter County's irrigated ground rents for $306 per acre, against $195 for non-irrigated, and the land itself was put at $9,579 per acre in 2022, up 41.6 percent since 2017. The bigger story in the insurance record is heat and drought. Their share of indemnities went from 9 percent in 2010-2019 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 16 weeks of severe drought in 2003 alone, though only 7 weeks in 2021-2025. Excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause over the whole record at 40 percent. The loss ratio of 0.42 means the premiums have paid back more than the claims over the closed years, with 3 of 22 crop years paying out more than premium.

18133.text: Putnam County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so rain decides the crop. Heat and drought took 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-2025's closed years during 2010-2019, and 29 percent in 2020-2025. The 2012 corn yield was 61.4 bushels per acre, against a median of 181.3. Crop insurance has paid out $90.8 million since 1989, and the ten closed years 2016-2025 ran a loss ratio of 0.23. Non-irrigated cash rent is $224 per acre for 2026, up 6.7 percent from 2016, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings was $8,265 per acre.

18135.text: The county's heat-and-drought story is mostly in the claims. Heat and drought made up 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 44 percent in 2010-2019, then 39 percent in 2020-2025. The crop insurance loss ratio is 0.54 over 1989-2025, and five of the 26 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. The last ten closed years are lighter, at 0.24. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $209 per acre, up 14.2 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $9,308 per acre in 2022, so rent came to 2.13 percent of value that year. CRP is small here at 1386 acres, but 232 of those acres come out in fiscal years 2027-2029.

18137.text: The first thing I'd look at in Ripley County is the water side of the ledger. Floods and excess moisture drove 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2025, and the county's loss ratio over those years was 0.75, with 8 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $174 per acre, up 11.5 percent since 2016. The county's corn yield trend since 2008 is up 3.2 bushels per acre a year, and the worst year was 2012 at 101.3 bushels.

18139.text: Rush County is a dry-year county, and the insurance record shows it. Heat and drought made up 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities over the closed years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio was 0.52 over that span, but only 2 of 26 crop years paid out more than premium. The last ten closed years was 0.19. Heat and drought share went from 51 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 64 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $242 per acre for 2026, up 18 percent since 2016.

18141.text: Heat and drought claims stand out in St. Joseph County. They were 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 39 percent in 2000-2009, fell to 16 percent in 2010-2019, then rose to 54 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood, at 33 percent, is the largest cause over the full record. The county's loss ratio of 0.56 for 1989-2025 means claims have paid out more than premium overall, though only 5 of 22 closed crop years did that. Non-irrigated cash rent is $196 per acre in 2026, up 22.5 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $312 per acre.

18143.text: Scott County's heat and drought picture has eased while water-related losses have stayed the biggest cause of claims. Excess moisture and flood account for 70 percent of the $30.3 million paid in closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.74. Heat and drought went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025. The county's corn yield trend since 2008 is up 3.6 bushels per acre a year, and non-irrigated rent is $155 per acre in 2026, up 19.2 percent since 2016.

18145.text: Shelby County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the water that is used all comes from groundwater. The heat and drought share of crop insurance claims went from 53 percent in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, though it peaked at 67 percent in 2010-2019. Indemnities have paid out 0.62 of premium since 1989, and only 4 of 26 closed crop years paid more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $249 per acre for 2026, up 29.7 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $10,164 per acre, and that figure is the operators' own estimate.

18147.text: Spencer County's crop insurance record leans heavily on weather. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities at 47 percent, and its share went from 41 percent in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025, after a peak of 62 percent in 2010-2019. The ten most recent closed crop years show a loss ratio of 0.25, well below the 0.49 for the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $185 per acre in 2026, up 42.3 percent since 2014. The census put land and buildings at $6,525 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators themselves estimated. Solar is operating at 51.5 MW, and CRP covers 1336 acres.

18149.text: Heat and drought is the main thing to watch in Starke County. It was 39 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 49 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are costing more of the claims money now than they used to. The county has paid out $54.2 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.81 over that span, with 6 of 22 crop years paying more than premium. The 2015 corn crop was 97.6 bushels per acre against a median of 149.5. Irrigation is a small piece of the picture: $251 per acre irrigated rent against $170 non-irrigated in 2024 and 2026, and $26,649 in irrigation failure claims over all the closed years.

18151.text: Steuben County is a dryland corn and soybean county, and the one thing that stands out is how the insurance claims have moved. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025, after sitting at 13 percent and 10 percent in the years between. Closed crop years paid out $53.5 million against a loss ratio of 0.74 over 1989-2025, and 2016-2025 alone was 0.45. Non-irrigated cash rent is $153 per acre for 2026, up 25.4 percent since 2014. Irrigation is only 7 percent of harvested cropland, and CRP takes 3.9 percent of the cropland base.

18153.text: Sullivan County's heat and drought claims stand out less than its water problems. Most of the claim dollars here have come from too much rain and flooding, which made up 52 percent of the indemnities over the closed years. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025, with a spike to 48 percent in 2010-2019. The county has 255.2 MW of solar operating and 200 MW of solar proposed, and 355 CRP acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. Non-irrigated cash rent is $230 per acre for 2026, up 39.4 percent from 2016.

18155.text: Switzerland County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought made up 48 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio for those closed years was 0.96, meaning claims paid came close to premiums collected. Heat and drought share went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025. The county's corn yield trend over 2008-2023 is 4.6 bushels per acre a year, and the July nightly low has warmed since 1976. Non-irrigated cash rent is $134 per acre for 2026.

18157.text: Tippecanoe County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 66 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 67 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out $65.9 million on closed crop years, with loss ratio 0.4 over the full record. Three of the 30 closed years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $267 per acre for 2026, up 18.7 percent from 2016, and the 2022 census land value is $8,601 per acre, which the operators themselves put on the ground. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation failure has paid just $41,281 in all.

18159.text: Tipton County's heat and drought claims have moved most in the record. Heat and drought made up 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 29 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is the largest cause overall at 36 percent. Insurance has paid out $24.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, with a loss ratio of 0.34. Cash rent is $275 per acre, up 25 percent since 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $11,110 per acre in 2022, and the 2022 rent was 2.47 percent of that value.

18161.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Union County. It caused 67 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and its share went from 39 percent in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 78 percent in 2010-2019. The worst corn year was 2012, when yields fell to 91.7 bushels per acre against a county median of 195.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $220 per acre for 2026, up 17 percent since 2016. The census land value of $9,913 per acre for 2022 is far above that rent, at 2.1 percent of it.

18163.text: Vanderburgh County is a rainfed county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater, so the corn ground mostly lives or dies on rain. The clearest thing in the record is the insurance history: heat and drought made up 59 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019, the single worst stretch, and 2012 was the bad year with a corn median of 60.4 bushels per acre against a 179.6 median. Indemnities have been 0.63 of premium over 1989-2025, and only 2 of 18 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated rent is $233 per acre for 2026, up 33.1 percent since 2014.

18165.text: Vermillion County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of claims, and its share went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019 and 42 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.59, but over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 it is 0.21, so recent years have paid out far less than premium. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county average non-irrigated cash rent is $270 per acre, up 25.6 percent since 2016. Census land value was $8,513 per acre in 2022.

18167.text: Vigo County's biggest claims story is wet years, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of the $76.7 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.78, with 7 of 24 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 46 percent in 2010-2019 and 27 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years have mattered in recent decades too. Non-irrigated cash rent is $244 per acre for 2026, up 28.4 percent since 2016, and the county's corn yield trend is up 4.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024. Worst year was 2012 at 65.9 bushels.

18169.text: Wabash County's standout number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought claims were 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 42 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 0.66 across 1989-2025. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground is dryland. The county corn yield trend is up 2.9 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, but the worst year, 2012, was 105.4 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $201 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings was $8,802 per acre in 2022.

18171.text: Warren County is mostly rainfed ground. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought is the biggest cause of insurance claims, and its share went from 62 percent in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, though it jumped back to 57 percent in 2010-2019 along the way. Crop insurance has paid out $52.5 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.36 across 1989-2025, with only 2 of 30 years paying more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $303 per acre in 2026, up 21.2 percent from 2016.

18173.text: Warrick County is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 4 of its 22 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.75 over the full span. Heat and drought went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $175 per acre, up 25 percent since 2016. CRP covers 963 acres, and 186 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

18175.text: Washington County is dryland ground, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census, so the weather record and the claims history carry most of the story. Heat and drought made up 53 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has come down over time. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 was 0.57, but over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 it was 0.27, which is the more recent picture. Non-irrigated rent is $168 per acre for 2026, up 46.1 percent since 2016. Weeks in severe drought or worse were zero from 2021 through 2025.

18177.text: Wayne County's notable number is heat and drought. It made up 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 53 percent in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2010-2019 before it fell back to 55 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought claims are the main reason this county has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 0.65 across the closed years. The worst year was 2012, with a corn yield of 79.8 bushels per acre against a median of 179.3. Non-irrigated rent is $214 per acre in 2026, up 28.9 percent since 2016, and census land value was $7,341 per acre in 2022.

18181.text: White County is mostly dryland, and that shows in the claims. Irrigation covers only 3 percent of harvested cropland, and heat and drought went from 49 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed years 1989-2025, the loss ratio is 0.58, with 4 of 31 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $263 per acre in 2026, up 9.6 percent since 2014. The county has 1217.2 MW of wind operating and 550 MW of solar, so a lot of the land is working on more than crops.

18183.text: Whitley County is mostly dryland. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rest waits on rain. Heat and drought went from 20 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2010-2019 period hit 35 percent, the highest share of the three. The county's loss ratio is 0.74 across 1989-2025, and five of 23 closed crop years paid out more than premium. The loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.45, so the recent decade has been calmer than the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $199 per acre in 2026, up 38.2 percent since 2014.

19001.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Adair County. It was behind 9 percent of crop insurance claims in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full record at 53 percent. The county's loss ratio is 0.75 across the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 6 of 31 years paid out more than the premium. Not much of the ground is irrigated, and the worst drought week count was 19 weeks in 2000, with 32 weeks in severe drought or worse across 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $237 per acre for 2026, up 21.5 percent since 2016.

19003.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Adams County. It made up 11 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 27 percent in 2000-2009, 52 percent in 2010-2019, and 72 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the closed crop years paid out $55.5 million, and the loss ratio is 0.52, with 3 of 26 crop years paying more than the premium. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 33 in 2021-2025 alone, after a worst year of 2003 at 30 weeks. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $232 per acre, up 12.1 percent since 2016.

19005.text: Allamakee County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the rent and the weather record are the two things to watch. Heat and drought has been a bigger share of crop insurance claims lately, going from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the loss ratio was 0.65, and the county has paid out more than premium in 5 of 19 crop years. The county's non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $252 per acre. Census land value was $7,375 per acre in 2022.

19007.text: Appanoose County is a dryland county, and the weather has been expensive for the people farming it. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over all closed crop years is 1.09, with 5 of 22 years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $173 per acre, up 9.5 percent since 2016. The county has 20402 CRP acres, 16.4 percent of the cropland base, and 3668 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

19009.text: Heat and drought is the story in Audubon County. It was 7 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-1999, and it was 67 percent over 2020-2025. The county has paid out $102.5 million on closed crop years since 1989, with heat and drought the largest cause at 60 percent of that. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.36, well under the 0.61 for the full record, so the recent years have paid less than the long run. Non-irrigated cash rent is $302 per acre for 2026, up 16.6 percent from 2016. Wind is the other thing on the land: 303.5 MW is operating, and nothing is proposed.

19011.text: Benton County is a rainfed county where heat and drought, not heat alone, has been the main thing that costs farmers money. Heat and drought was 57 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019, and it was 33 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full 1989-2025 record the loss ratio is 0.83, and 8 of 37 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $303 per acre, up 29.5 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $10,970 per acre, so rent in 2022 was 2.46 percent of that value.

19015.text: Boone County's heat and drought history is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities in the 2010-2019 period, and that share was 2 percent in 1989-1999, so the big payouts came in one stretch and not across the whole record. Since then it has eased to 10 percent for 2020-2025. The county loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 record is 0.62, and five of 33 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $263 per acre, up 11 percent from 2016.

19017.text: Bremer County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $118.4 million since 1989, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 44 percent of that. Its share went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2010-2019 and 45 percent in 2020-2025. Seven of the 27 closed crop years paid out more than the premium collected, with the 1989-2025 loss ratio at 0.75. Non-irrigated cash rent is $291 per acre in 2026, up 11.1 percent from 2016, and the 2025 CRP enrollment is 14410 acres.

19019.text: Heat and drought is the story in Buchanan County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 17 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out more than premium in 6 of 31 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.65 over the full period. Irrigation covers 1 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $293 per acre in 2026, up 20.1 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $9,819 per acre in 2022. That census figure is the operators' own estimate, so treat it as a reference point rather than a sale price. Corn yields have trended up 3.2 bushels per acre a year since 2008.

19021.text: Buena Vista County is mostly dryland, and the water story is in the claims. Heat and drought was 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 47 percent in 2000-2009, and 27 percent in 2020-2025, so it is still the biggest cause on the books at 36 percent overall. The county has no irrigated cropland, so every dry year lands on the crop. Non-irrigated rent is $260 per acre for 2026, up 6.1 percent since 2016. The loss ratio over the closed years is 0.61, and five of 34 crop years paid out more than premium. Wind is the other large item, with 369.6 MW operating and nothing proposed.

19023.text: Butler County is a dryland county with a heat and drought problem that has grown. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.85 over closed crop years 1989-2025, with 7 of 31 crop years paying out more than premium. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $301 per acre in 2026, up 32 percent since 2016, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $8,547 per acre. Corn yields show a trend of 2.5 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 193.1 bushels and a worst year at 122 in 2012.

19025.text: Calhoun County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the weather does the watering here. Heat and drought claims were 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 63 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst year, 2013, was 132.6 bushels per acre against a median of 194. Indemnities for irrigation failure total $39,924 across all closed years. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.67, but the last ten closed years are at 0.27, so the recent claims have been light against premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $267 per acre, up 6.4 percent from 2016, and the census value of land and buildings for 2022 was $10,686 per acre.

19027.text: Carroll County has a loss record that stands out. Crop insurance has paid out $231.5 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 67 percent of that. The share went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 78 percent in 2010-2019. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground runs on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $305 per acre, up 25 percent from 2016.

19029.text: Cass County's heat and drought claims stand out. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 13 percent in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2020-2025, and the largest cause over the whole record is heat and drought at 52 percent. Corn yields have still trended up 2.5 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with 2012 the worst year at 120.4. Non-irrigated cash rent is $259 per acre for 2026, up 19.9 percent from 2016. The county also has 489.3 MW of wind operating and no solar.

19031.text: Cedar County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $117.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 41 percent of that. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities ran $1.64 per $100 of insured value, and the loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 span is 0.55, with 8 of 36 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 52 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $297 per acre in 2026, up 14.7 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $10,621 per acre in 2022.

19033.text: Cerro Gordo is a dryland county with a lot of rain-driven loss. Only 0 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.74, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 37 percent. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, so that is the trend to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $260 per acre, up 8.3 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings for 2022 is $9,033 per acre, and the rent that year was 2.57 percent of it, so the ground is priced well above what it rents for.

19035.text: Cherokee County is dryland all the way, with no irrigated ground in the 2022 census, so the water question shows up in the claims more than anywhere else. Heat and drought made up 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 61 percent in 2000-2009, and 57 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's largest cause of loss overall is heat and drought at 45 percent. Crop years have paid out more than premium in 4 of 31 closed years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.41. Non-irrigated cash rent is $301 per acre in 2026, up 21.9 percent from 2016, against a 2022 census land value of $11,186 per acre.

19037.text: Chickasaw County is mostly dryland, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the drought claims are what stand out. Heat and drought went from 12 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio is 0.78 over 1989-2025, and 7 of 31 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $284 per acre for 2026, up 7.6 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $9,461 per acre, which is an operator estimate, so it is well above rent. Wind is the one big non-crop use, with 202.4 MW operating.

19039.text: Clarke County's crop insurance record leans toward dry years, and that has changed over time. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $167 per acre for 2026, down 21.2 percent from 2014. Corn yields have trended up 5.4 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2024, but the worst year, 2012, was 76.7 bushels. Crop insurance has paid out more than premium in 7 of 24 closed crop years, so the claims have been real. CRP covers 30 percent of the cropland base.

19043.text: Clayton County's cropland is all non-irrigated, so every bushel here depends on rain falling when it's needed. The heat and drought share of crop insurance claims went from 21 percent in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025, and that is the trend to watch. The worst corn year in the 2008-2025 series was 2012, at 152.9 bushels per acre, against a median of 194.2. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $266 per acre, up 9 percent since 2016. The county's losses have run high over the full record: the loss ratio for closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.58, and five of 24 years paid out more than premium. The 2016-2025 loss ratio is lower at 0.33.

19045.text: Clinton County is a dryland county, and the water question shows up most in the insurance record. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, and the crop years paying out more than premium were 7 of 36. Rent is $304 per acre, up 26.1 percent since 2016, while the census value of $9,600 per acre was 27.3 percent higher in 2017-2022 than before. Trend yield is climbing 2.9 bushels per acre a year, but 2012 fell to 139.6 bushels, so a dry year still bites hard here.

19047.text: Crawford County's crop insurance record is the story here. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims, at 60 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 14 percent in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2010-2019. Indemnities came to $235.4 million over those closed crop years, and the loss ratio was 0.65, with 7 of 37 crop years paying out more than premium. The corn yield trend is 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the worst year was 2012 at 131.3. Non-irrigated cash rent is $281 per acre for 2026, up 14.2 percent from 2016.

19049.text: Dallas County is a dryland county. Not one acre of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn you see out there is living on rain. The loss ratio since 1989 is 0.65, and heat and drought made up 44 percent of the indemnities paid out. That share was 7 percent in 1989-1999 and 59 percent in 2010-2019, and it fell back to 23 percent in 2020-2025. The county's average corn yield trend is up 2.8 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2025, and the 2012 crop bottomed out at 129 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $241 per acre for 2026, up 5.2 percent since 2016.

19051.text: Davis County is non-irrigated, and that matters more here than the rent figure. Heat and drought claims went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the full closed period is 1.11, with 6 of 23 crop years paying out more than premium. Corn yield has trended up 4.5 bushels per acre a year since 2008, but the worst year, 2012, was 52.4 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $182 per acre for 2026, up 19.7 percent since 2016. CRP covers 13.7 percent of the cropland base, and 5668 acres come out of it in fiscal years 2027-2029.

19053.text: Decatur County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Insurance has paid out $78.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.88, which means the claims came in under what farmers paid in premium over that whole span. The ten most recent closed years are a different story, with a ratio of 0.4. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims that matter now mostly come from dry weather, not wet springs. None of the county's cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $167 per acre.

19055.text: Delaware County is rainfed ground: 0 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the story here is dry weeks and heat, not water on tap. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the claims paid out $150.3 million, and the loss ratio is 0.7, with 6 of 31 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $298 per acre in 2026, up 21.1 percent from 2016. The county is also home to 104.1 megawatts of operating wind, and none of solar.

19061.text: Dubuque County is a dryland county in the most literal sense: none of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and the heat-and-drought share of crop insurance claims has climbed from 17 percent in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. The big shift in claims came in 2010-2019, when heat and drought went to 55 percent, and it has held there since. The county corn yield trend over 2008-2025 is 3.3 bushels per acre a year, and the worst year, 2012, was 149.4 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $303 per acre in 2026, up 16.1 percent since 2016, while the census value of land and buildings is $10,692 per acre. CRP covers 3.8 percent of the cropland base.

19063.text: Emmet County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at here. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for the largest cause at 46 percent. The county has no irrigated cropland, so every dry spell lands on the crop. The loss ratio of 0.81 over 1989-2025 means claims have run close to premium, and six of 30 closed crop years paid out more than premium was collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $239 per acre in 2026, up 6.7 percent since 2016.

19065.text: Fayette County's heat and drought claims are the thing to watch here. Heat and drought went from 18 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025. The county paid out more than it took in premium over the full record, with a loss ratio of 0.68, and seven of the 31 closed crop years paid more than premium. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 58 in 2021-2025, and 2023 alone had 26. Non-irrigated cash rent is $270 per acre for 2026, up 13 percent from 2016, and the census value of $9,138 per acre is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

19067.text: Heat and drought is the story in Floyd County. It went from 2 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium over the full record, with a loss ratio of 0.79 across the closed crop years from 1989 through 2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $293 per acre for 2026, up 40.9 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $9,857 per acre in 2022, a figure operators gave as their own estimate. CRP covers 8.9 percent of the cropland base, with 5431 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

19069.text: Franklin County's crop insurance record is led by wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 36 percent, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.72, with 6 of 34 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought has grown from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $271 per acre, up 9.7 percent since 2016. Corn yields have trended up 2.9 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with 2012 as the worst year at 150 bushels per acre.

19071.text: Fremont County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 7 of the 34 closed crop years, and the 1989-2025 loss ratio is 0.63. Excess moisture and flood have caused most of the claims, at 70 percent, but heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the dry years land on mostly unwatered ground. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $215 per acre, down 1.8 percent since 2016.

19073.text: Heat and drought is the story in Greene County. It caused 56 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and its share went from 3 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2010-2019, then 32 percent in 2020-2025. The county's corn yield trend is up 3.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the worst year, 2012, was 124.6 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $268 per acre for 2026, up 18.1 percent from 2016. There are 13,467 CRP acres, 4.7 percent of the cropland base.

19075.text: Heat and drought has become the biggest cause of insurance payments in Grundy County. It was 9 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and is 29 percent for 2020-2025. The loss ratio over all closed crop years is 0.55, and five of the 34 years paid out more than the premium, with 2012 the worst at 161.5 bushels per acre. Non-irrigated cash rent is $322 per acre in 2026, up 16.2 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $12,121 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 6575 acres, with 1856 of those expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

19077.text: Guthrie County's crop insurance record is shaped mostly by heat and drought. Across the closed crop years 1989-2025, claims paid out $120.6 million, and heat and drought made up 59 percent of that. Its share went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 55 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the whole stretch is 0.71, though the last ten closed years have run at 0.42. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $248 per acre.

19079.text: Hamilton County is a dryland county with no irrigation at all, so what matters here is how the ground holds up in a dry year. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 33 percent in 2020-2025. The worst year in the record was 2013, with a median-breaking yield of 135 bushels per acre, against a county median of 188.9. The loss ratio is 0.72 over 1989-2025, and four of the 34 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $301 per acre in 2026, and the census land value of $11,157 per acre is the operators' own estimate.

19081.text: Hancock County is a county where the ground is mostly watered by the ground itself. Every acre of irrigation water here comes from groundwater, and the county's crop insurance has paid out $179.7 million since 1989, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 35 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025, peaking at 32 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $265 per acre in 2026, up 15.7 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $292. The census puts land and buildings at $9,457 per acre, a number the operators estimated, not a sale price.

19083.text: Hardin County's cropland is all dryland, and the insurance record shows how hard the wet years have hit. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 23 percent, and the county paid out more than it took in premium in 6 of 34 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.75 across 1989-2025. Heat and drought share of claims went from 5 percent in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $280 per acre in 2026, up 9.8 percent since 2016. The census land value is $10,393 per acre, and that rent is 2.46 percent of it.

19085.text: Harrison County is a dryland county with a small irrigated edge, and the irrigated edge is priced close to dryland ground. Irrigated cash rent is $273 per acre against $255 for non-irrigated, and that gap was wider in 2009, when irrigated rent was 1.20 times the dryland rent. Heat and drought claims have grown from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.69 across the closed crop years since 1989, and only 4 of 33 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is up 14.9 percent since 2016.

19087.text: Henry County's notable number is the claims history. Excess moisture and flood have paid out the most, at 46 percent of indemnities since 1989, and six of the 33 closed crop years paid out more than the premium behind them. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2010-2019, and 34 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low is 65.3 F for 2017-2026 against 64.6 F for the 1991-2020 normal. Cash rent is $253 per acre, up 11 percent since 2016, and CRP covers 13.1 percent of the cropland base.

19089.text: The loss numbers in Howard County stand out more than the rent does. Indemnities have paid $158.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought has grown from 4 percent of that in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the whole 1989-2025 stretch is 0.83, and 7 of 32 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. The last ten closed years are a different story at 0.4, so the bad years have been bunched. Non-irrigated cash rent is $283 per acre for 2026, up 16 percent from 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $8,461 per acre in 2022. Wind is the big non-crop use here, with 165 MW operating and nothing proposed for solar.

19091.text: Humboldt County's notable number is on the claims side. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is still the largest single cause at 40 percent of all indemnities since 1989. Insurance has paid out more than it took in across the 1989-2025 closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.63, and seven of the 31 crop years paid more than premium. The county has no irrigated cropland, so the rent of $262 per acre is non-irrigated ground that depends on rain. Land and buildings were valued at $10,740 per acre in the 2022 census, which is the operators' own estimate.

19093.text: Ida County's loss history stands out more than its rent. Crop insurance has paid out $118.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought was the largest cause at 59 percent of that. The share went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the whole stretch is 0.58, and 6 of 32 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $291 per acre for 2026, up 3.6 percent from 2016. Wind is the other big presence, with 502.1 MW operating and nothing proposed.

19095.text: Iowa County's headline is the claims, not the yields. Heat and drought went from 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 39 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is still the largest single cause over the full record at 36 percent, and the loss ratio of 0.58 says the policies have paid out more than premium over the long run. Land is priced well above the rent: the census value was $7,674 per acre in 2022, and the non-irrigated rent that year was 3.47 percent of that. Wind is the only energy build-out here, at 252.5 MW operating, with nothing solar and no new projects filed.

19097.text: Jackson County's loss record is what stands out. Crop insurance has paid $88.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought were the largest cause at 53 percent of that. Their share went from 41 percent in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, and the worst corn year, 2012, was 114.6 bushels per acre against a median of 189.2. The non-irrigated cash rent is $275 per acre for 2026, up 16.5 percent from 2016, and the 2022 census value of $8,284 per acre means rent was 2.92 percent of land value. Nothing is installed for solar or wind here, and CRP covers 6.8 percent of the cropland base.

19099.text: Jasper County is a rain-fed county where the loss record is the thing to look at. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities, at 30 percent of the $111.3 million paid on closed crop years since 1989. Its share went from 6 percent in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2010-2019, then came down to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.31, so claims have run well under premium lately, though 5 of 34 crop years since 1989 paid out more than premium. The 2026 non-irrigated cash rent is $264 per acre, up 10.5 percent from 2016.

19101.text: Jefferson County's biggest story in the claims is water, and it's too much of it. Excess moisture and flood account for 46 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 8 of the 31 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 19 percent of the total in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $244 per acre, up 15.6 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $6,951 per acre, and rent that year was 3.5 percent of it.

19103.text: Johnson County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often heat and drought have shown up in claims. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio is 0.59 over 1989-2025, with 7 of 33 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $277 per acre for 2026, up 22 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $10,307 per acre for 2022. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

19105.text: Jones County is rain-fed ground, and the weather record is what you'll see first. Heat and drought made up 25 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 52 percent in 2020-2025, and it was the largest cause of payouts overall at 49 percent. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.79, and 7 of 32 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Median corn yield was 190.1 bushels per acre, with 2012 the worst year at 127.3. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $279 per acre, up 13 percent since 2016.

19107.text: Keokuk County is mostly dryland, and the heat-and-drought claims are the thing to look at. Heat and drought went from 17 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out $131.6 million on closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio of 0.6 says the insurance has paid back less than the premiums over the full record, but 11 of 37 crop years paid more than the premium. Rent is $236 per acre, up 7.8 percent since 2016. Corn yields have a trend of 3.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the worst year, 2010, was 111.2. CRP covers 15.4 percent of the cropland base, and 9699 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

19109.text: Kossuth is a wet county more than a dry one. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.71, with 8 of 37 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $282 per acre in 2026, up 24.2 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $10,771 per acre in 2022, and the rent was 2.5 percent of that value. Wind is the main energy use here, with 442 MW operating.

19113.text: Linn County is a county where heat and drought drive the insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2010-2019 and 53 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.83, and 7 of 33 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Rent is $258 per acre, up 10.7 percent since 2016, and the census value of $10,758 per acre was set in 2022, after land values rose 29.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. Solar is the only renewable with any footprint here at 204.5 MW operating.

19115.text: Louisa County's irrigated ground is a small share of the cropland, 9 percent in the 2022 census, and all of that water comes from groundwater. The bigger story in the claims is dry weather. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.49, and only 3 of 32 closed crop years paid out more than premium. In the last ten closed years it was 0.21. Non-irrigated cash rent is $242 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings is $7,815 per acre for 2022.

19117.text: Lucas County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much the insurance claims have shifted toward heat and drought. That share went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2023 drought was the worst in the county's record with 27 weeks in severe drought or worse. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $176 per acre in 2026, up 17.3 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $5,715 per acre in 2022, and cash rent that year was 2.96 percent of it. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.93 since 1989.

19119.text: Lyon County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 3 of 33 closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.52 across 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are where the claims come from now. The county's worst year, 2012, had 42 weeks in severe drought or worse, and the county has had 24 weeks of it since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $284 per acre in 2026, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

19121.text: Madison County's heat and drought story is the one to look at first. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 57 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.5, and 5 of 27 years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $221 per acre, up 20.8 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $7,700 per acre in 2022, which is well above what the ground rents for.

19123.text: Mahaska County has a lot of wet-year pain in its record. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and only 4 of 34 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought has been climbing as a share of claims, from 9 percent in 2000-2009 to 46 percent in 2020-2025. The county also has 168 MW of wind operating and no solar. Corn yields show a trend of 3.7 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a worst year of 116.6 in 2010. Non-irrigated cash rent is $244 per acre in 2026, up 13.5 percent from 2016.

19125.text: Heat and drought are where this county's claims have changed. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2010-2019 share was 47 percent. Flood and excess moisture is still the largest cause over the full record at 45 percent, and the county has no irrigated cropland, so dry years land on the ground directly. Corn yield trend is up 4.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 175.2 and a worst year of 112.7 in 2010. Non-irrigated cash rent is $230 per acre in 2026, up 17.9 percent since 2016.

19127.text: Marshall County's corn is mostly dryland, and the county has leaned on rain rather than irrigation. 19131.text: Heat and drought is the story in Mitchell County. 19137.text: Montgomery County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the weather is the whole story for the crop. 19139.text: Muscatine County's notable number is in the insurance claims. 19141.text: What stands out in O'Brien County is the heat and drought claims, which went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. 19159.text: Heat and drought used to be a small share of crop claims in Ringgold County, and now it is the main one. Non-irrigated rent is $266 per acre for 2026, up 38.5 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings census value in 2022 was $5,970 per acre.

Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, the loss ratio is 0.86, and 7 of the 27 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $197 per acre for 2026, up 16.6 percent from 2016. Census land value is $5,451 per acre, and CRP covers 16.6 percent of the cropland base.

Non-irrigated cash rent is $288 per acre in 2026, and the census put land and buildings at $8,352 per acre in 2022.

Heat and drought went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are showing up more in claims. Non-irrigated cash rent is $241 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings for 2022 is $9,241 per acre, with 350.9 MW of wind operating in the county.

19197.text: Wright County is a rain county more than a dry one.
