The census put land and buildings at $1,856 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 17.4 percent of the cropland base.

20169.text: Saline County is mostly dryland, and the heat and drought claims are what stand out. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 87 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.97, and the county has paid out more than premium in 7 of 25 closed years. Non-irrigated rent is $65 per acre for 2026, up 5.7 percent from 2016. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of that water comes from groundwater.

20171.text: Scott County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought was 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 81 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 13 of 30 closed crop years. Only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre in 2026, up 31.4 percent since 2016, and the median county corn yield for 2009-2024 is 119.5 bushels per acre, with a worst year of 42.4 in 2022.

20173.text: Heat and drought are what stand out in Sedgwick County. They made up 26 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 84 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than premium over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.94. Irrigated ground is a small slice at 12 percent of harvested cropland, but irrigated cash rent is $169 per acre against $56 for non-irrigated, and the gap has widened since 2009. The corn yield trend is 1.5 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 129.9 bushels and a worst year of 96 in 2011. Census land value was $3,923 per acre in 2022.

20175.text: Seward County is an irrigated county, and that shows in the rent. Irrigated ground is 54 percent of harvested cropland, the irrigation water all comes from groundwater, and irrigated rent is $137 per acre against $37 for dryland. Heat and drought is the main claim cause, at 57 percent of indemnities since 1989. Its share went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2010-2019, then 56 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $2,215 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 31.6 percent of the cropland base, with 11943 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

20177.text: Shawnee County is mostly dryland, and the risk shows up in the claims. Heat and drought made up 74 percent of the $29.8 million paid out in closed crop years since 1989, and their share climbed from 36 percent in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025. Only 14 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the rest rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $71 per acre in 2026, up 34 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $201. Corn has averaged a median 138.8 bushels per acre since 2009, with a rough 2012 at 85.

20181.text: Sherman County is a dryland county with a sharp irrigated premium. Irrigated ground rents for $193 per acre against $63 for non-irrigated, and irrigation is 28 percent of harvested cropland, all drawn from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out more than it collected, with a loss ratio of 1.03 over the closed years 1989-2025. Heat and drought made up 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 62 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is up 37 percent since 2016, to $63 per acre.

20183.text: Heat and drought is the story in Smith County. It was 15 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 87 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 85 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out $177.9 million on closed crop years, against a loss ratio of 0.74, and the median corn yield of 118.3 bushels per acre hides a worst year at 39.5 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $76 per acre in 2026, up 17.1 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground ran $195 per acre in 2021, with 89 percent of irrigation water pulled from groundwater. Nothing is operating in wind or solar.

20185.text: Stafford County's notable number is how much of the trouble has come from heat and drought. Heat and drought made up 15 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 79 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the county's insurance losses ran at 0.87 of premium, and 10 of 27 closed crop years paid out more than they took in. Irrigation is a fifth of the harvested cropland, and it is all groundwater, so irrigated ground rents for $151 per acre against $48 for dryland.

20187.text: Stanton County is an irrigated county more than a dryland one, and that shapes the whole picture. Irrigated ground rents for $101 per acre, against $32 for non-irrigated, and that gap has widened: irrigated rent was 2.81 times non-irrigated in 2009 and is 3.11 times now. Water comes entirely from groundwater, and the crop insurance record is heavy: indemnities have run at a 1.06 loss ratio since 1989, and heat and drought went from 22 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 75 percent in 2020-2025.

20189.text: Stevens County is an irrigation county. Irrigated ground rents for $131 per acre, against $36 for dryland, and the gap has widened, from 2.63 times in 2009 to 3.64 times in 2026. Every irrigation point in the county draws on groundwater, and 57 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census. Heat and drought claims went from 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2020-2025. The county's weeks in severe drought or worse ran 417 of 1357 weeks across 2000-2025, with 53 weeks in 2013 alone. Land and buildings were valued at $1,792 per acre in 2022.

20191.text: Sumner County's loss record is the first thing to look at. Crop insurance has paid out $429.2 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the indemnities came to 1.07 times the premium, with 12 of 32 crop years paying more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $57 per acre, up 15.2 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground was $124 per acre in 2022. Groundwater supplies 95 percent of the irrigation water.

20195.text: Trego County is a dryland county, and the notable thing is how much of its insurance money now comes from heat and drought. In 1989-1999 heat and drought made up 8 percent of indemnities, and in 2020-2025 it was 94 percent. Across the closed crop years 1989-2025, the county has paid out $150.3 million, and the loss ratio is 0.98, with 10 of 25 crop years paying more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $41 per acre, up 30.2 percent since 2016. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and CRP covers 15.4 percent of the cropland base.

20197.text: Heat and drought is the story in Wabaunsee County. It made up 29 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 86 percent in 2020-2025, and it is 82 percent of the total paid since 1989. The loss ratio is 0.62 over the closed crop years, and 4 of 20 crop years paid out more than the premium. The worst year was 2011, when the median corn yield fell to 56.7 bushels per acre. Irrigation is small at 8 percent of harvested cropland, and 77 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $63 per acre in 2026, up 15.6 percent since 2016.

20201.text: Washington County is mostly dryland, so the rent to watch is the $92 per acre non-irrigated figure, up 14.4 percent since 2016. Heat and drought is what drives the insurance claims here. It was 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 90 percent in 2020-2025. The county's worst corn year was 2012 at 79.7 bushels per acre, against a median of 118.8. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 5 of 32 closed crop years, though the ten years from 2016 to 2025 have run a loss ratio of 0.36. Groundwater supplies 71 percent of the irrigation water. There are no solar or wind projects operating yet.

20203.text: Wichita County's crop insurance record leans hard on heat and drought. Of the $245.0 million paid out on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, heat and drought made up 70 percent, and its share went from 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed years is 1.05, so claims have paid out more than premium overall, though over 2016-2025 it is 0.77. Only 15 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation water comes entirely from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre in 2026, up 24.7 percent since 2014.

20205.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Wilson County. It took 56 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999, 24 percent in 2000-2009, 59 percent in 2010-2019, and 72 percent in 2020-2025. Only 2 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is taking the weather as it comes. The loss ratio is 0.93 over the closed crop years, and 6 of 22 years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is $75 per acre for 2026, up 8.7 percent since 2016.

20207.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Woodson County. It was 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 86 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has no irrigated harvested cropland to fall back on. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.98, with 5 of 18 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $58 per acre, up 17 percent since 2016. The census land value of $2,005 per acre was 20.6 percent higher in 2017-2022 than before, so rent is still a small share of the land's value. Corn yield trend is 1.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 105.9 bushels.

20209.text: Wyandotte County's notable number is the drought share of crop claims, which went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025, with the 2000-2009 period at 54 percent. Flood and excess moisture still cause most of the money paid out over the full record, at 76 percent. The closed-year loss ratio is 0.61 across 1989-2025 and 0.44 across 2016-2025. Census land and buildings were $9,876 per acre in 2022, after a 46.5 percent rise from 2017 to 2022. Heat and drought weeks ran to 22 for 2021-2025, and the county has 277 active points of diversion, with 29 for irrigation.

26001.text: Alcona County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Flood and excess moisture are the largest cause of claims at 47 percent, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.76, so claims have paid out less than premiums over the long run. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, with a dip to 17 percent in 2000-2009 in between. None of the cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated rent is $45 per acre in 2026, up 87.5 percent from 2016, against a census value of $3,069 per acre in 2022.

26003.text:
Alger County is mostly ground that stays dry and cool in summer, and that is the first thing I'd look at here. No cropland is irrigated, and the July nightly lows have held close to the 1991-2020 normal, with 54.7 F for 2017-2026 against 54 F before. Severe drought has been rare: 29 of 1,357 weeks since 2000, with the worst year being 2005 at 11 weeks. Only 5 of those weeks came in 2021-2025.

Rent is $20 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026. The 2022 census put land and buildings at $2,348 per acre, up 15.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. That rent is 0.85 percent of the census value. No CRP acres and no wind or solar are on the books here.

26005.text: Allegan County's heat-and-drought story is the one to look at first. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of insurance payouts in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 27 weeks of severe drought in 2000-2025, with 5 of those in 2021-2025 alone. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $155 per acre in 2026, up 19.2 percent since 2016. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.67, and 7 of 26 crop years paid out more than the premium.

26007.text: Alpena County is a rain county more than a heat county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the biggest insurance cause here is excess moisture and flood at 43 percent of indemnities, ahead of anything tied to dry weather. Heat and drought claims were 31 percent in 1989-1999 and are 31 percent again in 2020-2025, so that share has held steady. The county's corn loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.72, but over 2016-2025 it is 0.41. The 2016 corn yield, at 88.9 bushels per acre, was the worst year in the published run. Non-irrigated cash rent is $55 per acre for 2026, up 69.2 percent from 2016.

26009.text: Antrim County is a county where the notable thing is cold, not heat. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here at 59 percent, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.09, meaning claims paid out more than premiums collected. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 3 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $41 per acre, down 18 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $5,870 per acre in 2022, up 39.7 percent from 2017. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater.

26011.text: Arenac County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities paid $29.0 million over 1989-2025, and the largest cause was excess moisture and flood at 42 percent, so wet springs and standing water do more damage here than heat or dry spells. Heat and drought claims are still rising, though. They were 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 36 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 18 weeks of severe drought in 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $128 per acre in 2026, up 50.6 percent since 2014, and the county is only 1 percent irrigated.

26015.text: Barry County's corn is mostly rain-fed, and the loss record is the thing to look at. Insurance has paid out $30.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 39 percent. Its share went from 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 47 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 0.5, and the county paid out more than premium in 4 of 19 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $129 per acre for 2026, up 18.3 percent since 2016. The corn yield trend is 2.4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 153 and a worst year of 121 in 2012.

26017.text: Bay County's notable number is the water side. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $185 per acre in 2026, up 40.2 percent since 2014, and irrigated ground rents for $325 per acre. Most of the crop insurance money paid here came from excess moisture and flood, at 40 percent of indemnities, and the county's loss ratio of 0.56 across 1989-2025 is well under 1. Heat and drought claims went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. The corn yield trend is up 1.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

26019.text: Benzie County's most notable feature is how little heat and drought have cost its growers. Freeze and frost make up 82 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and heat and drought went from 10 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.71, but over the last ten closed crop years it has come down to 0.45. Corn yields have trended up 3.2 bushels per acre a year since 2008, and the county has 0 MW of solar and 0 MW of wind operating. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre, and the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $6,283 per acre.

26021.text: Berrien County's notable number is the irrigation. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, but irrigated ground rents for $240 per acre against $125 for non-irrigated, and 76 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $105.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and freeze and frost, at 57 percent, is the largest cause. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025, with 11 percent in 2010-2019 between them. The loss ratio is 0.82, so claims have run below premiums over the whole period.

26023.text: Branch County is mostly non-irrigated ground, and the heat and drought claims are where the story is. Heat and drought went from 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.56, so the policies have paid out more than the premiums they have collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $133 per acre in 2026, up 2.3 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $190. The census puts land and buildings at $5,315 per acre in 2022, up 25.5 percent from 2017. Corn yields have trended up 2.6 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with 2012 the worst year at 112.8.

26025.text: Heat and drought is the main thing to look at in Calhoun County. It was 26 percent of insurance claims in 1989-1999 and 52 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 43 percent in 2020-2025. The county's corn yields have been trending up 2.3 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 144.4 bushels and a worst year of 87.1 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $132 per acre for 2026, up 25.7 percent since 2016. Insurance indemnities have paid out more than premiums in 5 of 23 closed crop years. Land and buildings were valued at $5,072 per acre in 2022, down 4.5 percent from 2017.

26029.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

26031.text: Cheboygan County is a small cropland county where the ground is mostly rain-fed and the crop insurance record is light. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the closed crop years since 1989 paid $568,970 in indemnities against a loss ratio of 0.45, so claims have run well under premiums. Heat and drought was the largest cause of those claims at 31 percent, but its share was 21 percent in 1989-1999, and the county has had only 2 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021. Non-irrigated rent is $27 per acre in 2025, up 8 percent since 2014.

26033.text: Chippewa County's big story is the rent. Non-irrigated ground went from a rent of $29 per acre in 2026 after rising 61.1 percent since 2016, and that jump is worth watching against the census value of $2,840 per acre for land and buildings in 2022. Heat and drought are the biggest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 45 percent of indemnities since 1993, though that share fell from 49 percent in 2000-2009 to 42 percent in 2010-2019. July nightly lows have warmed to 55 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.8 F. Strong CRP presence at 15472 acres, or 29.4 percent of cropland, is also part of the picture.

26035.text: Clare County's heat and drought story is mostly in the claims. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025, and it is now the largest cause of claims over the full record at 44 percent. The yield trend is up 2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, with a median of 125.7 bushels and a worst year of 105 in 2018. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre, up 55.8 percent since 2016. The county's loss ratio of 0.85 over 1989-2025 means claims have run a bit below premiums overall. CRP covers 374 acres, 1.9 percent of cropland.

26037.text: Clinton County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the water risk that shows up in the claims is too much of it, not too little. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of loss at 36 percent of indemnities since 1989. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.59, and the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.62, so insurers have paid out less than premiums over the long run. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 23 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $171 per acre for 2026, up 23 percent since 2016.

26039.text: Crawford County is a dry-ground county with little drought on record, and the notable thing is the land value. Census operators put land and buildings at $4,483 per acre in 2022, and that estimate was up 28 percent from 2017, or 5.1 percent a year. Not one farm reported irrigated harvested cropland, and there is no CRP or wind and solar on the books. The July nights are a little warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, with the average low at 56.3 F for 2017-2026 against 55 F. Severe drought weeks have been rare, 26 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with the worst year 2003 at 13 weeks, and 13 weeks in severe drought or worse for 2021-2025.

26041.text: Delta County's farmland is mostly rain-fed, and that is what drives the picture here. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation failure claims total $60,254 across all closed years. Heat and drought made up 84 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 21 percent in 1989-1999. The loss ratio of 0.94 over 1989-2025 is near the top of what a county pays back in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, down 25 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $2,340 per acre in 2022, a number that comes from operators' own estimates.

26043.text: Heat and drought is the story in Dickinson County. It caused 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989 through 2024, and its share went from 4 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 96 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.64, so claims paid out less than premiums came in. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $22 per acre, and the census put land and buildings at $3,012 per acre in 2022. Irrigation failure claims total $51,721 across all closed years, which is small.

26045.text: Eaton County's heat and drought claims have climbed sharply in the latest stretch. The share of indemnities from heat and drought was 24 percent in 1989-1999 and is 38 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood remains the largest cause over the whole record at 41 percent. The loss ratio of 0.68 for 1989-2025 means insurers paid out less than the premiums collected, and only 5 of 23 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $123 per acre in 2026, down 6.8 percent from 2016, and only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

26047.text: Emmet County's notable number is the claims record. Freeze and frost took 49 percent of the closed crop-insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2024, and heat and drought went from 8 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2000-2009. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so dry years land hard on the ground that is there. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre in 2026, down 55 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $5,871 per acre in 2022, which is well above that rent, and the land value rose 55.9 percent from 2017 to 2022. Heat and drought are not the main story here, but they have claimed more of the record than they used to.

26049.text: Genesee County's corn ground is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather risk that shows up here is wet springs more than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood made up 54 percent of the $43.7 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 14 weeks in severe drought or worse over 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $131 per acre for 2026, up 45.6 percent from 2016, and the loss ratio of 0.68 over 1989-2025 means claims have run below premiums on average.

26051.text: Gladwin County is mostly ground that gets its water from the sky. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and crop insurance paid $11.1 million on closed crop years 1989-2025, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 41 percent. Heat and drought went from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $137 per acre for 2026, up 30.5 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $4,647 per acre in 2022, and the 2022 rent was 1.32 percent of that value.

26055.text: Grand Traverse County's biggest flag is freezing, not heat or drought. Freeze and frost make up 58 percent of the $18.7 million in crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over those closed years is 0.96, with 2 of 10 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 7 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $65 per acre, and the land value is $9,197 per acre.

26061.text: What stands out in Houghton County is how little of the ground is irrigated, 2 percent of harvested cropland in 2022, and how seldom the county has been hit by long dry stretches. Only 50 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and none of those weeks came in 2021-2025. The worst year was 2007 with 25 weeks. July nights are a little warmer than they were, with the average low at 55.3 F for 2017-2026 against a 53.9 F normal from 1991-2020. The census value of land and buildings was $3,467 per acre in 2022, and it rose 47.3 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP holds 178 acres, 2.1 percent of the cropland base.

26063.text: Huron County's most notable number is the rise in heat and drought claims. They were 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 50 percent in 2020-2025, and the single largest cause over the whole record is still heat and drought at 40 percent. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground has nothing to fall back on in a dry July. The county paid out more than the premium in 4 of 31 closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.44 over the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $239 per acre in 2026, up 11.7 percent from 2016, and the 2022 census value of land and buildings was $7,652 per acre.

26065.text: Ingham County is a rainfed county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop depends on the sky. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 33 percent, and its share went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields trend up 2.1 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 157.4 bushels, but 2012 fell to 120.5. Non-irrigated cash rent is $140 per acre, up 21.7 percent since 2014, and the land and buildings value is $5,227 per acre.

26069.text: Iosco County's notable number is the crop insurance shift. Heat and drought went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, while flood and excess moisture is still the largest cause over the full record at 51 percent. The loss ratio over the closed years 2016-2025 was 0.46, so premiums have run ahead of claims in the recent decade. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $52 per acre, up 44.4 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $3,856 per acre, and the 2022 rent came to 1.23 percent of that. The July nightly low has averaged 59.4 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 57.4 F.

26071.text: Iron County is a quiet one on most fronts. The land value jump stands out: the census put it at $4,200 per acre in 2022, and it was up 112.6 percent from 2017, or 16.3 percent a year. Cash rent was $17 per acre that same year, so the ground is priced far above what it rents for. July nights have run 53.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 52.2 F. Drought is the main thing to watch: 54 of the 1357 weeks from 2000-2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. The worst year was 2007 with 24 weeks. From 2021-2025 there were 5 such weeks. There are no CRP acres, and no wind or solar operating or proposed.

26073.text: Isabella County's insurance record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $65.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the claims ran more than premium in 5 of 27 years, for a loss ratio of 0.65 over the full span. Heat and drought claims went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. The non-irrigated rent is $135 per acre for 2026, up 35 percent from 2016. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Wind turbines are running at 544.8 MW, and the county has 172 MW of solar proposed.

26075.text: Jackson County's most telling number is the crop insurance picture. Indemnities have paid out $57.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.7, with 4 of 22 crop years paying more than premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 49 percent of that, and its share went from 42 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $97 per acre, up 12.8 percent since 2016, and the corn yield trend over 2008-2025 is up 3.2 bushels per acre a year.

26079.text: Heat and drought used to be the main reason claims got paid in Kalkaska County, and that has eased. Heat and drought was 85 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 43 percent in 2010-2019. Across all closed crop years since 1993, the county has paid $326,244 in claims, and heat and drought is still the largest single cause at 50 percent. Drought got bad enough to matter here, with 12 weeks of severe drought in 2003 and 7 weeks from 2021-2025. Rent is $58 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and the census land value is $3,799 per acre.

26085.text: Lake County's notable items are in the insurance and drought records. Heat and drought claims went from 30 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 70 percent in 2020-2025. Closed crop years since 1989 paid out $827,512, and the loss ratio is 0.82, so premiums have come back to growers at a fair rate for the risk. Drought has been light, with 11 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and none since 2021. The July nightly low is up to 57.3 F from a 1991-2020 normal of 56.3 F. Cash rent is $50 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,054 per acre in 2022.

26087.text: Lapeer County's ground has been wetter than dry. Excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's losses have run above premium in 4 of 22 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025, so it is growing but still the smaller share. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $98 per acre for 2026, up 27.9 percent from 2016.

26091.text: Heat and drought is the claim story in Lenawee County. Its share of indemnities went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full record at 33 percent. Corn yields have trended up 3.2 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 169 bushels and a worst year at 100.3 in 2012. Crop insurance has paid out $142.4 million on closed years, and the loss ratio of 0.63 means claims have run ahead of premium over time, with 7 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Irrigation is rare here, at 2 percent of harvested cropland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $165 per acre in 2026, up 9.3 percent since 2016.

26093.text: Livingston County is mostly rain-fed ground, and what stands out is the wet side of the ledger. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 39 percent, and the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 show a loss ratio of 0.58, with indemnities paid per $100 of insured value at $5.46. Heat and drought was 41 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and is 44 percent in 2020-2025, so it is a growing share of the claims, though flood still leads. Corn yields have trended up 2.3 bushels per acre a year since 2008, and the median is 154.8 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $105 per acre for 2026, against a census land value of $7,380 per acre for 2022.

26095.text: Luce County is a quiet one on the numbers. Drought weeks are rare, with 25 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, and the worst year, 2005, had 11 of them. Only 5 of those weeks came in 2021-2025. The July nightly low has crept up, now at 54.4 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 53 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre for 2026. The land and buildings census value was $3,109 per acre in 2022, which the operators estimated themselves, and it rose 23.3 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP takes up 931 acres, 20.6 percent of the cropland base, and none of it expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

26099.text: Macomb County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.05 for 2016-2025, and the largest cause over the whole span was excess moisture and flood at 65 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 5 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $102 per acre, up 50 percent from 2016. The county's census value of land and buildings is $7,741 per acre for 2022, and that figure is the operators' own estimate.

26101.text: Manistee County is mostly a non-irrigated county, with only 16 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. The notable thing here is the freeze and frost history. Freeze and frost make up 72 percent of the $6.9 million in closed crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over those years is 1.26, which means claims have paid out more than the premiums collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, up 25 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025, and no CRP acres or wind and solar are on the books here.

26103.text: Marquette County's notable number is its crop insurance record. Claims paid out $2.9 million across the closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.79, so the county has taken back more in indemnities than it paid in premium. Heat and drought was the biggest cause at 55 percent of that. Its share went from 74 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2010-2019, then back up to 74 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $3,434 per acre in 2022, up 55.7 percent from 2017. Severe drought weeks have been few, with 38 weeks across 2000-2025 and 1 week in 2021-2025.

26105.text: Heat and drought claims are the thing to look at in Mason County. They were 28 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, fell to 8 percent in 2010-2019, and were back up to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.7, and only 1 of 13 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $62 per acre, up 6 percent since 2014, and irrigated ground rents for $100 per acre. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 73 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

26107.text: Mecosta County's story is in the heat-and-drought claims. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst drought year, 2025, had 12 weeks at severe drought or worse. Irrigation is a small piece here, with groundwater supplying 95 percent of irrigation water in 2015, and non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre in 2026. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.71, so claims have paid out more than premiums through that stretch. The census land value of $4,348 per acre in 2022 was a farmer estimate, and the county has no solar or wind operating yet.

26109.text: Menominee County is a dry-weather county. Heat and drought has taken the biggest share of crop insurance payouts since 1989, and in the last five crop years it made up 83 percent of claims, up from 9 percent in 1989-1999. The loss ratio over the full record is 0.98, and eight of the 18 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. None of the cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 2.3 percent from 2016, and the census land and buildings value was $3,061 per acre in 2022.

26111.text: Midland County's heat and drought claims stand out. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than premium in only 1 of 19 closed crop years. Flood and excess moisture is still the largest cause at 42 percent of the total. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $179 per acre for 2026, up 43.2 percent from 2016.

26113.text: Missaukee County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the water question has been moving under it. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.18, so the claims have been light even as the share tilts toward heat. Most irrigation water comes from groundwater, 88 percent in 2015. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $98 per acre, up 58.1 percent since 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $4,867 per acre in 2022.

26115.text: Monroe County's loss history leans toward wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 41 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.69 across the closed years 1989-2025, with 5 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 50 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $172 per acre in 2026, up 21.1 percent from 2016. Irrigation is a small part of the picture here, with irrigated rent at $220 per acre in 2023.

26117.text: Montcalm County's heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought went from 18 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the largest single cause over the full record is heat and drought at 36 percent. The county paid $38.1 million in closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.43, so claims have run well under premium overall. Non-irrigated cash rent is $107 per acre in 2026, up 28.9 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,937 per acre in 2022. Irrigated ground rents for $241 per acre.

26119.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

26121.text: Muskegon County's most unusual number is the insurance record. Crop insurance has paid out $37.1 million across 1989-2025, and freeze and frost caused 60 percent of it, so the county's losses have come more from cold than from heat or drought. The loss ratio over the whole period is 0.65, and the county paid out more than it took in premium in 3 of 17 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigation matters here too: 61 percent of water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $111 per acre in 2026.

26123.text: Newaygo County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the rent reflects that. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 61.2 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $130 per acre, but only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county is leaning on rain. The corn yield trend is up 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the median year was 138.2 bushels. Heat and drought went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, with 2000-2009 the high at 47 percent. Freeze and frost, not heat, is the largest cause of claims.

26125.text: Oakland County is a wet-ground county. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 48 percent, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.34, which means insurers paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought are a real part of the claims but not the lead. Their share went from 39 percent in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, with 45 percent in 2000-2009 and 33 percent in 2010-2019 in between. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most corn here depends on rain. The median corn yield for 2009-2024 was 142.6 bushels per acre, and the worst year was 2009 at 119.

26127.text: Oceana County's notable number is the freeze and frost claims: they make up 61 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and heat and drought is a smaller share. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2000-2009, then 9 percent in 2010-2019 and 9 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $106 per acre in 2026, up 86 percent since 2016. Only 12 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the census put land and buildings at $5,348 per acre in 2022. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.83, with 3 of 14 closed crop years paying out more than premium.

26129.text: Ogemaw County is mostly a rain-fed county, and its notable number is the rent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $64 per acre in 2026, and it was up 71.6 percent from 2016. The census land value of $3,407 per acre is high next to that rent, and the 2022 rent was only 1.19 percent of it, so the land is priced well above what it brings in. Crop insurance has paid out $9.2 million on closed years since 1989, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 43 percent. Heat and drought went from 25 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 21 weeks of severe drought since 2021.

26131.text: Ontonagon County's cash rent is the thing to look at first. Non-irrigated ground rented for $22 per acre in 2025, and it was down 25.9 percent from 2014. Land and buildings were valued by operators at $3,563 per acre in 2022, a 123.1 percent rise from 2017, which is far above what rent alone would suggest. Heat has not been the pressure here: the July average nightly low was 55.1 F for 2017-2026 against a 54 F normal. Drought has been light, with 69 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2007 was the worst year at 25 weeks.

26133.text: Osceola County's most notable number is its crop insurance history. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities, at 58 percent of the $7.5 million paid for closed crop years, and its share rose from 39 percent in 2000-2009 to 75 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 was 0.76, and it was 0.65 over the last ten closed crop years, 2016-2025. The worst corn year was 2018 at 99 bushels per acre, against a median of 130.5. Non-irrigated cash rent is $79 per acre for 2026, up 43.6 percent from 2016. The county has no drought weeks in 2021-2025, and 80 percent of irrigation water comes from groundwater.

26137.text: Otsego County is a small corn county where the heat-and-drought story has grown much louder. Heat and drought made up 45 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, dropped to 25 percent in 2010-2019, and then jumped to 62 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record the loss ratio is 0.74, so premiums have covered the claims paid. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,545 per acre in 2022, which was up 27.5 percent from 2017. The July nightly lows have run warm, with 56.2 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 54.7 F.

26139.text: Ottawa County's cropland is mostly dryland. Only 22 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the irrigated share is high enough to matter because the irrigated rent is $250 per acre against $143 for non-irrigated ground. Non-irrigated rent is up 25.4 percent since 2016. Corn yields have trended up 2.8 bushels per acre a year since 2008, and the median is 151.7, with 2012 the worst year at 111.2. Freeze and frost is the biggest cause of insurance claims, and heat and drought fell from 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.64, so claims have run below premiums over the long haul.

26141.text: Presque Isle County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what shows up in its claims. Heat and drought went from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, while the closed-year loss ratio since 1989 is 0.65. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, up 19.7 percent from 2016. The 2022 census puts land and buildings at $3,642 per acre, and rent was 1.48 percent of that value.

26143.text: Roscommon County's notable number is land value. The census put land and buildings at $4,073 per acre in 2022, and that figure is up 66.2 percent since 2017, or 10.7 percent a year. The county's July nights have warmed too, with average lows of 56.7 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 55.3 F. Drought has been light here: 26 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2003 had the most with 13 weeks. Only 65 CRP acres were enrolled in 2025, and there is no wind or solar operating.

26145.text: Saginaw County's notable number is the claims record: excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the $94.0 million paid out since 1989, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.57 over those closed years, with 5 of 31 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has grown, though it has not moved steadily. The rent is $159 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 4.6 percent since 2016. Groundwater supplies 94 percent of irrigation water, and the July nightly low has warmed to 61.9 F in 2017-2026.

26147.text: Excess moisture and flood is what stands out in St. Clair County. It caused 65 percent of the $59.0 million in crop insurance indemnities paid on closed years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.03, meaning the county paid out more than it took in premium. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is climbing. None of the cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre for 2026, up 30.6 percent from 2016.

26149.text: Irrigation is the big fact in St. Joseph County. Irrigated cash rent is $321 per acre in 2026 against $131 for non-irrigated ground, and 67 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census. Most of that water comes from groundwater, 81 percent in 2015. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims over 1989-2025, at 41 percent of the $21.5 million paid. Its share moved from 62 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent rose 12.9 percent from 2016 to 2026, to $131 per acre.

26151.text: Sanilac County is a rainfed county, and its notable risk runs toward too much water more than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it collected in premium in only 4 of 31 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is climbing even though the county has had only 8 weeks of severe drought since 2000. Non-irrigated cash rent is $157 per acre in 2026, up 31.9 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings are valued at $6,380 per acre in 2022.

26153.text: Schoolcraft is a dry-land county with no irrigation at all, so the water question here is rain, not pumps. Its drought record is light: 27 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year, 2005, had 11 of those weeks. Only 5 weeks have qualified in 2021-2025. July nights are running a little warmer, with the 2017-2026 average low at 55.3 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 54.6 F, though that trend is not a clear one. Land and buildings were valued at $2,839 per acre in 2022, up 56 percent from 2017, and 1360 acres sit in CRP, 31.9 percent of the cropland base. No solar or wind is operating or proposed.

26155.text: Shiawassee County is a rented-ground county, and the rent has climbed fast. Non-irrigated cash rent is $148 per acre for 2026, and it was up 64.4 percent from 2014 to 2026. Crop insurance is the other thing to look at here. Excess moisture and flood, not heat, drove the largest share of indemnities, at 47 percent. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 was 0.61, and indemnities ran past premium in 4 of 24 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, so that side is picking up.

26157.text: Tuscola County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have been paid on 4 of 31 closed crop years in a loss ratio of 0.54, and the largest cause is excess moisture and flood at 40 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is the one to watch. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $222 per acre, up 22 percent since 2016. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and wind power is the one energy use on the books, at 629.2 MW operating.

26159.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

26161.text: Washtenaw is a rain-fed county, and the notable part is how much of the insurance money has gone to heat and drought. That share went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025, and it was the largest cause over the full record at 44 percent. The county has paid out $65.6 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio of 0.81 means claims have run ahead of premium over the long haul, with payouts above premium in 4 of 20 crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $92 per acre in 2026, up 22.7 percent since 2016. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

26163.text: Wayne County's cropland is mostly dryland, and what stands out here is the insurance side. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025 the county's loss ratio is 1.82, and over the last ten closed years it climbed to 2.23, meaning indemnities have run well ahead of premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 50 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, so it is back in the picture after a quieter stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $90 per acre for 2026.

26165.text: Wexford is a county where the heat-and-drought story runs through the claims. Heat and drought made up 55 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the share was 52 percent in 2000-2009 and 60 percent in 2010-2019. Corn has been a reliable crop here most years, with a median yield of 103.3 bushels per acre from 2008 to 2022, but 2013 was 54.5. Only 27 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. The loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 span is 0.59, and the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.31. The county's non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre, up 36.6 percent since 2016.

27001.text: Aitkin County's crop insurance record is dominated by wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 60 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.32, which means claims have paid out more than premiums taken in. Heat and drought claims went from 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years are showing up more in the record than they used to. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation failure claims total $31,517 across all closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre in 2026.

27003.text: Anoka County is a small irrigated ground county in the northern Twin Cities metro, and heat and drought is what stands out in its claims. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.74, down from 0.98 across all closed years. Only 22 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 68 percent of that water from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre in 2026, up 16.5 percent since 2016, and census land and buildings value is $9,535 per acre.

27005.text: Becker County is mostly dryland, and what stands out is who pays the claims. Flood and excess moisture took 41 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio across those closed crop years was 0.5, with 5 of 32 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $127 per acre, up 21 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $3,413 per acre in 2022, and rent was 3.9 percent of that value.

27007.text: Beltrami County is mostly a wet-ground county. The biggest claim cause since 1989 is excess moisture and flood, at 55 percent of the $25.9 million paid out, and the county has paid more than its premiums in only 3 of 16 closed crop years. Irrigation is barely present, with 6 percent of harvested cropland watered. The change that stands out is heat and drought, which went from 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $54 per acre in 2026, up 125 percent from 2016, against a 2022 census land value of $3,063 per acre.

27009.text: Benton County's heat and drought claims stand out. They were 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 88 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid $110.9 million on closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio over those years is 0.94, and 12 of 24 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $128 per acre in 2026, up 53.3 percent since 2016. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's corn yields have trended up 3.1 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 154.3.

27011.text: Big Stone County is mostly dryland ground, so what stands out here is the water. Corn has come off the ground in a wet pattern more than a dry one, and flood and excess moisture were the largest cause of claims, at 55 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are showing up more in the claims book than they used to. The county's own nightly July lows are not a clear trend, and the crop loss ratio over the last ten closed years was 0.78, so premiums have been covering more than the claims. Non-irrigated rent is $184 per acre for 2026, up 11.5 percent from 2016.

27013.text: Blue Earth County is mostly dryland, and its notable pattern is water from the sky rather than heat. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the loss ratio over the closed crop years is 0.66, with payouts above premium in 6 of 36 years. Excess moisture and flood, at 51 percent, is the largest claim cause, while heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $252 per acre in 2026, up 15.1 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings is $7,755 per acre.

27017.text: Carlton County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at here. Heat and drought made up 4 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 31 percent in 2000-2009, and 12 percent in 2010-2019. Freeze and frost is the largest cause over the whole span, at 42 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $19 per acre for 2026, up 31 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,040 per acre in 2022, after rising 41.1 percent from 2017. The county has 50 CRP acres, with 4 expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029, and no wind or proposed wind and solar capacity beyond 1 MW of solar operating.

27019.text: Carver County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $69.7 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.81 over the closed crop years, with 6 of 23 years paying more than premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 51 percent. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 64 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $252 per acre in 2026, up 29.2 percent from 2016.

27021.text: Cass County's heat and drought story is the one to start with. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid $12.7 million in closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio is 0.91 over the full period and 0.65 over 2016-2025, so the last ten years have been easier on the insurers than the whole record. Non-irrigated rent is $30 per acre in 2026, and the county had 157 of 1357 weeks in severe drought or worse since 2000, with 30 of those weeks in 2024 alone.

27023.text: Chippewa County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $213.4 million since 1989, and excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of that, which tells you the county's losses have mostly come from too much water rather than too little. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has grown. The loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.85, and 9 of 37 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $212 per acre for 2026, up 12.8 percent since 2016.

27025.text: Chisago County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of claims, and its share rose from 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.88, and insurers paid out more than premium in 7 of the 19 closed crop years. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $81 per acre in 2026, up 17.4 percent from 2016.

27027.text: Clay County is mostly rain-fed ground, and its risk has come from too much water more than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of the $243.6 million paid out since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over the closed crop years is 0.5, with 6 of 37 years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is growing. Non-irrigated cash rent is $172 per acre in 2026, up 31.3 percent from 2016.

27029.text: Clearwater County is a rain-wet county more than a dry one. Its biggest insurance cause is excess moisture and flood, at 43 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989. Still, heat and drought claims went from 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the closed crop years is 0.8, so the claims have been running close to the premiums. Irrigation is only 11 percent of harvested cropland, and the county paid just $14,399 for irrigation failure in all closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 60 percent from 2016.

27031.text: Cook County is a cool, wet corner of the state, and the Atlas shows very little irrigation here, only 8 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the crop depends on rain. Drought is the main thing to watch. Severe drought or worse covered at least 50 percent of the county for 143 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with 2007 the worst year at 35 weeks, and 40 weeks in just 2021-2025. July nights have stayed cool, averaging 52.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 51.4 F. The census puts land and buildings at $7,495 per acre, which rose 26.5 percent from 2017 to 2022, a value the operators estimated themselves.

27033.text: Cottonwood County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is the wet side of the ledger. Excess moisture and flood account for 40 percent of the indemnities paid here since 1989, and the county's loss ratio is 0.6 over the closed crop years, with 5 of 35 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. 27153.text: Todd County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, claims paid $102.3 million, and heat and drought was the largest cause at 48 percent of that. Its share went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed years is 0.7, and 8 of 27 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $110 per acre in 2026, up 73.2 percent since 2016. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain.

27155.text: Traverse County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here lives on rain, and the insurance record shows that rain has been more often too much than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of the $271.9 million paid out on closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.88 across those years. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry side is picking up. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $182 per acre, up 9 percent from 2016.

27157.text: Wabasha County is mostly dryland ground, and that shapes what the numbers say. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, so the rent of $241 per acre is for ground that depends on rain. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 30 percent, and heat and drought's share of indemnities went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought claims have been the bigger story lately. Crop insurance has paid out more than premium in 4 of 25 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.75 over the full period. Land and buildings were valued at $6,636 per acre in 2022.

27159.text: Wadena County is mostly dryland, and the heat and drought claims are what stand out here. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than premium in 4 of 19 closed crop years. The non-irrigated cash rent is $39 per acre in 2026, up 21.9 percent since 2016. The census land value is $3,230 per acre, and the county's corn yield trend is up 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

27161.text: Waseca County's notable number is the water. Excess moisture and flood took 53 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the county has paid out more than premium in only 3 of 31 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 37 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $263 per acre in 2026, up 13.4 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings census value is $8,825 per acre for 2022. Corn yields have a trend of 1.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

27163.text: Washington County is a dryland county with a small irrigated edge. Only 138 acres are in CRP, and the county has no wind and 42.3 MW of solar. The notable thing for the ground is the insurance record: indemnities have totaled $22.2 million since 1989, and heat and drought made up 58 percent of them. Its share went from 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 was 0.55, and the county paid out more than premium in 4 of 19 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $145 per acre in 2026, up 9 percent from 2016.

27165.text: Watonwan County's heat and drought story has changed in a way worth looking at. Heat and drought claims were 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, then 39 percent in 2000-2009, and 15 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause over the full record at 51 percent, and the loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.89, so claims have paid out close to the premium that was collected. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $252 per acre in 2026, and the census land value was $8,091 per acre in 2022. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland.

27167.text: Wilkin County is mostly dryland, and what stands out is the insurance record. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 44 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for 56 percent of the total paid since 1989. The loss ratio is 0.64 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 7 of 37 years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $180 per acre in 2026, and the census put land and buildings at $5,418 per acre in 2022.

27169.text: Winona County is a dryland county, and its weather risk has shifted toward heat and drought. Every acre of harvested cropland is non-irrigated, and the water that does exist comes from groundwater. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and that is the number to watch. Losses have run above premium in 4 of 24 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.69 across 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $208 per acre, down 8.8 percent since 2016.

27171.text: Wright County is mostly dryland, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the heat and drought story is the one to look at first. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2000-2009, then came back to 54 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record, the county's closed crop years paid out $114.9 million, and the loss ratio is 0.81, so indemnities have run ahead of premium overall. The 2016-2025 stretch is calmer at 0.51. Non-irrigated cash rent is $192 per acre for 2026, up 28.9 percent since 2016.

27173.text: Yellow Medicine County is a rent-and-insurance county first, and the insurance story is the one to look at. Indemnities over 1989-2025 have run at 0.66 of premium, and in the last ten closed crop years that ratio reached 0.73. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, so the losses have shifted toward dry years even though excess moisture and flood still lead at 41 percent. Cash rent on non-irrigated ground was $230 per acre in 2025, up 13.3 percent from 2014. The county has no irrigated cropland, and the corn yield trend since 2008 is 2.2 bushels per acre a year.

29001.text: Adair County's heat and drought claims are the story here. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 20 percent in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 34 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025. Excess moisture and flood still caused the most loss at 57 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over all closed crop years is 0.75. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $121 per acre, up 31.5 percent from 2016.

29003.text: Andrew County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have run ahead of premium over the long haul, with a loss ratio of 0.61 across 1989-2025 and payouts above premium in 4 of 25 closed crop years. Heat and drought was the biggest cause, and its share of claims went from 17 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019, then 33 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county's corn depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $175 per acre for 2026, up 15.9 percent from 2016.

29009.text: Barry County's heat and drought story is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 1 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 24 percent in 2000-2009, and 93 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 89 percent for 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.95, so claims have been close to premiums lately. Rent is $45 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 3.4 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $4,384 per acre in 2022, and land values rose 27.9 percent from 2017 to 2022.

29011.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Barton County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium over the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.06. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 93 percent of that water comes from groundwater, so most of the ground is dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $83 per acre for 2026, up 12.2 percent since 2016. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 59 across 2021-2025 alone, with 29 of them in 2006.

29013.text: Bates County is mostly dryland, and what stands out is how often the crop insurance checks have been for heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 55 percent in 2020-2025. Five of the 29 closed crop years paid out more than the premium, and the loss ratio over the whole period is 0.78. Non-irrigated cash rent is $155 per acre for 2026, up 69.4 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $4,006 per acre in 2022, and that figure is the operators' own estimate.

29015.text: Benton County is a dryland county, and heat and drought is the thing that stands out here. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance payouts since 1989, at 68 percent of $28.7 million. That share went from 57 percent in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.63, so premiums have covered the claims more than they have not. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre in 2026, up 9.6 percent from 2016.

29019.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Boone County. It was behind 41 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 55 percent in 2020-2025, and the claims have been paid out more than premium in 5 of the 19 closed crop years. Corn yields have trended up 4 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a worst year of 41.1 bushels in 2012. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $143 per acre in 2026, up 1.4 percent since 2016.

29021.text: Buchanan County's notable number is flood, not drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 69 percent of the $55.0 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and the county's loss ratio is 0.57 across those closed years. Only 5 of 23 crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought claims were 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 11 percent in 2020-2025, so they have stayed a small share. Non-irrigated cash rent is $164 per acre in 2026, up 13.9 percent since 2016, and the county has 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated. The July nightly low has stayed near its 1991-2020 normal, at 67.3 F for 2017-2026.

29023.text: Butler County's ground is mostly dryland, but the cropland is hard to separate from water. Irrigated land rented for $226 per acre in 2025, and the non-irrigated rate of $74 per acre in 2026 was down 17.7 percent from 2016. Excess moisture and flood account for 80 percent of the $72.9 million in indemnities paid since 1989. Heat and drought claims went from 36 percent in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.06.

29025.text: Caldwell County's notable number is its crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $59.8 million since 1989, and heat and drought drove 55 percent of that. The sharewas 20 percent in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2010-2019, then came down to 41 percent in 2020-2025. Six of the 19 closed crop years paid out more than the premium collected, and the loss ratio over the whole period is 0.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $158 per acre for 2026, and the county has 1711 CRP acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

29027.text: Callaway County's corn ground is mostly dryland, with just 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. The thing that stands out is heat and drought in the claims. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2000-2009, and it has held near that level since, at 53 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.77, and insurers paid out more than premium in 6 of 23 crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $131 per acre for 2026, up 14.9 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $4,653 per acre in the 2022 census, and the 250 MW solar project proposed to EIA is the only energy build on the table.

29031.text: Cape Girardeau County is notable for heat and drought claims. They were 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 43 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood still account for the largest share of claims, at 58 percent over the full record. Crop insurance paid out more than premium in 7 of 18 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.77. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $117 per acre, up 27.2 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground is only 7 percent of harvested cropland, and it rents for $257 per acre.

29033.text: Carroll County's notable feature is how much of its insured loss comes from too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 67 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground here is mostly rain-fed. Heat and drought claims went from 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, which is worth watching. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $192 per acre, up 18.5 percent since 2016, and the county has 40231 CRP acres, 13.6 percent of the cropland base.

29037.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

29039.text: The notable thing in Cedar County is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $14.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.52, so claims have run ahead of premium. Heat and drought caused 66 percent of that, and its share went from 42 percent in 2000-2009 to 71 percent in 2020-2025. The worst corn year in the 2010-2024 run was 2013 at 77.2 bushels per acre, against a median of 131.5. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre in 2026, up 16.7 percent from 2016.

29041.text: Chariton County's notable pattern is water, not heat. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the county's crop depends on rain, and insurance has paid out $129.9 million since 1989, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 64 percent. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2010-2019, then 28 percent in 2020-2025. The county's worst corn year was 2012 at 57.2 bushels per acre. Non-irrigated cash rent is $156 per acre in 2026, up 31.1 percent from 2016.

29043.text: Heat and drought is the story in Christian County. It caused 82 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1995 to 2025, and its share rose from 74 percent in 2010-2019 to 94 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1995-2025 is 1.57, meaning the county has been paid out more than it paid in premium. The county has no irrigated cropland, so the dry weeks show up directly in the crop. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre in 2026, up 44.4 percent from 2016. The median corn yield for 2008-2020 was 109.9 bushels per acre, with 2011 the worst year at 60.

29045.text: Heat and drought claims are the trend to watch in Clark County. Their share of indemnities went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's 2012 drought weeks are the worst in the record at 19. Most of the cropland is not irrigated, and only 3 percent is, so dry years land on the crop directly. Rent is $157 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 11.3 percent since 2016. Crop insurance indemnities have paid out more than premiums over the full record, with a loss ratio of 0.71 across 1989-2025.

29049.text: Clinton County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 25 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, and that share was 62 percent in 2000-2009 and again in 2010-2019, before falling to 53 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record, indemnities totaled $69.6 million, and the loss ratio was 0.69, with 3 of 22 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $200 per acre, up 28.2 percent since 2016. Corn yields have trended up 3.4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but 2012 was 57.6 bushels per acre.

29051.text: The heat and drought share is what stands out in Cole County. It went from 3 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025, and the weeks in severe drought or worse were 40 for 2021-2025 alone. Most of the claims over the whole record still came from excess moisture and flood, at 62 percent. The loss ratio is 0.81 across 1989-2025 and 0.7 over the last ten closed crop years, so the insurance has paid out less than it took in premium over the long run. Non-irrigated cash rent is $84 per acre, up 67 percent since 2016, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

29053.text: Cooper County's notable number is heat and drought. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 54 percent in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's 1989-2025 loss ratio is 0.81, with 7 of 26 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $144 per acre in 2026, up 50.8 percent from 2016. The 2017-2026 July nightly low is 68.4 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.6 F.

29055.text: Heat and drought is the main reason claims get paid in Crawford County. Of the $656,995 in closed-year indemnities from 1989 to 2025, 60 percent came from heat and drought, and the share was 66 percent in 2010-2019 and 59 percent in 2020-2025. The county went through 15 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2012, the worst year in the record, and 18 such weeks in 2021-2025. Rent is $24 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 44.1 percent from 2016 to 2026. The census put land and buildings at $2,882 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate.

29057.text:
Heat and drought is the story in Dade County. It was 11 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 80 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for closed crop years is 0.87, and 3 of 18 years paid out more than premium. Most cropland here is not irrigated, at 6 percent irrigated in 2022, so the rest rides on rain.

The county averages $66 per acre for non-irrigated rent in 2026, up 20 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,520 per acre in 2022. The worst corn year in the published record was 2011, at 36.8 bushels per acre, against a median of 118.5. Corn yield trend is 1.4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

29059.text: Dallas County is a dryland county with a heat problem more than a drought one. Heat and drought together made up 75 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1995-2025, and their share went from 74 percent in 2010-2019 to 78 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.7, which means claims have paid out well above premiums over that span. The July nightly low averaged 67.8 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026, up 14.5 percent since 2016. Median corn yield for 2011-2023 was 111.5 bushels per acre, with 2011 the worst year at 42.5.
