29061.text: Daviess County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often heat and drought have driven the claims. They were 36 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2010-2019, then 46 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $175 per acre in 2026, up 15.1 percent from 2016. Crop insurance has paid out $86.9 million since 1989, with the loss ratio at 0.69 over the full run. The 2018 crop was 93.2 bushels against a median of 142.4, so one bad year can wipe out a lot of ground's worth of income.

29063.text: The thing that stands out in DeKalb County is how little of the ground gets water beyond rain. Not one acre of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, so every crop here lives or dies on the sky. Heat and drought made up 31 percent of the crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 63 percent in 2010-2019, and that share was 40 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full 1989-2025 span, the claims paid out $69.8 million, and in 6 of 22 closed crop years the payments ran above the premiums collected. The last ten closed years have been quieter, with a loss ratio of 0.36. Non-irrigated cash rent is $156 per acre in 2026, down 6.6 percent from 2016.

29065.text: The most notable thing in Dent County's numbers is the land itself. Census land and building values were $2,920 per acre in 2022, and they rose 39.6 percent from 2017 to 2022, which is 6.9 percent a year. Those are the operators' own estimates, not sale prices, but they moved a lot. Rent went the other way: non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, down 24.5 percent from 2016. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground is mostly dryland. Drought has been a real factor, with 55 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought or worse, and 10 of those weeks came in 2021-2025.

29067.text: Heat and drought are the main reason claims get paid in Douglas County. They made up 72 percent of the $321,712 in closed crop-year indemnities from 2013 to 2025, and their share went from 54 percent in 2010-2019 to 82 percent in 2020-2025. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $32 per acre, up 28.6 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $2,936 per acre in 2022, up 39.8 percent from 2017. Only 256 acres sit in CRP, and no solar or wind is operating or proposed.

29069.text: Dunklin County is an irrigated county. Groundwater supplies all the irrigation water, and 64 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so irrigated rent of $203 per acre in 2024 is the number to watch, against $131 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2025. The county's losses are mostly from too much water: excess moisture and flood account for 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.11. Heat and drought claims fell from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025. Census land value was $6,938 per acre in 2022, up 36.3 percent from 2017.

29071.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

29073.text: Gasconade County is dryland, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census, and the thing that stands out is how the risk has been shifting. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause over the full record at 61 percent. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.91, and over the last ten closed crop years it was 0.79. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre in 2026, down 13.6 percent from 2016. The census land value of $3,826 per acre in 2022 was up 37.3 percent from 2017.

29075.text: Gentry County is a dryland county, and it has had more trouble with too much water than with heat or drought. Flood and excess moisture is the largest cause of crop insurance payouts here, at 50 percent of the $101.1 million paid over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for that span is 0.85, with 8 of 24 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $160 per acre in 2026, down 14.4 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims went from 24 percent in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2010-2019, then came back to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The county also has 39908 CRP acres, 25.2 percent of the cropland base.

29077.text: Greene County is a non-irrigated county, and heat and drought is what shows up in the claims. None of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 86 percent of crop insurance indemnities for closed years 1995-2025. That share went from 82 percent over 2010-2019 to 89 percent over 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio is 1.55, so indemnities have run above premiums over the long stretch. The worst corn year in 2008-2021 was 2018 at 66.7 bushels, against a median of 135.6. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre for 2026, up 35.6 percent since 2016.

29079.text: Grundy County's notable number is how much of its insurance money has come from wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 46 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 7 of 24 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2020-2025, so dry weather is part of the picture too. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $165 per acre in 2026, up 16.2 percent from 2016. CRP covers 23787 acres, which is 16.1 percent of the cropland base.

29081.text: Harrison County is a dry-weather county. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance payouts over 1989-2025, at 55 percent of the $112.7 million paid, and its share went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2010-2019 before settling at 54 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed years was 0.74, and 7 of 26 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $136 per acre for 2026, down 7.5 percent from 2016, and the 2022 census value of $3,799 per acre works out to a rent that was 3.84 percent of land value.

29085.text: Hickory County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $7.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 68 percent of that. The share went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2020-2025, so the heat and drought claims have been growing as a part of the total. Over the last ten closed years the loss ratio was 1.47, meaning claims ran above premium. Rent is $58 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 57.5 percent since 2016. The worst corn year was 2020, at 93.5 bushels per acre against a median of 127.8.

29087.text: Holt County's claims history leans toward too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 80 percent of the $167.0 million paid out from 1989 through 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 8 of 31 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $217 per acre in 2026, up 20.6 percent from 2016. Census land value was $5,713 per acre in 2022, and only 18 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

29089.text: Howard County's cropland is not irrigated in any meaningful share, and the rent for it is $142 per acre in 2026, up 17.4 percent since 2016. Excess moisture and flood carry most of the crop insurance claims here, at 60 percent of $37.1 million in indemnities over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 17 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is the one to watch. The county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.69, and the median corn yield for 2008-2023 was 135.1 bushels per acre, with 2012 the worst at 81.3.

29093.text: Iron County is mostly dryland, and the drought record is the part that stands out. There were 53 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, out of 1357 weeks, with 2012 the worst year at 12 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent was $20 per acre in 2025, down 13.3 percent since 2013. The census value of land and buildings was $2,697 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. The July nightly low averaged 65.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 64.3 F normal for 1991-2020, and Julys with an average low at or above 70 F have not occurred since 1900. Cropland here is not irrigated, and there is little CRP ground or energy development to speak of.

29095.text: Jackson County is a non-irrigated county, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so its corn depends on rain. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2020-2025 share is the one to watch. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 was 0.68, and insurance paid out more than premium in 3 of 19 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $158 per acre for 2026, up 58 percent from 2016.

29099.text:
Jefferson County's loss record is driven by heat and drought, and that share has grown. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.56. Dry years are the main story here, with 40 of 1357 weeks in severe drought or worse since 2000 and a worst year of 2012 with 12 weeks.

Nights are warmer too. The July average low for 2017-2026 is 68.6 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.4 F. Cash rent is $52 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and the census value of land and buildings is $5,915 per acre.

29101.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Johnson County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2020-2025, and it has been the largest cause of loss at 62 percent over the whole record. The loss ratio is 0.76 across the closed crop years 1989-2025, and only 2 of 22 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $105 per acre in 2026, up 51.1 percent from 2016. The county has only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the median corn yield for 2008-2024 is 136.1 bushels per acre.

29103.text: Knox County is dryland from top to bottom, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census. Heat and drought has been the biggest source of crop insurance claims, and its share went from 39 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks in severe drought or worse have clustered in recent years, with 32 weeks in 2021-2025 alone. The county has paid out $149.1 million in indemnities against a loss ratio of 0.93 over the closed years, so claims have run above premium in 10 of 27 crop years. The non-irrigated cash rent is $173 per acre, up 36.2 percent since 2016.

29105.text: Laclede County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of claims for decades, and its share barely moved: 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 65 percent in 2000-2009, 68 percent in 2010-2019, and 68 percent in 2020-2025. Since 1992 the loss ratio is 1.25, so claims have paid out more than premiums came in. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre in 2026, up 13.2 percent from 2016. The county corn trend is 1.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2023, with 2012 the worst year at 80.8 bushels.

29107.text: Heat and drought is the story in Lafayette County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 21 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 51 percent in 2020-2025. Corn is the largest source of those claims. The median county corn yield for 2008-2025 was 173.3 bushels per acre, but 2012 fell to 80.1. Loss ratio over the 1989-2025 closed years is 0.43, and only 2 of 30 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $226 per acre, up 59.2 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $7,328 per acre in 2022.

29109.text: Lawrence County is a dryland county. Only 2 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of that water comes from groundwater, so the crop rides on rain. That shows in the claims. Heat and drought went from 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 84 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.12, so insurers have paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $68 per acre in 2026, up 72.2 percent since 2014. The county has 149.4 MW of operating wind and no solar, and CRP is small at 153 acres.

29111.text: Heat and drought is the story in Lewis County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 36 percent in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out more in claims than it took in premium in 11 of 27 closed crop years. The corn trend is up 4.5 bushels per acre a year on the published years 2008-2025, with a worst year of 41 bushels in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $176 per acre in 2026, up 30.4 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $4,861 per acre in 2022, and rent that year was 3.48 percent of that value.

29113.text: Lincoln County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities over 1989-2025 have been $68.7 million, and the loss ratio is 0.76, but over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 it was 0.42, so claims have been light lately. Excess moisture and flood cause 56 percent of all indemnities, which is more than any other cause. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 45 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $149 per acre, up 43.3 percent since 2016.

29115.text: Linn County's cropland is all dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often the insurance has paid out. Crop insurance indemnities came to $101.6 million over 1989-2025 on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.89, with 8 of 22 crop years paying out more than the premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 49 percent. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2010-2019, then 42 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $134 per acre, up 14.5 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $4,261 per acre.

29117.text: Livingston County is a rainfall-and-flood county more than a heat county. Its largest insurance cause is excess moisture and flood at 59 percent of indemnities, and the county has seen only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated. Heat and drought claims went from 18 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, with the peak at 42 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $185 per acre for 2026, up 9.5 percent from 2016. The insurance loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.71, but over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.48. CRP covers 9.7 percent of the cropland base, and 1597 acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

29119.text: Heat and drought is the story in McDonald County. Crop insurance has paid out $3.9 million on closed crop years since 1995, and heat and drought caused 83 percent of it. The loss ratio over those years is 1.72, meaning claims have run well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought was 90 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 and 74 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre in 2026, down 15.6 percent from 2016, while the census value of land and buildings is $3,910 per acre.

29121.text: Heat and drought is the story in Macon County. It took 31 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 64 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 54 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over all closed crop years is 0.77, and six of the 22 years paid out more than premium, so the insurance has paid well above what growers put in. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, which is why dry years hit this ground hard. Non-irrigated cash rent is $135 per acre, up 7.1 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $4,026 per acre in 2022, so rent ran 2.96 percent of that. There are 18270 acres in CRP, and 760 of them expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

29123.text: Madison County is a small county where the biggest number is the weather. Heat and drought made up 81 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, and the share went from 71 percent in 2010-2019 to 84 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026, up 22.4 percent since 2016. Census land and building value was $2,627 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated. Only 10 CRP acres are in the county, none of them expiring through 2029.

29127.text: Marion County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated. Heat and drought claims have grown as a share of indemnities, from 39 percent in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood remain the largest cause overall at 46 percent. The loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 record is 0.7, but over 2016-2025 it is 0.44. Non-irrigated cash rent is $185 per acre for 2026, against a census land and buildings value of $6,203 per acre for 2022. CRP holds 6536 acres, and 612 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

29129.text: Mercer County is a dryland county with a lot of flood and wet-spring loss on the books. None of the harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, and excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the $57.7 million paid out since 1989. Heat and drought claims went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2010-2019, and they were 47 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.46, and non-irrigated cash rent is $139 per acre in 2026.

29131.text: Miller County's crop insurance record stands out. Claims have paid out more than premiums over the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.07 across 1989-2025 and 1.03 over the last ten closed years. Heat and drought was 25 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, 47 percent in 2010-2019, and 73 percent in 2020-2025. The rent has dropped to $55 per acre for non-irrigated ground, down 12.7 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,272 per acre in 2022, up 31 percent from 2017, so the rent and the land value are moving apart. Corn yields show a trend of 1.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

29133.text: This county leans on irrigation more than most. Irrigated ground is 46 percent of harvested cropland, all of it watered from groundwater, and irrigated rent is $251 per acre against $183 for dryland. Heat and drought claims went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry-weather side of the ledger has stayed a real part of it. The bigger story in the claims is excess moisture and flood, at 79 percent of the $103.0 million paid since 1989. Loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.94, meaning insurers paid out a bit less than premium in that stretch. Land and buildings were valued at $6,746 per acre in 2022.

29137.text: Monroe County's heat and drought claims have climbed steadily. Heat and drought was 61 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999 and 77 percent in 2020-2025. Over the 1989-2025 closed years, insurance paid out $156.3 million, and the loss ratio is 0.92, with 8 of 30 crop years paying out more than premium. July nights have been warm, averaging 67.1 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.4 F. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 28 in 2023, and 31 weeks have come in 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $171 per acre in 2026, up 23.9 percent since 2016.

29141.text: Heat and drought is the story in Morgan County. It caused 74 percent of the crop insurance payouts since 1989, and its share went from 79 percent in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025. The county has no irrigated cropland, and the worst corn year in the 2008-2022 record was 2012, at 40.5 bushels per acre against a median of 136.2. Non-irrigated cash rent is $64 per acre for 2026, down 26.7 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $5,025 per acre in the 2022 census, up 31 percent from 2017. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years was 0.78, lower than the 1.01 over the full record.

29143.text: New Madrid County is mostly irrigated ground, and the water comes from wells. Sixty percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, and all of the irrigation water is groundwater. The irrigation premium has grown, with irrigated cash rent at $227 per acre against $161 for non-irrigated ground in 2026, up from 1.26 times the non-irrigated rent in 2009 to 1.41 times now. Flood and excess moisture cause 72 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1989, and claims paid out more than premium in 6 of 30 closed years. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025.

29145.text: Newton County is dryland from end to end. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the weather is the whole story here. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.47, and heat and drought made up 79 percent of the indemnities. That share went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 73 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,732 per acre, a figure the operators themselves estimated. The ten closed crop years from 2016 through 2025 was 0.98, so recent claims have run closer to premium.

29147.text: Heat and drought is the story in Nodaway County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 10 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 38 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought is the largest cause of indemnities over the whole record at 46 percent of $108.6 million. The county's loss ratio of 0.48 over 1989-2025 means claims ran well under premium overall, but 6 of 32 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $192 per acre in 2026, and the county has 528.9 MW of wind operating with no solar yet.

29151.text: Osage County's most notable number is how the crop insurance claims have shifted. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for 72 percent of all indemnities over the full record. The loss ratio is 0.67 across 1989-2025 and 0.59 across 2016-2025, so claims have run below premiums over the long haul. Non-irrigated cash rent is $68 per acre for 2026, down 25.1 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,470 per acre in 2022.

29155.text: Pemiscot County is mostly dryland rent, but the water is all from wells. Groundwater supplied 100 percent of irrigation water in 2015, and irrigated ground rents for $185 per acre against $157 for non-irrigated. Heat and drought claims went from 39 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood made up 66 percent of the total $107.6 million paid since 1989. The county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.71, and six of 30 years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is up 41.4 percent since 2016.

29157.text: Perry County's crop insurance record has changed shape more than anything else here. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause over the whole record at 48 percent. The county has paid out $37.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.49, so claims have run below premium lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $116 per acre for 2026, up 12.6 percent from 2016. July nights have warmed a little, with the 2017-2026 average low at 68.7 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.3 F.

29159.text: Heat and drought is the story in Pettis County. It was 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 82 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 6 of 26 closed crop years. Nothing here is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. The county had 35 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2023 alone, and 41 such weeks across 2021-2025. Rent is $149 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 60.2 percent since 2016. The July nightly low is 68 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.4 F.

29161.text: Phelps County's notable number is the rent. Non-irrigated cash rent was $17 per acre in 2025, and it is down 55.8 percent from 2014. Heat and drought claims were 47 percent of indemnities over 2020-2025, but the largest single cause over 1992-2025 was excess moisture and flood, at 43 percent. The county has seen 16 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021, and 2012 was the worst year with 13 weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $3,912 per acre in 2022, up 48.4 percent from 2017-2022. Solar is small at 2.8 MW, and no wind is operating.

29163.text: Pike County's notable number is the crop insurance picture. Heat and drought accounted for 50 percent of the $130.8 million in indemnities over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and its share went from 42 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those years is 0.85, and 7 of 27 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $148 per acre in 2026, up 23.3 percent since 2016, while the census land and buildings value in 2022 was $4,561 per acre.

29165.text: Platte County is mostly dryland, and its main risk on the insurance books is too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 64 percent of the $48.8 million paid out from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 0.59. Heat and drought claims have climbed as a share, from 6 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $168 per acre, up 12 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings census value is $5,713 per acre. The county had 35 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2003, and 12 weeks from 2021 through 2025.

29167.text: Polk County is a dryland county where drought and the insurance claims that follow it are the main story. Heat and drought made up 71 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 51 percent in 2010-2019 and 65 percent in 2000-2009. Crop insurance has paid out $1.55 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years 1993-2025, and the ten years 2016-2025 ran at 1.45. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 20.3 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,857 per acre in 2022.

29169.text: Pulaski County is a non-irrigated county, with 0 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so the ground is carrying its own water. Heat and drought claims went from 20 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 54 percent in 2020-2025, and that is the change I'd look at first. The July nightly low has averaged 68.5 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.8 F, and July lows have been at or above 70 F in 5 Julys since 1900. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre in 2026, up 34.9 percent since 2016. Crop insurance has paid out $1.6 million over 1994-2025, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 58 percent.

29171.text: Putnam County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause over the full record at 55 percent. Losses have been heavy, with a 0.9 loss ratio since 1989 and 7 of 18 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $118 per acre in 2026, up 21.6 percent from 2016, and the county has no irrigated cropland to fall back on. The 2012 corn yield of 65.6 bushels is the bad year to keep in mind.

29173.text: Ralls County's heat and drought problem is getting bigger in the claims. Heat and drought was 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 76 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid $112.0 million in indemnities since 1989. The loss ratio over the full span is 0.95, and six of 25 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $165 per acre for 2026, up 19.6 percent from 2016, while the census value of land and buildings is $5,816 per acre for 2022.

29175.text: Randolph County is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather risk falls on rain-fed corn and beans. Heat and drought made up 60 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and their share went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out more than premium over the full span, with a loss ratio of 0.75. Non-irrigated cash rent is $144 per acre for 2026, up 19 percent from 2016. The 2012 drought brought the corn yield down to 39.5 bushels per acre, against a median of 151.7.

29177.text: Ray County is mostly dryland. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. The county's bigger insurance story is wet years, not dry ones: excess moisture and flood account for 63 percent of the $65.0 million paid out since 1989. Heat and drought claims have grown, from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $187 per acre, up 27.2 percent since 2016. Census land value was $5,276 per acre in 2022, so rent was 3.03 percent of that figure.

29181.text: Ripley County's losses have come mostly from wet springs and flooding, not from heat or drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 85 percent of the $16.9 million in indemnities paid over closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.68. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2020-2025. Most cropland is non-irrigated, and cash rent for that ground is $74 per acre in 2026, up 92.2 percent from 2016.

29183.text: Heat and drought claims have climbed the most here. They were 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and reached 25 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for 78 percent of all indemnities paid since 1989. The loss ratio over the full span is 0.68, and five of the 30 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $157 per acre in 2026, up 22.7 percent from 2016. Groundwater supplies 79 percent of the irrigation water.

29185.text: St. Clair County is dryland, with no irrigated harvested cropland in the 2022 census, so the weather risk falls on the crop itself. Heat and drought went from 25 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 70 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.02, meaning claims have run above premium. The median corn yield for 2010-2025 was 125.6 bushels per acre, with 2011 the worst year at 35.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $109 per acre for 2026, and land and buildings were valued at $3,962 per acre in the 2022 census, up 61.5 percent from 2017.

29186.text: Ste. Genevieve County is mostly dryland, and what stands out is the shift in what has been costing the insurance pool. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025, and that is the change worth watching here. Excess moisture and flood still account for 62 percent of the closed-year total of $19.6 million since 1989. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.58, and the 2017-2026 July nightly low averages 68.3 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $104 per acre in 2026, up 26.8 percent since 2016.

29187.text: St. Francois County's story is dryland ground that has paid its way for most of the years on record. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so rain decides the crop. Heat and drought made up 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019, and 52 percent in 2020-2025, so it is still the main claim cause. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.94, which means indemnities came in just under premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $63 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,052 per acre in 2022.

29189.text: Heat and drought is the thing to watch in St. Louis County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 2 percent in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for 86 percent of all indemnities since 1989. Irrigation is 3 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground depends on rain. The county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.81, and the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.65. Non-irrigated cash rent is $142 per acre for 2026, down 4.1 percent from 2016.

29195.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Saline County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 24 percent in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 42 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land. Non-irrigated cash rent is $196 per acre for 2026, up 30.7 percent since 2016. Insurance has paid out $109.2 million since 1989, and in the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio was 0.37. The census put land and buildings at $6,325 per acre in 2022.

29197.text: Schuyler County's heat-and-drought claims have climbed sharply while its losses from excess moisture and flood remain the largest cause overall. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's ten most recent closed crop years show a loss ratio of 0.44, well under the 0.92 for the full 1989-2025 span. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $97 per acre, down 14.9 percent from 2016. Heat is not the main story in July nights, which averaged 65.8 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.1 F.

29199.text: Scotland County's cropland is all non-irrigated, and the weather that has hurt it most is wet weather, not dry. Excess moisture and flood make up 51 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, while heat and drought went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2020-2025. The crop insurance loss ratio is 0.72 over the full record, but only 0.26 over 2016-2025, and 8 of 30 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Cash rent is $175 per acre for 2026, up 31.6 percent since 2016, while the 2022 census value of $5,438 per acre is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

29201.text: Scott County is mostly dryland with a sizable irrigated share, and the water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims have grown: they were 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 38 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.79, so insurance has paid out more than the premiums taken in over that stretch, and in 3 of 23 closed crop years it paid more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $176 per acre in 2026, and irrigated rent is $260 per acre. Census land and buildings value was $6,405 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 3.7 percent of the cropland base.

29205.text: Heat and drought is the story in Shelby County. It caused 43 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, and that share went up to 56 percent in 2010-2019 and again in 2020-2025. The county has had 23 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021, with 19 of its 64 bad weeks since 2000 falling in 2023 alone. Insurance losses have run above premiums over the full span, with a loss ratio of 0.82 and payouts higher than premium in 5 of 26 crop years. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $177 per acre, up 14.2 percent since 2016. CRP covers 6.6 percent of the cropland base.

29207.text: Stoddard County is mostly dryland, but the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $208 per acre against $113 for non-irrigated, and 55 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 99 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Most of the insurance pay here has come from too much rain, not dry weather: excess moisture and flood account for 62 percent of the $189.2 million in indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $6,814 per acre in 2022, up 27.3 percent from 2017.

29209.text: Stone County is mostly dry ground, and its heat is showing up in the nights more than the days. The July average low has been 68.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 66.9 F normal for 1991-2020, and five Julys since 1900 averaged 70 F or higher. Irrigation is barely there, with 3 percent of harvested cropland watered in 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent was $37 per acre in 2023, up 34.5 percent from 2012. Land and buildings were valued at $4,003 per acre in 2022, which rose 38.3 percent from 2017 to 2022. The county has 23 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025, and 2012 stands out as the worst year with 16 weeks.

29211.text: Heat and drought claims are the thing to watch in Sullivan County. Their share of indemnities went from 16 percent in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.57, with $8.58 paid per $100 of insured value. Corn has been paying out more than premium in 7 of 18 closed crop years over the full record. Not a single acre here is irrigated, so the corn crop rides on rain. Cash rent is $123 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 34.4 percent since 2016. CRP covers 18.2 percent of the cropland base, with 1151 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

29213.text: Taney County's rent is what stands out. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, and it was down 27.3 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,385 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 51.5 percent between 2017 and 2022, so the ground is worth far more than the rent it brings in. Drought has been a smaller factor here, with 72 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2012 the worst year at 18 weeks. July nights have run close to the normal, averaging 67.9 F over 2017-2026 against 66.8 F for 1991-2020.

29215.text: Rent here is $56 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 73.8 percent since 2016. That is a big climb for a county where heat and drought did most of the damage. Heat and drought made up 95 percent of crop insurance claims paid from 2017 to 2025, $418,455 in all, and 94 percent of claims in 2020-2025. Drought weeks in severe drought or worse ran 59 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, with 19 of them in 2012. July nights have averaged 67.1 F since 2017, against a 65.7 F normal for 1991-2020. Land and buildings were valued at $3,220 per acre in 2022, up 55.9 percent from 2017.

29217.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

29219.text: Warren County is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the water that does get pumped comes from groundwater. The thing that stands out is the insurance record. Closed crop years paid out $27.2 million on $0.6 for every dollar of premium, and three of 18 years paid out more than the premium. Excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 47 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $107 per acre and has not moved since 2016. Solar is operating at 139 MW, with 300 MW more proposed, and there is no wind.

29221.text: Washington County is a dryland county. None of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and the 2022 census put the land and buildings at $2,926 per acre, up 23.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, down 38 percent from 2016. Heat and drought are behind 95 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 2018-2025, which came to $122,877 on closed crop years. Severe drought hit at least 50 percent of the county for 53 weeks from 2000-2025, with 12 of those weeks in 2012, and 15 weeks in 2021-2025 alone. July nightly lows are running 65.5 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.7 F, and the July trend since 1976 is not a clear trend.

29223.text: Wayne County is a rainfall county more than a heat county. The indemnity record is led by excess moisture and flood at 48 percent, and the loss ratio is 1.29 over the last ten closed crop years, meaning claims have run above premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 31 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is climbing even as the county is not in severe drought often. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre, up 16.9 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $2,495 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 220 acres, with 144 of those expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

29225.text: Webster County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn crop lives or dies on rain. The median corn yield for 2008-2022 was 123 bushels per acre, and the worst year, 2022, was 56.1. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 81 percent of indemnities over 1994-2025. Its share went from 80 percent for 2010-2019 to 84 percent for 2020-2025. The loss ratio for closed crop years is 1.73, so claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre for 2026, up 5.7 percent since 2016, while the census puts land and buildings at $4,559 per acre.

29227.text: Worth County's notable number is how much its insurance claims have moved toward heat and drought. Those claims were 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 53 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for the largest share overall at 44 percent. Corn yields have trended up 4.7 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 144.4 bushels and a worst year of 60.4 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $188 per acre in 2026, and the census put land and buildings at $3,888 per acre in 2022. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

29229.text: Heat and drought is the story in Wright County. It caused 89 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid on closed years from 1995 to 2025, and its share went from 88 percent in 2010-2019 to 94 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those years is 2.04, meaning the county has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premiums. The Atlas also counts 15 weeks of severe drought in 2021-2025 alone. Cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 64.3 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,310 per acre in 2022. No cropland is irrigated.

31003.text: Antelope County is mostly irrigated: 70 percent of harvested cropland, and 99 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $320 per acre, against $173 for non-irrigated, and the gap has held near the same ratio since 2008. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 33 percent of $144.6 million paid since 1989. Its share was 20 percent in 1989-1999 and 42 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $5,999 per acre in 2022, and 2683 irrigation wells have no decommission date on record.

31005.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Arthur County. Their share of crop insurance claims went from 1 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 65 weeks in severe drought or worse since 2021. Hail still causes the most claims over the long run, at 44 percent. The loss ratio is 1.8 over the last ten closed crop years, so claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Land values were $1,091 per acre in 2022, and 35 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all of it from groundwater.

31007.text: Banner County is a dryland-leaning county with most of its ground in non-irrigated production, but the water picture is where it stands out. Groundwater supplies 92 percent of irrigation water, and the July nightly low has climbed from a 1991-2020 normal of 57 F to an average of 58.3 F over 2017-2026. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.03, with 9 of 24 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre and irrigated is $177 per acre.

31009.text: Blaine County is a groundwater county. Groundwater supplies 92 percent of the irrigation water, and irrigated ground rents for $187 per acre in 2025, while non-irrigated ground rents for $39 per acre in 2023 and is down 9.3 percent from 2013. Hail is what has been paying claims here, at 71 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.07, meaning insurers paid out more than premiums came in. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 1 percent in 2020-2025. Census land value was $1,317 per acre in 2022.

31013.text: Box Butte County is a dryland county with an irrigated edge. Irrigated ground rents for $203 per acre in 2026, against $38 for non-irrigated, and the gap has narrowed from 8.10 times in 2013 to 5.34 times now. Most of the crop insurance money paid here has come from hail, at 57 percent, and the loss ratio over the closed years is 0.82, with 11 of 35 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $2,034 per acre in 2022, and CRP holds 40.7 percent of the cropland base.

31015.text: Boyd County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what has been costing the ground here. Heat and drought was 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 90 percent in 2020-2025, and it accounts for 86 percent of all indemnities since 1989. The county has paid out more in claims than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 0.96 over the closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $126 per acre in 2026, up 13.5 percent since 2016, and the Census put land and buildings at $2,664 per acre in 2022. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

31017.text: Brown County's irrigated ground is the thing to look at first. Irrigated rent is $186 per acre for 2026, and the census puts 44 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, with 58 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Non-irrigated rent was $62 per acre in 2025, up 148 percent from 2014. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 256 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2000. The corn yield trend is up 2.8 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.52. Hail is the largest cause of claims, at 35 percent.

31021.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Burt County. It was 5 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 37 percent in 2000-2009, 28 percent in 2010-2019, and 57 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is still the largest single cause over the full record at 38 percent. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 201 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, with 2023 the worst at 52 weeks. Irrigated ground rents for $276 per acre against $252 for non-irrigated, and the premium has been slipping from 1.14 times in 2009 to 1.10 times in 2026. The census puts land and buildings at $7,150 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate.

31025.text: Cass County is mostly dryland, and most of its corn is decided by rain. Heat and drought made up 79 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019, the largest share in any period the Atlas shows, and 56 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the county paid out $107.2 million on insured crops, and the loss ratio was 0.52, with 5 of 34 closed crop years paying more than the premium they brought in. Irrigated ground is rare here, at 1 percent of harvested cropland, and non-irrigated cash rent is $226 per acre for 2026, up 12.4 percent from 2016.

31027.text: Cedar County is a dryland-and-irrigated county where heat and drought have become the main reason claims get paid. Heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 77 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out $188.0 million on closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.69, and over the last ten closed years it is 0.53. Irrigated ground rents for $352 per acre against $247 for non-irrigated, and 46 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 96 percent of that water from groundwater. The county's worst drought year was 2022, with 40 weeks in severe drought or worse.

31029.text: Chase County is a dryland-and-irrigation county with a heavy claims history from hail and a rising share of drought losses. Irrigation covers 61 percent of harvested cropland, all of it fed from groundwater, and irrigated ground rents for $258 per acre against $58 for non-irrigated. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, while hail still accounts for 56 percent of the $207.5 million paid since 1989. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.86, and the county paid out more than premium in 7 of 34 years. The census put land and buildings at $2,558 per acre in 2022, and CRP takes 14.9 percent of the cropland base.

31031.text: Cherry County is mostly dryland, but the irrigated ground that exists is where the money is: $176 per acre irrigated against $36 for non-irrigated, and 18 percent of harvested cropland is under pivots, pumping from wells that draw on groundwater for 93 percent of irrigation water. Heat and drought went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025, while hail still leads at 49 percent of the total. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.58, so insurance has paid out less than premium in recent years. Median corn yield for 2008-2021 was 180.5 bushels per acre, with 2011 the worst at 155.2.

31033.text: Cheyenne County is mostly dryland, but the irrigated ground carries the rent: irrigated ground rents for $190 per acre, against $42 for non-irrigated, and the gap has been wide and steady enough that it is not a clear trend. Groundwater supplies 96 percent of the irrigation water, and 588 irrigation wells have no decommission date on record. The bigger shift is in claims. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and hail still leads the list at 40 percent overall. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.92.

31035.text: Clay County is mostly irrigated ground. Irrigation covers 79 percent of harvested cropland, and 95 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $320 per acre in 2026 against $157 for dryland, and both rents have barely moved since 2016. The bigger story is the weather. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, and 107 weeks of severe drought or worse have hit the county since 2021. The closed-year loss ratio is 0.49, with 3 of 30 crop years paying out more than premium. Irrigation wells are still open with no decommission date on 2,566 of 3,945 registered wells.

31039.text: Cuming County's notable number is how much of its loss history has come from heat and drought. Their share of indemnities went from 27 percent in 1989-1999 to 84 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out $219.0 million on closed crop years since 1989. The insurance loss ratio is 0.84, and 7 of 31 crop years paid out more than premium. Only 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent is $289 per acre against $344 for irrigated ground. The county's worst corn year in the published record was 2012 at 95.7 bushels per acre.

31041.text: Custer County is a heavily irrigated county, with 58 percent of harvested cropland under pivots and 93 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $240 per acre against $100 for dryland, and the county's wells have a median depth of 315 feet. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities, at 46 percent of the $192.1 million paid over 1989-2025. Its share went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2000-2009, and was 41 percent in 2020-2025. Dryland rent is up 30.9 percent since 2016, and the county has 2,323 irrigation wells with no decommission date on record.

31043.text: Dakota County is mostly watered from the ground. Irrigated ground rents for $322 per acre, against $264 for dryland, and 99 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought has been the biggest cause of crop insurance claims since 1989, and its share went from 20 percent in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks in severe drought or worse have been frequent here, with 42 in 2022 alone. Land is valued at $7,081 per acre, but that figure is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

31045.text: Dawes County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at first. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 4 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 6 of 10 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 50 percent from 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $170. CRP covers 49.1 percent of the cropland base, with 650 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

31047.text: Dawson County is mostly irrigated ground, and that drives most of what follows. The census says 80 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 87 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Irrigated rent is $273 per acre against $128 for dryland, and the ratio has stayed near 2.13 in 2026 and 2.11 in 2008. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2010-2019 and 17 percent in 2020-2025. Hail still accounts for the largest share of claims at 48 percent. Dryland rent is up 31.3 percent since 2016.

31049.text: Deuel County is a dryland county with a sizable irrigated edge, and the irrigated ground is where the cash rent gap really shows. Irrigated ground rents for $172 per acre in 2026, against $44 for non-irrigated, and irrigated is only 10 percent of harvested cropland, so the county's rent picture depends on which ground you're looking at. Heat and drought is the biggest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 47 percent of the $91.2 million paid since 1989, and its share went from 4 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025. The county's median corn yield over 2008-2024 was 113.4 bushels per acre, with 2021 the worst year at 81.5.

31051.text: Dixon County's notable number is the water. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, yet the irrigated rent is $343 per acre against $256 for non-irrigated ground, and that gap has widened since 2016 when the multiple was 1.20. Heat and drought made up 72 percent of closed crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and the share went from 29 percent in 1989-1999 to 77 percent in 2010-2019. The county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.78, so claims have run ahead of premiums over the full span, though 2016-2025 was 0.46.

31053.text: Heat and drought is the thing to watch in Dodge County. It was 11 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2020-2025. The county paid out $108.9 million on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.54, so claims have run ahead of premium. Irrigated ground rents for $306 per acre against $225 for dryland, and 39 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 91 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 82 in 2021-2025.

31055.text: Douglas County is a county where heat and drought claims have become the main story. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 194 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2000. Irrigated ground rents for $269 per acre against $248 for non-irrigated, and 94 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 0.63, so claims ran below premium in that stretch.

31057.text: Dundy County is an irrigated county with a lot of dry years. Irrigation covers 48 percent of the harvested cropland, and the water comes from groundwater, 98 percent of it. Irrigated ground rents for $237 per acre this year, against $51 for dryland. Crop insurance has paid out $158.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, with an overall loss ratio of 0.85, and heat and drought went from 6 percent of those indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks of severe drought ran to 105 in 2021-2025 alone, with the worst year at 2013 with 53 weeks.

31059.text: Fillmore County has a lot of irrigated ground, 71 percent of harvested cropland in 2022, and that water comes from wells that pull 95 percent groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $314 per acre this year, against $174 for dryland, and the county's indemnities have leaned on heat and drought. That share went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2000-2009, then came down to 33 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio since 1989 is 0.49, and for the last ten closed crop years it climbed to 0.62. Of the 2,482 irrigation wells with no decommission date on record, the median one is 222 feet deep.

31061.text: Franklin County is a irrigated county on paper more than in the field, and the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $284 per acre against $115 for non-irrigated, and irrigated rent was 2.47 times the dryland rate in 2026. Irrigated land is 56 percent of harvested cropland, and 91 percent of that water comes from groundwater, so the wells are the thing to watch. Heat and drought made up 20 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 51 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out more than premium in 8 of 26 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.65.

31063.text: Frontier County is a county where irrigation makes most of the money. Irrigated ground rents for $211 per acre in 2026, against $68 for dryland, and irrigation covers 33 percent of harvested cropland, with 99 percent of that water pulled from groundwater. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance claims, and its share went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 90 in 2021-2025 alone, and the county's worst year, 2013, had 53 such weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $2,370 per acre in 2022, and the county has 27656 acres in CRP.

31065.text: Heat and drought is the big story in Furnas County. It caused 68 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and its share went from 25 percent in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2010-2019. The county paid out $259.6 million on closed claims, and the loss ratio of 1.03 means claims have run a little above premiums over the full stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $88 per acre, and irrigated ground rents for $235. Land and buildings were valued at $2,895 per acre in 2022, a number from the operators themselves, not a sale.

31067.text: Gage County's notable pattern is the heat and drought claims. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid $145.3 million on closed crop years overall. Irrigation is a big part of the picture too: irrigated ground rents for $278 per acre against $176 for dryland, and 79 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. The county has 802 irrigation wells with no decommission date on record. Corn yields have trended up 2.1 bushels per acre a year since 2008, and the ground was worth $5,474 per acre on the 2022 census.

31069.text: Garden County is a dry-land and pivot county where the heat-and-drought claims have taken over. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 75 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out $62.1 million on closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio is 0.95, and six of the 22 closed crop years paid more than the premium. Most of the irrigation water comes from groundwater, at 86 percent, and the 2026 irrigated rent is $189 per acre against $44 for non-irrigated ground. CRP covers 46.6 percent of the cropland base, with 483 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

31071.text: Garfield County is an irrigated county where the water comes from the ground. Only 27 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, but 80 percent of the irrigation water is pumped from groundwater, and there are 786 registered wells. Heat and drought claims were 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 11 percent in 2020-2025, while hail is the largest single cause at 33 percent. Corn yields have trended up 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, and the loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.83. Irrigated cash rent was $233 per acre in 2025, against $90 for non-irrigated ground.

31073.text: Gosper County has a lot of irrigated ground, and it draws most of its water from the ground below it. Irrigated cash rent is $280 per acre against $98 for non-irrigated, and the census put the land and buildings at $4,514 per acre in 2022. Heat and drought claims went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.57. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 85 over 2021-2025, and 2013 alone had 53.

31079.text: Hall County is an irrigated county first. Irrigated ground makes up 83 percent of harvested cropland, all of the irrigation water comes from groundwater, and irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $279 per acre against $130 for non-irrigated ground in 2025. Crop insurance has paid out $127.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, with hail the largest cause at 36 percent. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, and 52 weeks of severe drought or worse were logged in 2023.

31087.text: Hitchcock County is a dryland county with an irrigated edge, and the heat and drought side is what stands out. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more in claims than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 1.18 over closed crop years 1989-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $198 per acre against $60 for dryland, and 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, most of it on groundwater, with 576 irrigation wells showing no decommission date. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 53 in 2013 and 112 across 2021-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $2,181 per acre in 2022, up 38.6 percent from 2017.

31093.text: Howard County is mostly irrigated: 67 percent of harvested cropland, and 57 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $245 per acre against $132 for dryland, and irrigated rent was 2.34 times dryland in 2008 and 1.86 times in 2026. The county's crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 0.61 over 1989-2025 and 0.67 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought was 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 44 percent in 2020-2025. The worst drought year was 2023, with 52 weeks in severe drought or worse.

31097.text: Heat and drought is the story in Johnson County. It drove 64 percent of the crop insurance payouts over 1989-2025, and its share went from 20 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025. The county corn yield trend is up 2 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 147 bushels and a worst year at 86.7 in 2012. Only 12 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the irrigated rent of $298 per acre was 1.54 times the non-irrigated $184 in 2025, down from 1.78 in 2010.

31099.text: Kearney County is mostly irrigated ground, and the water comes from wells: 68 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, and 90 percent of the water is groundwater. Irrigated cash rent is $263 per acre in 2026 against $129 for non-irrigated ground, and the 2010 ratio was 1.85 with no clear trend since. Heat and drought claims went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, which is the part of the record I'd watch. Insurers have paid out $119.3 million on closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.59, and 4 of 30 years paid more than premium. Census land and buildings were valued at $7,608 per acre in 2022.

31101.text: Keith County is an irrigated county first. Irrigated cash rent is $218 per acre, and non-irrigated is $56, so the gap is wide. Heat and drought has become the main reason claims get paid: its share of indemnities went from 5 percent in 1989-1999 to 79 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.72, and over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.73. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 401 of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 67 of those weeks in 2021-2025. Groundwater supplies 90 percent of the irrigation water.

31103.text: Heat and drought is the claim story in Keya Paha County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 5 percent in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, and it was the largest cause over the whole record at 33 percent. The county paid out more than premium in 2 of 15 closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.58 across 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $43 per acre, down 8.5 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $193. Corn yields trend up 2.3 bushels per acre a year on the published years 2008-2025.

31105.text: Kimball County is mostly dryland, but the irrigated ground is what sets the rent. Irrigated cash rent is $192 per acre in 2026, against $34 for non-irrigated, and that gap has widened from 4.80 times in 2009 to 5.57 times now. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years the insurance loss ratio was 0.83, so claims have run ahead of premiums. CRP covers 48.2 percent of the cropland base, and 17776 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

31107.text: Knox County leans on irrigation more than most of Nebraska's ground, and the water comes from wells. Irrigated cash rent is $300 per acre against $217 for dryland, and in 2009 irrigated ground rented for 1.82 times dryland, against 1.38 times in 2026. Heat and drought was 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 101 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021. The corn yield trend is up 2.4 bushels per acre a year, with a county median of 171.3 bushels. The census value of land and buildings is $5,161 per acre, and that figure is the operators' own estimate.

31109.text: Lancaster County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought made up 73 percent of the $133.0 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, and its share went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 76 percent in 2020-2025. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $190 per acre in 2026, up 16.6 percent from 2016, and irrigated rent is $274 per acre. The corn yield trend is 1.2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024.

31113.text: Logan County is a dryland-and-pivot county, and the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $191 per acre in 2026 against $49 for non-irrigated ground, and the irrigated rent has pulled further ahead of the dryland rent over the last few years. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 29 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.74, and only 3 of 17 crop years paid out more than the premium. Groundwater supplies 99 percent of the irrigation water, and 307 irrigation wells have no decommission date on record.

31117.text: Most of the cropland in McPherson County is irrigated, and the water comes from the ground: 89 percent of irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $146 per acre, against $40 for non-irrigated ground in 2025. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in premium over the last ten closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.27. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2020-2025, and 129 irrigation wells have no decommission date on record.

31121.text: Merrick County is an irrigated county, and that shapes everything else here. Irrigated cash rent is $272 per acre in 2026, against $121 for non-irrigated ground in 2022, and 82 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all of it drawing on groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $79.5 million since 1989 against premiums that the loss ratio of 0.58 says were more than the claims. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 52 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2023. Land and buildings were valued at $5,476 per acre in 2022, a number the operators gave, not a sale price.

31123.text: Morrill County is a county where most of the cropland is irrigated, and the land is mostly under the pivots. The 2022 census put the irrigated share of harvested cropland at 64 percent, and 63 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater, so the wells are the operation. Irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $178 per acre, while non-irrigated rent for 2025 is $40. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 0.74 across 1989-2025, and hail is the largest cause at 48 percent. Heat and drought claims have grown from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025.

31127.text: Heat and drought is the story in Nemaha County. It made up 9 percent of crop insurance claims in 1989-1999, 60 percent in 2000-2009, and 41 percent in 2020-2025. Over all the closed crop years the county has paid out more than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 0.52 and 3 of 32 years paying more than premium. Irrigated ground rented for $288 per acre in 2023, against $213 for non-irrigated in 2026, and 66 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Census land value was $6,778 per acre in 2022, up 49 percent from 2017.

31129.text: Nuckolls County is a county where heat and drought drive most of the insurance payouts. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 86 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.27, so payouts have run past premiums. Irrigated ground rents for $296 per acre against $148 non-irrigated, and irrigated ground is 32 percent of harvested cropland, with 82 percent of that water from groundwater.
