Corn yields have been close to flat, at a trend of 0.8 bushels per acre a year. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.82, so premiums have mostly covered the claims. Cash rent is $64 per acre in 2026, up 27.7 percent from 2016. Wind is the other thing on the ground here, with 149 MW operating.

38071.text: Ramsey County's biggest story in the claims data is water in the wrong place. Excess moisture and flood account for 64 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, while heat and drought went from 2 percent in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 span is 0.88, and the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 0.67. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre for 2026, up 15.8 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $1,885 per acre for 2022. CRP covers 5.1 percent of the cropland base.

38073.text: Ransom County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the bigger story in its insurance history is wet years, not dry ones. Flood and excess moisture account for 75 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and heat and drought went from 4 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $118 per acre, up 24.2 percent since 2016. Irrigation is a small slice here, at 6 percent of harvested cropland, so the $198 irrigated rent matters mostly to the few operators who have it. CRP holds 11.9 percent of the cropland base.

38075.text: Renville County is a dryland county with no irrigated harvested cropland reported in 2022, so water is a question of rain, not a pump. What stands out here is excess moisture: flood and wet weather account for 62 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the county has paid out more than its premiums in 14 of 34 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.14. Heat and drought went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $64 per acre in 2026, up 35.8 percent since 2014, and the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $2,334 per acre.

38077.text: Richland County is mostly dryland, and the water that's there is spoken for by a few wet years. Flood and excess moisture account for 70 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and only 7 of 37 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025, so that's the part to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $163 per acre for 2026, up 27.3 percent from 2016, and the census land value of $4,419 per acre for 2022 was a 38.6 percent move from 2017.

38079.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

38081.text: Sargent County's heat and drought story is small, but the weather that hurts here is wet. Flood and excess moisture make up 74 percent of the $377.8 million in indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the county's loss ratio over those closed years is 0.82. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, which is worth watching. Irrigation is not much of a factor: irrigated rent is $177 per acre against $135 for non-irrigated ground, and the gap has narrowed since 2010.

38083.text: Heat and drought is the story in Sheridan County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst weeks of drought have come in the last five years, with 56 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025. The loss ratio of 0.73 over 1989-2025 means claims have paid out more than the premiums over the whole record, and 2016-2025 ran at 0.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre for 2026, up 27 percent from 2016. The county is not showing a clear trend in its July nightly lows, so that stays out of the picture.

38085.text: Sioux County is a dryland county with no irrigated harvested cropland reported in 2022, so the rent of $46 per acre is for ground that lives or dies on rain. Heat and drought are the main reason claims get paid here, at 51 percent of indemnities since 1989, and their share went from 15 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out more than premium over the period, with a loss ratio of 0.84 and 5 of 20 crop years paying more than they cost. Land and buildings were valued at $1,367 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 15.2 percent of the cropland base.

38087.text: Slope County is dryland all the way through. No farm reported irrigated harvested cropland in 2022, and heat and drought drove most of the insurance money here. Heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2000-2009, then 35 percent in 2010-2019 and 62 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought weeks were 289 of 1357 between 2000 and 2025, with 42 of those weeks in 2008 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $47 per acre, up 38.2 percent since 2016. Crop insurance paid out $131.0 million on closed crop years, a loss ratio of 0.89 against premium.

38089.text: Stark County is dryland all the way. Not a single harvested acre is irrigated, and the crop insurance record shows why it matters: heat and drought drove 54 percent of the $221.7 million paid out from 1989 through 2025. Its share went from 21 percent in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2000-2009, and it has run 44 percent in 2010-2019 and 46 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.84 for the full stretch, and nine of 31 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $48 per acre, up 33.8 percent since 2016.

38091.text: Steele County's land is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much of the loss comes from too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood made up 51 percent of the $268.6 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and the county's loss ratio was 0.66 over those closed years. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is climbing. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $99 per acre, up 15.1 percent since 2016.

38093.text: Stutsman County is mostly dryland, and the county's crop insurance history is shaped more by wet years than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 53 percent of indemnities from 1989 to 2025, while heat and drought went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields show a trend of 2.2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with the worst year 2021 at 98.7 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $96 per acre in 2026, up 26.1 percent since 2016. There are 200 MW of wind operating and no solar.

38095.text: Towner County's crop insurance story is wet years more than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 66 percent of the $441.4 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.87, with 17 of 37 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought is the part that has grown, from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. No farm reported irrigated harvested cropland in 2022, so every acre here is dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $64 per acre, up 42.7 percent since 2016.

38101.text: Ward County's crop insurance record has leaned toward drought lately. Heat and drought went from 18 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, and the single worst corn year, 2021 at 58.5 bushels per acre, came in the same stretch as 52 weeks of severe drought. Over the full record the county paid out $587.1 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.91, so claims have run close to premium. None of the cropland is irrigated, so dry years land on the ground directly. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026.

38103.text: Wells County is dryland from top to bottom, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census, so the rent and yield numbers below are all rain-fed. The thing that stands out is the insurance record. Heat and drought went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.77, with indemnities at $11.56 per $100 of insured value. Non-irrigated cash rent is $81 per acre, up 25.6 percent since 2016. The corn yield trend is 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the 2021 crop was 84.2 bushels against a median of 130.5.

38105.text: Williams County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the weather record is where the county stands out. Heat and drought made up 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 and 54 percent in 2020-2025, against 15 percent in 1989-1999. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.73, and $12.49 was paid per $100 of insured value. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre in 2026, up 10.1 percent since 2016, and the median corn yield for 2008-2025 is 84.6 bushels per acre, with 2021 down to 58.

39001.text: Heat and drought is the thing to watch in Adams County. It caused 49 percent of the crop insurance payouts from 1989 to 2025, and its share went from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out more than it took in premiums in 5 of 18 closed crop years, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.73. Non-irrigated cash rent is $136 per acre for 2026, up 57.2 percent since 2016. The land and buildings value in the 2022 census was $5,254 per acre, up 35.3 percent from 2017.

39003.text: Allen County is mostly rain-fed ground. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on the rain that falls. The insurance record shows that. Excess moisture and flood was the largest cause of claims at 32 percent, but heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The worst corn year was 2012, at 111.1 bushels per acre, against a median of 169.9. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $226 per acre, up 27 percent from 2016, while the 2022 census land value is $8,341 per acre. Rent in 2022 was 2.55 percent of that value.

39005.text: The county's biggest story is water, and it's mostly too much of it. Excess moisture and flood have been the largest cause of claims over 1989-2025, at 50 percent, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 4 of 22 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 0 weeks in severe drought since 2021. Rent is $129 per acre, up 13.2 percent since 2016, and the census land value of $7,886 per acre was set by operators, not sale prices.

39007.text: The thing that stands out in Ashtabula County is the water, and it is too much of it, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 71 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1989, and the county has paid out more than its premiums in 5 of the 20 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 39 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, but none of the 2021-2025 weeks reached severe drought, and the county has no irrigated cropland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $53 per acre in 2026, down 27.9 percent from 2016, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings was $5,435 per acre.

39009.text: Athens County's story this year is the drought claims. Heat and drought made up 60 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 18 percent in 2010-2019. The county's worst corn year in the published record was 2012, at 114.9 bushels per acre, against a median of 151.8. The county's 1989-2025 loss ratio of 0.77 means the insurers have paid out less than the premiums collected over the long run, though that changes in the bad years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $55 per acre, unchanged from 2016 to 2026. The census land value, at $4,123 per acre in 2022, is the operators' own estimate and is well above what the rent alone would suggest.

39011.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Auglaize County. It was 44 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 63 percent in 2000-2009, then came back to 52 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out $73.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.58, so claims have run ahead of premium more often than not. Rent is $234 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 14.7 percent since 2016. Corn yields show a trend of 4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 171.8 bushels and a worst year at 104.5 in 2012.

39013.text: Belmont County is a dryland county. Not one acre of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the cash rent of $26 per acre reflects ground that depends entirely on the sky. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 57 percent since 1989, and it rose to 64 percent of indemnities over 2020-2025. The county had 24 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2024 alone, and 26 such weeks across 2021-2025. Corn yields have a median of 125 bushels per acre, and the worst year, 2012, was 96.7. July nights are also running warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, with a 63.2 F average low over 2017-2026. Land and buildings were valued at $4,446 per acre in 2022.

39015.text: The first thing I'd look at in Brown County is the crop insurance record. Indemnities over 1989-2025 came to $52.5 million, and the loss ratio is 0.59, so claims have run well under premium over the long haul. The big single cause is excess moisture and flood at 53 percent. Heat and drought share of claims went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025, after dipping to 15 percent in 2010-2019, so the recent years look more like the early ones. Rent is $161 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 43.8 percent since 2016, and none of the harvested cropland is irrigated.

39019.text: Carroll County's crop insurance has paid out more than it took in. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 1.15, and heat and drought drove most of it, at 75 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 47 percent in 1989-1999. Nothing here is irrigated, so a dry July lands straight on the corn. Rent is $64 per acre in 2026, down 1.5 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $5,992 per acre in 2022, so rent on that value is 0.96 percent, a thin return for the ground. Median county corn yield is 123.5 bushels per acre, with 2012 the bad year at 82.

39021.text: Champaign County is mostly a rain-fed county, and most of the ground is leased that way. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $217 per acre in 2026, up 18.6 percent since 2016. The weather risk shows up in the insurance claims. Heat and drought was 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, and it was 47 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out $71.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.52. Over the last ten closed years it is 0.38, so claims have been lighter lately. Land and buildings were valued at $9,173 per acre in the 2022 census, and rent was 2.21 percent of that value.

39023.text: Clark County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much of the insurance money paid out has come from heat and drought. That share was 55 percent in 1989-1999 and 26 percent in 2020-2025, so the pattern has eased some over time. Over the closed years 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.46, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 4 of 25 crop years. The median corn yield for 2008-2025 is 189.5 bushels per acre, with a worst year of 138.3 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $247 per acre, and the census land value is $9,200 per acre.

39025.text: Clermont County is a non-irrigated county, and the crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Flood and excess moisture took 39 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for those closed years is 0.61, with 3 of 22 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 50 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $129 per acre for 2026, against a 2022 census land value of $7,599 per acre, which the operators themselves put on the ground.

39027.text: Clinton County is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is the thing to look at first. Flood and excess moisture cause the largest share of indemnities, at 44 percent, and the 1989-2025 loss ratio is 0.41, with 4 of 26 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims were 58 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 29 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry-year pattern has come back after a quiet stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $170 per acre, up 8.3 percent from 2016. Census land value was $8,247 per acre in 2022.

39029.text: Heat and drought is the thing to watch in Columbiana County. It was 38 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-1999 and 41 percent over 2000-2009, dipped to 21 percent over 2010-2019, then jumped to 67 percent over 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio is 0.55 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and only 1 of 19 years paid out more than premium. The July nightly low has warmed to 62 F in 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 60.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre in 2026, up 24.5 percent from 2016. Corn yields have a trend of 0.8 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the median is 148.8 bushels.

39031.text: Coshocton County's loss history leans toward wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of the $19.4 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, and insurance has paid more than premium in only 2 of 16 crop years. The 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.51, so recent years have been quieter. Heat and drought share went from 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2020-2025, which is worth watching. Cash rent is $95 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 2.7 percent since 2016.

39033.text: Crawford County's most notable number is the flood risk. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here at 35 percent, and crop years have paid out more than premium in 4 of 23 closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.46 across 1989-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 20 percent in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, so they matter too, but water that comes in too fast is the bigger worry. Non-irrigated cash rent is $209 per acre for 2026, up 28.2 percent since 2016. Solar is 117 MW operating and no wind is operating or proposed.

39037.text: Darke County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid $122.4 million on closed crop years, and the ratio of indemnity to premium is 0.56 across 1989-2025, with four of 27 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 53 percent of that, but its share went from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yield fell to 100.1 bushels in 2012, while the median since 2008 is 174.9. Non-irrigated cash rent is $287 per acre in 2025, and land and buildings are valued at $10,913 per acre in 2022.

39039.text: Defiance County is a rain-wet county more than a dry one. The biggest cause of claims is excess moisture and flood, at 44 percent of indemnities since 1989, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Heat and drought made up 23 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has been climbing. The crop insurance loss ratio was 0.84 over 1989-2025 and 0.64 over the last ten closed years, and the county's land value was $7,824 per acre in 2022, with non-irrigated cash rent at $177 per acre for 2026. Rent is up 18.8 percent since 2014.

39041.text: Delaware County is a rainfed county where the wet years cost more than the dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over those closed crop years is 0.61, with 4 of 23 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $190 per acre in 2026, up 38.7 percent from 2016, against a census land value of $9,771 per acre in 2022.

39043.text: Erie County's most notable number is the water, and it's the wet side of it. Excess moisture and flood took 46 percent of the crop insurance payouts from 1989 to 2025, and the county's loss ratio was 0.5 over those closed years. Only 2 of 21 crop years paid out more than premium, so the claims have mostly been modest. Heat and drought went from 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has climbed from a 1991-2020 normal of 64.6 F to 66.1 F over 2017-2026. Non-irrigated rent is $191 per acre in 2026, up from 2016 by 36.4 percent.

39045.text: Fairfield County is rain-fed all the way through. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so every bushel depends on what falls from the sky. Heat and drought is the biggest cause of insurance claims here, with 53 percent of indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2010-2019 and 53 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.48 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and only 3 of 22 crop years paid out more than premium, so the insurance has mostly been a cost to the farmer. Non-irrigated cash rent is $188 per acre for 2026. The corn yield trend is up 2.2 bushels per acre a year, but 2012 was 105.7 bushels, so a dry year still shows up hard.

39047.text: Fayette County is a non-irrigated county, and that's the first thing to know: none of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so every bushel depends on rain. Heat and drought claims went from 75 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, which is the change to watch. The county has paid out $79.1 million in closed crop years, and four of 26 years paid more than the premium. Cash rent is $240 per acre for 2026, up 34.8 percent since 2016, and the census value of $8,758 per acre was the operators' own estimate. The median corn yield is 180.9 bushels per acre, with 2012 down to 125.8.

39049.text: Franklin County is a rent story more than a weather story. Non-irrigated cash rent is $218 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 50.3 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims went from 52 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has come back up after a dip. The county has held a loss ratio of 0.58 across 1989-2025, with 2 of 19 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Corn yield has a median of 166.4 bushels per acre for 2008-2022, but 2008 was 131. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so dry years land on the ground that has no irrigation to fall back on.

39051.text: Fulton County is a rain county more than a heat or drought county. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 43 percent, and the crop insurance loss ratio is 0.59 over 1989-2025, paying out more than premium in 4 of 23 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 42 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and 2025 alone had 13 weeks of severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated cash rent is $226 per acre in 2026, and census land and buildings value was $7,946 per acre in 2022.

39053.text: Gallia County is a rain-and-flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 56 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio over those closed crop years is 1.03, meaning claims have run a little above premium. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, so that part has picked up lately. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $62 per acre, up 27.6 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings is $3,625 per acre. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

39055.text: Geauga County is not a corn-and-drought story. What stands out here is flood and wet springs: excess moisture and flood account for 75 percent of the $6.6 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had no weeks of severe drought from 2021-2025. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 span is 0.88, but over the last ten closed crop years it was 0.6. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, up 33.7 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $9,272 per acre.

39057.text: Greene County is a rainfed county with a heat and drought problem that has grown over time. Heat and drought went from 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, and it is still the largest cause across 1989-2025 at 39 percent. Loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.29, so claims have run well under premium recently, though two crop years out of 23 paid more than premium overall. Non-irrigated cash rent is $226 per acre in 2026, up 26.3 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $9,290 per acre in 2022, so rent was 2.13 percent of that value. Corn yield trend is up 2.3 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 187.8 bushels per acre.

39059.text: Guernsey County is mostly rain-fed ground, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather that matters here is wet springs and floods more than dry spells. Excess moisture and flood have caused 68 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.75, meaning claims have run below premiums. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 23 weeks of severe drought in 2024, the worst year on record here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre for 2026, up 34.9 percent from 2016. The land and buildings value was $5,198 per acre in 2022, up 39.7 percent from 2017.

39061.text: Hamilton County is a small-acreage place for a corn county. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop lives or dies on rain. Heat and drought made up 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 85 percent in 2010-2019, and 54 percent in 2020-2025, so that risk has been the main driver of claims in every stretch. Crop insurance has paid out $3.3 million since 1989 on a loss ratio of 0.64, and the ratio over 2016-2025 is 0.32. Non-irrigated cash rent is $167 per acre in 2025, and the census puts land and buildings at $13,985 per acre in 2022.

39063.text: Hancock County's notable number is the flood and wet-year claims. Excess moisture and flood make up 44 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in only 2 of 23 closed crop years, so the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.56. Heat and drought claims have swung widely, going from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2010-2019 and back up to 34 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $212 per acre for 2026, up 23.3 percent from 2016.

39065.text: What stands out in Hardin County is the flood side of the ledger. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's loss ratio of 0.73 over the closed years means the insurers have paid out more than they collected. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, so the recent claims tell a different story than the long run. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $250 per acre, up 34.4 percent since 2016.

39067.text: Harrison County is a dryland rent county with a wet-year insurance history. The non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre for 2026, up 13.5 percent since 2016. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.46, well below the 0.56 for the full 1989-2025 record, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 42 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 22 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2024 alone.

39069.text: Henry County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities paid $75.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the county paid out more than premium in only 3 of 22 crop years, with the excess moisture and flood cause leading at 36 percent. Heat and drought claims fell from 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent is $200 per acre, up 13 percent since 2014. Land is valued at $7,859 per acre by the census, and 2022 rent was 2.34 percent of that value. Wet years have driven most of the claims here.

39071.text: Highland County has no irrigated cropland, so every bushel here rides on rain, and the insurance record shows the dry years are where the money has gone. Heat and drought made up 37 percent of indemnity claims in 1989-1999 and 56 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.77, and insurers paid out more than premium in 4 of the 23 closed crop years. Rent is $173 per acre for 2026, up 37.3 percent since 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $6,081 per acre in 2022. Solar is operating at 667 MW, and 200 MW more has been proposed.

39073.text: Hocking County is a non-irrigated county, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so rain carries the crop here. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.04, which means insurance paid out more than the premiums collected in that stretch. 40143.text: Tulsa County is mostly dryland. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $28 per acre, up 12.2 percent since 2016. The notable thing here is the insurance record. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.83. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse reached 34 in 2022. The census land value was $7,122 per acre in 2022, and it rose 22.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

40145.text: Wagoner County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $22.6 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought drove 47 percent of that, rising from 34 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019 before dipping to 45 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.69 over the whole run, and 3 of 18 crop years paid out more than premium. Rent is $26 an acre for non-irrigated ground, down 5.4 percent since 2016. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the crop rides on rain.

40147.text: The rent is the first thing to see here: non-irrigated ground in Washington County is $34 per acre for 2026, up 56.8 percent from 2016. That rise lines up with a county where heat and drought has become the main reason claims get paid. Heat and drought went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.97, close to a dollar paid back for every dollar of premium. The county had 77 weeks in severe drought or worse across 2021-2025, and 2022 alone had 34 weeks at the worst. Every acre here is dryland, so a dry year lands on the whole crop.

40149.text: Heat and drought is the story in Washita County. It made up 44 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 80 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has held near its 1991-2020 normal, at 70.9 F for 2017-2026.

Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, down 8 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $1,550 per acre in 2022, but that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

40153.text: Woodward County is notable for how often heat and drought have cost the crop. 46097.text: Miner County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at first. Heat and drought was 3 percent of insurance indemnities over 1989-1999 and 59 percent over 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full 1989-2025 record at 43 percent. The loss ratio is 0.73 across closed crop years, and 8 of 31 years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $146 per acre in 2026, up 20.7 percent since 2016. The 2022 census value of land and buildings is $4,428 per acre, which puts the 2022 rent at 3.23 percent of that value. CRP covers 11.9 percent of the cropland base, with 5200 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

46099.text: Minnehaha is a county where the ground does most of the work and the heat-and-drought claims are the story. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than premium in only 3 of 33 closed crop years. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the corn rides on rain. The median corn yield for 2008-2025 was 172 bushels per acre, with 2012 down to 117.5, and the yield trend is up 2.5 bushels per acre a year. Non-irrigated cash rent is $221 per acre for 2026, up 23.5 percent since 2016.

46102.text: Heat and drought is the story in Oglala Lakota County. It was 2 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 70 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.13, with 9 of 15 years paying out more than the premium. Over 2016-2025 the ratio is 1.23, and indemnities ran $27.51 per $100 of insured value. Non-irrigated cash rent was $34 per acre in 2024, up 39.6 percent since 2012. Census land and buildings value was $871 per acre in 2022, up 29.2 percent from 2017. CRP covers 7924 acres, and none of that expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

46103.text: Pennington County is mostly dryland, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent and the insurance picture are both shaped by dry years. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.9. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre in 2026, up 7.2 percent from 2016. Conservation ground is a big part of the land here, with 60925 CRP acres, 28.8 percent of the cropland base, and 362 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. Solar is the only power on the list, at 128 MW operating.

46105.text: Perkins County is dryland from end to end, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent and the weather picture both turn on rain. Heat and drought is the main cause of crop insurance claims, at 62 percent of the $103.0 million paid since 1989, and its share went from 20 percent in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $39 per acre in 2026, up 69.6 percent since 2014. The loss ratio is 0.77 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 6 of 25 years paid out more than premium. CRP covers 41.2 percent of the cropland base.

46107.text: Most of the ground in Potter County is dryland, and the numbers say the weather is what decides a year here. Heat and drought made up 70 percent of the indemnities paid in 2000-2009 and 56 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out $203.9 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025. The loss ratio is 0.66, and in 9 of 32 crop years the payouts ran higher than the premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $111 per acre, up 15.6 percent from 2016. The corn yield trend is 1.7 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with the worst year at 93.3 bushels in 2012.

46109.text: Roberts County is mostly dryland, and its notable story is wet years. Flood and excess moisture account for 62 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years was 0.77. Heat and drought claims went from 4 percent in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $179 per acre for 2026, up 20.9 percent from 2016, and the census land value was $4,089 per acre in 2022. CRP covers 11.1 percent of the cropland base, with 5956 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

46111.text:
Sanborn County's insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities paid out $164.6 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.88, with 13 of 29 crop years paying more than the premium taken in. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought weeks ran to 77 in 2021-2025, so the dry years have been costing the county more.

Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $138 per acre, up 20 percent from 2016. Corn yields have held near a median of 145.2 bushels per acre, with a bad year at 104.1 in 2022.

46115.text: Spink County's notable pattern is water and wet years, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of the $481.6 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025, while heat and drought went from 2 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 41 percent in 2000-2009. The loss ratio of 0.61 across closed crop years means insurers paid out more than premium, and 12 of 36 years paid above premium. Non-irrigated rent is $139 per acre in 2026, up 26.4 percent since 2016. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the irrigated rent of $179 per acre in 2025 is 1.42 times the dryland rent, down from 2.19 in 2012.

46117.text: Heat and drought are the story in Stanley County. They made up 4 percent of crop insurance claims in 1989-1999, 50 percent in 2000-2009, and 79 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record the county has paid out $152.1 million, with heat and drought the largest cause at 61 percent. Claims have paid more than premium in 10 of 29 closed crop years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.75. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 36.6 percent from 2016, and census land value was $1,135 per acre in 2022.

46119.text: Sully County is a dryland county, and the numbers say the weather has been the main story. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims at 57 percent of the $302.6 million paid since 1989. That share went from 7 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio is 0.6, and 8 of 33 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is $96 per acre for 2026, up 7.2 percent since 2016.

46121.text: Todd County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at here. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out $35.7 million on closed crop years since 1989. Only 9 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rest is dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $45 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,168 per acre for 2022. The county has had 46 weeks in severe drought or worse since 2021, against 219 weeks of that kind over 2000-2025.

46123.text: Tripp County is mostly dryland, and the loss record is where it stands out. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of the $163.0 million in crop insurance indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and its share went from 14 percent in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 0.78, and 9 of 31 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre in 2026, up 36.9 percent from 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $2,124 per acre in 2022, which the census shows as the operators' own estimate.

46125.text: Turner County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often the insurance has paid. Indemnities have totaled $306.5 million since 1989, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 54 percent, up from 7 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.05, so claims ran above premium in that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $218 per acre for 2026, up 19.1 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $7,125 per acre in 2022, and the 2022 rent was 2.72 percent of that figure.

46127.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Union County. It caused 5 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 45 percent in 2000-2009, 46 percent in 2010-2019 and 53 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.74, and in 6 of 31 years the payouts were more than the premium. Only 17 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and 97 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The county had 85 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $252 per acre in 2026, up 14.5 percent since 2016.

46129.text: Walworth County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rest waits on rain. The heat and drought share of crop insurance claims went from 8 percent in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.49 over 1989-2025, with 5 of 25 crop years paying out more than premium. Corn yields have a trend of 2.5 bushels per acre a year, and the county's median is 125.6 bushels, with 2010 the worst year at 101.1. Non-irrigated cash rent is $105 per acre in 2026, up 21.4 percent since 2016. CRP covers 19.7 percent of the cropland base, and 3594 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

46137.text: Ziebach County has a lot of ground in the Conservation Reserve Program, 119,513 acres in 2025, which is 46.8 percent of the cropland base. That shapes what rent means here. Non-irrigated cash rent was $46 per acre in 2025, up 40 percent since 2014. Heat and drought claims have grown as a share of indemnities, from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.95, and 8 of 23 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Worst year was 2003 with 50 weeks of severe drought or worse.

48001.text: Anderson County is mostly dryland, with only 4 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so the rain that falls is the crop's whole water supply. The biggest source of insurance claims has been excess moisture and flood at 65 percent, while heat and drought went from 89 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Still, the loss ratio is 1.93 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, meaning claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre in 2026, up 81.2 percent since 2014. The July nightly low averaged 73.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.7 F.

48003.text: Andrews County is mostly dryland rent ground, and the water is all from the Ogallala. Every acre of irrigation water comes from groundwater, and the crop insurance record shows heat and drought doing most of the damage: 61 percent of the $108.0 million paid out from 1989-2025. Those claims were 66 percent of the total in 1989-1999 and 66 percent again in 2020-2025, with a dip to 47 percent in 2000-2009. Crop years paid out more than the premium in 15 of 20 closed years, and the loss ratio is 2.13. The July nightly low has averaged 70.1 F since 2017, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.8 F.

48007.text: Heat and drought has been the main cause of crop insurance claims in Aransas County for a long time, but its share has come down. It was 98 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 29 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 0.82, and indemnities paid $15.07 per $100 of insured value. Land and buildings were valued at $1,831 per acre in 2022, up 8.7 percent from 2017. July nights have warmed too, with an average low of 78.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 77.7 F.

48009.text: Archer County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid $47.8 million across closed crop years since 1989, with heat and drought behind 76 percent of it, and the loss ratio is 1.33, so claims have paid out more than premiums. Heat and drought went from 66 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 87 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land, and non-irrigated rent is $34 per acre in 2026.

48011.text: What stands out in Armstrong County is how much of the ground is in grass. CRP covers 45368 acres, or 47.3 percent of the cropland base, and none of those contracts expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre, up 39.2 percent since 2016, and irrigated rent was $60 per acre in 2023. Crop insurance has paid out $104.4 million since 1989, and heat and drought account for 74 percent of that. Heat and drought share went from 66 percent in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025.

48013.text: Atascosa County is mostly dryland, but the ground that is irrigated is irrigated from wells, and heat and drought now drive most of the crop insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.45, meaning insurers paid out more than they took in premium. Irrigated rent was $140 per acre in 2025, and non-irrigated rent was $19 per acre in 2026, up 22.6 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $2,767 per acre in 2022, up 21.2 percent from 2017.

48015.text: Austin County is a rain-fed county: only 4 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. That makes the heat and drought record the thing to look at first. Heat and drought was 71 percent of indemnity claims in 1989-1999 and 49 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1. July nightly lows have averaged 75.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre in 2026, up 65.2 percent since 2016, and census land and buildings were valued at $6,189 per acre in 2022.

48017.text: Bailey County is a dryland-and-pivot county, and the water is the story. Irrigated ground rents for $124 per acre, against $48 for non-irrigated, and the two prices have held their ratio, 2.58 this year and 2.91 in 2009. Groundwater supplies all of the irrigation water, and 36 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Heat and drought claims went from 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 55 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out more than premium in 23 of 36 closed crop years, so the claims have been real. The July nightly low has warmed, now averaging 65.4 F over 2017-2026.

48021.text: Bastrop County is a county where the ground's water and the summer heat show up in the claims more than anywhere else on the page. Heat and drought made up 93 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 13 percent in 2020-2025, while the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.25, meaning claims have run above premiums across the whole record. Only 25 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 84 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, up 81.5 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 74.6 F over 2017-2026, against 73.2 F for the 1991-2020 normal.

48023.text: Heat and drought are what stand out in Baylor County. They caused 81 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and their share went from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 89 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance paid out more than the premiums in 11 of 23 closed crop years, and the loss ratio over those years was 1.44. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre for 2026, up 8.9 percent from 2016. Wind is the only power on the books, with 380.8 MW operating and nothing proposed for solar.

48025.text: Bee County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what has driven its crop insurance payouts. Heat and drought accounted for 79 percent of the $95.0 million paid out from 1989-2025, and it rose from 50 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 90 percent in 2010-2019 before easing to 79 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed crop years was 1.11, and 9 of 26 crop years paid out more than the premium. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre in 2026, up 40 percent since 2016.

48027.text: Bell County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what has been costing the farmers here. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 85 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 53 percent over 1989-2025. The loss ratio is 0.92, and 8 of 27 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre in 2026, up 29.6 percent from 2016, while the census puts land and buildings at $4,587 per acre in 2022. Solar is the big change on the ground, with 780.8 MW operating and no wind.

48029.text: Heat and drought is the story in Bexar County. It accounts for 75 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and its share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1, meaning the claims paid matched the premiums collected. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse reached 52 in 2025, tied with 2006. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre, up 71.4 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $72 per acre.

48033.text: Borden County's cropland is all watered from wells, and the insurance record is where the county stands out. Crop insurance has paid out $145.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 87 percent of that. The share was 95 percent over 2010-2019 and 83 percent over 2020-2025. Over the ten closed years 2016-2025 the loss ratio is 1.3, so claims have run ahead of premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026.

48035.text: Bosque County's notable number is the claims record. Heat and drought made up 60 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 45 percent in 1989-1999, and the county's loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 1.75, meaning insurers have paid out more than premiums taken in. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $26 per acre, up 79.3 percent since 2016. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county's crop is dryland. The July nightly low averaged 74.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.1 F. Solar is running at 490.9 MW, with no wind.

48037.text: Bowie County is a non-irrigated county in the sense that matters most: just 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance record is dominated by wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of indemnities from 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.33 over those closed years, with 10 of 17 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, up 17.5 percent since 2016, and census land value is $3,614 per acre for 2022.

48039.text: Brazoria County's cropland is mostly dryland, with 27 percent of harvested acres irrigated in 2022 and only 7 percent of that water drawn from groundwater. The county's bigger story in the claims is excess moisture and flood, the largest cause at 34 percent, and insurance has paid out more than the premium over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.3. Heat and drought went from 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, so it is climbing back. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 38.8 percent since 2014, and irrigated ground rents at $60.

48041.text: Brazos County is a dryland county where heat and drought drive most of the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 84 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2020-2025, and the largest cause over the full record is heat and drought at 58 percent. Only 18 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio over the closed years is 1.27, with 6 of 12 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, down 11.6 percent from 2016.

48045.text: Briscoe County's cropland is mostly dryland, so the irrigated rent is the number to watch: $62 per acre in 2024, and all of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought is the main reason claims get paid here. It went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 49 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out $161.9 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.21, with 18 of 31 crop years paying out more than the premium collected. The non-irrigated rent is $20 per acre in 2026, up 25 percent since 2016.

48047.text: Brooks County is a dryland ground county where heat and drought drive most of the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 98 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 83 percent in 2010-2019, and the closed-year loss ratio is 2.92, so claims have paid out well beyond premium. Non-irrigated cash rent was $8 per acre in 2023, down 46 percent from 2013. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Census land and buildings value is $1,945 per acre, up 25.3 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low averaged 75.9 F over 2017-2026 against a 74.9 F normal, and 48 weeks in severe drought or worse came in 2021-2025.

48049.text: Brown County's cropland is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is the cause that keeps showing up in the claims. Heat and drought was 58 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 57 percent in 2000-2009, and 77 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 28 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the full closed period is 1.11, so insurers have paid out more than the premiums came in. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $16 per acre, up 37.5 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $3,221 per acre in 2022.

48051.text: Heat and drought is the story in Burleson County. It was 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 79 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid $33.0 million in indemnities over the closed years 1989-2025. The loss ratio over those years is 0.96, and 7 of 18 crop years paid out more than the premium. Only 14 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre, down 6 percent since 2014.

48055.text: Caldwell County's heat and drought losses are the story here. Heat and drought made up 94 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 90 percent in 1989-1999. Insurers have paid out more than they took in on this ground, with a loss ratio of 1.08 across the closed years 1989-2025. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most acres ride on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $33 per acre, up 65 percent since 2014, while the census puts land and buildings at $4,814 per acre.

48057.text: Calhoun County's corn record is thin, and the losses show up mostly in the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 64 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, and that share fell to 29 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over closed crop years is 1.11, with 11 of 27 years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre, up 21.2 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $3,345 per acre in 2022, after a 56 percent rise from 2017 to 2022. There is 196.3 MW of solar operating in the county and no wind.

48059.text: Heat and drought is the story in Callahan County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 65 percent in 1989-1999 to 86 percent in 2020-2025, and insurance has paid out $14.4 million on closed crop years since 1989. Over the ten closed years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 1.3, so claims ran ahead of premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre for 2026, up 73.9 percent from 2016. Wind is the other big presence here, with 602.9 MW operating and 415 MW of solar proposed. CRP is small at 148 acres, and none of it expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

48063.text: Camp County is a small non-irrigated place, with only 7 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, so the ground mostly lives or dies on the weather it gets. The insurance record is the thing I'd look at first. Losses have run past premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.63 over 1990-2025 and 1.29 over the last ten closed crop years. Freeze and frost, not heat, is the biggest cause at 44 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought claims went from 4 percent in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 3 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 18.9 percent from 2016.

48065.text: Carson County is a dryland county with a large irrigated share and heat and drought claims that stand out. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities, at 50 percent of $250.8 million paid over 1989-2025, and its share went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio of 1.25 means claims have run above premiums over the full span, with the ten years 2016-2025 at 1.31. Irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre against $48 for non-irrigated ground, and the census value of land and buildings is $1,561 per acre. Groundwater supplies all of the irrigation water.

48069.text: Castro County is a dryland-and-pivot county in a hurry. Heat and drought has gone from 15 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.9. Irrigation is in place on 57 percent of harvested cropland, all of it fed from groundwater, and irrigated ground rents for $145 per acre while non-irrigated is $49. Land has a census value of $2,130 per acre, up 54.3 percent from 2017 to 2022. Wind is the energy story here, 442.4 MW operating, with no solar yet.

48073.text: Cherokee County's notable thing is how little of its cropland is irrigated: 3 percent of harvested cropland, so the ground here lives or dies on rain. Freeze and frost drove 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities over the closed years, and the county's loss ratio of 0.28 says the premiums have paid out well under what farmers put in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre for 2026, up 24.1 percent from 2016. The land and buildings census value was $4,007 per acre in 2022, a number the operators reported themselves. Heat and drought claims were 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, and 25 weeks of severe drought have shown up since 2021.

48075.text:
Childress County is a dryland county first. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $182.5 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 72 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.54, so claims have run above premiums over the whole record. The share of claims from heat and drought was 59 percent in 1989-1999, 73 percent in 2000-2009, 79 percent in 2010-2019, and 68 percent in 2020-2025.

Non-irrigated cash rent is $25 per acre for 2026, and the census land value is $1,687 per acre. CRP covers 32 percent of the cropland base.

48077.text: Clay County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Insurers have paid out $27.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.32, so claims have run well past the premiums. Heat and drought was 41 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the ground here is dryland, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so a dry summer lands on the crop with nothing to fall back on. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre in 2026, up 1.9 percent from 2016.

48081.text: Coke County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought make up 84 percent of the $12.7 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, and claims for that cause went from 58 percent of the total in 1989-1999 to 79 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have run ahead of premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.42 across those years and 1.36 over 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 130.8 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings were valued at $1,542 per acre in 2022, up 60.3 percent since 2017. The county has 525 MW of wind operating and no solar yet.

48083.text: Heat and drought is the story in Coleman County. It was 42 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-1999 and 80 percent over 2020-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.76 over the last ten closed crop years, which means the insurance companies paid out more than was collected in premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre and has moved up 68.2 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $2,174 per acre in 2022, and the county had 63 weeks in severe drought or worse over 2021-2025. Nothing is operating in solar or wind yet, though 396 MW of solar has been proposed.

48085.text: Collin County is a non-irrigated county: only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 20 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Rent is $32 per acre and has moved up 90.9 percent since 2016, which is a lot of ground to pay more for. The crop insurance record is the thing I'd look at first. Excess moisture and flood account for 60 percent of indemnities, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.1, with 12 of 25 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025.

48087.text: Collingsworth County is a dryland county that has leaned hard on crop insurance. Only 24 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums in 16 of 30 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.57, and heat and drought account for 73 percent of the payments. Their share went from 78 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025, and that is still the biggest cause. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre in 2026, up 161.3 percent from 2016.

48091.text: Comal County is a dry-ground county with most of its cropland unirrigated, and heat and drought is what drives its claims. Heat and drought made up 88 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and the indemnities paid out came to $1.8 million against a loss ratio of 1.06, so claims have run past premiums. Its share rose from 82 percent in 1989-1999 to 86 percent in 2020-2025. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $12 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings is $5,507 per acre.

48093.text: Comanche County is a dryland place where heat and drought drive most of the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 68 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and the share went from 69 percent in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 81 percent in 2000-2009. Crop insurance paid out more than premium in 5 of 11 closed crop years, and the loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 1.3. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $35 per acre, up 89.2 percent from 2016. Only 27 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 85 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

48095.text: Concho County is mostly dryland, and the dry ground is where the trouble shows. Heat and drought made up 83 percent of insurance claims in 2020-2025, and 88 percent in 2010-2019, against 65 percent in 1989-1999. Crop insurance paid out $161.1 million over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio of 1.52 means claims ran well past premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $27 per acre, down 8.5 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $74 per acre, but only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 92 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

48097.text: Cooke County's corn is mostly rain-fed, and the risk on the books here is wet springs more than dry summers. Excess moisture and flood account for 39 percent of the $8.7 million paid out since 1989, and heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the full closed period is 0.8, and the last ten closed crop years came in lower at 0.68. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $4,391 per acre in 2022. Wind operating is 413.4 MW, and 150 MW of solar has been proposed.

48099.text: Coryell County is mostly dryland, and drought is what shows up in the claims. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 67 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 64 percent in 1989-1999. Crop insurance has paid out $18.7 million on closed years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.98, which is close to what farmers paid in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, up 25 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $3,621 per acre for 2022, after a 38.9 percent rise from 2017.

48101.text: Cottle County is mostly dryland, and drought is what stands out here. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 78 percent of the $97.4 million paid out on crop insurance claims from 1989-2025, and the share rose from 52 percent in 1989-1999 to 76 percent in 2020-2025, with 86 percent in 2010-2019. Insurance has paid out more than the premiums in 12 of 18 closed crop years, for a loss ratio of 1.57. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,059 per acre in 2022.

48103.text: Crane County's biggest story is the water-stress record, with 323 of 1,357 weeks from 2000-2025 (23.8 percent) at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. The worst year was 2011, with 50 weeks. Since 2021, 81 weeks have been in severe drought or worse. July nights have warmed too: the 2017-2026 average low of 72.8 F is above the 1991-2020 normal of 71.9 F, and the nightly low trend since 1976 is 0.63 F per decade. Land is priced at $1,444 per acre by the 2022 census, and values rose 70.3 percent from 2017-2022. There is 150 MW of solar operating, with no wind and no CRP expiring through 2029.

48111.text: Dallam County is mostly irrigated ground, with 70 percent of harvested cropland watered and all of that water pulled from groundwater. The rent split shows it. Non-irrigated ground rents for $20 per acre in 2026, down 63.1 percent from 2016, while irrigated ground is $127 per acre. The insurance record is the other thing to look at. Crop insurance has paid out $412.9 million on closed years since 1989, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 37 percent of that. Its share went from 21 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have run ahead of premium, with a loss ratio of 1.43 over the closed years.

48113.text: Dallas County is a place where the water is the story more than the heat. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 38 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $15.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the largest cause is excess moisture and flood at 54 percent. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2000-2009, then 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2023 was $20 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $8,455 per acre.

48115.text: Dawson County is a heat and water county first. Groundwater supplies 99 percent of irrigation water, and heat and drought account for 74 percent of the $1.08 billion paid out in crop insurance indemnities since 1989. The loss ratio of 1.32 means claims have paid out more than premiums over the closed years, and 19 of 37 crop years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 74 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $48 per acre in 2025, and irrigated rent was $109 per acre in 2023.

48117.text: Deaf Smith is a county where the heat and the water are both showing up in the claims. Heat and drought went from 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio is 1.28 over closed crop years, with 22 of 37 years paying out more than premium. The county is all groundwater for irrigation, and the July nightly low has reached 66 F in the 2020s. Irrigated cash rent is $101 per acre against $32 for non-irrigated ground, and the census value of land and buildings was $1,838 per acre in 2022.

48119.text: Delta County's heat-and-drought claims have come back hard. That share went from 26 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 54 percent in 2020-2025, and 41 weeks of severe drought or worse fell in 2021-2025 alone. The bigger number over the whole record is flood and excess moisture, which caused 45 percent of the $44.2 million paid since 1989. Closed crop years show a loss ratio of 1.08, and 1.26 over 2016-2025, so claims have run above premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, down 9.4 percent from 2016. Solar is the one large new use on the books, at 204.5 MW operating and 110.1 MW proposed.

48121.text: Denton County's notable number is the flood side of the ledger. Excess moisture and flood cause 47 percent of the indemnities paid here since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.09 across the closed crop years, with insurance paying out more than premium in 8 of 14 years. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, so it has held steady. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which means most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre, up 10 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $12,287 per acre.

48123.text: Heat and drought has been the main source of crop insurance claims in DeWitt County, and that stands out. The county's insurance loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.06, meaning claims have run slightly above premiums over the full stretch, though 2016-2025 was 0.64. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 55.2 percent since 2014, while the census value of land and buildings is $3,823 per acre. Heat and drought was 70 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 93 percent in 2010-2019.

48125.text: Dickens County is a dry-ground county with heat and drought doing most of the damage. Heat and drought went from 57 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 89 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out more than it took in premium over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.94. Only 34 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of the water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, up 165 percent since 2016. Census land and building value was $1,791 per acre in 2022, and 68.4 percent of the cropland base is in CRP, with none of those acres expiring through 2029.

48127.text: Dimmit County is mostly irrigated, and the water comes from wells. The census shows 53 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, and 94 percent of irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought went from 36 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2010-2019, and the county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.69, so claims have run well ahead of premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent was $18 per acre in 2020, up 20.7 percent from 2010. The census value of land and buildings was $1,777 per acre in 2022, a 26 percent rise from 2017.

48129.text: Donley County is a dryland and irrigated mix with a heavy heat-and-drought history. Heat and drought made up 35 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 58 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full record at 60 percent. Insurance paid out $35.0 million on closed claims against premiums that were only a little less than that, a loss ratio of 0.96. Irrigation is 43 percent of harvested cropland, and all of its water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, up 32.3 percent since 2016, while irrigated rent was $106 per acre in 2024. Wind is the only power development operating in the county, at 174 MW.

48133.text: Eastland County is mostly dryland, and the water and heat numbers are what stand out. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 92 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.55, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, up 70.8 percent from 2016. The July nightly low averaged 72.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.3 F, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,026 per acre in 2022.

48139.text: Ellis County is a dryland county. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn yield swings with the weather. Heat and drought claims were 57 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, a shift that tracks the weeks in severe drought, which were 41 from 2021-2025 alone. The loss ratio is 0.98 over 1989-2025, and 1.14 over 2016-2025, so in recent years the insurers have paid out more than the premiums. The 2026 non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $5,374 per acre, so the rent is a small share of what the ground is worth.

48141.text: El Paso County is notable for how much of its cropland runs on irrigation, 73 percent by the 2022 census, and for what happens when the water fails. Crop insurance has paid out $84.2 million since 1992, and irrigation failure accounts for 64 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.58 over the closed crop years, and it was 2.15 over 2016-2025, so claims have outrun premiums in recent years. Heat and drought claims went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. July nights have warmed, with the average low at 70.9 F for 2017-2026. Groundwater supplies 21 percent of irrigation water.

48143.text: Erath County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the weather risk has moved into the claims. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2020-2025, with 91 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.69, so premiums have covered the claims lately, but the long run since 1989 is 2.27. The county had 52 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2022, and the July nightly low over 2017-2026 averaged 73.5 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre, up 41.2 percent since 2016.

48145.text: Falls County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought has been the biggest cause of crop insurance claims, though its share has dropped from 83 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the closed crop years paid out $95.8 million, and the loss ratio is 0.91, with 8 of 27 years paying more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026, against a census land value of $3,689 per acre in 2022.

48147.text: Fannin County's cropland is mostly dryland, and what stands out is how much the rain decides the crop. Its corn yields have a median of 82 bushels per acre, but the worst year, 2009, was 45, and insurance has paid out $98.1 million since 1989 with excess moisture and flood as the largest cause at 65 percent. Heat and drought went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre in 2026, up 76.2 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $72. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

48149.text: Fayette County is a dryland county where heat and drought drive most of the losses. Heat and drought made up 73 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and their share went from 72 percent in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks were highest in 2011 at 45 weeks, and 69 weeks of severe drought or worse have come since 2021. The county's loss ratio was 0.95 over 1989-2025 and 0.5 over the last ten closed crop years. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain.

48151.text: Fisher County is a dryland county with very little irrigation to fall back on. Only 98 percent of the water used for irrigation comes from groundwater, and irrigation failure has paid just $18,689 across all closed years, so the risk sits in the dry years rather than in the pump. Heat and drought are the main claim cause, at 76 percent of the $410.9 million paid since 1989. That share went from 61 percent in 1989-1999 to 87 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 67 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.57 across closed years, and it was 1.64 over 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre for 2026, up 24 percent from 2016.

48153.text: Floyd County's heat and drought pattern is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid out $644.4 million in closed crop years with a loss ratio of 1.14. Irrigation failure paid only $621,720 across all closed years, and the county's irrigation water is all groundwater. Non-irrigated rent is $30 per acre and irrigated rent is $76, with the 2026 figures set against a census land value of $1,186 per acre in 2022. July nights have warmed, with the average low at 68.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.4 F.

48155.text: Foard County's cropland runs on groundwater: 100 percent of its irrigation water came from the aquifer in 2015. The heat and drought share of crop insurance claims went from 71 percent in 1989-1999 to 91 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.17, meaning claims paid more than premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent was $18 per acre in 2025, down 27.5 percent since 2014. The county has 555.3 MW of wind operating and 300 MW of solar proposed, while its 1,298 CRP acres have none expiring through 2029.

48157.text: Fort Bend is a county where irrigation carries a lot of the weight. Irrigated cash rent was $98 per acre in 2023, against $42 for non-irrigated ground in 2026, and that is a wide gap for a county where only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated rent has not moved at all since 2016. Crop insurance has paid out $92.8 million on closed years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 1.01, which means the claims have run a little above the premiums. Heat and drought was 71 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 and 41 percent in 2020-2025. The county also has 1221.2 MW of solar operating and no wind.

48159.text: Franklin County is a dryland county with very little irrigation. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of the water comes from groundwater.
