Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 41 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025. Its share fell from 70 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, up 10.6 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $4,816 per acre, with values up 55.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. The county has 257.5 MW of solar operating and none of wind.

48161.text: Freestone County's cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $25 per acre in 2026, and it has risen 138.1 percent since 2016. Very little of the harvested cropland is irrigated, just 5 percent in the 2022 census, so most of the crop depends on rain. Heat and drought claims were 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 0 percent in 2020-2025, while other causes made up 51 percent of closed-year payouts from 1990 to 2020. The biggest thing on the ground right now is 758.8 MW of solar proposed to the EIA, against 10 MW operating.

48163.text: Frio County is mostly irrigated ground, and the water comes from wells. The census put 77 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, and all of the irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. That is why an irrigated acre rents for $173 while dryland goes for $41, a ratio of 4.22 in 2026 against 2.17 in 2009. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed years 1989-2025 is 1.03, so claims have run a bit over premium.

48165.text: Gaines County is a county where the water decides the rent. Irrigated ground rents for $190 per acre, against $50 for dryland, and that gap has widened from 3.22 times in 2010 to 3.76 times in 2026. Irrigation failure has paid only $9.9 million in claims, so the county's losses come mostly from dry years on dryland, not from wells going dry. Heat and drought went from 41 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 52 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2022.

48167.text: Galveston County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the water problem here is too much of it, not too little. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 40 percent of the $3.9 million paid from 1989-2024, and the county's loss ratio over all closed crop years is 1.11, meaning claims have run above premiums. Heat and drought was 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and 9 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre in 2026, down 3.3 percent from 2016. July nights have warmed too: the average low was 78.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 77 F. No solar or wind is operating in the county.

48169.text: Garza County's crop claims are dominated by heat and drought, which made up 80 percent of the $110.2 million paid from 1989 through 2025. The share went from 72 percent in 1989-1999 to 77 percent in 2020-2025, peaking at 87 percent in 2010-2019. Every acre of irrigation water comes from groundwater, and the county paid out more than it took in premium in 14 of 26 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 9.6 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $1,244 per acre in 2022.

48171.text: Gillespie County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $16.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought has been the largest cause at 46 percent of that. Its share went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.02, so insurers paid out more than was collected in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre in 2026, up 24.1 percent since 2016.

48173.text: Glasscock County is mostly irrigated, and it's all groundwater. Irrigation covers 51 percent of harvested cropland, and every acre of that water comes from the ground. Heat and drought drove the losses: they made up 71 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 86 percent in 2000-2009, 95 percent in 2010-2019, and 75 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.28 across the closed crop years, and insurers paid out more than premium in 18 of 31 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, and irrigated rent was $68 per acre in 2016.

48175.text: Goliad County is mostly dryland, and the water question runs through most of what the numbers say. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $14.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, with heat and drought behind 77 percent of it. That share was 43 percent in 1989-1999 and 93 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 80 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is $29 per acre, up 70.6 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings are valued at $3,741 per acre by operators in 2022.

48177.text: Gonzales County is mostly dryland, with only 18 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and it is a county where heat and drought drive the claims. Heat and drought was 91 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 93 percent in 2020-2025, and the 1989-2025 loss ratio of 1.08 means insurers have paid out more than the premiums collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $27 per acre in 2026, up 107.7 percent since 2016, while census land and buildings were valued at $4,484 per acre in 2022. The county has no wind or solar operating and no CRP acres expiring through fiscal 2029.

48179.text: Gray County is a dry-land country that leans heavily on water it pumps. Irrigated ground rents for $84 per acre in 2022, but the county's non-irrigated rent is only $23 per acre, and the irrigation water all comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 61 percent of the $91.3 million in crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio of 1.17 means insurers paid out more than they took in premiums. Over the last ten closed crop years that ratio was 1.15. Heat and drought claims went from 58 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025. In 2014 the county spent 46 weeks in severe drought or worse.

48181.text: Grayson County is a dryland county in a hard-to-predict spot. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has not paid out the way the insurance was built to. Crop insurance indemnities came to $71.0 million across 1989-2025, and the loss ratio was 0.97, with 9 of 20 crop years paying out more than premium. Excess moisture and flood, not heat, drove 56 percent of those claims. Heat and drought share of claims went from 42 percent in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre, up 50 percent since 2014, and the census put land and buildings at $7,774 per acre in 2022. Weeks in severe drought or worse have been 37 across 2021-2025.

48183.text: Gregg County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. That makes rain the main question for a crop here. Drought has been the thing to watch: 182 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2011 alone had 51 of them. The last five years have had 18 such weeks. Nights in July have averaged 72.9 F from 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.7 F, and the longer trend since 1976 is not a clear trend. Non-irrigated cash rent was $16 per acre in 2020, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $6,992 per acre.

48185.text: Grimes County is a dryland county with a lot of rain-driven ground, and its summers have been getting warmer. The July nightly low averaged 74.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.3 F, and it has been rising 0.6 F per decade since 1976. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre for 2026, up 28.6 percent from 2016. The land and buildings value from the 2022 census was $3,448 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

48187.text: Guadalupe County is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather and the insurance record tell most of the story here. Heat and drought was the cause behind 88 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and its share rose from 77 percent in 1989-1999 to 94 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities paid out more than premium in 5 of 19 closed crop years, though the 2016-2025 loss ratio was 0.66. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 31.1 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,941 per acre in 2022.

48189.text: Hale County is an irrigated county first. Irrigated ground rents for $147 per acre in 2026, against $50 for dryland, and every acre of that irrigation water comes from groundwater. The corn yield trend over 2008-2023 is down 3.4 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 147.8 bushels and a bad year at 114.3 in 2022. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, indemnities ran at 1.39 times premium, and the county has 478 MW of wind operating with no solar yet.

48191.text: Hall County is a dryland rent county, and the rent is low for a reason. Non-irrigated cash rent was $26 per acre in 2025, and it is down 23.2 percent since 2014. Heat and drought made up 77 percent of the $235.7 million in crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the county's loss ratio of 1.45 means claims have run well past premiums. Heat and drought went from 61 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 75 percent in 2020-2025. Only 32 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and CRP covers 49.8 percent of the cropland base, with none of those acres expiring from 2027 through 2029.

48193.text: Heat and drought is the story in Hamilton County. It accounted for 66 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 63 percent in 2000-2009 to 82 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.38, meaning claims paid out more than premiums taken in. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county had 315 weeks of at least 50 percent severe drought or worse from 2000 through 2025, with 52 of those weeks in 2022 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $19 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings is $3,215 per acre. The July nightly low averaged 73.1 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.9 F.

48195.text: Hansford County is a dryland-and-irrigation county, and the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated rent is $160 per acre in 2026 against $34 for non-irrigated ground, and 59 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all of it from groundwater. Heat and drought has been the biggest cause of insurance claims since 1989, though its share went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 70 percent in 2000-2009 and 41 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years the loss ratio is 1.14, and 21 of 35 crop years paid out more than the premium. Land and buildings were valued at $2,037 per acre in 2022, up 51.8 percent from 2017. Wind is the only power development here, at 1220.8 MW operating.

48197.text: Hardeman County leans hard on groundwater and heat-and-drought claims. Every acre of irrigation water comes from the aquifer, and the county has paid out $102.3 million in crop insurance indemnities since 1989, with heat and drought the largest cause at 61 percent. The loss ratio over those closed crop years is 1.42, and insurers paid out more than premium in 10 of 18 crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $23 per acre for 2026, up 24.3 percent from 2016. Heat and drought share of claims went from 64 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. The census value of land and buildings was $1,525 per acre in 2022.

48199.text: Hardin County is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 34 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, the biggest single cause, and heat and drought claims went from 15 percent in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Only 21 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre in 2026, up 26.9 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $5,546 per acre, and that jumped 77.4 percent between 2017 and 2022. There is no CRP ground here, and no wind or solar in operation, though 456 MW of solar has been proposed.

48201.text: Harris County's rent story starts with heat and water. July nights now average 75.9 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 74.8 F, and the July nightly low has been warming at 0.49 F per decade since 1976. Heat and drought made up 39 percent of insurance claims in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2010-2019, then 26 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 74.4 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground rented for $72 per acre in 2013, and 39 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so water access matters more here than the average rate suggests.

48205.text: Most of the cropland in Hartley County is irrigated, and every drop of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $205 per acre this year, while non-irrigated ground goes for $49, and the non-irrigated rent is up 172.2 percent since 2016. Crop insurance has paid out $1.14 for every dollar of premium over 1989-2025, and 1.32 over the last ten closed years. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 30 percent, rising from 25 percent in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2010-2019. Land and buildings are valued at $1,824 per acre, and CRP covers 5.8 percent of the cropland base.

48207.text: Haskell County is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is where the county stands out. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of claims, at 75 percent of the $390.2 million paid from 1989-2025, and the share went from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 79 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio over the closed crop years was 1.42, with 21 of 37 years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre for 2026, up 20.8 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings value was $1,928 per acre in 2022.

48209.text: Hays County is a dry-ground county in a hot, dry stretch of Texas, and most of the trouble shows up as heat and drought. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 90 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 87 percent in 1989-1999. The loss ratio is 1.07 over 1989-2025, so claims have paid out more than premiums came in. The median corn yield for 2011-2022 was 82.4 bushels per acre, but 2011 fell to 12.6. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, down 11.7 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $11,177 per acre.

48211.text: Hemphill County is mostly dryland, but the crop insurance record shows how hard the dry years have hit. Heat and drought was 64 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 81 percent in 2010-2019, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.25, meaning claims have run above premiums. Irrigated ground is all watered from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $23 per acre for 2026, up 53.3 percent from 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $1,181 per acre in 2022. CRP acres total 5780 with none expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

48213.text: Henderson County's crop insurance record is led by excess moisture and flood, which took 60 percent of indemnities, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.4, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, with the peak at 47 percent in 2010-2019. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 89 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The county's July nightly lows averaged 73.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 72.8 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre in 2026.

48215.text: Hidalgo County is mostly irrigated ground, and the water comes from surface sources, not wells. Irrigated cash rent is $109 per acre against $48 for non-irrigated ground, so the water is worth a lot. Heat and drought claims were 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 10 percent in 2020-2025, but the loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 1.36, meaning claims have paid out more than premiums in recent years. Corn yields trend up 1.9 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025. Irrigation failure claims total $81.8 million over the full record.

48217.text: Hill County's notable thing is how much of its corn ground has been hit by heat and drought, and how little of it is irrigated. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 51 percent of the $174.4 million in crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025. Its share fell from 73 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, but it is still the largest cause. The 2011 corn crop was 46 bushels, against a median of 89.1 bushels for 2008-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre for 2026, up 23.5 percent since 2016.

48219.text: Hockley County is a dryland-and-irrigation county where the water comes from the ground and the heat has been building. Irrigated ground rents for $75 per acre, against $46 for non-irrigated, and irrigated acres are 42 percent of harvested cropland. Heat and drought was 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 66 percent in 2010-2019, and the closed crop years since 1989 paid out $813.8 million on $1.38 of indemnity for every premium dollar. The July nightly low averaged 67 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.3 F. CRP holds 95198 acres, 45 percent of the cropland base, with 508 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

48221.text: Hood County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the water that matters here is the rain that falls on it. Only 14 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, and heat and drought made up 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2024. That share was 67 percent again in 1989-1999, so it has held steady rather than climbing. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $28 per acre, up 55.6 percent from 2016. The census land and buildings value is $5,910 per acre in 2022, up 72.4 percent from 2017.

48223.text: Hopkins County is a dryland county in most ways that matter. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance record leans wet: excess moisture and flood account for 65 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over those years is 1.25. Heat and drought claims went from 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025, peaking at 36 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 15.1 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $4,732 per acre in 2022, after a 62.2 percent rise from 2017.

48225.text: Houston County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Claims paid out $12.9 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.57, meaning indemnities ran above premiums across that stretch. Over the last ten closed years the ratio is 1.65. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 51 percent of claims. Heat and drought was 60 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and 40 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 25 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, up 2.6 percent from 2016.

48227.text: Howard County is a groundwater county. Every acre of irrigation water comes from the aquifer, and the crop insurance record shows what that dependence costs in dry years. Heat and drought went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 92 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 82 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full stretch, indemnities paid out $467.7 million against premiums, a loss ratio of 1.33, with 20 of 37 crop years paying out more than was collected. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 52 in 2022, and 103 weeks have come since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026.

48231.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

48235.text: Heat and drought account for most of what has been paid out on crop insurance claims here. Of the $7.1 million paid across the closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, 87 percent came from heat and drought, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 1.9, meaning claims ran well ahead of premium. The share of claims from heat and drought went from 54 percent in 1989-1999 to 82 percent in 2020-2025, peaking at 95 percent in 2010-2019. Irrigated ground is not something I can see in these numbers, but the non-irrigated cash rent was $9 per acre in 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $1,345 per acre in 2022, up 35.2 percent from 2017.

48237.text: Jack County's most notable number is that heat and drought has been the main cause of crop insurance claims for three decades. It made up 80 percent of the $800,477 in indemnities paid from 1995 through 2025, and 86 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 161.9 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,320 per acre in 2022, up 42.3 percent from 2017. Wind is operating at 380 MW, and 650 MW of solar has been proposed, with no CRP acres set to expire from fiscal 2027 through 2029.

48245.text: Jefferson County is a mostly non-irrigated county, and the rent story is the big move: non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre in 2026, up 443.2 percent since 2016. Irrigation water comes from surface sources, not wells, and 36 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The loss record is the thing to look at. Insurance has paid out $96.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 2.65. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, and excess moisture and flood is still the largest single cause at 47 percent.

48249.text: Heat and drought drive most of the claims in Jim Wells County. Since 1989, crop insurance has paid $164.4 million, and heat and drought made up 84 percent of it. The share was 51 percent in 1989-1999 and 95 percent in 2000-2009, and it is 86 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 17 of 32 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.47. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre in 2025, and only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain.

48253.text: Heat and drought is the story in Jones County. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 80 percent of the $415.9 million paid from 1989-2025, and its share went from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2020-2025. Claims have paid out more than premium in 22 of the 37 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.53. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 86 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 15.7 percent since 2016.

48255.text: Karnes County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what has cost the most. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 52 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 92 percent in 2010-2019. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 0.68, and insurers paid $15.46 for every $100 of insured value. Non-irrigated cash rent is $25 per acre for 2026, up 19 percent from 2016. The July average nightly low was 74.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.5 F. Corn yields have been a median 73.8 bushels per acre since 2010, and the worst year, 2011, was 20.8.

48257.text: Kaufman County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the rent and the weather claims are where the story sits. Crop insurance indemnities for closed years total $29.6 million, and the loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 1.71, meaning the county has paid out well more than it took in premium. Heat and drought went from 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, and excess moisture and flood still lead the list at 48 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre in 2026, up 36.8 percent since 2016, and the census land value was $5,522 per acre in 2022. Solar is running at 146.7 MW, with 601 MW proposed, and no CRP acres are left to expire.

48261.text: Kenedy County is a hot, dry place to farm, and it has been getting hotter at night. The July average low was 76.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 76 F, and it has climbed 0.48 F per decade since 1976. The county has seen 127 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F, and the 1900s were the first decade the July average low reached 66 F. Severe drought, with at least 50 percent of the county in it, has covered 270 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with 2012 the worst at 48 weeks. Wind is the only energy use on the ground, at 1075.4 MW operating, and there is no CRP ground.

48263.text: Kent County is a county where heat and drought drive most of the claims. Heat and drought made up 46 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 89 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 79 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance paid out $1.66 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years, which tells you the ground has been hard on crops here. The county also has 57.5 percent of its cropland in CRP, and the July nightly low has been warming since 1976.

48271.text: Kinney County's notable number is water. Every acre of irrigation water comes from groundwater, and crop insurance has paid $2.6 million on closed claims since 1995, with heat and drought behind 77 percent of that. The loss ratio on those closed years is 1.48, meaning the county has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premiums. Heat and drought was 74 percent of claims in 2000-2009 and 82 percent in 2010-2019, then 68 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $11 per acre for 2026, and census land and buildings were $1,573 per acre in 2022, up 26.8 percent from 2017.

48273.text: Kleberg County grows no irrigated crops, so every acre depends on rain, and the insurance record shows what that means. Heat and drought caused 79 percent of the $162.0 million paid out on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the county paid out more than it took in premium in 12 of 35 years, for a loss ratio of 1.16. Heat and drought went from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre in 2026, up 37.9 percent since 2016, while the census puts land and buildings at $1,396 per acre in 2022.

48275.text: Knox County's notable feature is how much of its insurance money has gone to heat and drought. Of the $162.2 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, heat and drought accounted for 74 percent, and the share was 46 percent in 1989-1999 and 78 percent in 2000-2009. Loss ratio is 1.31 over 1989-2025, with 15 of 30 crop years paying more than the premium. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $27 per acre, up 3.8 percent since 2016, and land and buildings are valued at $1,983 per acre in 2022.

48277.text: Lamar County's loss ratio is the number that stands out. Over the closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, crop insurance paid out $74.1 million, and the payouts ran 1.07 times the premiums. Excess moisture and flood, not drought, is the largest cause at 51 percent of indemnities, and heat and drought was 33 percent in 1989-1999 and 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre for 2026, down 4.4 percent from 2016, and only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The July nightly low has averaged 73.1 F over 2017-2026 against a 72.1 F normal.

48279.text: Lamb County is a county where most of the cropland is watered from the ground, and that is the first thing a reader should weigh. Irrigated land is 56 percent of harvested cropland, and all of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $107 per acre against $66 for dry ground. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 51 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 21 percent in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025. Loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.73, so claims have paid out more than premiums in recent years.

48281.text: Lampasas County is a dryland county where heat and drought drive most of the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 79 percent of the $451,837 in indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, and the share went from 87 percent in 2010-2019 to 95 percent in 2020-2025. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. The county has had 99 weeks in severe drought or worse since 2021, and 2022 alone had 47 weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in that condition. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, up 100 percent from 2016.

48287.text: Lee County is a dryland county, and the weather is what decides a crop here. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and crop insurance has paid out $2.2 million on closed claims since 1989, with heat and drought behind 69 percent of it. The loss ratio of 1.45 says those payments have run above the premiums paid in. Heat and drought went from 63 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 63 percent again in 2010-2019. Worst year was 2011, with a corn yield of 13 bushels per acre and 52 weeks of severe drought. Non-irrigated cash rent is $13 per acre in 2026, down 23.5 percent from 2016.

48289.text: Leon County's notable number is the crop insurance record: indemnities have run above premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.59 over closed crop years 1990-2025 and 1.73 over the last ten. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of what was paid, so wet years, not dry ones, are what have cost insurers here. Heat and drought claims were 52 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 34 percent in 2010-2019, and came back to 46 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low averaged 74 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.9 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre in 2026, up 33.3 percent since 2016.

48291.text: Liberty County is a flood-and-wet-year county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 63 percent of the $82.3 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.52 across those closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $23 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,253 per acre in 2022. There is 109.9 MW of solar operating, with 150 MW proposed.

48293.text: Limestone County is mostly dryland, with only 4 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the crop insurance record shows why the weather matters. Heat and drought claims were 75 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 33 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is the largest cause overall at 41 percent. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.1, so claims have run above premiums lately. Non-irrigated cash rent was $16 per acre in 2025, down 38.5 percent from 2014, and the census put land and buildings at $2,658 per acre in 2022.

48295.text: Lipscomb County is a dryland county on paper, but the irrigated ground is worth a look. Irrigated cash rent is $113 per acre against $18 for non-irrigated, and every acre of irrigation water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities at 40 percent, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.52, meaning insurers paid out more than was collected in premium. Heat and drought claims went from 50 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025.

48297.text: Live Oak County is a dryland county where heat and drought is the main thing that shows up in the books. Heat and drought made up 79 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, $31.3 million in all, and the loss ratio over those closed crop years was 1.27, meaning more was paid out than was collected in premium. The share of claims from heat and drought went from 49 percent in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2020-2025. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is riding on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre, up 30 percent since 2016.

48299.text: Llano County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 14 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $10 per acre for 2026, up 32 percent since 2016. The county has had 461 of 1357 weeks since 2000 with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2011 alone had 46 weeks. Since 2021 there have been 105 such weeks. July nightly lows averaged 73 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72 F, and the July low trend since 1976 is 0.37 F per decade, warming. The census value of land and buildings was $3,097 per acre in 2022.

48303.text: Lubbock County's ground is mostly watered from underneath: 65 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. The insurance record shows the strain. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.35, meaning claims have paid out more than the premiums collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, up 44.8 percent since 2016, and irrigated rent is $76 per acre. The July nightly low averaged 68.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.5 F.

48305.text: Lynn County leans hard on heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 46 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio of 1.27 means insurance has paid out more than the premiums collected. Only 37 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $47 per acre in 2026, up 16 percent since 2014, while irrigated ground rents for $92. Land and buildings were valued at $1,306 per acre in 2022, and 29.9 percent of the cropland base is in CRP, with 803 acres expiring over fiscal years 2027-2029.

48307.text: Heat and drought is the story in McCulloch County. It caused 82 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and its share went from 65 percent in 1989-1999 to 86 percent in 2020-2025. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 91 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Closed crop years paid out $66.5 million against premiums, a loss ratio of 1.41, and the last ten years ran at 1.46. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, up 30 percent since 2016. Wind is the one big piece of new ground use, with 340 megawatts operating.

48309.text: McLennan County is a dryland county. Only 2 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain, and the insurance claims show it. Heat and drought made up 61 percent of the $103.4 million paid out from 1989 through 2025, and 9 of the 27 closed crop years paid more than the premium collected, with a loss ratio of 1.01 over the full span. The share of claims from heat and drought went from 78 percent in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025. The 2017-2026 July nightly low averaged 74.5 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $43 per acre in 2026, up 24.6 percent since 2016.

48313.text: Madison County is a dryland rent county, and its notable feature is how little ground is irrigated. The non-irrigated cash rent is $15 per acre, down 23.1 percent since 2014, while the irrigated rent is $37 per acre. Severe drought or worse covered at least 50 percent of the county in 189 of 1357 weeks since 2000, and the worst year was 2011 with 52 weeks. Since 2021 it has been 25 weeks. July nights have warmed slightly, with the 2017-2026 average low at 74.1 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 73 F. The census value of land and buildings was $4,028 per acre in 2022, up 34.4 percent from 2017. There is no CRP ground and no operating solar or wind.

48319.text: Mason County is mostly irrigated ground, and the water comes from wells. Irrigated land is 71 percent of harvested cropland, and 98 percent of that irrigation water is groundwater. Heat and drought made up 59 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and that share rose to 81 percent in 2020-2025. Dry weeks have been frequent: 103 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025, with 46 of those weeks in 2011 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 53.6 percent since 2016, and irrigated cash rent was $115 per acre in 2022.

48321.text: Matagorda County's ground is mostly dryland, and its insurance history is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $297.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, against premiums that were smaller than that, with a loss ratio of 1.43 and 18 of 31 years paying out more than premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest single cause at 32 percent. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $62 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground rents for $68.

48323.text: Maverick County is mostly irrigated, with 82 percent of harvested cropland watered, and none of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims have been climbing in the insurance record, going from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks are a bigger part of the story, with 458 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 96 of those weeks falling in 2021-2025. Irrigated cash rent was $50 per acre in 2019, and the census value of land and buildings was $1,705 per acre in 2022.

48325.text: Medina County is mostly dryland in rent terms but heavily irrigated in ground, and that split shapes everything here. Irrigated ground rents for $102 per acre in 2026, while non-irrigated is $21, and non-irrigated rent is down 10.6 percent from 2016. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 72 percent of indemnities, and it went from 48 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.22, so claims have paid out more than premium over the full record. Irrigation covers 60 percent of harvested cropland, and 60 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

48327.text: Heat and drought is the story in Menard County. It accounted for 90 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 49 percent in 1989-1999, and it was the largest cause across all closed crop years at 71 percent. Only 24 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the July nightly low averaged 70.8 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre in 2026, up 130.4 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $1,968 per acre in 2022, a 32.8 percent gain from 2017. Solar is running at 7.5 MW, and no wind is operating.

48329.text: Midland County is a groundwater county, and every acre of irrigation here draws on the Ogallala. The heat and drought part of the insurance record is the story. It went from 66 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 92 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 80 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full closed years, the loss ratio is 1.32, and 14 of 23 crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent was $22 per acre in 2016. Census land value was $1,618 per acre in 2022, with only 0.6 percent change from 2017. Wind is operating at 140 MW, and no solar is running yet.

48331.text: Milam County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the weather risk shows up in the claims. Heat and drought made up 59 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and the share went from 88 percent in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. The county paid out more than it took in premium over those closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.92. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre for 2026, up 6.7 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has been warming, averaging 74.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.8 F.

48333.text: Heat and drought is the story in Mills County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 23 percent in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2000-2009, then came back down to 37 percent in 2010-2019 and climbed again to 64 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years from 2016 to 2025, insurance paid out $1.38 for every dollar of premium, and losses in the county were $40.21 per $100 of insured value. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground is dryland, and the county has 330 weeks of severe drought in the 2000-2025 record, with 52 of those in 2022. Non-irrigated rent is $24 per acre in 2025.

48335.text: Mitchell County is a dryland county, and the numbers say the dry years are what the ground is built around. Heat and drought made up 69 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 70 percent in 2020-2025, with 86 percent in 2000-2009, and the loss ratio over the closed years is 1.47, so claims have paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $23 per acre, up 17.9 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground is only 14 percent of harvested cropland, and the 2012 irrigated rent was $50 per acre. CRP covers 12986 acres, or 33.2 percent of the cropland base, with just one acre expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

48337.text: Montague County's loss ratio is 1.47, meaning crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums taken in over 1989-2025, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 44 percent of the $3.0 million in indemnities. Its sharewas 59 percent in 1989-1999 and 48 percent in 2020-2025, so the pressure is still there. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which leaves most ground dependent on rain. The county averages $23 per acre for non-irrigated cash rent in 2026, up 7 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,879 per acre in 2022.

48339.text: Montgomery County is a land-value and heat county more than a water-trouble one. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance loss ratio is 0.02 over 1998-2023, so claims have paid out very little against premiums. The county's census land and buildings value is $13,070 per acre, up 14.5 percent from 2017 to 2022, while non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre in 2026, up 10.3 percent from 2016. July nights have warmed, with the average low at 74.9 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.8 F. Severe drought has covered at least 50 percent of the county in 134 of the 1357 weeks since 2000, with 2011 the worst at 47 weeks.

48341.text: Moore County is an irrigated county first. Groundwater runs all of the irrigation water here, and irrigated ground made up 54 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census. Irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $146 per acre, against $29 for non-irrigated ground in 2025. Non-irrigated rent is up 28.9 percent from 2014 to 2025. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 44 percent of indemnities, and it went from 30 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2000-2009, then 34 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance paid out $1.19 for every dollar of premium over 1989-2025, and $1.35 over the last ten closed crop years.

48345.text: Motley County is a dryland county with a loss record that stands out. Indemnities have run at 1.72 times premium over the closed crop years since 1989, and the ten years from 2016 through 2025 was 1.76. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of those claims at 69 percent overall, and its share went from 75 percent in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $16 per acre in 2024, up 50 percent since 2013. Census land value was $1,118 per acre in 2022, and irrigation water is 100 percent groundwater.

48349.text: Navarro County is a dryland county with a loss record that stands out. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $58.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.18, with 9 of 17 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 42 percent of indemnities, and it was 38 percent in 1989-1999 against 42 percent in 2020-2025. Land is priced well above rent: $3,770 per acre in the 2022 census against $36 per acre of non-irrigated cash rent for 2026.

48353.text: Heat and drought is the main thing in Nolan County. It was behind 76 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 68 percent in 1989-1999 to 83 percent in 2010-2019 before falling to 72 percent in 2020-2025. Claims paid $182.0 million against premiums, a loss ratio of 1.49, and 14 of 31 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 77 over 2021-2025, and 2022 alone had 52 weeks. Groundwater supplies 97 percent of irrigation water. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $27 per acre, and irrigated was $109 per acre in 2023.

48355.text: Nueral Nueces is a county where the ground is dry and the crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the long run. Heat and drought claims took 83 percent of the $505.9 million in indemnities from 1989-2025, and their share went from 45 percent in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed crop years is 1.09, with 15 of 37 years paying out more than premium. None of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $70 per acre, up 14.8 percent since 2016. Corn yields in the county have been trending up 3.2 bushels per acre a year since 2008.

48357.text: Ochiltree County is a dryland county with a water question underneath it. Only 40 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 31 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $99 per acre. Heat and drought was 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 77 percent in 2000-2009, and 38 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 1.33, so insurance paid out more than the premiums. The census put land and buildings at $1,893 per acre in 2022, with CRP covering 25.3 percent of the cropland base.

48359.text: Oldham County is a dryland county where heat and drought drive the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 53 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the closed crop years have paid out $59.1 million, a loss ratio of 1.29, with 11 of 18 years paying more than premium. Only 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and that water is all groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, up 13.9 percent since 2016. CRP covers 48.1 percent of the cropland base, and 755.2 MW of wind is operating.

48363.text: Palo Pinto County is a dryland county. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Heat and drought are the cause behind 79 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid from 1990 to 2025, and that share went from 45 percent in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated rent is $21 per acre for 2026, down 10.6 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $2,869 per acre in 2022, an estimate from operators, and that is well above what the rent alone would suggest.

48365.text: Panola County is a dryland county with an unusual pattern in its insurance record: the big losses have come from too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood made up 43 percent of the $758,050 paid out on closed crop years from 2021 through 2025, and heat and drought made up none of it. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre in 2026, down 18.2 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,130 per acre in the 2022 census, a figure the operators supplied themselves.

48367.text: Parker County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 4 percent irrigated in 2022, so the rent and the weather both matter more here than the water. Non-irrigated cash rent was $16 per acre in 2024, up 32 percent from 2014. The loss story is heat and drought: that cause made up 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 54 percent in 1989-1999 to 93 percent in 2000-2009. The census put land and buildings at $6,899 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate. Solar has 773 MW proposed to EIA and nothing operating yet.

48369.text:
Parmer County is a dryland-and-irrigation county where the water is the story. Two-thirds of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $116 per acre in 2026, against $36 for non-irrigated, and the gap is large.

The loss ratio is the number to watch. Crop insurance has paid out $1.5 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 22 of 36 years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 52 in 2012 and again in 2022.

48375.text: Potter County's most notable number is that all of its irrigation water comes from groundwater, and heat and drought have driven most of its crop insurance claims for years. Heat and drought went from 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 89 percent in 2020-2025. Closed-year claims total $13.7 million since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.43, meaning claims have run above premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre, up 138.7 percent since 2016, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $1,217 per acre.

48379.text: Rains County is a dryland county. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground lives or dies on what the sky gives it. The bigger story is the drought weeks: 211 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 31 of those came in just 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 69.2 percent since 2014. The July nightly low has warmed by 0.32 F per decade since 1976, and the 2017-2026 average is 73 F against a normal of 72.4 F. Land and buildings were valued at $5,667 per acre in the 2022 census, a number that comes from operators' own estimates.

48383.text: Reagan County is mostly dryland, and drought is what shows up in its claims. Heat and drought made up 82 percent of the $179.8 million paid out on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the share went from 78 percent in 1989-1999 to 93 percent in 2010-2019 before it came down to 74 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground is 39 percent of harvested cropland and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent was $38 per acre in 2023, up 17.2 percent from 2013. Insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 1.47, and the census put land and buildings at $1,249 per acre in 2022.

48387.text: Red River County is a dryland county where the crop insurance record has run against the farmer more often than not. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 11 of 17 closed crop years since 1989, and the last ten closed years came in at a loss ratio of 1.62. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are doing more of the damage than they used to. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre for 2026, and census land value was $3,398 per acre in 2022.

48391.text: Refugio County is mostly ground that depends on well water. All of its irrigation water comes from groundwater, and heat and drought account for 68 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1989. The share was 83 percent in 2000-2009 and 61 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 19.8 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings were valued at $2,528 per acre in 2022, a jump of 102.2 percent from 2017. The county also has 220 MW of wind operating and 394.4 MW of solar proposed, with no CRP acres.

48393.text: Roberts County is mostly dryland, and the water here comes from underground: all of its irrigation water is pumped from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $10.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought made up 50 percent of that. Its share went from 44 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 1.12, meaning claims ran above premiums in that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent was $10 per acre in 2022, while irrigated rent was $90 in 2020. The census land value was $950 per acre in 2022, and there are 288.6 MW of wind operating with 500 MW proposed, but no solar.

48395.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Robertson County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 60 percent in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2000-2009 and then back up to 62 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's 1989-2025 loss ratio is 1.01, with 5 of 20 crop years paying out more than premium. Only 18 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 97 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent was $11 per acre in 2025, down 59.3 percent since 2014, while irrigated rent was $98 per acre in 2026. July nightly lows have averaged 74.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73 F.

48397.text: Rockwall County is a place where the water problem is wet ground, not dry. Crop insurance has paid out $10.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and excess moisture and flood account for 67 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.05 for the whole period and 1.08 for the last ten closed years, so claims have run past premiums. Heat and drought share of claims went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, with 33 percent in 2000-2009 in between. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $7,370 per acre.

48399.text: Runnels County is mostly dryland, with only 8 percent of harvested cropland irrigated and 85 percent of that water pulled from groundwater. Heat and drought is the cause behind most of the crop insurance payouts here: 83 percent of the $297.5 million paid since 1989. The share was 47 percent in 1989-1999 and 91 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, up 16.7 percent since 2016. The loss ratio is 1.56, so claims have run past premiums over the full record, and the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.7. Land and buildings were valued at $1,978 per acre in 2022.

48405.text: Most of what stands out here is the heat and the land prices, not the rent. July nights have been warm for a long time. The July average low for 2017-2026 is 72.7 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.9 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.44 F per decade. Julys with an average low at or above 70 F number 94 since 1900. Rent for non-irrigated ground was $16 per acre in 2023, up 24 percent from 2013. The census value of land and buildings was $4,336 per acre in 2022, and it rose 53.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, which is operators' own estimate and not a sale price.

48407.text: San Jacinto County is a dryland county. Only 3 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the rent you see here is for ground that lives on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre in 2026, up 12.5 percent from 2016. The land and buildings are valued at $4,840 per acre in the 2022 census, and that figure is the operators' own estimate. The July nights are the part to watch: the average low for 2017-2026 is 74.2 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.4 F. Since 1976 the July low has been warming at 0.45 F per decade, and 127 Julys since 1900 have averaged a low at or above 70 F.

48409.text: Heat and drought is the story in San Patricio County. It made up 97 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 and 73 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.18, with 12 of 36 crop years paying out more than premium. Corn yields have not trended up or down over 2010-2025, but the 2022 crop was 34.9 bushels per acre against a median of 81.4. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 98 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $84 per acre, up 24.6 percent since 2016.

48411.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in San Saba County. It was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, at 67 percent of the $18.3 million paid, and its share rose from 42 percent in 1989-1999 to 70 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed years 2016-2025 is 1.37, so the claims paid have run ahead of the premiums. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $11 per acre in 2026.

48415.text: Scurry County is a dryland county with heat and drought on the books more than anything else. Heat and drought took 82 percent of the $249.3 million paid out in closed crop years from 1989-2025, and its share was 92 percent in 2010-2019. Insurance claims have paid out more than premium in 20 of 35 closed crop years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.37. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 85 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre, up 25.5 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $1,279 per acre, and CRP covers 31.9 percent of the cropland base, with none of those acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

48417.text: Shackelford County's crop insurance record is the first thing to notice. Indemnities have run above premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.22 across 1989-2025 and 1.25 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 82 percent of the $16.7 million paid, and its share went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 84 percent in 2000-2009 and 83 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $20 per acre, up 73.9 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $1,885 per acre in 2022, and 565.6 MW of wind is operating in the county.

48419.text: Shelby County is a non-irrigated county, with just 2 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in the 2022 census, so rain sets the crop here. The most useful number on the drought side is the 167 of 1357 weeks, or 12.3 percent, since 2000 with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. The worst year was 2011, with 52 weeks. Between 2021 and 2025 there were 39 such weeks. Cash rent is $18 per acre for 2026, up 2.9 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,584 per acre in 2022, a figure operators gave, and it rose 2.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

48421.text: Sherman County's cropland is mostly dryland in the census sense, but the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $170 per acre against $40 for non-irrigated, and the non-irrigated rent has risen 95.1 percent since 2016. Groundwater supplies all of the irrigation water. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.14 over 1989-2025, and 1.42 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 42 percent, and its share went from 31 percent in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 61 percent in 2000-2009. Weeks in severe drought or worse have been frequent, with 80 of them in 2021-2025 alone.

48423.text: Smith County is a county where freeze and frost, not heat or drought, has driven most of the crop insurance claims. Freeze and frost made up 56 percent of indemnities from 1989-2025, while heat and drought went from 44 percent of claims in 1989-1999 down to 0 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed crop years was 0.38, so premiums have run well ahead of payouts. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which puts most of the ground on rain alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 18.9 percent from 2016, and the census land and buildings value was $7,161 per acre in 2022.

48427.text: Starr County is a dry-land county where most of the cropland is not irrigated, and that shows up in the rent. Non-irrigated ground rents for $18 per acre in 2026, down 39.3 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $96 per acre in 2024. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims, and it made up 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 46 percent in 2020-2025. The county's July nights are warmer now, averaging 76.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 75.5 F.

48431.text: Sterling County's crop insurance record stands out. Claims paid out $3.5 million from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio is 1.15, meaning indemnities ran above the premiums collected. Heat and drought caused 89 percent of those claims. The share was 59 percent in 1989-1999 and 100 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 90 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $5 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,186 per acre in 2022, up 74.9 percent from 2017. The July nightly low has averaged 71.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.4 F.

48433.text: Stonewall County's crop insurance record is the first thing I'd look at. Claims paid out $60.5 million over 1989-2025, and heat and drought caused 80 percent of that. The share went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 90 percent in 2010-2019, then came back to 78 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.53, and insurers paid more than the premium in 11 of 16 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026. CRP covers 48.9 percent of the cropland base, with no contracts expiring through fiscal 2029.

48437.text: Swisher County's most striking figure is how much the water is worth. Irrigated cash rent is $72 per acre against $39 for non-irrigated ground, and that gap has widened from 1.29 times in 2009 to 1.85 times in 2026. All of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought has grown from 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.28, with 20 of 36 years paying out more than premium. July nightly lows averaged 67.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 66 F normal. The county has 1,100 MW of solar operating and 120,582 CRP acres.

48439.text: Tarrant County is mostly dryland, with 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather risk falls on rainfall more than on pumps. The clearest signal is heat and drought in the claims. They made up 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.03, so insurance has paid out slightly more than was collected in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre in 2026, up 31.8 percent since 2016. The census land and buildings value of $6,750 per acre is the operators' own estimate, and it rose 2 percent a year from 2017 to 2022. July nights have also warmed, with the 2017-2026 average low at 75.4 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 74.6 F.

48447.text: Throckmorton County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums over the full closed period, with a loss ratio of 1.36 and 11 of 18 crop years paying more than was collected. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 66 percent of claims, and its share went from 59 percent in 1989-1999 to 88 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre for 2026, and all irrigation water comes from groundwater. Land and buildings were valued at $2,232 per acre in the 2022 census, up 58.5 percent from 2017.

48449.text: Titus County is mostly dryland. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and crop insurance paid $377,682 over 1990-2025 on closed claims, with heat and drought behind 52 percent of that. The July nightly low averaged 73.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.1 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.5 F per decade. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, up 90.5 percent from 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $3,394 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 34.7 percent between 2017 and 2022.

48451.text: Tom Green County is an irrigated county first. Irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre in 2026 against $50 for non-irrigated ground, so irrigated ground now rents for 3.00 times the dryland rate, up from 1.70 in 2009. Groundwater supplies 95 percent of the irrigation water, and 45 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Heat and drought made up 75 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, down from 85 percent in 2000-2009. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.87, so claims have run well above premium. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 46 in 2021-2025.

48455.text: Trinity County is mostly ground that gets no irrigation, and most of what makes it stand out is the water and the heat. Drought has been a steady presence here, with 135 weeks of severe or worse drought between 2000 and 2025 and 52 of those weeks in 2011 alone. The July nightly low averaged 73.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.9 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre for 2026, down 20 percent from 2016. Census land and building value was $3,266 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate and not a sale price. Land value rose 23.5 percent between 2017 and 2022.

48461.text: Upton County is a groundwater county. All of its irrigation water comes from the aquifer, and heat and drought have caused most of the crop insurance payouts since 1989, at 85 percent of $54.2 million. The loss ratio is 1.47, and insurers paid out more than they took in premiums in 12 of 17 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 74 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 90 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 82 percent in 2020-2025. The county's July nights averaged 72.3 F in 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.3 F. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2017 was $30 per acre. There is 949.3 MW of wind and 730 MW of solar operating here.

48467.text: Van Zandt County is mostly dryland, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. Its crop insurance record is light at a 0.22 loss ratio over 1990-2025, but heat and drought still lead the claims at 42 percent of indemnities over 1990-2023, after running 55 percent over 2000-2009. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 179 of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 2011 the worst year at 50 weeks, and 28 weeks in 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 12.8 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value was $4,736 per acre in 2022, up 28.9 percent from 2017. Solar operating is 59 MW, and there is no wind.

48469.text: Victoria County is a dryland county where the weather record and the insurance record tell the same story. Only 12 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities over 1989-2025, at 47 percent, and its share went from 63 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed years is 0.84, with 10 of 26 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre, unchanged from 2016.

48471.text: Walker County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent irrigated in the 2022 census, so rent is set by ground that depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, and it has risen 122.2 percent since 2016. The bigger change is in what the crop insurance claims are for. Heat and drought was 0 percent of indemnities in 1900 through 2019 but reached 50 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for 68 percent of all claims from 2015-2024. Our July nightly lows averaged 74.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.3 F. The loss ratio is 0.38 for closed crop years 1999-2025, meaning claims have run well under premiums over that stretch.

48473.text: Waller County's loss record is the first thing I'd look at. Crop insurance indemnities have run $19.8 million across the closed years since 1989, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.18, meaning the claims paid out more than the premiums brought in. Over the ten closed years 2016-2025 that ratio is 2.2. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 49 percent, and its share fell from 68 percent in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, with other causes picking up the rest. Non-irrigated rent is $44 per acre, up 102.3 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $64.

48477.text: Washington County is a dryland county. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the rent and the insurance record both reflect ground that waits on rain. Heat and drought is the largest cause of indemnities, at 47 percent over 1995-2025, and the county has paid out $3.6 million on closed crop years. The insurance loss ratio is 1.46 over that span, and it is 1.34 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought share of indemnities went from 64 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 32 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated rent is $29 per acre for 2026, up 75.8 percent from 2016.

48479.text: Webb County is a county where irrigation does most of the work. Forty-four percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of that water comes from groundwater, so the ground depends on surface supply when it's dry. Heat and drought claims rose from 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2000-2009, and the county had 52 weeks of severe drought in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $12 per acre for 2026, up 60 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $1,750 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price, and that value has crept up only 0.4 percent a year since 2017.

48481.text: Wharton County is a county where irrigation does a lot of the work. Irrigated ground rents for $105 per acre in 2026, against $63 for non-irrigated, and 38 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, most of it pumped from groundwater. The indemnity record is the other thing to look at. Insurance has paid out more than the premium in 16 of the 31 closed crop years since 1989, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.24. Heat and drought was the largest single cause of claims at 29 percent, but its share fell from 60 percent in 2000-2009 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigation failure claims have totaled $109.1 million over the whole period.

48485.text: Wichita County's heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought went from 53 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio is 1.37 across the closed crop years 1989-2025, with payouts above premium in 13 of 26 years. Irrigated ground rents for $86 per acre, against $38 for non-irrigated, and only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county depends on rain. Land and buildings were valued at $2,084 per acre in 2022, up 41.4 percent from 2017.

48487.text: Wilbarger County's crop insurance record is the story here. Indemnities total $178.1 million across the closed crop years, and heat and drought account for 78 percent of that. The share has climbed from 65 percent in 1989-1999 to 88 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.41 over the full record, and in the last ten closed years it was 1.1, so claims have run above premium. Rent is $30 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 17.3 percent since 2016. All of the irrigation water comes from groundwater, and the county's wind is 1015.2 MW.

48489.text: Willacy County is a heat and water story more than a rent story. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance payouts, reaching 84 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 74 percent in 2010-2019, before falling to 30 percent in 2020-2025. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, and irrigated rent is $98 per acre. Wind is the big non-crop use here, with 1444.6 MW operating and no solar.

48491.text: Williamson County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so heat and dry weeks do most of the work on the crop. Heat and drought went from 93 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 83 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 0.62, so claims have paid less than premium lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 7.9 percent since 2016. The census land value is $4,814 per acre, and the county's corn yield trend is 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

48493.text: Wilson County is a dryland county, and the insurance claims tell the story. Only 23 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 93 percent of indemnities paid over 2020-2025, up from 50 percent over 1989-1999. The loss ratio over the closed years 1989-2025 is 1.24, so claims have paid out more than premiums came in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre, up 44.2 percent since 2016, while the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $4,471 per acre. Heat and drought weeks ran 122 across 2021-2025, and the worst corn year was 2022 at 51 bushels per acre.

48495.text: Winkler County's notable number is the claims picture. Freeze and frost caused 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities over the 2023-2025 closed crop years, $382,390 in total, while heat and drought made up 11 percent of claims from 2020-2025. Land is being valued high, at $1,520 per acre in the 2022 census, and it went up 35.6 percent between 2017 and 2022. July nights have warmed too, averaging 71.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.3 F. Solar is the big land use here, with 250 MW operating and no wind.

48497.text: Wise County is mostly dryland, and the heat and drought numbers are what stand out. Heat and drought made up 39 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 58 percent in 2000-2009, and it was still the largest cause at 43 percent over the full record. The county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.16, so claims have paid out more than premiums. July nights now average 73.9 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre for 2026, down 6.1 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $6,259 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' estimate, not a sale.

48499.text: Most of the ground in Wood County is dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre for 2026, down 11.9 percent from 2016. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 210 of 1357 from 2000 through 2025, and 2011 alone had 52 of them. Heat and drought made up 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, and freeze and frost took 74 percent of the closed crop years from 1990-1997. The 2022 census value of land and buildings is $5,395 per acre, up 60.5 percent from 2017 to 2022.

48501.text: Yoakum County is mostly irrigation country, with 45 percent of harvested cropland irrigated and all of that water coming from groundwater. Irrigated cash rent is $158 per acre in 2026, against $30 for non-irrigated ground, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,606 per acre in 2022. Heat and drought claims are the largest loss cause at 55 percent of indemnities since 1989. Their share went from 45 percent in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $1.52 for every dollar of premium over the closed years, and $1.73 over 2016-2025.

48503.text: Young County is mostly dryland, and drought is what stands out. Heat and drought made up 95 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid for 2020-2025, up from 56 percent for 1989-1999. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.99, and in the full 1989-2025 record indemnities ran 1.13 times premium, with payouts above premium in 6 of 15 crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, up 25 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $2,496 per acre in 2022, a 47.6 percent rise since 2017. The county has 698 MW of wind operating and no solar.

48507.text: Zavala County is an irrigated county first. Irrigation covers 69 percent of harvested cropland, and 93 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated rent is $50 per acre against $23 for non-irrigated ground. The bigger story is in the insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.47, meaning claims have run past premiums. Drought weeks in 2021-2025 total 118, and the county's July nightly lows averaged 74.9 F across 2017-2026.

55001.text: Adams County is mostly dryland with a lot of irrigation on top. Two-thirds of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 81 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $341 per acre in 2026 against $74 for non-irrigated, and that gap has widened from 3.29 times in 2009 to 4.61 times now. Crop insurance has paid out $91.3 million since 1989, and excess moisture and flood, not drought, is the largest cause at 55 percent. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025, and 27 weeks of severe drought have been logged since 2021.

55003.text: Ashland County's crop insurance record leans toward too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims since 1989, at 41 percent, and the county's loss ratio of 0.58 over 1989-2025 is below 1. Heat and drought has grown in the last stretch: it was 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 54 percent in 2020-2025. The county's 2026 non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre, up 113.9 percent from 2016.

55007.text: Bayfield County's crop insurance record is shaped more by wet years than by dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 46 percent of the $4.4 million in indemnities paid over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.96, meaning claims came close to premiums paid in. Heat and drought claims went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years have started to matter here in a way they did not earlier. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 14 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $2,812 per acre in 2022.

55009.text: Brown County's corn is mostly watered by rain, and the bigger threat has been too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 44 percent of the indemnities paid here since 1989, and the county's loss ratio of 0.78 over closed crop years means insurers have paid out more than they took in premium. Heat and drought claims went from 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 9 percent in 2010-2019 and were 14 percent in 2020-2025.
