Rent has moved to $213 per acre for 2026, up 17.7 percent since 2016, and the census land value of $9,088 per acre is a much larger number than rent alone would suggest. Only 1 percent of cropland is irrigated.

55011.text: Heat and drought is the story in Buffalo County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 21 percent in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2000-2009, and it has been 43 percent in 2020-2025. The county's closed crop years paid out $35.0 million, with a loss ratio of 0.62, and 3 of the 19 closed years paid out more than premium. Corn yields have trended up 1.9 bushels per acre a year, and the median is 164.4 bushels, with 2013 the worst year at 141. Non-irrigated cash rent is $139 per acre in 2026, up 14.9 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $182 per acre in 2023, and all of its irrigation water comes from groundwater.

55013.text: Burnett County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought was the biggest cause of claims, at 55 percent of the $21.6 million paid out since 1989, and its share went from 9 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio of 0.82 means claims have run below premiums overall, though 4 of 15 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Rent is $56 per acre, up 28.4 percent since 2016, and the census land value is $3,584 per acre. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain.

55015.text: Calumet County's biggest number is water, and it runs the other way from drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 57 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's loss ratio is 0.65 across the closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, a small move. Non-irrigated cash rent is $187 per acre in 2026, up 20.6 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $8,232 per acre in 2022, so the 2022 rent was 2.08 percent of that value.

55017.text: Heat and drought is the story in Chippewa County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 23 percent in 1989-1999 to 75 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 26 percent in 2020-2025. Over all the closed crop years, the loss ratio is 0.63, and six of 29 crop years paid out more than the premium. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $125 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $4,325 per acre. The 2009 drought ran 21 weeks in severe drought or worse, the worst year in the record. Recent years have been quiet on drought, with zero weeks in 2021-2025.

55019.text: Clark County's notable number is flood, not drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of the $86.7 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, and the county's loss ratio is 0.74 overall, with 7 of 28 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims were 67 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and fell to 5 percent in 2020-2025, and there have been no weeks of severe drought since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $119 per acre in 2026, up 36.8 percent from 2016, while census land and buildings value in 2022 is $5,034 per acre.

55021.text: Columbia County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at first. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance payments here, at 40 percent of indemnities since 1989, and it held near 40 percent in every period since 2000. The crop insurance loss ratio is 0.56 over 1989-2025, and five of the 26 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Drought weeks are rare here, but 2021-2025 logged 28 weeks in severe drought or worse. The 2026 non-irrigated cash rent is $215 per acre, up 20.1 percent since 2016.

55023.text: Crawford County's heat and drought claims are the thing to watch. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 12 percent in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio is 0.61 over 1989-2025, with 4 of 17 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $167 per acre for 2026, up 34.7 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $4,494 per acre in 2022, a number the operators themselves estimated, and CRP covers 4649 acres, or 5.7 percent of the cropland base.

55025.text: Dane County's cropland is mostly non-irrigated, and the big story here is drought and heat claims. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $231 per acre in 2026, up 34.3 percent since 2016. Put that next to a census land value of $9,427 per acre in 2022 and the rent is a small slice of the ground's worth. Corn yields have trended up 3.3 bushels per acre a year since 2008, but the worst year, 2012, was 110.9.

55027.text: Dodge County's bigger story is water, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 62 percent of the $86.2 million in crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio is 0.56, with 5 of 26 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025. July nights have stayed close to normal, with the 2017-2026 average low at 61 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 59.9 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $212 per acre, up 20.5 percent since 2016. CRP covers 3879 acres, and 487 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

55029.text: Door County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $52.4 million since 1989, and in the closed years the county has paid back $0.74 for every dollar of premium, with 5 of 20 crop years paying out more than the premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 36 percent. Heat and drought was 56 percent of claims in 2000-2009 and 21 percent in 2020-2025. Rent is $120 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 48.1 percent since 2016. Corn yields have a trend of 2.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 132.5 and a worst year of 99.3 in 2011.

55031.text: Douglas County is a non-irrigated county with no irrigated cropland in the 2022 census, so the rent and the weather record are the story here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre for 2026, and it was up 6.7 percent from 2016. Excess moisture and flood made up 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2020, and the loss ratio for closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.76. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 8 percent in 2010-2019, and the county had 83 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 25 of them in 2007.

55033.text: Dunn County's notable number is the insurance record. Heat and drought made up 76 percent of indemnity payments in 2000-2009, but only 43 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full closed years, the loss ratio is 0.57, and 8 of 26 crop years paid out more than the premium. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $131 per acre in 2026, up 31.7 percent since 2016. Every acre here is irrigated from groundwater, and irrigated rent is $252 per acre. The county's corn yield trend has been rising 2.3 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 168.6 bushels.

55035.text: Eau Claire County's corn has been a steady performer, with a median yield of 159.2 bushels per acre across 2008-2025. The bad years are what stand out. The worst was 2012 at 116 bushels, and heat and drought went from 14 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2000-2009, before easing to 33 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $125 per acre in 2026, up 45.3 percent since 2016. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain.

55041.text: Forest County's loss history is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $1.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, against a loss ratio of 1.49, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Freeze and frost is the largest cause at 38 percent. Heat and drought went from 40 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 19 percent in 2010-2019, then back up to 31 percent in 2020-2025. The county's July nightly lows have averaged 53.8 F over 2017-2026, close to the 53.2 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026.

55043.text: Grant County is dryland from end to end: no harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has no irrigation to fall back on. Drought is what stands out here. Heat and drought went from 18 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 47 percent in 2020-2025. Over those same years the loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.65, and four of the 25 closed crop years paid out more than the premium collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $247 per acre for 2026, up 28.6 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value was $6,306 per acre in 2022, so rent ran 3.44 percent of that value. CRP covers 26033 acres, and 5065 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

55045.text: Green County is a dryland county with a clear weather story. Heat and drought made up 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 63 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 51 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.69, and crop years paid out more than premium in 7 of 26 closed years. The county averaged a 185.2 bushel corn yield from 2008 through 2025, with 2012 down to 76. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, all from groundwater, so most of the ground is riding on rain. The county's non-irrigated cash rent is $223 per acre in 2026, up 32 percent since 2016.

55047.text: Green Lake County's heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 51 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the county paid $31.9 million on closed crop years, and the largest cause was that same heat and drought at 50 percent. Corn yields have trended up 2.7 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 168.3 and a worst year of 97.3 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $195 per acre for 2026, up 36.4 percent from 2016.

55049.text: Heat and drought is the main thing that has cost this county's growers money. It was 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2010-2019, then 37 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, indemnities ran $75.7 million, and only 3 of 22 crop years paid out more than premium. Corn yields have still trended up 3 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 186.9 bushels per acre. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 99 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $196 per acre, down 1.5 percent since 2016.

55051.text: Iron County's notable pattern is in the claims. Freeze and frost caused 45 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2019 by closed crop year, and heat and drought went from 100 percent of the total in 2000-2009 to 22 percent in 2010-2019. July nightly lows have averaged 54.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 54.1 F. Drought has been less frequent recently too, with 41 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025 and the worst year, 2007, at 26 weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $4,086 per acre in 2022, up 20.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. There is no CRP, wind or solar on the books here.

55053.text: Jackson County is a dryland county, and its corn has been paying out mostly on heat and drought. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 47 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, with its share at 62 percent in 2000-2009 and 35 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $143 per acre in 2026, up 43.7 percent from 2016, and the 1989-2025 loss ratio of 0.67 means claims have run ahead of premiums over the full record. The corn yield trend is up 2.3 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2025, with the worst year at 116.1 bushels in 2012. The county has 4066 CRP acres, and 764 of them expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

55057.text: Juneau County is mostly dryland ground, and the thing that stands out is how often the crop has been hit by too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 31 percent of the $74.3 million in closed-year crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.78, with 5 of 22 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2010-2019, then 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $120 per acre in 2026, up 31.1 percent from 2016.

55059.text: Kenosha County is mostly dryland ground that floods more often than it dries out. Excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and only 2 of the last 20 closed crop years paid out more than premium overall. Heat and drought claims have been a smaller part of the picture, falling from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2010-2019, then climbing back to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $184 per acre for 2026, up 21.1 percent from 2016. The county's July nightly lows have been close to normal, averaging 62.8 F across 2017-2026 against 61.9 F for the 1991-2020 normal.

55061.text: Kewaunee County's biggest story is water, and it's too much of it. Excess moisture and flood made up 39 percent of the crop insurance indemnities, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.63, with 6 of 22 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2000-2009, then back to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent is $228 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 58.3 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $7,465 per acre in 2022, so rent is a small slice of that. Corn yields show a trend of 2.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024.

55063.text: La Crosse County's notable point is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid $16.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought drove 52 percent of that. Its share went from 28 percent in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 0.63, so claims have run well under premium lately. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $165 per acre, up 25 percent since 2016. The worst corn year in the record was 2012 at 137.1 bushels per acre.

55065.text: Lafayette County has no irrigated cropland, and heat and drought is the main reason crop insurance has paid out here. Heat and drought made up 18 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 24 percent in 2000-2009, 39 percent in 2010-2019, and 21 percent in 2020-2025. Since 1989 the loss ratio has been 0.7, and 4 of the 29 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. The worst corn year was 2012, at 77.6 bushels per acre against a median of 195.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $240 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $7,655 per acre in 2022.

55067.text: Langlade County is mostly a non-irrigated county, with irrigated ground at 38 percent of harvested cropland in 2022. Its drought history is the thing to look at. Heat and drought made up 54 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, down to 11 percent in 2010-2019, and back up to 30 percent in 2020-2025. The county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.79 over 1989-2025, and insurers have paid out more than premium in 5 of the 18 closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $103 per acre in 2026, up 25.6 percent since 2016.

55069.text: Lincoln County doesn't rise or fall much with the weather in July. The July nightly low averaged 56.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 55.9 F normal, and no July since 1900 has averaged 70 F or higher. The trouble here has mostly come from too much water: excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of insurance claims, at 38 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 10 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, with a spike to 64 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated rent is $70 per acre in 2026, up 58 percent since 2016.

55071.text: Manitowoc County is a rain-and-wet county more than a dry one. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 3 of 24 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.63 over the whole stretch. Heat and drought claims were 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 17 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had no weeks of severe drought since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $199 per acre, up 25.2 percent from 2016.

55073.text: What stands out in Marathon County is how little of the ground is irrigated, 3 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and that most of what water there is comes from groundwater, 82 percent in 2015. Heat and drought claims were 66 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, down to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood, at 44 percent, is the largest cause of claims over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio of 0.63 means claims have run below the premiums paid over that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $133 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,576 per acre in 2022.

55075.text: Marinette County's corn ground has been a fairly steady producer, with a median yield of 134.1 bushels per acre across 2008-2025 and a yield trend of 2 bushels a year. The notable number is heat and drought, which made up 65 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 42 percent in 2020-2025, after falling to 19 percent in 2010-2019. Over the full closed years, insurance paid $34.6 million against a loss ratio of 0.57, and only 3 of 21 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is $124 per acre, and the county is only 3 percent irrigated, so most of the crop depends on rain.

55077.text: Marquette County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at here. Heat and drought was 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, rose to 51 percent in 2010-2019, and was 41 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out more than it took in premium over the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.87 across 1989-2025, and 5 of 22 crop years paid more than premium. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $91 per acre in 2026, up 71.7 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground is $251 per acre. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

55078.text: Menominee County is a small county with few of the usual pressures showing up in the numbers. July nights have warmed a little, with the average low at 57.8 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 56.6 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.5 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Severe drought has covered at least 50 percent of the county in 50 of 1357 weeks since 2000, and 2009 was the worst year with 24 weeks. The 2021-2025 stretch recorded 11 weeks in severe drought or worse. There is no CRP ground, no operating wind or solar, and nothing proposed to the EIA. Those are the facts the county has on the record.

55079.text: Milwaukee County is a small-acreage county where the weather problem has mostly been too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 60 percent of the $2.2 million in crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county's loss ratio is 0.67 over that stretch, rising to 0.81 across the ten closed crop years 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $101 per acre, and the 2022 census land and buildings value is $25,512 per acre. Only 26 acres of CRP are enrolled, and none expire through 2029.

55081.text: Monroe County is mostly dryland, with 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather years do most of the sorting. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 38 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 5 percent in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out $53.2 million on closed crop years, and in four of the twenty closed years the payouts were more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $154 per acre for 2026, up 16.7 percent since 2016, and the census land value is $5,240 per acre. The worst corn year in the record was 2013, at 121.4 bushels per acre, against a median of 155.5.

55083.text: Oconto County is mostly dryland ground, and the water-related claims here come from wet springs more than dry summers. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of the $65.5 million in indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and heat and drought went from 21 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2000-2009, then back down to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $154 per acre, up 40 percent since 2016, while the census value of land and buildings is $5,367 per acre. The rent in 2022 was 2.22 percent of that value. Just 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

55085.text: Oneida County has had more crop insurance paid out than it collected in premium over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.47 for 2016-2025. Most of the losses in the long record came from freeze and frost, at 56 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought claims were 4 percent in 1989-1999 and 3 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 28 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2009 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent was $42 per acre in 2024. The census land and buildings value was $5,553 per acre in 2022, up 36.6 percent from 2017.

55087.text: Outagamie County is mostly a wet-year county. Excess moisture and flood account for 61 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.74 over the closed crop years, with 6 of the 31 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025, with a spike to 42 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $161 per acre for 2026, up 49.1 percent from 2016. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has had 5 weeks of severe drought across 2000-2025.

55089.text: Most of Ozaukee's ground is dry-land, and the county's notable story is wet years, not heat. Flood and excess moisture cause 60 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.63. Heat and drought claims were 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 17 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $118 per acre, against a census land value of $8,047 per acre from 2022, so the rent is a small share of the value. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

55091.text: Pepin County's notable number is the insurance record. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities, at 64 percent of the $15.8 million paid over 1989-2025, and the share went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2000-2009. Indemnities have paid more than premium in 3 of 17 closed crop years, though the last ten years run at a loss ratio of 0.27. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $185 per acre, up 42.3 percent from 2016. Heat and drought weeks have been few since 2021, with 8 weeks in severe drought or worse across 2021-2025.

55093.text: Pierce County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather years matter most here. Heat and drought made up 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 2000-2009, which is the largest single cause in the record. That share fell to 25 percent over 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $179 per acre for 2026, and it is up 32.6 percent since 2016. The county's census land value of $5,863 per acre was estimated in 2022, when rent ran 2.68 percent of that value. The 2013 drought year still stands out, with the corn yield at 140.3 bushels per acre against a median of 177.6.

55095.text: Polk County's most telling number is the insurance record. Heat and drought made up 9 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 69 percent in 2000-2009, and 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the closed crop years paid out $88.0 million with a loss ratio of 0.72. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 94 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Corn yields have trended up 2.2 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 156.2 bushels, though 2013 fell to 103. Non-irrigated cash rent is $122 per acre for 2026, up 66 percent since 2016.

55099.text: Price County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is the freeze and frost claims. Freeze and frost are the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here at 50 percent, while heat and drought went from 5 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 3 percent in 2020-2025, with a spike to 44 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre for 2026, up 32.1 percent from 2016. The county's corn yield trend is up 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.83.

55101.text: Racine County's notable number is the loss record on crop insurance. Indemnities from 1989 to 2025 came to $33.0 million, and in 4 of the 21 closed crop years the claims paid out more than the premium, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 49 percent. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $175 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $9,656 per acre in 2022. Groundwater supplies 98 percent of irrigation water.

55103.text: Richland County is fully dryland. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and the water that does exist comes from groundwater, so the ground carries the whole crop. Heat and drought are the main cause of insurance claims here: 52 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and their share went from 14 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 was 0.86, and 6 of 18 years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $155 per acre for 2026, up 50.5 percent since 2016.

55105.text: Rock County is a dryland county in most of its fields, and the water that does get used comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims have grown from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2010-2019, and they were still 51 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio was 0.26, so claims ran well under premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $223 per acre for 2026, up 22.5 percent since 2016.

55107.text: Rusk County's notable number is the water side. Heat and drought used to be a small share of crop insurance claims here, 12 percent in 1989-1999, then jumped to 70 percent in 2000-2009 before falling back to 16 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the county's cropland is non-irrigated, so a dry July still hits the crop directly. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims over the whole record, at 44 percent. Non-irrigated rent is $104 per acre in 2026, up 57.6 percent from 2016, and the closed crop years since 1989 paid out $34.2 million, a loss ratio of 0.89.

55109.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in St. Croix County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 12 percent in 1989-1999 to 77 percent in 2000-2009, and it has been 55 percent in 2010-2019 and 56 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the county's loss ratio is 0.64, and six of 28 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Most of the cropland is not irrigated, at 7 percent irrigated in 2022, and non-irrigated cash rent is $127 per acre for 2026, up 23.3 percent from 2016.

55111.text: Sauk County is mostly dryland ground, with only 6 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims here, at 45 percent of indemnities since 1989. Its share went from 20 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 43 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $158 per acre for 2026, and that is up 26.4 percent from 2016. The insurance loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.54, so claims have run below premiums lately.

55113.text: Heat and drought is the story in Sawyer County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 17 percent in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2000-2009, and it has been 34 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio is 0.67 over 1989-2025, and 0.3 over the last ten closed crop years, so the bad years have been bunched together. Corn yields show a trend of 1.7 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, with a median of 139.2 bushels and a worst year of 95 in 2008. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, up 72.9 percent from 2016. Groundwater supplies 5 percent of irrigation water.

55115.text: Shawano County's main story is wet years more than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 36 percent, and heat and drought went from 16 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2000-2009 before falling back to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields have trended up 2.5 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 152.6. The loss ratio is 0.63 across 1989-2025, but it is 0.39 over the last ten closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $142 per acre in 2026, up 46.4 percent since 2016.

55117.text: Sheboygan County's cropland is all non-irrigated, and the county's trouble has come from wet springs more than from heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.62, with 4 of 19 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $151 per acre for 2026, up 41.1 percent since 2016. Corn yields trend up 2.4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, from a worst year of 131 bushels in 2008 to a median of 157.4.

55119.text: Taylor County's notable number is wet springs, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 54 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio over those closed years is 0.81, with 6 of 19 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 57 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 7 percent in 2020-2025, and no county land is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $118 per acre in 2026, up 42.2 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $3,710 per acre.

55121.text: Trempealeau County is mostly rainfed ground, and the water question shows up more in the insurance claims than in the acres. Heat and drought made up 68 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has come down, though it still leads all causes over the whole record at 51 percent. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation failure has paid just $11,054 across all closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $144 per acre in 2026, up 10.8 percent from 2016. The county's average nightly July low is 61.3 F for 2017-2026 against 60.3 F for the 1991-2020 normal, and the Atlas shows a warming trend since 1976.

55123.text: Vernon County has no irrigated cropland, so the crop depends on rain. Heat and drought was 7 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 54 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 27 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2023 alone. Insurance paid out more than premium in 6 of the 19 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.81 over the full span. Non-irrigated cash rent is $145 per acre in 2026, up 12.4 percent since 2016. The county corn yield trend is 1.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

55125.text: Vilas County is mostly forest and lakes, so the notable part here is the crop insurance record. Freeze and frost cause most of the claims, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years, 2016-2025, is 1.45, meaning insurers paid out more than they took in premium. That is a short stretch, so it is worth reading next to the long run of 0.79 across 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 20 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. Summer nights are running close to normal, at 53.6 F over 2017-2026 against 53.4 F in the 1991-2020 normal. Groundwater supplies 9 percent of irrigation water, and no CRP acres or solar and wind capacity are operating here.

55127.text: Walworth County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought made up 48 percent of the $60.8 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and their share went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 0.32, so the policies have been paying less than premium lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $236 per acre for 2026, up 24.2 percent from 2016, and irrigated rent was $230 per acre in 2024. Weeks in severe drought or worse have been 19 since 2021, and 2012 was the worst year with 25 weeks.

55129.text: Washburn County is mostly dryland, and the water and weather record shows it. Heat and drought claims were 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 56 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 14 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021 alone. Corn has averaged 152.7 bushels per acre over 2008-2025, with a worst year of 81.9 in 2013. Non-irrigated cash rent is $68 per acre in 2026, up 20.5 percent from 2016. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in over the full record, at a loss ratio of 0.77, but the last ten closed crop years was 0.39.

55131.text: Washington County's cropland has been hit more by too much water than by heat or dry spells. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 46 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 20 percent in 2020-2025. Loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.59, but over the last ten closed crop years, 2016-2025, it is 0.36. Non-irrigated cash rent is $119 per acre for 2026, down 0.8 percent from 2016.

55133.text: Waukesha is a county where heat and drought claims stand out more than the corn trend does. Heat and drought was 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 45 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full record at 43 percent. The loss ratio of 0.59 over 1989-2025 means claims have paid back more than the premiums collected, though only 3 of 19 closed crop years paid out more than premium. The county has little irrigation, 2 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the corn rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $171 per acre in 2026, up 50 percent from 2016, and the 2022 census value of land and buildings was $8,589 per acre.

55135.text: Waupaca County's notable number is the heat and drought share of crop insurance claims: 55 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, down to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the money paid out here over the years came from excess moisture and flood, at 44 percent of all indemnities. The loss ratio of 0.67 says claims have run below premiums over the whole record, and only 3 of 22 closed crop years paid out more than was collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $129 per acre in 2026, up 48.3 percent from 2016, and the county's corn yield trend is up 1.7 bushels per acre a year. Only 9 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated.

55139.text: Winnebago County's flood-and-wet losses stand out more than anything in the heat or drought columns. Excess moisture and flood made up 65 percent of the $36.5 million in crop insurance indemnities paid for closed crop years 1989-2025, and four of the 22 closed years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $123 per acre in 2026, up 25.5 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $8,641 per acre in 2022, and rent that year was 1.15 percent of that value.

55141.text: Wood County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities paid $74.9 million across the closed years since 1989, and the loss ratio was 0.91, so claims ran close to premium over the whole stretch. Nine of 25 crop years paid out more than the premium. Excess moisture and flood made up 51 percent of those claims, and heat and drought went from 7 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent is $82 per acre in 2026, up 25.4 percent from 2016.

01001.text: Autauga County's crop insurance record leans hard on heat and drought. Across the closed crop years 1989-2025, indemnities paid came to $10.1 million, and heat and drought made up 55 percent of that. Its share went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2000-2009 and 52 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 41 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio over the closed years is 0.72, and the ten most recent closed years was 0.56. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and that water is all groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre, up 50.7 percent since 2016.

01003.text: Baldwin County is a non-irrigated county in practice: only 21 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the irrigated cash rent of $143 per acre is well above the non-irrigated $90. The bigger story for growers is wet weather. Excess moisture and flood has been the largest cause of indemnities at 37 percent, and the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 show a loss ratio of 0.83, so claims have run ahead of premium. Heat and drought went from 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is up 27.7 percent since 2016, to $90 per acre.

01005.text: Barbour County's notable number is the loss ratio. Crop insurance has paid out $1.22 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and in 4 of those 11 years payouts ran above premium. Heat and drought drove most of it, though that share has come down from 75 percent in 2000-2009 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $58 per acre for 2026, up 69.6 percent since 2016. The county's own census value of land and buildings was $2,617 per acre in 2022, and the 233 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2000 are spread across the record, with 2012 the worst at 52 weeks.

01009.text: Blount County's loss record is what stands out. Crop insurance indemnities have paid out at a loss ratio of 0.72 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, up from 0.55 across 1989-2025, and heat and drought went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. Corn is a dry-years crop here: the median yield 2009-2025 is 128.4 bushels per acre, but the worst year, 2012, was 70. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $48 per acre, up 95.9 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground is rare at 2 percent of harvested cropland.

01013.text: Butler County's heat and drought story is the one to look at first. Heat and drought made up 23 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 61 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities were paid out at a loss ratio of 1.15 over the last ten closed crop years, so claims have run ahead of premiums. July nightly lows averaged 71.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 69.8 F normal, and the nightly low trend since 1976 is warming at 0.57 F per decade. Non-irrigated cash rent was $33 per acre in 2024.

01015.text: Calhoun County's corn record is shaped more by wet years than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 46 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1995 through 2025, and the county's loss ratio has climbed from 0.56 over that full span to 0.83 across the ten closed crop years 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims fell from 64 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 30 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $64 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,855 per acre in 2022. The county has no irrigation drawn from groundwater.

01017.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Chambers County. It accounts for 72 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 2005 to 2025, and its share went from 54 percent in 2000-2009 to 79 percent in 2010-2019 before coming back to 61 percent in 2020-2025. The county has 1 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. July nights are also running warmer, with the average low at 69.6 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 27.3 percent from 2016.

01019.text: Cherokee County is mostly dryland ground, with 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the drought record is what stands out. Heat and drought made up 91 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 23 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims have shifted a lot even as the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.63. Only 2 of 18 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre for 2026, up 12.5 percent since 2016, and irrigated rent is $172 per acre. Land and buildings were valued at $3,646 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

01021.text: Chilton County is a dryland county with a small irrigated base. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $24 per acre, down 12.5 percent from 2016. The county's heat and drought claims have been a small share of insurance payouts, going from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 7 percent in 2020-2025. The bigger story is freeze and frost, which caused 71 percent of the $18.9 million paid out on closed crop years 1989-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.04, so payouts have run a little above the premiums collected.

01023.text: Choctaw County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so rain decides the crop here. Heat and drought has become the main reason insurance claims get paid. It was 20 percent of indemnities over 2010-2019 and 59 percent over 2020-2025, and the county's largest share across 1990-2024 was 38 percent. July nights have warmed too: the average low ran 72.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.9 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre for 2026.

01025.text: Clarke County's heat is the thing to look at. July nightly lows averaged 72.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.9 F, and 63 Julys since 1900 have had an average low at or above 70 F. Heat and drought made up 70 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 44 percent in 2020-2025, still the largest cause. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $17 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings is $2,688 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar operating in the county.

01031.text: Coffee County is mostly dryland, and the heat and drought shows up in the claims. Heat and drought was 46 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 69 percent in 2000-2009, and it has stayed in the 60s since. Indemnities total $134.2 million over the closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.26, with payouts above premium in 20 of 34 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre in 2026, up 15.1 percent from 2016. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rainfall.

01033.text: Colbert County is mostly dryland, with just 4 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather runs straight into the crop. Heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims at 57 percent, and its share went from 47 percent in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.06, which means claims paid more than premium in that stretch. Corn yield has been flat, with a trend of 0.2 bushels per acre a year, and the worst year was 2022 at 94 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $105 per acre in 2026.

01035.text: Conecuh County's notable number is heat and drought. They made up 52 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 46 percent in 1989-1999, and the county's largest cause over the full 1989-2025 record at 50 percent. The 2011 drought was the worst year, with 45 weeks of severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated rent is $28 per acre in 2026, down 24.7 percent from 2016. The county's corn yield trend has been up 4.9 bushels per acre a year over 2009-2025, with a median of 116.2 bushels.

01039.text: Covington County is mostly dryland, with only 4 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so heat and drought carry most of the risk here. Heat and drought made up 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 38 percent in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2010-2019. Insurance has paid out more than the premiums collected: the loss ratio is 0.97 across closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, up 18.8 percent since 2016, and the census land value is $3,400 per acre. CRP covers 5212 acres, 12.1 percent of the cropland base.

01041.text: Crenshaw County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here lives or dies on rain. Heat and drought made up 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities over the closed years 1989-2025, and that share went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 75 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out $13.9 million, and the loss ratio is 1.1, which means claims have run past the premiums paid in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre for 2026, up 11.1 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,002 per acre in 2022.

01043.text: Cullman County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance record shows heat and drought as the largest cause of indemnities at 41 percent of the total since 1989. That share went from 24 percent in 1989-1999 to 82 percent in 2020-2025, so heat and drought have been carrying more of the claims in recent years. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.75, and the July nightly low has averaged 70.5 F over 2017-2026 against a 68.6 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 14.5 percent since 2016.

01045.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

01047.text: Dallas County has a loss ratio of 1.23 over the last ten closed crop years, which means insurance has paid out more than the premiums taken in during that stretch. Heat and drought claims were 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2000-2009, and they were 41 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the ground here is non-irrigated, with irrigated land at 15 percent of harvested cropland, and non-irrigated rent is $36 per acre. The July nightly low has averaged 72.5 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.1 F. The census land value is $2,402 per acre, and it rose 28.1 percent from 2017 to 2022.

01049.text: Heat and drought is the main thing to watch in DeKalb County. Its share of crop insurance payouts went from 61 percent in 1989-1999 to 47 percent in 2020-2025, but it still led every period. Since 1989, closed crop years paid out $14.6 million, with a loss ratio of 0.52. Two of the fifteen closed crop years paid more than the premium collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre in 2026, up 15.4 percent since 2016, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Weeks in severe drought ran to 16 across 2021-2025, and the 2017-2026 July nightly lows averaged 68 F.

01051.text: Elmore County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 9 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the corn crop lives or dies on rain. Heat and drought was the biggest cause of insurance claims over 1989-2025, at 51 percent of the $9.8 million paid, and its share fell from 67 percent in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.81, up from 0.65 across 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre for 2026, up 15.6 percent since 2016.

01053.text: Escambia County's ground is mostly dryland, and the weather risk shows up most in the insurance claims. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities over 1989-2025 at 38 percent, and its share went from 33 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.85, so claims paid out more than premium over that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $101 per acre, up 18.1 percent since 2016. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county's corn rides on rain.

01055.text: Etowah County is a dryland county. Only 6 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the corn sees whatever rain falls, and when the rain stops the claims show it. Heat and drought is still the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities at 51 percent over 1994-2025, but its share fell from 82 percent in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.78, and the 2012 corn yield of 83.5 bushels per acre is the worst year in the record. Non-irrigated rent is $60 per acre in 2026, up 63 percent since 2016.

01057.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

01061.text: Geneva County is mostly dryland, and its weather record is the story. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims, taking 55 percent of the $171.3 million paid out from 1989-2025, and it went from 50 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025. Over those same closed crop years, the loss ratio is 1.19, with 22 of 35 years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre in 2026, up 20.2 percent since 2016. Only 12 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's corn yield trend is 3.1 bushels per acre a year.

01063.text: Greene County is a dryland county. Irrigated ground has no rent figure here, so the county average is for non-irrigated ground at $26 per acre in 2026, up 4 percent from 2016. The number that stands out is insurance. Crop insurance has paid out $7.2 million on closed crop years since 1989, and claims have paid back 2.83 times premium over the last ten closed years. Heat and drought was the largest cause, at 44 percent of indemnities over the full run. Its share went from 34 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 51 percent in 2010-2019. Land and buildings were valued at $2,573 per acre in 2022, a 31.9 percent rise from 2017.

01065.text: Hale County's crop insurance record leans hard on heat and drought, and the mix has shifted over the decades. Heat and drought made up 41 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 72 percent in 2000-2009, then came down to 29 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.16, so claims have run ahead of premiums recently. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $52 per acre, up 56.7 percent since 2016. Every bit of the irrigation water comes from groundwater.

01067.text: Henry County's corn is mostly rain-fed, and the insurance record is where the county's water trouble shows up. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of the $134.6 million paid out on closed crop years from 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.23, with 17 of 37 crop years paying more than the premium they took in. Heat and drought was 51 percent of claims in 1989-1999, rose to 77 percent in 2000-2009, and was 54 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre for 2026, up 27.2 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $129 per acre.

01069.text: Houston County is mostly dryland, and its farmers have been paying out more in crop claims than they've paid in premium. Heat and drought is the cause behind most of that: 59 percent of the $194.6 million in indemnities since 1989, and it went from 52 percent in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025. Only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground that does get water is rented at $203 per acre against $61 for dryland. Non-irrigated rent is up 38.6 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,685 per acre, and CRP covers 3.2 percent of the cropland base.

01071.text: Jackson County is mostly dryland, and the main thing to know is how often the rain has failed here. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims since 1989, and it made up 71 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, down to 52 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.87, and corn yields were cut to 80.5 bushels per acre in 2016 against a median of 124.8. Non-irrigated rent is $62 per acre, up 50 percent since 2016, while the census value of land and buildings was $3,511 per acre in 2022. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

01075.text:
Lamar County's crop insurance record leans on heat and drought more than most. Over the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio was 0.95, meaning claims ran close to the premiums paid in, and heat and drought was the largest cause of claims since 1989 at 39 percent. Its share was 49 percent in 1989-1999, 57 percent in 2000-2009, and 54 percent in 2010-2019, before falling to 27 percent in 2020-2025.

July nights have also warmed. The average July low for 2017-2026 is 71.4 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.8 F. Rent is $40 per acre in 2026, up 52.8 percent from 2016.

01077.text: Lauderdale County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn crop rides on rain. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims since 1989, and its share rose from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.85, which means the county has paid out more than it took in premium recently. The county's census land value is $5,183 per acre, and non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $78 per acre.

01079.text: Lawrence County's notable pattern is heat and drought in the claims. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2010-2019, and it was still 54 percent in 2020-2025. Over closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.94, with 8 of 27 years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $113 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,865 per acre, with irrigated ground only 5 percent of harvested cropland.

01081.text: Lee County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 19 percent of harvested acres irrigated in 2022, and heat and drought has been the main claim cause for a long time. Heat and drought went from 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio for 1990-2025 is 0.79. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 7.8 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $5,018 per acre in 2022, and the county's July nightly lows averaged 70.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.7 F.

01083.text: Limestone County is mostly dryland, and the risk that stands out is heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full record at 56 percent. Those claims add up to $78.5 million since 1989 against a loss ratio of 0.78, so the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 8 of 30 crop years. The median corn yield is 159.8 bushels per acre, but the worst year, 2012, was 71.9. Non-irrigated cash rent is $139 per acre in 2026, up 51.9 percent since 2016. Only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

01087.text: Macon County's notable number is the heat and drought claims. From 1989-1999 to 2010-2019 that share ran between 52 and 63 percent of indemnities, then fell to 17 percent for 2020-2025. Total indemnities across closed crop years are $5.8 million, with a loss ratio of 0.74. Non-irrigated cash rent is $41 per acre in 2026, up 13.9 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings were valued at $2,687 per acre in 2022. July nightly lows averaged 71.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.8 F.

01089.text: Madison County is mostly dryland, and the weather has been the main thing taking claims. Heat and drought made up 18 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 66 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025, indemnities totaled $60.4 million, and the county has paid out more than premium in 4 of 28 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.63. The yield trend is 2.3 bushels per acre a year, and the worst year was 2012 at 110.6 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $113 per acre in 2025, up 69.9 percent since 2014.

01091.text: Heat and drought is the main cause of claims in Marengo County. Its share of indemnities went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.44, so insurers have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which leaves most of the ground dependent on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre in 2026, up 23.4 percent since 2016. The county's July nightly lows have run warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, with the 2017-2026 average at 71.9 F against 70.9 F.

01095.text: Marshall County is a non-irrigated county, and the thing to watch here is the heat and drought claims. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, at 59 percent of $6.7 million. Its share went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio of 0.66 over those years means claims ran below premium overall, but the last ten closed crop years was 0.72. The non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026, up 8.1 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 70.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.1 F.

01097.text: Mobile County's most notable number is the rent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $84 per acre in 2026, and it has climbed 89.8 percent since 2016. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 96 percent of that water comes from groundwater, so most of the ground here is dryland. Heat and drought claims went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.74 over 1989-2025. Excess moisture and flood, not drought, is the largest cause of claims at 41 percent.

01099.text: Monroe County's heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought was 45 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 59 percent in 2020-2025, and it has been the largest cause over the full record at 51 percent. The loss ratio of 0.87 across closed crop years means insurers paid out more than premium in 4 of 24 years, and the worst corn year was 2011 at 72.4 bushels. Non-irrigated rent is $66 per acre in 2026, while the 2022 census value of $2,399 per acre was the operators' own estimate and the land value has held flat since 2017.

01101.text: Montgomery County's cropland is mostly dryland. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 88 percent of what water is used comes from groundwater. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities, at 44 percent since 1989. Its share was 47 percent in 1989-1999, 73 percent in 2000-2009, 32 percent in 2010-2019, and 39 percent in 2020-2025. The worst year was 2012, with 39 weeks of severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 7.3 percent from 2016. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.82, so claims have run above premium. CRP covers 17.1 percent of the cropland base.

01103.text: Morgan County's corn is mostly watered by sky, and the bad years show it. Heat and drought made up 16 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 69 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.99. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $65 per acre, up 132.1 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $6,130 per acre, a figure the operators themselves estimated, and the July nightly low has averaged 70.7 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F.

01105.text: Perry County is mostly dryland, with only 9 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and the groundwater behind that irrigation is the whole supply. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 47 percent, and its share went from 25 percent in 1989-1999 to 47 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.06, so claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre in 2025, up 40 percent since 2014, and the census value of land and buildings is $2,354 per acre in 2022.

01107.text: Pickens County is a dry-year county mostly by way of the claims, and the heat has been creeping up. Flood and excess moisture is the biggest cause of crop insurance payments since 1989, at 40 percent. Heat and drought was 73 percent of claims in 2000-2009 and only 6 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years have not come as often lately. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.11, which means the claims paid out more than the premiums brought in. The non-irrigated rent is $50 per acre, up 200 percent since 2016. There is no groundwater irrigation here.

01109.text: Pike County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid $43.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.28, with three of the ten closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 55 percent of those indemnities, and its share went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. The corn yield trend is up 3.1 bushels per acre a year over 2009-2025, with a median of 101.9 and a worst year of 64.8 in 2011. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre in 2026.

01111.text: Randolph County is a non-irrigated county, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the rent and the yield record mostly reflect dryland ground. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, up 2 percent from 2016. The corn yield trend fitted over 2011-2024 is up 4.5 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 98.3 bushels and a worst year of 2011 at 60. Heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims at 48 percent since 2002, and it went from 56 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Census land and buildings are valued at $4,005 per acre in 2022, up 26.9 percent from 2017.

01113.text: Heat and drought is the main reason claims get paid in Russell County. Since 1989 it has accounted for 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities, and the share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 70 percent in 2010-2019 before dropping to 46 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.88, and the July nightly low has averaged 71.2 F over 2017-2026 against a normal of 70.5 F. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre for 2026.

01115.text: St. Clair County's heat is the story here more than its drought. The July average nightly low for 2017-2026 is 70.2 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F, and the July low has been warming 0.51 F per decade since 1976. Julys with an average low at or above 70 F have happened 15 times since 1900. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026, up 55.3 percent from 2016. Heat and drought made up 59 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019 and 22 percent in 2020-2025. Flooding and excess moisture is the largest cause of claims over the whole record, at 75 percent.

01117.text: Shelby County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 10 percent irrigated in 2022, so rent and yield both depend on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, down 9.8 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $70. Heat and drought claims made up 66 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 29 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather risk that drove payouts earlier has shown up less in recent claims. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1994-2025 is 0.61, meaning indemnities have run below premiums overall. The census land value of $5,118 per acre in 2022 is well above the cash rent.

01119.text: Sumter County's notable number is the crop insurance loss ratio of 1.15 over closed crop years 1989-2025, meaning claims paid out more than premium collected, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 36 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought was 28 percent in 1989-1999 and 16 percent in 2020-2025, so it has been a smaller share of claims lately. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, down 4.8 percent from 2016. CRP covers 25.8 percent of the cropland base.

01121.text: Talladega County is mostly non-irrigated ground, and the rent reflects that: $54 per acre for non-irrigated land in 2026, up 25.9 percent since 2016. Irrigated rent was $105 per acre in 2024, and the gap between the two has widened from 1.83 in 2010 to 2.96 in 2024. Heat and drought was the largest source of crop insurance claims, at 55 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, though its share fell from 58 percent in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. The worst year for corn was 2024, at 113.6 bushels per acre against a median of 139.2. Land and buildings were valued at $3,914 per acre in 2022.

01123.text: Tallapoosa County is not a county where water is the main worry on paper. The census shows 36 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, and only 5 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The bigger story in the claims is heat and drought, which made up 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1995-2025, though that share was 62 percent in 1989-1999. July nights are warmer than they used to be: the average low is 69.7 F for 2017-2026 against a 68.7 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent was $21 per acre in 2024, down 8.7 percent from 2014. Census land and buildings value was $3,062 per acre in 2022.

01125.text: Tuscaloosa County is mostly dryland, and heat and drought is what has cost growers money here. Heat and drought made up 72 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 78 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 42 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.46 over 1989-2025, so claims have run below premiums, though the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.52. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre for 2026, up 16.5 percent since 2016. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

01127.text: Walker County is a non-irrigated county, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, so the rain it gets is the crop's water. Heat and drought are the story in the insurance claims: they were 9 percent of indemnities over 2010-2019 and 69 percent over 2020-2025, and they are the largest cause over 2016-2025 at 37 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $24 per acre, down 11.1 percent from 2016. The median corn yield for 2013-2025 is 123.8 bushels per acre, with 2024 the worst year at 73.1. The July nightly low has been warming at 0.39 F per decade since 1976, and the 2017-2026 average of 70.6 F is above the 1991-2020 normal of 69.6 F.

01129.text: Washington County's heat-and-drought story is mostly in the past. Heat and drought made up 60 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019, but only 5 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.47, well under the 0.69 for the full 1989-2025 record. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. July nightly lows averaged 72.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 71 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent was $38 per acre in 2025, up 48.1 percent since 2014. Census land and buildings were valued at $2,714 per acre in 2022, up 34 percent from 2017.

01131.text: Wilcox County is dryland, and it is a county where the heat shows up more than the drought. None of the harvested cropland was reported irrigated in 2022, so every crop here lives or dies on what the sky gives it. Heat and drought was still the largest cause of indemnities over 1989-2025, at 40 percent of the $4.7 million paid, though its share fell from 41 percent in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years was 0.82, so insurance has paid out less than the premiums taken in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 36.7 percent from 2016, and census land and buildings were valued at $2,163 per acre in 2022.

01133.text: Winston County is mostly dryland, and the weather record is what stands out. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so rain carries most of the crop. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 37 percent of indemnities, and it still made up 36 percent for 2020-2025. The county has also been in severe drought for 139 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with 40 of those weeks in 2007 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre in 2026, up 43.2 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,005 per acre in 2022.

02013.text: Aleutians East is a cool county and the numbers don't show much change. The July average nightly low for 2017-2026 is 47.2 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 46.5 F. The long trend since 1976 is 0.28 F per decade, which is not a clear trend. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, and the county has had no weeks with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse from 2000-2025. On the energy side, the county has 1 MW of wind operating and no solar, and nothing new is proposed to the EIA.

02050.text: The most notable thing here is how little has changed in the things that usually move this ground. There are no drought weeks on record for this county in 2000-2025, and no solar or wind operating or proposed. The July nightly low has come in at 48 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 47.4 F, and the long-run trend since 1976 is 0.36 F per decade, which is warming. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. For a grower or a landowner, that points to a stable, cool-summer picture rather than a heat or water problem.

02060.text: Bristol Bay Borough is a quiet county on the climate side. July nights have averaged 48 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 47.7 F. The July low trend since 1976 is not a clear trend, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Weeks with severe drought or worse covering the county are none for 2000-2025. There is no solar or wind operating here, and nothing proposed to EIA.

02068.text: Denali Borough is a place where the July nights are running a little warmer than they used to. The average July low over 2017-2026 is 45.1 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 43.9 F, and the long trend since 1976 is warming at 0.3 F per decade. No July since 1900 has had an average low at or above 70 F. The county has had no weeks with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse since 2000. Wind is the energy on the ground here, with 24.6 MW operating and nothing new proposed to EIA, and there is no solar operating.

02070.text: Dillingham is a cool county, and the summer numbers are steady. July nights averaged 47.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 47.3 F. That is a small difference, and the trend since 1976 is not a clear one. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. The county has had no weeks with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse from 2000-2025. There is no solar or wind operating here, and nothing proposed to EIA. For ground in this county, the main things to watch are the weather itself and the land's own use, not heat or dry spells.

02105.text: Hoonah-Angoon is a county where the heat and drought numbers are quiet. The July nights are a little warmer than they were: the average low for 2017-2026 is 46.2 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 45.7 F. Since 1976 the July low has been trending warmer at 0.45 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, and there have been no weeks since 2000 with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. There is no solar or wind capacity operating in the county, and none proposed to EIA.

02158.text: Kusilvak is a county where the story is warming nights, not drought. July nights averaged 48.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 48 F. The nightly low has trended warm at 0.51 F per decade since 1976. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, and no week in 2000-2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. There is no solar or wind capacity operating here, and none proposed to EIA.

02164.text: Lake and Peninsula Borough is a quiet one on the numbers here. July nights in 2017-2026 averaged 46.5 F, just above the 1991-2020 normal of 46 F. The nightly low trend since 1976 is not a clear trend, so I wouldn't read anything into it. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, and the county has had no weeks with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse since 2000. There is no solar or wind operating in the county, and nothing proposed to EIA.

02180.text: Nome in July is a cool place, and the nights are staying a bit warmer than they used to. The average July low over 2017-2026 is 46.6 F, against 45.3 F for the 1991-2020 normal, and the record since 1976 shows a warming trend of 0.49 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Wind is the only power on the books here, at 1.8 MW, with nothing proposed.

02188.text: Northwest Arctic Borough is a place where the warming shows up mostly as a slow drift in summer nights. The July average low for 2017-2026 is 47.8 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 46.7 F. Since 1976 the July nightly low has been trending warmer at 0.46 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, and no weeks since 2000 have had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. The county has 1.7 MW of solar and 3.3 MW of wind operating now, with nothing new proposed to EIA. For a farmer or landowner, the story here is cool nights getting a little less cool, not a dry summer.

02198.text: This is a cool, wet county where the heat numbers barely move. July nights have averaged 51 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 50.5 F, and the long-run trend is 0.35 F per decade. No July since 1900 has had an average low at or above 70 F. Drought has been rare here too: 58 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2019 accounts for 44 of those. The last five years show no such weeks. There is no solar or wind capacity operating in the county, and none proposed to EIA.

02230.text: Skagway's summers have been getting warmer at night, but slowly. July nightly lows averaged 44.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 43 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.63 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. The county has had no weeks with at least 50 percent of its land in severe drought or worse since 2000, and there is no solar or wind capacity operating or proposed here. For a farm or landowner, the story is a gentle warming trend with no drought pressure on record.

02261.text: Valdez-Cordova has no cropland in the Atlas and no insurance claims. The data here cover temperature only. July nights have warmed 0.4 F per decade since 1976. The recent decade, 2017-2026, averaged a nightly low of 44.2 F, compared to the 1991-2020 normal of 43.6 F. No July since 1900 has had an average nightly low at or above 70 F.

02282.text: Yakutat's summer nights are running a little warmer than they used to. July lows averaged 44 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 42.7 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.49 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. The county has had no weeks in severe drought or worse since 2000, so water hasn't been the pressure here. There is no solar or wind operating or proposed for the county.

04007.text: Gila County is a fully irrigated county, and that shapes everything else here. Every acre of harvested cropland in the 2022 census was irrigated. The July nights are getting warmer: the average low has been 66.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.2 F, and it has not yet hit 70 F in any July since 1900. Drought has been a steady pressure too. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 439 of 1357 over 2000-2025, with the worst year at 46 weeks in 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $356 per acre, and that figure was down 8.5 percent from 2017 to 2022.

04012.text: La Paz County is all irrigated cropland, and the insurance record shows it. The loss ratio was 1.72 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, meaning insurers paid out more than the premiums collected. Heat and drought claims went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, so the freeze and frost losses have taken up more of the picture. Irrigation failure claims total only $979,237 across all closed years. The July nightly low has averaged 81.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 79.2 F.

04015.text: Mohave County's July nights are the story here. The average July low for 2017-2026 is 72.8 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.8 F, and the July low has been warming 0.78 F per decade since 1976. Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F number 61. Water is the other piece: 44 percent of irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought made up 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1999-2018, and the loss ratio for closed crop years 1995-2025 is 0.23. Census land and buildings were valued at $1,045 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

04027.text: Yuma County is an irrigated county, and every acre of harvested cropland here is watered. Heat and drought is the largest cause of claims since 1993, and its share went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025. The crop insurance loss ratio for 2016-2025 is 1.1, so insurers have paid out more than they took in premium over that stretch. Groundwater supplies only 10 percent of irrigation water, so most of the supply comes from surface sources. Land is valued at $8,662 per acre in the 2022 census, which is the operators' own estimate and not a sale price.

05001.text: This county is mostly ground that has to be watered to pay. Irrigated ground rents for $158 per acre in 2026, and non-irrigated ground for $98 in 2025, so the wet ground is what carries the rent. The county's crop insurance has paid out more than it took in premiums over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.01 for 2016-2025. Most of the water comes from wells, 54 percent in 2015. Heat and drought claims went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst single year was 2009 at 160 bushels per acre.
