05003.text: Ashley County's biggest flag is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 7 of 31 closed crop years, and the loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 1.21. Excess moisture and flood account for 66 percent of the $79.8 million paid since 1989, so the wet years do most of the damage here, not the dry ones. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $46 per acre in 2017, and irrigated rent is $170 per acre in 2026. Groundwater supplies 89 percent of irrigation water.

05009.text: Boone County is a non-irrigated county, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the rent and the weather both have to be read against dry ground. Cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026, up 24.6 percent from 2016. The notable number on the insurance side is the loss ratio of 1.36 for closed crop years 2009-2025, which means claims paid out more than the premiums brought in. Freeze and frost made up 89 percent of those indemnities, and heat and drought went from 0 percent in 2000-2009 and 2010-2019 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks in the county were 15 for 2021-2025, with 2012 the worst year at 28 weeks.

05011.text: Bradley County's notable number is the crop insurance record: indemnities have run above premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.6 across closed crop years 1989-2025 and 1.38 over 2016-2025. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 48 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent was $12 per acre in 2022. The July nightly low averaged 72.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.1 F.

05015.text: Carroll County is a non-irrigated county, with none of its harvested cropland under irrigation in the 2022 census, so every drought week lands on the crop. The county rent is $50 per acre for 2026, up 47.1 percent from 2016. The 2022 census value of land and buildings is $3,992 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate and not a sale price, and it rose 45.2 percent between 2017 and 2022. Severe drought covered at least 50 percent of the county in 77 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, with 28 of those weeks in 2012. The county has 71 CRP acres, and 41 of them come up for expiration in fiscal years 2027-2029.

05017.text: Chicot County is a flood-and-rent county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 56 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.17, meaning claims ran past premiums. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025, with 35 weeks of severe drought in 2021-2025. Irrigated rent is $165 per acre against $159 for non-irrigated, a gap that was 1.77 times in 2009 and is now 1.04 times. Non-irrigated rent is up 63.9 percent since 2016.

05019.text: Clark County's claims history leans toward too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood make up 63 percent of the $15.0 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.44 for that span and 1.59 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims were 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 9 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has dropped. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026, up 146.9 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,036 per acre in 2022, after a 25.4 percent rise from 2017. July nightly lows have averaged 71.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 70.3 F normal for 1991-2020.

05021.text: Clay County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the water-related claims here have come mostly from too much rain, not too little. Excess moisture and flood make up 79 percent of the $103.9 million in indemnities paid since 1989, while heat and drought went from 17 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.1, so insurers paid out more than the premiums that came in. Non-irrigated cash rent was $42 per acre in 2025, and irrigated rent was $195 per acre in 2026, with 98 percent of irrigation water coming from groundwater.

05029.text: Conway County's notable number is the insurance record. Crop insurance has paid out $11.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 1.12, which means claims ran above premiums. Excess moisture and flood account for 67 percent of that, while heat and drought went from 60 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $24 per acre, up 58.1 percent from 2016. Two-thirds of irrigation water comes from groundwater.

05031.text: Craighead County's cropland leans on water from underground. Groundwater supplies 84 percent of irrigation, and irrigated rent is $159 per acre in 2026, against $54 for non-irrigated ground in 2023. That gap was 1.95 times in 2009 and is 3.32 times now, so irrigated ground has pulled well ahead. Insurance has paid out more than premium here over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.07, and the most recent ten years run at 1.42. Most of those claims come from excess moisture and flood, not heat. Heat and drought went from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 7 percent in 2020-2025.

05035.text: Crittenden County is mostly irrigated, and it is a county where wet years cost more than dry ones. Irrigated ground is 65 percent of harvested cropland and all of its irrigation water comes from groundwater. Flood and excess moisture make up 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.82 over closed crop years, with 6 of 32 years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims went from 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $109 per acre and irrigated is $157 per acre, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,236 per acre in 2022.

05037.text: Cross County is mostly irrigated ground, with 83 percent of harvested cropland watered and 92 percent of that water pulled from groundwater. The thing that stands out in the claims is flooding. Excess moisture and flood make up 77 percent of indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.16 over the closed years, with 14 of 28 crop years paying out more than premium. Over 2016-2025 that ratio climbed to 1.36. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $140 per acre and irrigated is $149, so the two sit close together now.

05043.text: Drew County is mostly irrigated, and that shapes everything else here. Irrigated ground is 78 percent of harvested cropland, and 82 percent of the water comes from groundwater. The irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre against $39 for non-irrigated ground, and the non-irrigated rent is up 143.8 percent since 2016. The loss ratio of 1.13 says insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the closed years, and in the last ten crop years it ran 1.38. Most of those claims were excess moisture and flood, not heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 7 percent in 2020-2025.

05045.text:
Faulkner County is a rain county more than a heat or water county. Crop insurance has paid out $12.2 million on closed crop years since 1989, and excess moisture and flood caused 77 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.32 over the full run and 1.51 over the last ten closed crop years, so claims have run above premium. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025.

Irrigated ground rents for $100 per acre, while non-irrigated rent is $26, down 20 percent since 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 71.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.4 F, and the nightly low trend since 1976 is warming at 0.37 F per decade.

05047.text: Franklin County's crop insurance record leans toward too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 53 percent of the indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 1.37, meaning the county has paid out more than it took in premium. Heat and drought claims have moved around a lot, from 38 percent in 1989-1999 down to 25 percent in 2000-2009 and up to 50 percent in 2010-2019, then 39 percent in 2020-2025. The non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, up 60.6 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,245 per acre in 2022, up 26.6 percent from 2017.

05049.text: Fulton County's notable number is the rent jump. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 42.2 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $2,239 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 19.9 percent from 2017 to 2022. Drought has been light here: 94 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2012 the worst year at 28 weeks. The July nights are running a little warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, 68.6 F against 67 F. Only 1 acre is enrolled in CRP, and there is 1 MW of solar and no wind operating.

05053.text: Grant County has no irrigated harvested cropland at all, so every acre here is dryland, and that makes its weather record the main thing to watch. The July nightly low has averaged 72 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.9 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.47 F per decade. Julys with an average low at or above 70 F have shown up 67 times since 1900. Non-irrigated cash rent is $13 per acre for 2026, down 13.3 percent from 2014. The census value of land and buildings is $3,912 per acre, up 8.3 percent from 2017 to 2022.

05055.text: Greene County's cropland is mostly watered from wells, and irrigated ground rents for $192 per acre against $105 for dry ground. Corn yields show a fitted gain of 2.9 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 176 bushels and a worst year at 110.3 in 2011. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premium over the years, with a loss ratio of 1.25, and excess moisture and flood account for 82 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought claims went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 4 percent in 2020-2025.

05057.text: Hempstead County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested acres irrigated in 2022. Heat and drought was a small share of crop insurance claims in 1989-1999, at 2 percent, and it rose to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Most indemnity dollars came from other causes, at 59 percent of the $712,254 paid for closed crop years from 1989 to 2024. July nights have warmed too: the average low was 71.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 50 percent from 2016, and census land and buildings were valued at $2,902 per acre in 2022.

05059.text: What stands out in Hot Spring County is the flood side of the ledger. Excess moisture and flood took 90 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1990-2024, and the loss ratio for closed crop years is 1.51, so claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought claims went from 10 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, up 70 percent since 2016. July nights have warmed a bit, with the 2017-2026 average low at 71.7 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.3 F.

05061.text: Howard County's biggest insurance story is frost, not heat. Freeze and frost made up 58 percent of crop indemnities paid from 1989-2023, and heat and drought made up 0 percent of claims in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 70.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.5 F, and 31 Julys since 1900 have averaged 70 F or higher. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026, up 18.5 percent since 2016. The land and buildings census value was $4,175 per acre in 2022, which rose 46.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

05063.text: Independence County is mostly dryland, but the loss record is where to look first. Indemnities have paid out more than premium, with a loss ratio of 1.05 across 1989-2025 and 1.22 over 2016-2025, and most of the money has come from excess moisture and flood at 81 percent. Heat and drought claims have been a smaller share, going from 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $28 per acre, down 25 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $143 per acre in 2023, and 44 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 70 percent of that water from groundwater.

05065.text: Izard County's most notable number is the rent jump. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 133.3 percent since 2016. Land values were $2,778 per acre in the 2022 census, up 35.7 percent from 2017, which is a fast climb for ground that is mostly dryland. Summers here have been warmer at night, with the July average low at 68.7 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.6 F. Drought weeks are a steady part of the record: 104 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with the worst year being 2012 at 28 weeks. The county has no CRP acres and no wind or solar operating or proposed.

05069.text: Jefferson County is an irrigated county more than a dryland one, and the water comes mostly from wells. Irrigated ground rents for $185 per acre against $82 for non-irrigated, which was $1.10 for every dollar of dryland rent in 2008 and is now $2.24. Insurance has paid out $173.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and excess moisture and flood account for 64 percent of that, against 39 percent for heat and drought in 1989-1999 and 22 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.3, with 11 of 31 years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought weeks are present in the record too, 124 weeks since 2000, with 36 of them in 2021-2025.

05071.text: Johnson County is mostly dryland, and the water trouble here shows up in the insurance claims more than anywhere else. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 47 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025. That share went from 36 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 56 percent in 2010-2019. The county has paid out more than it took in on claims over the full record, with a loss ratio of 0.95, though the last ten closed crop years came in lower at 0.64. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre, up 80.8 percent since 2016.

05073.text: Lafayette County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the insurance record here runs more on too much water than too little. Indemnities over 1989-2025 were $44.8 million, and excess moisture and flood made up 63 percent of that. Heat and drought claims went from 37 percent in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.44, so claims ran well ahead of premium in recent years. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2025 was $58 per acre, up 79.7 percent since 2014, and irrigated ground was $174 per acre for 2026.

05075.text: Lawrence County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the loss history is the thing to look at first. Insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2025 total $183.0 million, and 93 percent of that came from excess moisture and flood, not heat or drought. The loss ratio over closed crop years is 1.58, and 12 of 19 crop years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims fell from 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 3 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $90 per acre in 2026, up 74.8 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,609 per acre in 2022.

05077.text: Lee County's corn is mostly irrigated, and the water comes from the ground: 73 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, and 98 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. The county's insurance record has run worse than the premiums in recent years. The loss ratio was 1.15 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, and the 1989-2025 ratio is 0.96. Flood and excess moisture cause the largest share of claims, at 56 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 24 percent in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2000-2009, and were 24 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $152 per acre in 2026, against $100 for non-irrigated in 2025.

05081.text: Little River County is a wet-year county more than a dry-year one. Excess moisture and flood account for 61 percent of the indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio of 1.28 means claims have paid out more than premium in 9 of 12 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims have held between 28 and 34 percent of indemnities in every period since 1989. July nights are warmer than they used to be, with the 2017-2026 average low at 72.8 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.2 F. Only 22 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 30 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre for 2026, up 12 percent from 2016.

05083.text: Heat and drought is the story in Logan County. It was 25 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, 54 percent in 2010-2019, and 66 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed years 1989-2025 is 0.99, so claims have come close to matching premiums over the whole run. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most acres are riding on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $33 per acre, up 120 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $3,129 per acre, and it rose 25.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

05085.text: Lonoke County is an irrigated county first. Seventy-nine percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 65 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $174 per acre this year, while non-irrigated ground is $30, which is down 9.1 percent since 2016. The crop insurance record is the other thing to note: indemnities have paid out more than premium over the last ten closed crop years, at a loss ratio of 1.76. Excess moisture and flood, not heat, is the largest cause, at 71 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025.

05087.text: Madison County's non-irrigated cash rent is $53 per acre for 2026, and it has climbed 158.5 percent since 2016, so the ground is renting for a lot more than it did ten years ago. Land and buildings were valued at $4,232 per acre in the 2022 census, up 35.1 percent from 2017, which is the operators' own estimate rather than a sale price. The county has no CRP acres, and the only energy on the ground is 5 MW of solar in operation, with no wind and nothing proposed. July nights have averaged 67.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 66.4 F normal for 1991-2020, and the July nightly low has no clear trend since 1976. Weeks in severe drought or worse have been 16 across 2021-2025.

05091.text: Miller County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Closed crop years from 1989 to 2025 paid out $135.3 million, and the loss ratio is 1.59, with 15 of 24 years paying more than the premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 53 percent. Heat and drought went from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. The 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.95. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre, up 64.1 percent since 2016, and the census land value is $3,500 per acre, so rent is 1.54 percent of that value.

05095.text: Monroe County is mostly a dryland corn and rice ground story, and what stands out is how much the water claims have shifted. Excess moisture and flood account for 74 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, while heat and drought went from 34 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.56, so insurers have paid out more than they took in premium. Irrigated ground rents for $157 per acre in 2026, and 91 percent of the irrigation water comes from groundwater.

05097.text: Montgomery County is a small county where the notable thing is the heat. The July nightly low has averaged 69.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F, and the July nightly low trend since 1976 is 0.61 F per decade, trend warming. There have been 18 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Drought is present too: 127 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2011 the worst year at 30 weeks. Rent is $28 per acre for non-irrigated ground this year, up 39 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings value was $3,481 per acre in 2022. There are 6 CRP acres and no wind or solar yet.

05099.text: Nevada County is a dry-ground county in the sense that the trouble comes from the sky, not the ground. Drought hit hard in 2011, when 33 weeks had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 121 of 1357 weeks since 2000 went that way. Since 2021 the count is 10 weeks, so the county has been quieter lately. Nights are running warm, with the July average low at 71.4 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $19 per acre in 2026, up 11.8 percent from 2016. Cropland is not heavily signed up for CRP, at 148 acres, and 27 of those acres come up for renewal in fiscal years 2027-2029.

05101.text: Newton County is dryland all the way, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census, so rent and ground value are set by rain and by what a farmer can count on in a dry July. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $26 per acre for 2026, up 27.5 percent from 2014. The census put land and buildings at $3,159 per acre in 2022, a 29.7 percent rise from 2017. Severe drought has touched the county in 91 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with the worst year 2012 at 28 weeks, and 16 weeks in the last five years. The July nightly low averaged 67.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 66.5 F normal for 1991-2020.

05105.text: Perry County's biggest story on the insurance side is water, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 84 percent of the $6.0 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 1.72, meaning claims ran well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought claims fell from 15 percent of the total in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has crept up to 71.1 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $27 per acre, down 6.9 percent since 2016.

05111.text: Poinsett County is mostly irrigated and mostly watered from the ground, and the water problem here has been too much rain more than too little. Excess moisture and flood make up 72 percent of the insurance payments since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.98 over the full span, with 9 of 31 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $110 per acre in 2026 and irrigated rent is $184, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,440 per acre in 2022.

05113.text: Polk County's rent is up sharply from 2016, and that comes with a warm summer picture. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre for 2026, and it has gone up 77.1 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,901 per acre in 2022, which rose 31.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nights have been warmer too: the average low for 2017-2026 is 68.5 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.7 F, and the trend since 1976 is up 0.46 F per decade. Weeks of severe drought or worse were 16 over 2021-2025, and the worst year was 2012 with 28 weeks. The county has 1 MW of solar operating and no wind.

05115.text: Pope County's cropland is mostly dryland, with 21 percent irrigated in 2022, and the county's insurance record leans toward wet years. Excess moisture and flood made up 53 percent of indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.82, so claims have run well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $19 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $3,861 per acre in 2022.

05117.text: Most of Prairie County's cropland is irrigated, and that is what sets the rent here. Irrigated ground rents for $140 per acre in 2026, while non-irrigated ground goes for $26, and the irrigated rent was 1.53 times the dryland rent in 2009 and is now 5.38 times it. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.08 over closed crop years 1989-2025, and 1.27 over 2016-2025. Excess moisture and flood account for 72 percent of those indemnities. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $3,560 per acre in 2022.

05119.text: Pulaski County's notable number is the rent falling while the ground is still worth a lot. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $39 per acre, down 25 percent from 2014, yet the census puts land and buildings at $4,602 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 17.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. Flood and excess moisture is the biggest source of crop insurance indemnities at 62 percent, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.24, with 1.66 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, and 41 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

05121.text: Randolph County's ground is mostly irrigated, and that changes how the rent numbers should be read. Irrigated ground rents for $172 per acre in 2026, against $35 for non-irrigated, and the ratio between them has jumped around without a clear direction. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.26 over 1989-2025, and 1.51 over the last ten closed crop years, mostly from excess moisture and flood, which account for 89 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $4,053 per acre in 2022, a figure that reflects operators' own estimates.

05123.text: St. Francis County is a mostly irrigated county, and that shapes everything else. Irrigated cash rent is $152 per acre in 2026 against $136 for non-irrigated ground, and the county's 2022 census shows 74 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, with 94 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Non-irrigated rent has climbed 142.9 percent since 2016. Insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.06, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 59 percent. Heat and drought went from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025.

05125.text: Saline County is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent and the weather are what most growers here live with. Non-irrigated cash rent is $17 per acre in 2026, down 20.9 percent from 2016. The July nightly low averaged 71.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.4 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.58 F per decade. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 22 over 2021-2025, and the worst single year was 2012 with 21 weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $4,510 per acre in the 2022 census, up 31.7 percent from 2017, which is a census operator estimate, not a sale price.

05127.text: What stands out in Scott County is how little of the land is watered and how much of that water comes from the ground. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, and all of the irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Non-irrigated cash rent is $23 per acre for 2026, up 31.4 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,109 per acre in 2022, which the census takes from the operators' own estimates. The July nightly low has averaged 69.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F, and 18 Julys since 1900 have averaged 70 F or higher. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 13 over 2021-2025.

05131.text: Sebastian County's crop insurance record is leaning toward heat and drought lately. Heat and drought made up 56 percent of indemnities paid for 2020-2025, up from 16 percent in 2000-2009. Excess moisture and flood still account for the largest share over the full record, at 63 percent, and the loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.04, meaning claims ran above premiums. The July nightly low averaged 71.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, and the census land value in 2022 was $4,298 per acre.

05133.text: Flooding is the main claim story in Sevier County. Excess moisture and flood account for 62 percent of closed crop insurance indemnities since 1989, out of $1.4 million paid. Heat and drought claims were 36 percent of the total in 1989-1999 and 30 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 11 percent in 2000-2009. The county averaged $24 per acre in non-irrigated cash rent in 2026, up 6.7 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,481 per acre in 2022, a number the operators gave, not a sale price. July nights have warmed, averaging 71.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 70.1 F normal.

05137.text: Stone County's cash rent is $30 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, up 57.9 percent since 2016. The census land value of $2,891 per acre in 2022 rose 33.7 percent from 2017, so the land is priced well above what the rent alone would suggest. Drought is the main thing to watch here. The county was in severe drought or worse for 103 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, with 28 of those weeks in 2012. Nights in July have averaged 68.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.7 F. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar operating in the county.

05139.text: Union County is the rent story first. Non-irrigated ground rents for $8 per acre in 2025, and that rent is down 16.1 percent from 2013. The census puts the value of land and buildings at $2,912 per acre in 2022, which is up 5.3 percent over 2017-2022, so the value side has moved more gently than the rent side. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse ran 162 of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 2011 the worst year at 48 weeks, and there were 33 such weeks in 2021-2025. July nights are warmer now too: the average low for 2017-2026 is 71.9 F against a 70.9 F normal for 1991-2020.

05143.text: Washington County is a small grain and forage county, and the notable thing here is how little of the cropland is irrigated: 1 percent in the 2022 census, so most of the rent is paying for ground that depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $53 per acre for 2026, up 96.3 percent from 2016. The July nightly low averaged 68.7 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.3 F, and the county has seen 11 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Freeze and frost drive the crop insurance claims, at 53 percent of $457,510 paid over 1996-2023. Heat and drought went from 20 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 9 percent in 2000-2009.

05145.text: White County's cropland is largely non-irrigated, but the county's corn has a steady story: the fitted yield trend has been climbing 3.2 bushels per acre a year across 2010-2024, while the worst year, 2011, was 130.3 bushels. Excess moisture and flood have caused 71 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and insurers have paid out more than they collected in 14 of the 16 closed crop years, with a 2016-2025 loss ratio of 1.71. Heat and drought claims went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, with the lowest share at 9 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre, and the census land value was $3,384 per acre in 2022.

05147.text: Woodruff County is mostly irrigated, and the water comes from the ground. The 2022 census counts 90 percent of harvested cropland as irrigated, and 94 percent of irrigation water in 2015 came from groundwater. That shapes the rent: irrigated ground rents for $155 per acre against $127 for non-irrigated in 2026, and the gap was 2.34 times in 2009 but is now 1.22 times and falling. Crop insurance has paid out $147.2 million on closed years from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio is 1.39 over 2016-2025, so claims have run above premium for the last decade. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 75 percent of those claims, and heat and drought went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025.

05149.text:
Yell County's crop insurance record is the first thing to notice. Indemnities have paid out $1.04 for every dollar of premium over the closed years 1989-2025, and the last ten closed years was 1.51. Excess moisture and flood caused 55 percent of the losses. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025, and that's the part to watch. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land and depends on the rain coming in the right weeks.

06001.text: Alameda County's cropland is mostly irrigated, at 85 percent of harvested acres in 2022, and irrigation water is 70 percent groundwater. Irrigated cash rent was $566 per acre in 2025, while the non-irrigated county average is $27 per acre for 2026, up 68.8 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $13,473 per acre in 2022, after a 13.6 percent a year climb from 2017. Crop insurance has paid out little, with a loss ratio of 0.3 over the closed years 1989-2025. Heat and drought claims were 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 41 percent in 2010-2019, and 14 percent in 2020-2025.

06005.text: Amador County is mostly irrigated ground, 95 percent of harvested cropland, and that changes how the rent numbers read. Irrigated cash rent was $324 per acre in 2025, against $65 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, which was up 261.1 percent from 2016. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 2.87 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 42 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 19 percent in 2020-2025. Groundwater supplies 71 percent of irrigation water, so the wells matter as much as the weather.

06009.text: Calaveras is mostly irrigated ground, 93 percent of harvested cropland, and the water mostly comes from wells, 70 percent in 2015. That shapes the rent picture. Non-irrigated ground rented for $11 per acre in 2022, down 63.3 percent from 2011, while irrigated ground was $700 per acre in 2026. Crop insurance has paid out $3.6 million on closed years since 1989 against premiums that bring the loss ratio to 2.07, so claims have run ahead of premium. Freeze and frost is the largest cause at 38 percent. Heat and drought went from 10 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 35 percent in 2020-2025.

06013.text: Contra Costa is an irrigated county more than a dryland one. Irrigated ground was 87 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and irrigated cash rent is $379 per acre against $30 for non-irrigated. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 105 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025. The total loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.84, so the county has paid out less than it took in premium over that stretch. July nightly lows have warmed to 59.1 F in 2017-2026.

06015.text: Del Norte is a county where the land value is the story. Census operators put the land and buildings at $10,206 per acre in 2022, and that figure rose 22.7 percent from 2017 to 2022, which is 4.2 percent a year. Most of the county's irrigation water comes from groundwater, 71 percent in 2015. Drought has been the main pressure: 180 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2020 alone had 38 of them. The last five years show 18 such weeks. July nights are warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, averaging 54.7 F for 2017-2026 against 53.1 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.83 F per decade.

06017.text: El Dorado County's notable number is the water. Irrigated cash rent is $900 per acre against $33 for non-irrigated ground, and 88 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 71 percent of that water pumped from groundwater. Most of the trouble on the insurance side has come from freeze and frost, which made up 45 percent of indemnities over the full period. Heat and drought claims went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio of 2.45 over 2016-2025 says the claims have run well past the premiums paid in.

06033.text: Lake County's cropland is 81 percent irrigated, and 71 percent of that water comes from groundwater, so the ground here depends heavily on wells. The bigger story is the claims. Heat and drought went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 3.45, meaning insurers paid out well over what farmers put in. Freeze and frost remain the largest single cause over the full record at 30 percent. July nights have warmed too, averaging 61 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 58.9 F.

06035.text: Lassen County's cropland is 91 percent irrigated, and most of that water comes from groundwater, so the big story here is how much insurance has paid out for heat and drought recently. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio of 1.81 over 1989-2025 means claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Non-irrigated rent is $32 per acre and irrigated rent is $225 per acre in 2026, and census land and buildings were valued at $4,493 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators themselves estimated.

06037.text: Los Angeles County is a county where the water is the story. Two-thirds of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and 70 percent of that irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Irrigated cash rent was $1,000 per acre in 2026, against $84 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2024, so the gap between ground with water and ground without it is wide. Drought is the other part. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse went from 477 of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 122 of those weeks in 2021-2025 alone. Insurance indemnities have been small, with a loss ratio of 0.04, and heat and drought was the largest cause of what was paid.

06039.text: Madera County is a county where the water decides the rent. Irrigated ground rents for $410 per acre, against $66 for non-irrigated, and 98 percent of irrigation water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $380.0 million since 1989, with the largest cause being excess moisture and flood at 32 percent. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.03, meaning claims ran past premiums. Heat and drought went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks in severe drought or worse covered 98 of the weeks from 2021-2025.

06041.text: Marin's cropland is mostly dryland, and the rent is the first thing to know: $64 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, up 60 percent since 2014. Irrigated ground rents for $1,290 per acre in 2025. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 42 percent of indemnities over 2011-2025. Heat and drought fell from 36 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. The census puts land and buildings at $7,636 per acre in 2022, up 30.3 percent from 2017. Drought weeks in 2000-2025 came to 287 of 1357, and 94 of those weeks fell in 2021-2025.

06045.text: Mendocino is a county where the irrigated ground does most of the work. Irrigation covers 80 percent of harvested cropland, and 71 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought has become the main reason claims get paid: its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 1 percent in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 1.19, and the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 1.61, so claims have run ahead of premium. Irrigated cash rent was $1,290 per acre in 2026, while non-irrigated rent was $32 per acre in 2022.

06053.text: Monterey is an irrigated county, with 98 percent of harvested cropland watered and 71 percent of that water pulled from groundwater. The land is priced high next to what the ground rents for. Census land and buildings were $12,799 per acre in 2022, up 73.7 percent from 2017, while non-irrigated cash rent was $14 per acre in 2024 and irrigated rent was $1,810 per acre in 2025. The insurance record is the hard part. Indemnities have run above premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.65 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2010-2019, then 18 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 52 in 2016.

06057.text: Nevada County's cropland is mostly irrigated, at 85 percent of harvested acres in the 2022 census, and the water comes largely from groundwater, 71 percent in 2015. Most of the irrigated ground rents for $1,540 per acre in 2026, while the non-irrigated average was $20 per acre in 2024. The biggest claims here have been freeze and frost, 56 percent of the $923,869 paid out from 2015-2025. Heat and drought made up 0 percent of claims in 2010-2019 and 1 percent in 2020-2025. Census land and building value was $8,650 per acre in 2022.

06059.text: Orange County's cropland is the thing to look at first, and it's mostly water. Seventy-one percent of irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought claims went from 0 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 80 percent in 2010-2019, and they make up 49 percent of the crop insurance payouts over 1996-2024. The loss ratio was 0.12 over 1995-2025 but reached 0.6 for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, and insurers paid $1.03 per $100 of insured value over 2016-2025. The county's land and buildings were valued at $15,003 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 106 in 2021-2025, and the worst year was 2016 with 52 weeks.

06063.text: Plumas is an irrigated county. Groundwater supplies 71 percent of irrigation water, and irrigated ground is 69 percent of harvested cropland. Land and buildings were valued at $4,222 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 83.7 percent between 2017 and 2022, or 12.9 percent a year. The county had 342 of 1357 weeks since 2000 with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year was 2015 with 52 weeks. Nights are warming too: July lows averaged 51.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 50 F.

06065.text: Riverside County is a mostly irrigated place, with 90 percent of harvested cropland watered and 71 percent of that water pumped from groundwater. The irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $259 per acre, against $24 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2024. The crop insurance loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.13, meaning claims paid more than premiums collected. Heat and drought made up 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 52 percent in 2020-2025, so that is the cause to watch. The census puts land and buildings at $19,831 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators estimated themselves.

06067.text: Sacramento County is an irrigated county, and most of what gets grown here depends on water. Irrigated ground is 89 percent of harvested cropland, and irrigated rent is $276 per acre against $68 for non-irrigated ground. Irrigation failure has paid out $4.3 million over all closed years, and the county's loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 1.63, so claims have run well above premium in recent years. Heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks of severe drought over the county totaled 106 in 2021-2025 alone.

06069.text: San Benito County's cropland is mostly irrigated, 87 percent of harvested acres in 2022, and 71 percent of that water comes from groundwater. That shapes everything else here. Irrigated ground rents for $651 per acre, while non-irrigated ground rents for $16 per acre and is up 14.8 percent since 2014. Crop insurance has paid out $27.5 million over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for that span is 1.11, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 34 percent. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025.

06071.text: Irrigated ground is the whole story here. Irrigated cash rent was $304 per acre in 2026, while the non-irrigated average for 2024 was $23 per acre, and 99 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census. Most of the water comes from groundwater, 71 percent in 2015, so the pumping is the thing to keep an eye on. Heat and drought claims were 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 66 percent in 2010-2019, and the loss ratio for the last ten closed crop years is 1.47. The July nightly low averaged 76.3 F over 2017-2026.

06073.text: San Diego County is an irrigated county, with 94 percent of harvested cropland watered and 71 percent of that water pumped from groundwater. The insurance record tells the rest. Indemnities have paid $53.3 million since 1995, and heat and drought drove the largest share at 45 percent. Its share went from 38 percent in 2000-2009 to 68 percent in 2010-2019, then down to 35 percent in 2020-2025. The ten crop years from 2016 through 2025 paid out 1.59 times what farmers paid in premium. July nights have also warmed, from a 1991-2020 normal of 62 F to an average of 63.9 F over 2017-2026.

06075.text: San Francisco County is a land-value story first. The census put land and buildings at $48,425 per acre in 2022, and that estimate fell 37.7 percent from 2017 to 2022, which is down 9 percent a year. Cropland is not the main use here, and there are no CRP acres. July nights are close to normal, with an average low of 54.4 F in 2017-2026 against 54.1 F in the 1991-2020 normal, and the nightly low trend since 1976 is not a clear trend. Drought is present but not a constant. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 279 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, with 52 weeks in the worst year, 2014.

06079.text:
Irrigation is what sets this county apart. Irrigated cash rent was $811 per acre in 2026, against $27 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2023, and 86 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Most of the water comes from groundwater, 71 percent in 2015, so the wells matter as much as the rent. The 2022 census value of land and buildings was $12,118 per acre, and that jumped 60.6 percent between 2017 and 2022.

Heat and drought claims went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.27, so claims paid out more than premium in that stretch. Freeze and frost remain the largest cause overall, at 38 percent.

06081.text: San Mateo is a small county with most of its ground in non-irrigated use, and the rent reflects that. Non-irrigated cash rent was $50 per acre in 2023, while irrigated ground rented for $550 per acre in 2026. Drought has been the hard part here: 276 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2015 was the worst year with 52 weeks. Heat and drought made up 36 percent of crop insurance claims for 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $12,311 per acre in 2022, up 26 percent from 2017, and the county has 4.2 MW of solar operating with no wind and nothing proposed.

06085.text: Santa Clara is an irrigated county. Eighty-eight percent of harvested cropland gets water, and 70 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. Irrigated ground rents for $823 per acre in 2025, while the non-irrigated rent was $24 per acre in 2024, down 41 percent from 2014. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.47 over closed crop years 1995-2025. Excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 48 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought went from 17 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 15 percent in 2020-2025.

06087.text: Santa Cruz County is mostly irrigated ground, 95 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and the water comes mostly from wells, 71 percent in 2015. Irrigated cash rent was $2,220 per acre in 2025, against $75 non-irrigated back in 2014. The census put land and buildings at $38,401 per acre in 2022, and that is what operators think the ground is worth, not a sale price. Heat and drought claims were 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 51 percent in 2010-2019, so that is the pattern to watch. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims across 1995-2025, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 0.31.

06089.text: Shasta County is mostly irrigated ground, 93 percent of harvested cropland by the 2022 census, and most of that water comes from wells, 63 percent in 2015. Non-irrigated rent is $36 per acre in 2026, flat since 2014, while irrigated rent is $205 per acre. The loss ratio over 1995-2025 is 1.07, and over the last ten closed crop years it is 1.29, so claims have paid out more than premiums came in. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, and 114 weeks of severe drought fell in 2021-2025 alone.

06093.text: Siskiyou is a county where most of the cropland runs on water. The census says 91 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 71 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. That is why irrigation failure, not heat or drought, is the largest cause of claims, with $48.5 million of the county's $93.3 million in indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025. Over ten closed crop years, 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 2.39, so claims ran well past premiums. Irrigated cash rent was $250 per acre in 2026, against a census land value of $4,174 per acre in 2022.

06095.text: Solano County is mostly an irrigated county. Irrigation covers 84 percent of harvested cropland, and 71 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The irrigated cash rent is $257 per acre in 2026 against $30 for non-irrigated ground, and that gap has widened since 2010, when the irrigated rent ran 4.70 times the non-irrigated figure; now it is 8.57. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: a loss ratio of 1.11 over 1989-2025, and 1.78 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, with freeze and frost the largest cause overall at 38 percent.

06097.text: Sonoma County is mostly dryland for rent purposes, but the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $1,300 per acre in 2026, against $58 for non-irrigated, and irrigated rent was 22.61 times non-irrigated in 2026. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.39 for 1989-2025, and the last ten closed crop years ran 1.96, so claims have been paying out more than premiums. The county has 328 weeks of severe drought or worse at the 50 percent level since 2000.

06099.text: Stanislaus is an irrigated county. Of the harvested cropland, 98 percent is irrigated, and 58 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. That is why the irrigated cash rent of $450 per acre sits so far above the non-irrigated rent of $55. Irrigated rent is 8.18 times the dry rent in 2026, and the ratio has moved around without a clear direction since 2010. The census puts land and buildings at $20,208 per acre in 2022, and the operators who gave that figure are estimating, not reporting sales. Crop insurance has paid out more than premium in 9 of the 37 closed crop years, and the loss ratio for 2016-2025 is 1.14. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025.

06101.text: Sutter County is an irrigated county first. Irrigation covers 96 percent of harvested cropland, and 73 percent of the water comes from groundwater. The irrigated cash rent was $420 per acre in 2026, against $38 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2023. Irrigated rent was 12.11 times the non-irrigated rent in 2023, up from 4.00 in 2010. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.42 over closed crop years 1989-2025, and 1.74 over 2016-2025. Irrigation failure is the largest cause of claims, at 34 percent. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025.

06105.text: Trinity County is mostly irrigated ground. The 2022 census has 76 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, and 70 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. Land and buildings were valued at $2,661 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 38.5 percent between 2017 and 2022. July nights have warmed too, with the 2017-2026 average low at 55.8 F against 54.2 F for the 1991-2020 normal. For water, 328 of the 1357 weeks from 2000-2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. That is 24.2 percent of weeks, and 2014 was the worst year with 52 weeks. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar in operation on the list.

06107.text: Tulare County is mostly irrigated ground, 97 percent of harvested cropland, and the water comes mainly from wells, 82 percent of it in 2015. Irrigated cash rent was $450 per acre in 2026 against $42 for non-irrigated ground. Heat and drought has grown into the largest cause of crop insurance claims, going from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities over 1989-2025 ran at 0.85 of premium, and the 2016-2025 ratio was 0.95, so claims have been close to what growers paid in. The county has 699.3 megawatts of solar operating and no wind.

06111.text: Ventura County is mostly irrigated, with 97 percent of harvested cropland watered in 2022 and 71 percent of that water coming from groundwater in 2015. Irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $3,340 per acre, against $63 for non-irrigated ground in 2024, so the two rents are not in the same world. The heat and drought share of crop insurance claims went from 13 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019, then came down to 39 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities ran 1.26 times premium, and the county has had 121 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021.

09001.text: Fairfield County's notable story is the nights. The July average low has been 65.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.7 F, and the 2020s are the first decade the July average low reached 66 F. Julys have never averaged a low of 70 F or higher in the record since 1900. The farmland itself is mostly rain-fed, with 8 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. Crop insurance losses from 1999 to 2015 were mostly freeze and frost, at 67 percent, and heat and drought made up 2 percent of indemnities over 2010-2019, down from 0 percent in 2000-2009. Land and buildings were valued at $11,310 per acre in 2022, rising 0.9 percent a year since 2017.

09003.text: Hartford County's cropland is mostly rain-fed, and the risk on it has been wet years more than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2023, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 1.21, with claims paying out more than premium in 13 of 26 crop years. Heat and drought went from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $152 per acre in 2026, up 33.3 percent since 2016, while the census value of land and buildings was $15,160 per acre in 2022.

09005.text:
Litchfield County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the crop insurance record here is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out $3.0 million against a loss ratio of 1.28 over the closed crop years 1995-2023, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 41 percent. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, which is the shift to watch.

Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $47 per acre in 2025, up 42.4 percent since 2014. Census land and buildings value was $14,512 per acre in 2022. July nightly lows have averaged 61.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 59.3 F normal.

09007.text: Middlesex County's most notable number is the shift in crop insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 1 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, while freeze and frost is still the largest cause over the whole record at 43 percent. Total indemnities across closed crop years 2006-2023 came to $1.0 million, and the loss ratio is 0.47, so claims have run well under premiums. Nights in July have averaged 64.5 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 62.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $68 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings is $15,325 per acre.

09009.text: Most of the ground in New Haven County is not irrigated, and that matters more here than the rent does. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 22 percent in 2010-2019 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause over 1995-2023 at 40 percent. The county's loss ratio over 1995-2023 is 0.91, but over 2014-2023 it is 0.61. The rent is $80 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and the census value of land and buildings was $25,431 per acre in 2022.

09011.text: Heat and drought is the claim story in New London County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 6 percent in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood remains the largest single cause over the full run of closed years at 29 percent. Average indemnities over 1997-2023 total $730,189, against a loss ratio of 0.39, so premiums have mostly stayed ahead of claims. Non-irrigated cash rent is $86 per acre in 2026, up 77.3 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $12,043 per acre in 2022, a 5 percent change since 2017.

09013.text: Tolland County's notable number is the flood claims. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of the $10.0 million in closed-year indemnities since 1995, and the county's loss ratio of 0.7 shows the insurance has paid out more than it took in. Heat and drought claims have fallen from 58 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 1 percent in 2020-2025. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated rent is $90 per acre in 2026, up 8.4 percent since 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 62.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 60.7 F.

09015.text: Windham County's notable number is the insurance record. Crop insurance paid out $1.2 for every dollar of premium over the ten closed years 2014-2023, and the loss ratio is 1.03 across 1995-2023. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, so the heat is showing up in the claims even though freeze and frost is still the largest cause at 28 percent. Ground is expensive next to the rent: census value is $10,546 per acre, and non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre, up 30.2 percent since 2016. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

09110.text: Crop insurance paid out $10.6 million in Capitol County in 2024-2025. Other causes drove 42 percent of indemnities, with heat and drought making up 21 percent of claims in 2020-2025. The loss ratio was 0.53, meaning the county paid $0.53 in indemnities for every dollar of premium collected in that closed crop year. No solar or wind projects are operating or proposed to the EIA in the county.

09130.text: Lower Ct River Valley County had $318,440 in crop insurance indemnities in the 2024-2025 crop year, with hail claims taking 96 percent of that total. Heat and drought made up 3 percent of indemnities from 2020-2025. There's no solar or wind generation operating in the county, and nothing proposed to EIA.

09140.text: Freeze and frost took the biggest share of crop insurance payouts in 2024-2025, running 31 percent of the $150,238 in closed indemnities for the county. Heat and drought made up 17 percent of claims over 2020-2025. No solar or wind generation is operating in the county, and none is proposed to the Energy Information Administration.

09160.text: Crop insurance paid $177,231 in the 2024-2025 crop years, with other causes driving 40 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought made up 14 percent of indemnities from 2020-2025. No solar or wind capacity is operating in the county, and none has been proposed to EIA.

09170.text: Hail took out 67 percent of the crop insurance claims filed in this county in 2024-2025, with total indemnities at $211,528. Heat and drought made up 11 percent of claims over 2020-2025. No solar or wind projects are operating or proposed here.

09180.text: Nothing here to report on solar or wind. The county has no operating solar or wind capacity and no projects proposed to EIA.

10001.text: Kent County's worst signal is in its claims. Heat and drought has caused most of the crop insurance indemnities here since 1989, and the share was 84 percent in 1989-1999 and 67 percent in 2020-2025. Losses have paid out more than the premium in 4 of 23 closed crop years, and the 1989-2025 loss ratio is 0.56. Non-irrigated cash rent is $119 per acre, up 33 percent since 2016, while only 37 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The 2022 census value of land and buildings is $8,679 per acre.

10003.text: New Castle County's crop insurance record stands out. Heat and drought made up 72 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 37 percent in 2010-2019, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.33, so the claims have run lighter than premiums lately. Heat and drought was 78 percent in 1989-1999, so it has been the main claim cause for a long time. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $102 per acre, and only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland. The census land value was $11,212 per acre in 2022, which puts rent near 1 percent of value.

10005.text: Sussex County's notable number is the drought record. Heat and drought made up 86 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2020-2025, and the largest cause over the whole span is still heat and drought at 68 percent. Lots of dry years show up in the claims. The county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.61, with 3 of 23 years paying out more than premium. Irrigation is a real part of the picture, with 42 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022 and 85 percent of that water from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $106 per acre in 2026, up 19.8 percent since 2016.

12001.text: Alachua County is a county where the irrigated ground stands out. Irrigated cash rent is $164 per acre against $42 for non-irrigated ground, and 30 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all of it from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $26.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio of 1.27 means claims have run above premiums over that stretch. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 40 percent. Heat and drought claims were 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 15 percent in 2020-2025. 13011.text: Banks County is notable for how little of its ground is in drought trouble lately and how much its July nights have warmed. The July average nightly low for 2017-2026 was 70 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.8 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.44 F per decade. Julys with an average low at or above 70 F have happened 20 times since 1900. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 25 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $6,926 per acre in 2022, a 28.7 percent rise from 2017. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 14 across 2021-2025.

13013.text: Barrow County's most notable number is the July heat. The average nightly low for July over 2017-2026 is 70.1 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.8 F, and July has averaged a low at or above 70 F in 19 Julys since 1900. Land values have moved hard too, with the census value up 52.9 percent from 2017 to 2022, and the 2022 census value is $10,026 per acre. Against that, non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre for 2026. Drought weeks have been fewer here in recent years, with 11 weeks in severe drought or worse over 2021-2025, and no CRP acres are enrolled.

13015.text: Bartow County's notable number is the crop insurance record: the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.68, up from 0.48 across the full 1989-2025 span, and heat and drought has been the leading cause of claims at 52 percent overall. The share of claims from heat and drought went from 61 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025. The census put land and buildings at $7,089 per acre in 2022, a 17.7 percent rise from 2017 to 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $46 per acre, up 7 percent from 2016, and only 15 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Conservation acres total 967 in 2025, and none expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

13017.text: Ben Hill County's crop insurance record stands out. Claims paid out $43.9 million over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.48, meaning the county has paid back more than it took in premium, with 8 of 13 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 36 percent, going from 57 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $273 per acre against $95 for dryland, and the gap has widened from 2.31 times in 2009 to 2.87 in 2026.

13019.text: Berrien County's most notable number is the irrigated rent: $269 per acre in 2026, against $103 for non-irrigated ground. Irrigated rent has gone from 2.20 times the dryland rent in 2009 to 2.61 times now, so the water is getting more valuable every year. Only 38 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and 54 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025, but the county's loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 1.55, so claims have still paid out more than premiums. Land and buildings were valued at $4,188 per acre in 2022.

13021.text: Heat and drought has driven most of the crop insurance claims in Bibb County, and the share has come down over time. It was 98 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 42 percent in 2010-2019, and 37 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1995-2024, closed claims paid out $667,335 in total, with heat and drought at 53 percent of that. The county also logged 275 of 1357 weeks at 50 percent or more in severe drought or worse since 2000, with the worst year at 52 weeks in 2012. July nights have warmed slightly, averaging 71.1 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.1 F.

13023.text: Bleckley County's cropland is mostly dryland, with irrigation on only 16 percent of harvested acres in 2022, and most of that water comes from groundwater. The irrigated rent is $197 per acre in 2026 against $80 for non-irrigated ground, which is the gap that matters most when you're deciding where to put a pivot or whether to rent the wet ground. Heat and drought claims were 67 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 32 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather pressure has eased in the claims record even as July nights have warmed. Crop insurance has paid out $32.8 million over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio of 1.02 means claims have run slightly ahead of premiums over that stretch.

13025.text: Brantley County's heat and drought claims have shrunk sharply. Heat and drought made up 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and only 4 percent in 2020-2025. The bigger money has come from freeze and frost, which is the largest cause at 35 percent of the $11.2 million paid since 1989. The loss ratio of 1.27 over the closed years means claims have run above premiums over that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre for 2026, and irrigation covers 32 percent of harvested cropland, with 75 percent of that water from groundwater.

13027.text: Brooks County is mostly dryland, but the water it does have is worth a look. Irrigated ground rents for $223 per acre against $106 for non-irrigated, and that gap is where the county's money is. Only 23 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 96 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: a loss ratio of 0.98 over 1989-2025, and 1.22 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims were 36 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 11 percent in 2020-2025. The census value of $4,723 per acre is the operators' own estimate, up 35.1 percent from 2017 to 2022.

13029.text: Bryan County is a warm county, and the heat has been showing up in the nights. The July average low for 2017-2026 is 73.4 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.6 F, and the July nightly low has been trending warmer at 0.52 F per decade since 1976. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims over 1989-2025, at 44 percent, but its share went from 51 percent in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. The census value of land and buildings was $3,570 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

13031.text: Bulloch County's heat and drought story has changed hands. Heat and drought made up 71 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 9 percent in 2020-2025, while the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.63. Over the full span 1989-2025 the ratio was 0.87, and 13 of 32 crop years paid out more than premium. Irrigation is a small part of the ground here at 16 percent of harvested cropland, and irrigated rent is $194 per acre against $79 for dryland. Non-irrigated rent is up 17 percent since 2016. Solar is the one energy item on the books, at 14.6 MW operating.

13033.text: Burke County is an irrigation county, and the water comes mostly from wells. Irrigated cash rent is $182 per acre in 2026 against $48 for non-irrigated ground, a gap that was 2.77 times in 2009 and is 3.83 times now. Irrigated land is 42 percent of harvested cropland, and 85 percent of that water is groundwater. Heat and drought made up 85 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 14 percent in 2020-2025, while the county's loss ratio over the closed years is 0.96, meaning claims have run close to premium over the whole record. Its drought weeks have been few since 2021, with 2 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2021-2025.

13035.text: Butts County's July nights have warmed past the old normal. The 2017-2026 average low of 70.8 F is above the 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F, and the July low has been climbing 0.6 F per decade since 1976. In 21 Julys since 1900 the average low reached 70 F or higher. The worst drought stretch in the record came in 2012, with 52 weeks at or above the severe mark. Since 2000, 314 of 1357 weeks have had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, which is 23.1 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent was $26 per acre in 2024, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,127 per acre in 2022, up 31.6 percent from 2017.

13037.text: Calhoun County is more irrigated than most places I'd look at, and the water side is where the read starts. Irrigation is on 65 percent of harvested cropland, and 35 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 51 percent of the insurance indemnities paid out from 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.05, so claims have run a little ahead of premiums over that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $87 per acre in 2026, up 70.6 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $225.

13039.text: Camden County's most notable feature is its irrigation. Forty-two percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, so water access shapes what ground can do here. The county's July nights have warmed too. The July average low was 73.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 72.6 F normal for 1991-2020, and a warming trend since 1976. Land and buildings were valued at $3,536 per acre in 2022, up 23.4 percent from 2017, and the county has 30 MW of solar operating with no wind. Drought has been less of a factor here, with 150 of 1357 weeks since 2000 showing severe drought across at least 50 percent of the county, and only 2 such weeks in 2021-2025.

13043.text: Candler County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much the heat-and-drought claims have fallen while the rent has climbed. Heat and drought made up 67 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 10 percent in 2020-2025, but the county still paid out $51.0 million over the full span, and the loss ratio of 0.91 means the payouts ran close to the premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre in 2026, up 43.3 percent since 2014. Only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. The July nightly low has averaged 71.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 71.2 F normal, so the nights are running warm.

13045.text: Carroll County's rent is up 24.6 percent since 2016, to $36 per acre for non-irrigated ground, but the bigger story here is heat. The July average nightly low has run 69.5 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.9 F, and the county has seen 4 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Land values are high against that rent, with the 2022 census putting land and buildings at $6,433 per acre after a 34.4 percent gain from 2017 to 2022. Drought has been a steady claim on ground here too, with 235 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought or worse. Nothing in the last five years reached that mark.

13047.text: Catoosa County is notable for how little of its ground is watered. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, so most of the crop depends on rain. Heat and drought made up 88 percent of the crop insurance claims paid from 1995 through 2025, and that share was the same 88 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $34 per acre, while the census puts land and buildings at $8,374 per acre, a value the operators themselves estimated. The county had 186 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 2008 the worst at 50 weeks.

13049.text: Charlton County is mostly dryland. Only 1 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground carries its own water through the summer. That makes the drought numbers the ones to watch. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 178 of 1357 from 2000 through 2025, and 2011 alone had 52 of them. Heat and drought made up 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 2000 through 2017, and the July average low has reached 72.5 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.4 F. Land and buildings were valued at $3,119 per acre in the 2022 census, up 28.5 percent from 2017.

13055.text: Chattooga County's loss history is the first thing I'd look at. The crop insurance loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.94, but for the last ten closed crop years it is 1.15, which means the claims paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought was the largest cause of those claims at 56 percent across 1995-2025, and its share went from 62 percent in 2000-2009 to 45 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigation is 2 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground is dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $58 per acre, up 161.4 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,305 per acre in 2022.

13057.text: Cherokee County is mostly dryland, with only 4 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. The rent here is $46 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, and the census put land and buildings at $9,874 per acre, which the operators estimated themselves. The thing I'd look at first is the drought record. The county spent 232 of 1357 weeks since 2000 with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse, and 2008 alone had 51 of those weeks. Since 2021 the count is 7 weeks. July nights have been warm too, with the average low running 68.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 67.8 F normal for 1991-2020.

13059.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Clarke County. It was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1995-2024, at 29 percent of the closed claims, and its share grew to 48 percent for 2020-2025. Only 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land and depends on rain in July. July nights have warmed too: the 2017-2026 average low is 70.6 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F, and 28 Julys since 1900 have averaged 70 F or above. Land and buildings are valued at $19,535 per acre, and CRP covers 37.1 percent of the cropland base, with none of it expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

13063.text: Clayton County's notable feature is its heat. The July nightly low has averaged 70.8 F over 2017-2026, and 30 Julys since 1900 have averaged a low of 70 F or above. The nightly low has been warming at 0.43 F per decade since 1976. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse have run to 315 of 1357 since 2000, and 2012 was the worst year with 52 weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $6,922 per acre in 2022, the census estimate from operators rather than a sale price. There is no CRP, solar or wind in the county.

13069.text: Coffee County's loss ratio is the number to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $1.35 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 18 of 27 years paid more than the premium. Over the last ten closed years it was 1.47. Heat and drought was the largest cause of those claims at 26 percent, but its share went from 38 percent in 1989-1999 to 10 percent in 2020-2025, so the recent claims are coming from other causes. Irrigation is 38 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and irrigated rent is $231 per acre against $108 for dry ground.

13071.text: Colquitt County is notable for how much of its cropland is irrigated: 42 percent of harvested cropland in 2022, and irrigated ground rents for $255 per acre against $120 for dryland. The loss ratio of 1.09 over 1989-2025 means indemnities have paid out more than premiums, and over the last ten closed crop years it was 1.29. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims, at 30 percent overall, and its share went from 34 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2010-2019 before falling to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $4,183 per acre in 2022, up 26.5 percent from 2017.

13075.text: Cook County's notable number is the loss ratio. Crop insurance has paid out $1.06 for every dollar of premium since 1989, and over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 that climbed to 1.36.
