Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 33 percent, and its share went from 48 percent in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $243 per acre against $101 for non-irrigated, and irrigation water is 84 percent groundwater. Land and buildings were valued at $4,057 per acre in 2022, up 33.5 percent from 2017.

13077.text: Coweta County is mostly dryland. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the rent and the land value both depend on what the rain does. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre for 2026, up 31.8 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $6,209 per acre for 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, which rose 28.7 percent from 2017 to 2022. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 300 of 1357 over 2000-2025, and 2012 had 52 of them. The July nightly low has averaged 70.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69 F.

13079.text: Crawford County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have run ahead of premium, with a loss ratio of 1.38 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, and the county's largest claim cause over 1989-2025 has been freeze and frost at 57 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. Sixty percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent was $49 per acre in 2024, and the census put land and buildings at $5,223 per acre in 2022.

13081.text: Crisp County is a dryland county, and most of the cropland depends on rain. Only 36 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigated ground rents for $242 per acre against $83 for non-irrigated. Heat and drought has been the biggest source of insurance claims, at 52 percent of indemnities since 1989. Its share went from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 69 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 33 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the loss ratio was 0.92, with 14 of 35 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated rent is up 25.8 percent since 2014.

13085.text: Dawson County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. That makes the rain pattern the thing to watch. Drought weeks in the county have been heavy in some years: 227 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2008 alone had 53. The last five years have been quieter, with 15 weeks in that range. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2025 was $46 per acre. The 2022 census put land and buildings at $9,260 per acre, and the value rose 32.6 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nights have warmed a little, with the average low at 66.8 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 66 F.

13087.text: Decatur County is an irrigated county first. Irrigation covers 60 percent of the harvested cropland, and 98 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $266 per acre against $117 for dryland, and the gap was wider in 2009 than it is now. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities, at 35 percent of the total, and its share went from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.04, meaning claims have run a little above premium over the whole stretch. Solar is the only large energy use on the books, at 517 MW operating.

13089.text: The thing that stands out in DeKalb County is the July nights. The average low for July over 2017-2026 was 70.5 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F, and July has averaged a low at or above 70 F in 24 Julys since 1900. Nights have been warming at 0.49 F per decade since 1976. Drought has also been a regular part of the picture: 287 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2008 had 50 such weeks. Irrigation is limited, with 17 percent of harvested cropland watered. Land and buildings were valued at $99,639 per acre in the 2022 census, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

13091.text: Dodge County is a dryland county for the most part, and the water question is what sets its numbers. Only 38 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigated ground rents for $212 per acre against $82 for non-irrigated, a ratio that was 2.60 in both 2009 and 2026. Crop insurance has paid out $38.3 million on closed years since 1989, and loss ratio is 1.21, so claims have run ahead of premium over the long run. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 and 23 percent in 2020-2025. The July low has averaged 72.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.3 F, and the July low trend since 1976 is 0.39 F per decade. Non-irrigated rent is up 30.4 percent since 2016.

13093.text: Heat and drought is the story in Dooly County. It caused 62 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and its share was 63 percent in 1989-1999, 73 percent in 2000-2009, 70 percent in 2010-2019, and 41 percent in 2020-2025. Only 30 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and 87 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The July nightly low has been warming, with 72.2 F in 2017-2026 against a 70.9 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $75 per acre in 2026, up 18.1 percent since 2016. The county has 6449 CRP acres and no solar or wind operating.

13095.text: Dougherty County is an irrigated county. Groundwater supplies all of the irrigation water, and irrigated ground rents for $243 per acre against $58 on non-irrigated ground in 2017. The loss ratio is the number to look at: 1.48 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, with 7 of 18 years paying out more than the premium. Over the last ten closed crop years it was 2.18, and indemnity paid was $17.02 per $100 of insured value. Heat and drought went from 49 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025. The July average low has been 72.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.8 F.

13099.text: Early County is mostly dryland, but the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $261 per acre against $87 for non-irrigated, and the 2022 census put 43 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, with 87 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Heat and drought is the biggest source of insurance claims, though its share has come down, from 64 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out more in claims than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 1.13 over the closed years 1989-2025. Solar is the other thing to note, with 194 MW operating and nothing wind.

13101.text: Echols County is a dryland county where the big risk on the books has been wind, not heat or drought. Wind took 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1995-2025, while heat and drought fell from 16 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 2 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio of 1.49 over 2016-2025 says claims have paid out more than premiums in recent years, so the insurance has been working for growers here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $95 per acre for 2026, and only 17 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain.

13103.text: Effingham County is a dryland county where groundwater irrigation carries most of the water load: 92 percent of irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here since 1989, at 38 percent of indemnities, but its share fell from 58 percent in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $32 per acre, down 4.5 percent from 2016. Irrigated rent was $90 per acre in 2021, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $4,398 per acre.

13105.text: Elbert County is mostly dryland, with only 14 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the crop insurance record is where the weather shows up most plainly. Heat and drought made up 66 percent of indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1994 to 2025, and that share went from 86 percent in 1989-1999 to 79 percent in 2020-2025, with 22 percent in 2010-2019 in between. Indemnities have run at a loss ratio of 0.52 over 1989-2025, meaning payouts have stayed below premiums on average. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre for 2026, up 62.2 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $4,492 per acre in 2022.

13107.text: Emanuel County is mostly dryland, and the heat-and-drought share of crop insurance payouts is the story here. It was 75 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 15 percent in 2020-2025, a big drop. Overall, the county's crop insurance losses have run 0.94 times premium since 1989, but only 0.69 over the last ten closed crop years. Irrigated ground rents for $148 per acre, against $69 for non-irrigated, and only 15 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 89 percent of that water from groundwater. Cropland is valued at $2,816 per acre in the 2022 census, up 34.7 percent since 2017.

13109.text: Evans County is mostly dryland. Only 39 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 43 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent was $57 per acre in 2023, up 11.8 percent from 2013. The census value of land and buildings was $3,486 per acre in 2022, and it rose 29.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. Heat and drought used to drive the claims here, going from 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause over the full record at 35 percent.

13111.text: Fannin County is mostly a county of freeze losses, not heat. Crop insurance paid $450,618 from 1995 to 2021, and freeze and frost made up 92 percent of it. Heat and drought claims were 0 percent in both 2010-2019 and 2020-2025. The county is only 4 percent irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Land and buildings were valued at $10,817 per acre in the 2022 census, and that value rose 83.3 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nights have warmed a little, averaging 64.2 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 63 F. Severe drought has touched the county for 204 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with 52 of those weeks in 2008.

13113.text: Fayette County's most notable number is how far the summer nights have warmed. The July average low has run 70.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.3 F, and it has been 24 Julys since 1900 at or above 70 F. Land values here jumped 96.1 percent between 2017 and 2022, which is 14.4 percent a year, while the census value still is $10,668 per acre. Water is the bigger pressure: 309 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2012 the worst year at 52 weeks. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

13115.text: Floyd County's notable number is the heat-and-drought pattern in its claims. Heat and drought made up 81 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 88 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Over the whole record it is 63 percent, and the loss ratio is 0.71, so claims have paid out less than premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2025, up 18.3 percent since 2014. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most corn here is grown without it, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,568 per acre in 2022.

13117.text: Forsyth County is a long way from dry ground in the Atlas numbers, but the drought weeks are worth a look. Of the 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, 252 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2008 alone had 53 of them. Since 2021 there have been 10 such weeks. July nights have warmed slightly, with the 2017-2026 average low at 68.5 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $46 per acre, and the 2022 census put land and buildings at $12,514 per acre, up 58.8 percent from 2017. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar in the county.

13125.text: The thing that stands out in Glascock is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid $2.4 million on closed crop years since 1995, and the loss ratio is 0.58 over the full record. Heat and drought claims made up 100 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 10 percent in 2020-2025, so the losses have moved away from dry weather and toward other causes. Nights are warmer too: the July average low for 2017-2026 is 70.9 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.1 F. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2022 was $21 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings was $2,364 per acre.

13127.text: Glynn County's standout is the land value. The census put cropland and buildings at $32,706 per acre in 2022, and that figure was up 112.2 percent from 2017, or 16.2 percent a year. Those are operators' own estimates, so treat them as a read on where the market has been, not a sale. Irrigation is part of the picture too: 42 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022. Heat is climbing slowly, with the July average low at 73.9 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 73 F. Drought has been light lately, with 2 weeks in severe drought or worse over 2021-2025, though 2011 ran 52 weeks.

13129.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

13131.text: Grady County is a dryland-and-irrigated county where the water question shows up in the claims. Heat and drought was 69 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 26 percent in 2020-2025, but the county still paid out more than it took in premium over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.04. Irrigated ground rents for $303 per acre against $113 for non-irrigated, and only 23 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so that gap is what a grower is paying for. The median corn yield is 149.6 bushels per acre, with a worst year of 101 in 2008.

13137.text: What stands out in Habersham County is freeze and frost, not heat or drought. Freeze and frost was the largest cause of crop insurance claims from 1989 to 2024, at 41 percent of indemnities, and heat and drought went from 3 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2000-2009. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground depends on rain. The non-irrigated cash rent is $41 per acre, up 54.7 percent since 2016, and the census land and buildings value was $8,912 per acre in 2022, which was the operators' own estimate. July nights have warmed a little, with the average low at 67.6 F for 2017-2026 against a 66.2 F normal.

13139.text: Hall County is mostly ground that depends on rain. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the dry years show up in the claims. Heat and drought made up 91 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 49 percent in 2020-2025, a real shift, though the county still paid out $1.0 million over 1995-2025 with a loss ratio of 0.92. Non-irrigated rent is $41 per acre for 2026, up 57.7 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $13,855 per acre in 2022, which is high next to that rent.

13141.text: Hancock County is a dryland county with very little irrigation, only 8 percent of harvested cropland in 2022. That makes the water side of the ledger lean on rain. Crop insurance claims from 2006-2025 came to $1.2 million on closed crop years, and wind was the largest cause at 33 percent. Heat and drought made up 35 percent of claims in 2010-2019 and 0 percent in 2020-2025, so that pressure has eased on paper even as the July nights run warm. Non-irrigated rent is $29 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $2,478 per acre in 2022.

13147.text: Heat and drought is the story in Hart County. It made up 83 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 2020-2025, up from 55 percent over 2010-2019, and the loss ratio for closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.82, so claims have run below premiums on the whole. The worst corn year in the record was 2022 at 72.3 bushels per acre, against a median of 152.1. Nights are getting warmer too: the July average low over 2017-2026 is 70.2 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69 F. Cash rent is $40 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, up 40.4 percent since 2016.

13151.text: Henry County is a dry-weather county more than a hot one. Heat and drought took 61 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and that share was still 59 percent in 2020-2025. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. The worst stretch on record for drought was 2012, with 52 weeks at or above that bar. Land and buildings were valued at $8,949 per acre in the 2022 census, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. The July average low over 2017-2026 was 70.8 F, against 69.4 F for the 1991-2020 normal.

13153.text: Houston County's most notable number is the heat and drought line. Heat and drought claims were 64 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2000-2009, then 62 percent in 2010-2019 and only 11 percent in 2020-2025. The county has been paid $28.1 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.89, so claims have run below premium over the full span. Irrigation is 31 percent of harvested cropland, and 98 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $59 per acre in 2026, up 55.3 percent since 2016.

13155.text: Irwin County's irrigated ground is the story here. Irrigated cash rent is $220 per acre against $113 for non-irrigated ground, and the census puts 54 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation. Heat and drought claims were 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 16 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry-year pressure has eased in the claims record. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.69, meaning insurers paid out more than the premiums collected. Irrigation failure claims total $194,571 across all closed years. Land and buildings were valued at $3,053 per acre in 2022, down 6 percent from 2017.

13157.text: Jackson County is mostly dryland, with only 9 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. Land and buildings were valued at $8,356 per acre that year, up 31.2 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 5.6 percent a year. Non-irrigated cash rent was $32 per acre in 2024, up 14.3 percent from 2014. Severe drought or worse covered at least 50 percent of the county in 284 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, with 2008 the worst at 53 weeks, and 12 of those weeks came in 2021-2025. July nightly lows have averaged 70.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.1 F, and 23 Julys since 1900 have averaged at or above 70 F.

13161.text: Jeff Davis County is notable for how much of its crop insurance money has come from heat and drought, and for how much of its cropland is irrigated compared with the rest of the state. Heat and drought was 48 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 48 percent again in 2010-2019, then fell to 17 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 was 1.28, and 11 of 19 crop years paid out more than the premium. Irrigated cash rent was $224 per acre in 2026, against $111 for non-irrigated ground.

13165.text: Jenkins County is an irrigated-ground story as much as a rent story. Only 25 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 77 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims over 1989-2025 at 51 percent, but it went from 83 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre in 2026, up 50 percent from 2016. The median county corn yield for 2008-2023 is 175.8 bushels per acre, with 2010 the worst year at 150.

13167.text: Johnson County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Claims have paid out $1.09 for every dollar of premium over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, and heat and drought drove most of the payouts across the full record. That share fell from 91 percent in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025, so the losses have been coming from more kinds of trouble lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre in 2026, up 51.7 percent from 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $2,716 per acre in 2022.

13169.text: Jones County is a dryland county with very little irrigation, and that's the first thing to know. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the crop depends on what the rain does. Non-irrigated cash rent was $25 per acre in 2025. Severe drought has been a big part of the record: weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 282 of 1357 from 2000-2025, with 2012 the worst year at 52 weeks. July nights have also been warmer, with the average low at 71 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.8 F. The census value of land and buildings was $3,562 per acre in 2022, and it rose 26.9 percent from 2017-2022.

13171.text: Lamar County's most notable number is heat and drought, which caused 72 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1997 through 2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.6, with indemnities paid per $100 of insured value at $9.51. Heat and drought share of indemnities went from 86 percent in 2000-2009 to 60 percent in 2010-2019 and then 84 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 70.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, unchanged from 2016.

13175.text: Laurens County's most notable number is the heat and drought claims record. Heat and drought was 66 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 79 percent in 2000-2009, and 31 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio is 1.19 over 1989-2025, with 4 of 12 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Irrigated ground rents for $187 per acre against $48 for non-irrigated, and 32 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 76 percent of that water from groundwater. Dry-year risk is real here, but the share of claims tied to it has come down.

13177.text: Lee County's irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $270 per acre in 2026, against $74 for non-irrigated, and that gap has widened from 2.24 times in 2010 to 3.67 times now. Irrigation covers 39 percent of harvested cropland, and 86 percent of the water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought made up 43 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, but that share fell from 59 percent in 2000-2009 to 31 percent in 2020-2025. The insurance loss ratio is 1.69 over the last ten closed crop years, meaning claims have run well above premium lately.

13179.text: Liberty County's most notable number is that flood and excess moisture drive the largest share of crop insurance claims, at 39 percent of $513,382 in indemnities paid over 1989-2024. Heat and drought claims were 20 percent in 1989-1999, went to 0 percent in 2000-2009, and reached 62 percent in 2010-2019. The July average low has been 73.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.7 F, and the July nightly low trend since 1976 is 0.54 F per decade. Census land and buildings value was $3,406 per acre in 2022. Solar is operating at 30 MW, with 150 MW more proposed.

13183.text: Long County's crop insurance record is the first thing to notice: $2.2 million paid out on closed crop years, against a loss ratio of 1.58, which means claims have run well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought was the biggest share of those claims in 1989-1999 at 45 percent, and it fell to 3 percent in 2020-2025. Only 6 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent was $37 per acre in 2022, against a census land and buildings value of $4,019 per acre.

13185.text: Lowndes County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Claims paid out $32.2 million over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio of 1.59 for 2016-2025 means the county has paid out more than it took in premiums in the last ten closed years. Wind is the largest cause at 40 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 47 percent in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather risk has shifted toward wind. Irrigated ground rents for $182 per acre against $92 for non-irrigated, and 86 percent of irrigation water comes from groundwater.

13191.text: McIntosh County's biggest insurance story is water from above, not heat. Excess moisture and flood made up 63 percent of the $505,070 in indemnities paid on closed crop years from 2023 through 2025, and heat and drought claims were 0 percent over 2020 through 2025. The county had 43 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2011, but only 3 weeks in 2021 through 2025. July nights are running a little warmer, with the 2017-2026 average low at 74.1 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.3 F. The land and buildings were valued at $2,056 per acre in 2022, and the county has no CRP acres, solar, or wind on the books.

13193.text: Macon County's cropland is mostly watered, and the irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $196 per acre against $88 for dryland, and that gap is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought used to make up 65 percent of crop insurance claims in 1989-1999, and in 2020-2025 it was 24 percent, so the losses have moved toward other causes. Groundwater supplies 78 percent of irrigation water, which is worth keeping in mind if you rent watered ground. Solar is running at 80 MW, with 150 MW proposed.

13195.text: Madison County is a dryland county, and its weather record is what stands out. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most crops live on rain. Heat and drought made up 66 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1995-2025, and that share held near 65 percent in 2010-2019 and 64 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre in 2026, up 24.6 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value is $7,085 per acre for 2022, which the operators themselves put on the ground.

13197.text: Marion County's heat and drought story is the one to look at first. Heat and drought made up 72 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 47 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has come down, but it is still the main cause of claims. The county has only 17 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land. The median corn yield over 2008-2024 was 130 bushels per acre, with a worst year of 81 in 2011. Non-irrigated rent is $36 per acre in 2026.

13199.text: Meriwether County's notable number is freeze and frost, which caused 86 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2024. Heat and drought claims were 2 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 0 percent in both 2010-2019 and 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.98, so claims paid came close to premiums. Irrigated land is 10 percent of harvested cropland, and CRP covers 1061 acres, or 7.9 percent of the cropland base. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre in 2026, up 11.5 percent since 2016.

13201.text: Miller County is a county where the irrigated ground is the story. Irrigated cash rent is $259 per acre in 2026, and the 2026 rent is $96 per acre for non-irrigated ground, so the irrigation premium is there every year you look. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here, at 48 percent of the $163.8 million paid over 1989-2025. Its share went from 53 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 1.15, so claims ran above premiums. Groundwater supplies 99 percent of irrigation water, and 63 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

13205.text: Mitchell County is an irrigated county. Six in ten acres of harvested cropland get water, and 96 percent of that water comes from groundwater, so the irrigated ground is the part of this county that carries the most weight. Irrigated cash rent is $260 per acre in 2026 against $112 for non-irrigated ground, and that gap has held steady, with the ratio at 2.32 in 2026 and 2.96 in 2009. Heat and drought claims have been the biggest cause of insurance payouts here, but their share fell from 52 percent in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $1.08 for every dollar of premium over the full record.

13207.text: Monroe County is a dryland county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.1, meaning insurers paid out more than farmers paid in premiums. Freeze and frost was the largest cause of indemnities at 48 percent, but heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 45 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2023 was $36 per acre, up 50 percent since 2012, and the Julys have been getting warmer at night.

13209.text: Montgomery County is a dry-ground county in the sense that most of its cash rent is for land without irrigation, and heat and drought have been the biggest source of crop insurance claims here over the long run, at 28 percent of indemnities since 1989. The share has moved a lot by period, from 39 percent in 1989-1999 to 9 percent in 2020-2025, so the last few years have been quieter on that front. The county paid $14.09 per $100 of insured value over 2016-2025, and the loss ratio for the full run of closed crop years is 0.9. Non-irrigated rent is $80 per acre for 2026, and irrigated ground rented for $185 per acre in 2020. July nights are warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, averaging 72.2 F over 2017-2026.

13211.text: Morgan County's heat and water claims stand out more than its rent does. Heat and drought made up 87 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2020-2025, and the ten closed crop years from 2016 to 2025 show a loss ratio of 1.11, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, up 22.8 percent since 2016. July nightly lows averaged 71.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F.

13213.text: Heat and drought claims have climbed in Murray County. They were 37 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, 23 percent in 2010-2019, and 52 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.16, which means the county paid out more in claims than it took in premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $43 per acre for 2026, up 34.4 percent from 2016. July nights have been warmer too, averaging 68.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.3 F. The county has 1030 CRP acres, which is 8.6 percent of the cropland base.

13219.text: Oconee County's rent is low, and the notable thing is how little of the land is irrigated and how little of its loss has come from water. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, and crop insurance losses since 1995 total $565,548, with heat and drought at 50 percent of that. Heat and drought went from 41 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 58 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent was $34 per acre in 2025, and the census value of land and buildings was $6,873 per acre in 2022, which was down 5 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low now averages 70.7 F, up from 69.2 F in the 1991-2020 normal.

13221.text: Oglethorpe County's heat and drought claims are the story here. Heat and drought made up 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019 and 88 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.27, meaning claims have run above premiums. The July nightly low averaged 70.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.1 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 59.5 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings were valued at $5,655 per acre in 2022.

13225.text: Peach County's cropland is mostly irrigated, 73 percent of harvested acres in 2022, and 96 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre in 2026 and has not moved since 2016. Irrigated ground rented for $197 per acre in 2023. The July nightly low has averaged 71 F over 2017-2026 against a 70.1 F normal. The bigger story in the claims is freeze and frost, which caused 47 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 4 percent in 2020-2025.

13227.text: Pickens County is a dry-weeks county more than a hot one. Drought weeks reached 218 of 1357 between 2000 and 2025, 16.1 percent, and the worst year was 2008 with 51 weeks. The 2021-2025 stretch had 20 weeks in severe drought or worse. July nights have not been a problem: the 2017-2026 average low is 67 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.4 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged 70 F or above. Non-irrigated cash rent was $25 per acre in 2022, with census land and buildings at $9,671 per acre and a 13.4 percent rise from 2017 to 2022.

13229.text: Pierce County's heat and drought claims have dropped off a lot. Heat and drought made up 44 percent of insurance indemnities over 1989-1999 and 9 percent over 2020-2025. Most of the big payouts here came from excess moisture and flood, at 32 percent of the total. The loss ratio is 1.21 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and insurers paid out more than premium in 12 of 24 years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $119 per acre in 2026, up 41.7 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground is a different animal, with a 2022 average of $248 per acre, and 85 percent of the water comes from groundwater.

13231.text: Pike County's ground is mostly dryland, and the insurance record tells the story of how that has changed. Heat and drought made up 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 and 49 percent in 2010-2019, but only 4 percent in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost remain the largest cause over 1995-2024, at 50 percent of $588,572 in closed claims. Non-irrigated cash rent was $44 per acre in 2025, up 64.8 percent since 2013. The census value of land and buildings was $6,000 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated.

13235.text: Pulaski County's notable number is the heat and drought claim record. Heat and drought made up 72 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 77 percent in 2000-2009, and 62 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 25 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over all closed crop years is 1.01, with 12 of 31 years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $142 per acre in 2026, up 57.8 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents at $216 per acre. Three weeks of severe drought or worse have been recorded since 2021.

13239.text: Quitman County's most notable number is the crop insurance record: $4.7 million in indemnities over 1989-2025, with heat and drought behind 66 percent of it, and a loss ratio of 1.28 across those closed years. The share from heat and drought went from 61 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 81 percent in 2000-2009. Over 2016-2025 the loss ratio fell to 0.96, and insurers paid $11.09 per $100 of insured value. July nights have warmed too: the average low was 71.2 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.6 F. Land and buildings were valued at $3,653 per acre in 2022, up 58.3 percent since 2017.

13241.text: Rabun County's notable thread is freezes, not heat. Freeze and frost made up 57 percent of crop insurance claims from 1989-2018, and heat and drought went from 1 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2010-2019. That's a rising share, but it's still a small one. The July nightly low was 65.1 F for 2017-2026 against a 63.2 F normal for 1991-2020, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low of 70 F or higher. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre for 2026. Census land and buildings were $11,517 per acre in 2022, up 39.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. There's no CRP ground and no wind or solar in the county right now.

13243.text: Randolph County's irrigated ground is the story here. Irrigated cash rent is $207 per acre against $62 for non-irrigated, and that gap has held wide since 2010. Heat and drought claims went from 39 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio of 1.04 means claims have paid out more than premiums over the closed years. Groundwater supplies 48 percent of irrigation water, and CRP covers 7.8 percent of the cropland base, with 437 acres expiring fiscal years 2027-2029.

13245.text: Richmond County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the insurance record leans on heat and drought more than most places do in this state. Crop insurance paid out $1.4 million on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio is 1.03, meaning the claims slightly outran the premiums. Heat and drought made up 90 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 10 percent in 2010-2019, and came back to 25 percent in 2020-2025. The census put land and buildings at $4,332 per acre in 2022, up 17.7 percent from 2017. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the crop rides on rain.

13247.text: Rockdale County is a Georgia county where the nights in July are the story. The July average low for 2017-2026 is 70.5 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F, and the trend since 1976 runs warm at 0.54 F per decade. July has averaged a low of 70 F or higher in 24 of the years since 1900. Drought has been a regular visitor too: 310 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2008 the worst at 50 weeks. Census land and buildings are valued at $7,472 per acre in 2022, up 5.8 percent from 2017, and there is no CRP ground and no wind or solar operating here.

13249.text: Heat and drought is the main story in Schley County. It was 82 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 45 percent in 2020-2025, so the share is falling, but it is still the largest cause. The loss ratio over 2016-2025 is 1.29, meaning insurers paid out more than farmers paid in premiums. Weeks of severe drought over the whole county ran 257 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, with 52 in 2012 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre, and July nightly lows averaged 71.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.9 F.

13253.text: Seminole County's notable number is the irrigation split. Irrigated ground rents for $274 per acre, against $108 for non-irrigated, and 56 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 99 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here at 35 percent, and it went from 37 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 26 percent in 2010-2019 before rising to 36 percent in 2020-2025. The insurance loss ratio is 1.11 over the closed years, which means claims have paid out more than premiums. Land and buildings were valued at $3,993 per acre in 2022, up 27.1 percent from 2017.

13255.text: Spalding County is mostly dryland, with only 14 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so rain sets the crop here more than anything else. The closed insurance claims from 1989-2019 total $181,720, and freeze and frost caused 44 percent of that, which is the cause to watch. Heat and drought made up 8 percent of claims in 1989-1999, and the county had 52 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2012, the worst year since 2000. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $27 per acre, and the census put land and buildings at $6,320 per acre in 2022, with the operators' own estimate of value up 23.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. No CRP acres are in the county now, and nothing wind or solar is operating or proposed.

13259.text: Stewart County's heat and drought claims have been falling as a share of the total, though they still carry most of the weight. Heat and drought went from 93 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out $24.8 million over the closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio of 1.25 says claims have run above premium over that stretch. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. July nights are warmer too, with an average low of 70.8 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70 F.

13261.text: Sumter County's corn is mostly irrigated and most of the water comes from groundwater, so the irrigated rent is the number to watch: $222 per acre in 2025, against $65 for non-irrigated ground in 2026. Heat and drought made up 54 percent of the $109.2 million in indemnities paid since 1989, and its share went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.16. Non-irrigated rent rose 22.6 percent from 2016 to 2026.

13263.text: Talbot County's heat is the thing to look at first. The July nightly low has averaged 70.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.3 F, and the trend since 1976 runs warm at 0.32 F per decade. July has averaged a low at or above 70 F in 16 years since 1900. Drought is the other side of it: 280 of 1357 weeks from 2000-2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2012 hit 52 weeks. Over 2021-2025 there were 12 such weeks. Cropland in CRP is 12.7 percent, with 160 acres and none expiring through fiscal 2029. Non-irrigated cash rent was $23 per acre in 2022.

13267.text: Tattnall County is a dryland corn county where irrigation matters more than anything else in the numbers. Only 26 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, but irrigated ground rents for $220 per acre against $61 for non-irrigated, and that ratio was 1.89 in 2009 and 3.61 in 2026 (for that comparison, the trend is not a clear trend, so read the two points only). Non-irrigated rent is up 13 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims fell from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 44 percent. Irrigation failure has paid $164,552 across all closed years.

13269.text: Taylor County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $27.6 million since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.71, meaning claims have run well ahead of premiums. Freeze and frost caused 47 percent of those payouts, the largest single cause. Heat and drought used to drive the claims, at 70 percent in 1989-1999, but fell to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $160 per acre, against $50 for non-irrigated, so water is worth a lot here. Solar is the other thing to watch, with 405.7 MW operating and none proposed for wind.

13271.text: Heat and drought is the story in Telfair County. It was the largest cause of crop insurance claims over 1989-2025, and its share went from 50 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. The county paid out $46.2 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio was 1.63, with 10 of 11 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent was $58 per acre in 2024, and the 2022 census value of land and buildings was $2,451 per acre. Groundwater supplies 85 percent of irrigation water.

13273.text: Terrell County is an irrigation county, and the water is the thing to watch. Irrigated cash rent is $234 per acre in 2026, against $77 for non-irrigated ground, and the gap has widened from 2.80 times in 2009 to 3.04 times now. Two-thirds of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims made up 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 43 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premium over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.19. Corn yields trend up 2.8 bushels per acre a year, and the county's worst year was 2009 at 143 bushels.

13275.text: Thomas County is a dryland county with a small irrigated share, and the water it does use comes mostly from wells. Irrigated cash rent is $252 per acre against $121 for non-irrigated ground, and the corn yield trend over 2008-2025 is 6.7 bushels per acre a year. Heat and drought made up 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 15 percent in 2020-2025, while the loss ratio for 2016-2025 was 1.23, so insurers have paid out more than they took in recently. Non-irrigated rent is up 50.3 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,110 per acre in 2022. CRP covers 4300 acres, and 845 of those contracts expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

13277.text: Tift County's insurance record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $96.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.39, which means claims have run above premiums over the long haul. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 35 percent, but its share went from 40 percent in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $111 per acre in 2026 and irrigated rent is $256, so irrigated ground rents for 2.31 times as much. The county corn yield trend is up 2.8 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, against a median of 172.9 bushels.

13279.text: Toombs County's irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $242 per acre in 2026, against $68 for non-irrigated ground, so an irrigated acre rents for 3.59 times as much as a dry one. That gap was 3.84 in 2009, and it has been rising. Heat and drought claims also stand out: they were 60 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 7 percent in 2020-2025. Since 2016 the non-irrigated rent is up 43.6 percent. The county has no solar or wind operating, and CRP covers 358 acres.

13283.text: Treutlen County's crop insurance record stands out. Claims paid out $9.2 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio of 1.16 means the county has paid back more than it took in premium. Over the last ten closed crop years that ratio is 1.47. Heat and drought was the largest single cause, at 28 percent of indemnities, though its share fell from 60 percent in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $74 per acre, and 39 percent of irrigation water comes from groundwater.

13287.text: Turner County is an irrigated county. Irrigated ground rents for $284 per acre in 2026, more than three times the $90 non-irrigated rate, and the gap has been widening since 2009, when irrigated rent was 2.15 times the dryland rate. The census says 68 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 64 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims at 46 percent, but its share fell from 69 percent in 2000-2009 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Claims have paid out more than premiums in 12 of 33 closed crop years.

13291.text:
Union County is a dry-weather county more than a hot one. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 214 of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 2008 the worst year at 53 weeks. Those weeks have been less common lately, with 17 in 2021-2025. July nights have averaged 63.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 62.4 F normal for 1991-2020, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F.

Non-irrigated cash rent is $45 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $8,109 per acre in 2022, up 40.5 percent from 2017.

13293.text: Heat and drought is the story in Upson County. It was 47 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 2005-2025, and it went from 17 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 85 percent in 2020-2025. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 286 of 1357 from 2000-2025, and the worst year was 2012 with 52 weeks. The July nightly low averaged 70.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.2 F. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dry-land. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre for 2026, up 62.8 percent from 2016.

13295.text: Walker County's heat-and-drought claims have climbed sharply, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.06, meaning farmers have been paid out more than they paid in premium. Heat and drought went from 34 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 70 percent in 2020-2025. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre in 2026, up 37.9 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,860 per acre in 2022.

13297.text: Heat and drought drive most of the crop insurance claims in Walton County. They made up 61 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county's loss ratio over those years was 0.69. The share was 67 percent in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2020-2025. Only 3 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. The July average low has reached 70.3 F over 2017-2026, up from a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 51.1 percent from 2016.

13299.text: Ware County is a dryland county with a loss record worth knowing about. Crop insurance has paid out $50.6 million over the closed years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.29, meaning claims ran above premiums in 8 of 12 years. Heat and drought was 58 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 and 6 percent in 2020-2025, so the main driver has shifted over time. Non-irrigated cash rent is $82 per acre in 2025, and the census put the land and buildings at $3,041 per acre in 2022. The July nightly low has been running warmer, at 72.6 F in 2017-2026 against a 71.3 F normal for 1991-2020.

13301.text: Warren County is a non-irrigated county, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, so the dry years land on the crop directly. Heat and drought made up 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 2010-2019 and 8 percent over 2020-2025, so that share has come down. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.57, and most of the payouts came from area and index plans with no peril assigned. July nightly lows averaged 70.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.7 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $21 per acre in 2023, up 20 percent from 2013.

13303.text: Heat and drought has been the main source of crop insurance claims in Washington County, but its share has fallen sharply. It was 78 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and is 10 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.02, so claims have paid out slightly more than premiums collected over the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $57 per acre, up 70.1 percent since 2016, and irrigated cash rent was $162 per acre in 2020. Only 30 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 83 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

13305.text: Wayne County's notable number is water and loss. Crop insurance has paid out $46.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 1.01, so claims have run a little above premiums lately. Heat and drought went from 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause overall at 37 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $76 per acre for 2026, up 67.8 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,579 per acre in 2022.

13307.text: Webster County is a dryland county: only 34 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and groundwater supplies 22 percent of the irrigation water. The heat and drought share of crop insurance indemnities went from 57 percent in 1989-1999 to 84 percent in 2000-2009 and 38 percent in 2020-2025, so the big claim years were the 2000s. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $35 per acre, down 23.9 percent since 2014. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 1.27 over 1989-2025. The July nightly low averaged 71.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.9 F.

13309.text: Wheeler County's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.9, meaning insurers paid out more than the premiums that came in, and heat and drought has been the largest cause of claims, though its share fell from 48 percent in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the irrigation water comes from groundwater, 64 percent in 2015. Non-irrigated cash rent was $63 per acre in 2013, and the census value of land and buildings reached $3,641 per acre in 2022, up 99.1 percent from 2017. The county had 4 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025, after 39 weeks in 2011. CRP covers 326 acres, and 80 MW of solar is proposed.

13311.text: White County is a non-irrigated county, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, so the ground depends on rain in July. The July nightly low has averaged 66.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.9 F, and 2020s is the first decade the July average low reached 66 F. Crop insurance has paid $613,318 since 1989, and heat and drought made up 69 percent of that. Its share went from 83 percent in 2000-2009 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims are less concentrated on heat and drought now than they were. Non-irrigated cash rent is $53 per acre for 2026.

13313.text: Whitfield County's notable number is flood, not heat. Excess moisture and flood made up 53 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1998 to 2025, and heat and drought made up 11 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 14.6 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value was $6,983 per acre in 2022, and it rose 12.9 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low has averaged 69.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 68 F normal, and six Julys since 1900 have averaged 70 F or higher. CRP holds 395 acres, 6 percent of the cropland base, and none of it expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

13315.text: Wilcox County is a dryland county with a lot of rent movement behind it. Non-irrigated cash rent is $125 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 86.6 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $205 per acre, which is 1.64 times the dryland rate, down from 2.36 times in 2010, so the gap between irrigated and dryland has narrowed a lot. Heat and drought made up 60 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 21 percent in 2020-2025. Closed crop years paid out more than premium in 11 of 31 years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.07.

13317.text: Wilkes County's most notable number is the weather. Heat and drought made up 68 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1995 to 2025, and that share is the same for 2020-2025 alone. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse went from 301 out of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 2008 the worst year at 53 weeks. July nightly lows have averaged 70.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.7 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, up 9.3 percent since 2016. Census land and building value was $3,614 per acre in 2022.

13319.text: Wilkinson County is a dryland county where heat and drought have driven most of the crop claims, though that share has fallen sharply lately. Heat and drought made up 78 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio across closed crop years is 1.26, so claims have paid out more than premiums brought in. The county's non-irrigated cash rent in 2024 was $40 per acre, and census land and buildings were valued at $2,292 per acre in 2022. Drought has been severe here, with 262 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2012 hit 52 weeks.

13321.text: Worth County is a dry-year county, and the claims show it. Heat and drought made up 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 56 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 30 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record, the county has paid out more than it took in premium: a loss ratio of 1.04, with 16 of 37 closed crop years paying more than premium. Only 26 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 80 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated ground rents for $113 per acre in 2026, while irrigated is $251.

15001.text: Hawaii County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums in 11 of 24 closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.09 across 1989-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years it is 1.94. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims, at 41 percent of $42.1 million since 1996, but its share went from 91 percent in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigation failure claims total only $385,328, and 54 percent of irrigation water comes from groundwater. Census land value is $8,886 per acre in 2022, up 28.2 percent from 2017.

15003.text: Honolulu County is an irrigated county, with 86 percent of its harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, and most of that water comes from sources other than groundwater, which was 18 percent in 2015. The July nights have warmed, with an average low of 71.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.8 F, and 19 Julys since 1900 averaged 70 F or above. Crop insurance paid $113,086 in indemnities over 1997-2005, and excess moisture and flood made up 79 percent of that, while heat and drought made up none of the claims in 2000-2009. Land and buildings were valued at $29,887 per acre in the 2022 census, up 20.5 percent from 2017, and the solar and wind on the grid is 354.7 MW solar and 126.6 MW wind.

15009.text: Most of Maui County's cropland is irrigated, 86 percent of harvested acres in the 2022 census, and the water comes mostly from surface sources, with groundwater at 17 percent in 2015. The notable thing is the insurance record. Indemnities paid out were $4.2 million over 2018-2025, and heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 43 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2017-2025 is 3.3, which means claims ran well ahead of premiums. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 67 in 2021-2025, with 32 of them in 2022 alone.

16005.text: Bannock County's biggest number is the water. Forty-two percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 2026 cash rent is $167 per acre there against $22 for non-irrigated ground, so the gap between wet and dry ground is wide. Freeze and frost lead the crop insurance claims at 36 percent of indemnities, while heat and drought went from 28 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 55.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.1 F. The county has no wind or solar operating and none proposed, and CRP covers 39.6 percent of the cropland base, with 3847 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

16009.text: Benewah County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out $30.1 million since 1989, and in six of the twelve closed crop years the payments came to more than the premium, for a loss ratio of 1.34. Heat and drought is the cause behind most of that money, and its share went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre in 2026, up 15.9 percent from 2016, and in 2022 the rent was 2.66 percent of the census land value of $2,747 per acre.

16017.text: Bonner County's cropland is mostly dryland. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, so the rent and the crop claims both come from ground that depends on rain. Heat and drought made up 61 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 2014-2025, and the share went from 46 percent in 2010-2019 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. The county's July nightly lows averaged 52 F in 2017-2026, up from a 1991-2020 normal of 50.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $53 per acre in 2026, up 45.2 percent since 2014.

16019.text: Bonneville County is an irrigated county first. Irrigated ground is 68 percent of harvested cropland, and it rents for $146 per acre in 2026, against $33 for non-irrigated ground in 2025. That gap was 3.24 times in 2009 and is 4.24 times now. Heat and drought made up 49 percent of insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 and 45 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio for 2016-2025 is 0.94, so the insurance pays out close to what it takes in. Most of the water comes from surface sources, with groundwater at 25 percent. Land and buildings were valued at $4,884 per acre in 2022, up 67.5 percent from 2017.

16021.text: Heat and drought is the story in Boundary County. It paid 68 percent of the crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 17 percent in 2000-2009 and 29 percent in 2010-2019. Heat and drought is the largest cause over the full 2001-2025 span too, at 46 percent of the $5.1 million paid. The county's closed-year loss ratio for 2016-2025 is 1, which means claims have matched premiums over the last ten years. The July nightly low is up to 52.2 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 49.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $81 per acre for 2026, up 14.9 percent since 2016. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland.

16023.text: Butte County is all irrigated, and irrigation is where the insurance money goes. Irrigation failure is the largest cause of claims here, at 36 percent of the $17.7 million paid since 1989, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 1.03, so claims have run slightly above premiums. Groundwater supplies 52 percent of the irrigation water. Heat and drought claims went from 8 percent in 1989-1999 to 3 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has fallen. The July nightly low averaged 52 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 50.5 F. Ground here has been selling for $3,430 per acre by the census count.

16025.text: Camas County is mostly dryland ground, and it has the heat and drought record to show for it. Heat and drought was 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 70 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.84. The July nightly low has averaged 52.2 F over 2017-2026, up from the 1991-2020 normal of 49.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2023, and the census value of land and buildings is $2,055 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate.

16027.text: Canyon County is mostly irrigated ground, 95 percent of harvested cropland by the 2022 census, and irrigated cash rent was $300 per acre in 2026. The notable number is crop insurance. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.21, so the claims have run ahead of premium. Irrigation failure itself has paid only $1.9 million across all closed years. Land and buildings were valued at $13,588 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. The non-irrigated rent of $46 per acre in 2019 is thin ground, and the county has no CRP acres or wind and solar to speak of.

16031.text: Cassia County is an irrigated county, with 91 percent of harvested cropland watered and 59 percent of that water coming from groundwater. The insurance record is the thing to look at. Indemnities have paid $59.4 million since 1989, and 6 of 27 closed crop years paid out more than premium, so the loss ratio over the whole stretch is 0.66 and over the last ten years it is 0.77. Heat and drought claims went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 35 percent in 2000-2009. Irrigated cash rent is $405 per acre and the census land value is $4,486 per acre, so the ground is priced well above what it rents for.

16033.text: Clark County is an irrigated county, and that shapes most of what follows. Irrigation covers 84 percent of harvested cropland, and 36 percent of the water comes from groundwater. The loss ratio is 1.73 over the last ten closed crop years, meaning insurers paid out more than the premiums taken in, and the largest single cause was freeze and frost at 49 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 3 percent in 2020-2025. Land is valued at $3,102 per acre, and that value rose 76.8 percent between 2017 and 2022.

16035.text: Heat and drought is the story in Clearwater County. Its share of crop insurance claims went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years was 2.1, meaning claims paid out more than premiums taken in. Nightly July lows have been warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, and the county had 84 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $57 per acre in 2026, up 4.6 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value is $3,570 per acre for 2022, which rose 44.6 percent from 2017.

16039.text: Elmore County is a county where the irrigation does most of the work. Irrigated ground is 91 percent of harvested cropland, and the irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $405 per acre, against $34 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2025. The crop insurance record is the part to watch. Closed crop years from 1989-2025 show a loss ratio of 1.1, and the ten years from 2016-2025 come in at 1.29, so claims have run ahead of premium. Heat and drought was the largest single cause of those indemnities, but its share fell from 38 percent in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The census put land and buildings at $3,233 per acre in 2022, up 29.7 percent from 2017.

16041.text: Franklin County is mostly irrigated ground, with 65 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, and the irrigated rent is the number to watch. Irrigated cash rent was $106 per acre in 2026 against $34 for non-irrigated ground, and the irrigated rent was 4.24 times the dryland rent in 2009 and 3.07 times in 2026. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in on the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.69 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, and July nightly lows have been warming.

16043.text: Fremont County is a county where the water decides the rent. Irrigated ground now rents for $180 per acre against $58 for dry ground, and that gap has widened from 1.79 times in 2010 to 3.10 times in 2026. Irrigation covers 54 percent of harvested cropland, and groundwater supplies only 15 percent of the water used on it. Heat and drought claims went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2020-2025, with irrigation failure paying $8.9 million over all closed years. The county's loss ratio of 0.78 over closed years means claims have run below premiums overall.

16045.text: Gem County is mostly irrigated, with 97 percent of harvested cropland watered and only 5 percent of that water coming from groundwater. The thing that stands out is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $5.4 million since 1990, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.42, meaning claims have run above premiums. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields have trended up 3.1 bushels per acre a year since 2008, so the county is producing more even as the dry years hit harder. The July nightly low has been warming, from a 1991-2020 normal of 56.5 F to 58.9 F over 2017-2026.

16049.text: Idaho County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent and the insurance record are the story here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre for 2026, and it was up 11.1 percent from 2016. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the closed crop years paid $93.5 million in indemnities, with a loss ratio of 1.15, so the insurance paid out more than the premiums brought in. The census put land and buildings at $2,367 per acre in 2022, up 44 percent from 2017.

16055.text: Heat and drought is the story in Kootenai County. It was 47 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 and 32 percent in 2010-2019, then jumped to 83 percent in 2020-2025. Losses have run ahead of premiums: the loss ratio is 1.39 over closed crop years 1989-2025, and 1.44 over the last ten. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $65 per acre, up 225 percent from 2014, and irrigated ground was $70 per acre in 2026. Land and buildings were valued at $11,050 per acre in 2022, with ground values up 100 percent from 2017 to 2022.

16057.text: Heat and drought is the story in Latah County. It caused 33 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities ran 1.33 times premium, and 8 of 18 closed years paid out more than the premium. July nightly lows have averaged 50.6 F since 2017 against a 1991-2020 normal of 49.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre for 2026, up 6.7 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value was $3,464 per acre in 2022.

16069.text: Heat and drought is the story in Nez Perce County. It was 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 76 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have paid out $126.6 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.24, so claims have run ahead of premiums over the full record. The county is dryland with no irrigated harvested cropland, and the July nightly low has warmed to 54.9 F in 2017-2026 from a 1991-2020 normal of 53.4 F. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $89 per acre in 2026, up 15.6 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,156 per acre in 2022. Drought weeks peaked at 30 in 2021, and 95 weeks have come in 2021-2025 alone.

16071.text: Irrigation is what sets this county apart. Irrigated ground rents for $127 per acre, and non-irrigated ground for $26, so the irrigated rent is 4.88 times the dryland rent in 2026. Non-irrigated rent is down 31.6 percent from 2016. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of claims at 51 percent, but heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2000-2009 and then down to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out 1.31 times the premium over the closed years, and 7 of 10 crop years paid more than the premium.

16073.text: Owyhee County is an irrigated county, with 93 percent of harvested cropland watered, and that shapes everything else here. Irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $254 per acre, while non-irrigated ground rented for $20 per acre in 2023, and that dryland figure was down 52.3 percent from 2013. Corn yields have a trend of 2.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the worst year, 2008, was 178 bushels. Crop insurance has paid $13.8 million on closed years since 1989, with a loss ratio of 0.78. Heat and drought claims were 24 percent of that over 1989-1999 and 19 percent over 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $2,025 per acre in 2022.

16077.text: Power County is an irrigated county. Irrigation covers 58 percent of harvested cropland, and most of that water comes from groundwater, 64 percent in 2015. Irrigated ground rents for $290 per acre against $32 for dryland, so the irrigated ground carries most of the value. The county's crop insurance has paid out more than it took in for 6 of 28 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.09 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025. CRP covers 36.1 percent of the cropland base, and 16,282 of those acres come up for renewal in fiscal years 2027-2029.

16081.text: Teton County is mostly an irrigated county. Irrigated land is 59 percent of harvested cropland, and irrigated ground rents for $60 per acre against $26 for dry ground. Heat and drought has been a bigger part of claims lately: it went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost is still the largest cause at 37 percent. Two of the ten closed crop years paid out more than premium, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.66. Groundwater supplies 24 percent of irrigation water, and the July nightly low has been warming.

16083.text: Twin Falls is an irrigated county, and that shapes everything else here. Irrigation covers 99 percent of harvested cropland, and irrigation failure is the largest cause of insurance claims, with $23.4 million paid for it out of $56.0 million in closed years since 1989. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. The county's irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $319 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings for 2022 is $6,129 per acre. Non-irrigated rent was $50 per acre in 2014. Groundwater supplies 25 percent of irrigation water.

21001.text: Heat and drought is the story in Adair County. It was 62 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 35 percent in 2010-2019, and was back to 60 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 68.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.5 F, and the county has warmed 0.77 F per decade since 1976. Corn has yielded a median of 158.5 bushels per acre since 2008, with 2012 the worst year at 71.6. Non-irrigated cash rent is $129 per acre for 2026, up 14.2 percent since 2016.

21003.text: Allen County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums in 13 of the 17 closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the full run is 1.53. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 50 percent of claims, but heat and drought went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, which is now the bigger share of claims. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $129 per acre, up 32.3 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $5,163 per acre in 2022, and it rose 49.1 percent from 2017 to 2022.

21007.text: Ballard County is a rain-fed county, and the wet years cost more than the dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in only 3 of 19 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.65 across the whole period. Heat and drought claims went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 47 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $161 per acre for 2026, up 45 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $4,478 per acre for 2022.

21009.text: Barren County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Since 1989, insurance has paid out $138.9 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio of 1.77 means indemnities have run ahead of premiums in 15 of 16 crop years, with excess moisture and flood the largest single cause at 53 percent. Heat and drought claims have shrunk as a share, going from 68 percent in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. The median corn yield over 2008-2025 is 174.5 bushels per acre, with a trend of 3 bushels per acre a year. Non-irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre in 2026.

21011.text: Bath County is a dryland county with no irrigated acres, and its notable story is water in the wrong amount. Crop insurance indemnities total $14.9 million since 1989, and excess moisture and flood account for the largest share at 41 percent. The loss ratio over all closed years is 1.3, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 65 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2020-2025, and that recent share is the figure to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent was $96 per acre in 2023, and the census value of land and buildings was $3,111 per acre in 2022.

21013.text: Bell County is mostly a dry-ground county. Only 1 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop depends on rain. Drought has been the bigger test: 67 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 2007 the worst year at 29 weeks. The last five years, 2021-2025, have had 4 such weeks, so that stretch has been quieter. Land and buildings were valued at $2,647 per acre in the 2022 census, and that figure is the operators' own estimate. Values rose 33 percent from 2017 to 2022. Nothing here is in CRP, and there is no wind or solar on the ground yet.

21015.text: Boone County is a non-irrigated county, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so dry years land on the crop directly. Heat and drought made up 72 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 41 percent in 2020-2025, a steady fall, while the loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.71, well under 1. Non-irrigated cash rent is $45 per acre in 2026, down 22.4 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $8,920 per acre in 2022, up 48.6 percent from 2017. Weeks in severe drought or worse have been few since 2021, just 2 through 2025.

21017.text: Bourbon County's notable number is how much of its loss history comes from heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 68 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2010-2019, then back up to 55 percent in 2020-2025. The closed crop years from 1989 to 2025 paid out $41.3 million, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 1.36, with 6 of 14 crop years paying more than premium. No irrigated acres are reported, so the county depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $105 per acre, down 25 percent from 2016. Census land value was $7,039 per acre in 2022.

21021.text: Boyle County is a dryland county, and the heat and drought record is what stands out. Not one acre of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. Heat and drought took 46 percent of the $9.8 million in crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch was 0.97, meaning claims came close to premiums. The share fell from 69 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025, but it is still the biggest cause. Nights are getting warmer too: the July average low was 66.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 65.2 F normal, and 2020s is the first decade it reached 66 F.

21025.text: Breathitt County's main risk on the books has been wet weather, not dry. Excess moisture and flood account for 64 percent of the $1.3 million in crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1995-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 74 percent of the total in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county had 4 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $36 per acre in 2011, and census land and buildings were valued at $2,132 per acre in 2022.

21027.text: Breckinridge County is all rainfed ground, and the insurance record is where the county stands out. Crop insurance has paid out $48.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the losses have run above premium, with the loss ratio at 0.92 and payouts exceeding premium in 5 of 18 crop years. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 45 percent, though its share fell from 60 percent in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $127 per acre for 2026, up 21 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,848 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators supplied themselves.

21031.text: Butler County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the water trouble here has been too much rain more than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 0.76, so claims have run below premium overall. Heat and drought went from 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025.
