Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $144 per acre, up 25.2 percent since 2016, and census land and buildings value in 2022 was $4,286 per acre. Corn yield has risen 3.6 bushels per acre a year over the published years 2008-2024, with the 2012 drought year at 105.3 bushels.

21033.text: Caldwell County's heat and drought story is the thing to look at here. Heat and drought was 51 percent of the indemnities in 1989-1999, 52 percent in 2000-2009, 59 percent in 2010-2019, and 42 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record, 52 percent of the indemnities paid out were from heat and drought, and the loss ratio is 0.71, with 4 of 19 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $170 per acre for 2026, up 23.2 percent since 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $4,783 per acre in 2022, and the county had 4977 acres in CRP in 2025.

21035.text: Calloway County is mostly dryland, and its loss history is the thing to look at first. Insurance indemnities have run above premium over the full record, with a loss ratio of 1.07 across 22 closed crop years, and heat and drought account for 43 percent of the $92.1 million paid since 1989. That share was 27 percent in 1989-1999 and 51 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $161 per acre in 2026, up 40 percent from 2016. The county's own census value for land and buildings was $5,167 per acre in 2022, and the 2022 rent was 2.71 percent of that figure.

21037.text: Campbell County is a non-irrigated county where the notable number is the heat and drought claim record. Heat and drought made up 44 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1995 to 2025, and it was 35 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $45 per acre in 2026, up 12.5 percent from 2016. The census land and buildings value was $6,228 per acre in 2022, a 23.1 percent rise from 2017. Severe drought has been rare here, with 25 of 1357 weeks since 2000 and none from 2021 through 2025, while July nightly lows averaged 66.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 65.2 F normal.

21039.text: Carlisle County is a dryland county that has leaned on water less than most. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the big insurance story here is wet weather, not heat: excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 43 percent. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 50 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $180 per acre in 2026, up 29.5 percent from 2016. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.79, and four of 18 crop years paid out more than premium.

21041.text: Carroll County's crop insurance claims have leaned toward wet years. Excess moisture and flood account for 57 percent of the $6.3 million paid on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.21 over that stretch, meaning the county has paid out more in indemnities than farmers paid in premiums. Heat and drought claims were 56 percent of the total in 1989-1999, fell to 25 percent in 2010-2019, and were back to 47 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $4,769 per acre in 2022.

21043.text: Carter County is a non-irrigated county in northeastern Kentucky, and the notable thing in its numbers is the insurance record. Crop insurance has paid out $3.6 million against a loss ratio of 1.78, which means claims have run well ahead of premiums. Excess moisture and flood account for 57 percent of indemnities, and heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 40 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2025, and the July nightly low averaged 65 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.3 F. The county has no irrigated cropland and no wind or solar capacity.

21045.text: Casey County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain, and the insurance record shows where that has hurt. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims over 1989-2025, and its share went from 43 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 71 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 0.86, but across 1989-2025 it is 1.15, so the claims have run ahead of premium over the full record. Non-irrigated cash rent is $111 per acre for 2026, up 40.5 percent since 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $3,369 per acre in 2022.

21047.text: Heat and drought is the main cause of crop insurance claims in Christian County, though its share has eased. It made up 56 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 42 percent in 2020-2025. Since 1989, insurance has paid $171.2 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.78, so payouts have run ahead of premium in 7 of 31 years. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $200 per acre in 2026. Corn yields show a trend of 3.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025.

21051.text: Clay County's notable thing is the claims history. Heat and drought went from 26 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 to 12 percent in 2010-2019, then 35 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood still lead the all-time total at 61 percent of $2.6 million paid since 1995. The loss ratio is 1.55 for closed crop years 1989-2025, so claims have paid out more than premiums over that stretch. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland. Non-irrigated rent was $51 per acre in 2025, and the census value of land and buildings was $2,956 per acre in 2022.

21053.text: Clinton County is a dryland county with a loss record that stands out. Indemnities have run higher than premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.09 across 1989-2025, and heat and drought have caused 51 percent of the claims. Their share went from 45 percent in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2020-2025. Cropland is 0 percent irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $85 per acre for 2026, up 41.7 percent from 2016, and the census land value is $4,298 per acre.

21057.text: Cumberland County's most notable thing is how little of its trouble comes from dry weather. Excess moisture and flood have caused 46 percent of the crop insurance payouts since 1989, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 0.68, so claims have run below the premiums paid in. Heat and drought went from 50 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Summer nights are warming, too: the July average low is 68.3 F for 2017-2026, against a 66.1 F normal for 1991-2020. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $80 per acre in 2026.

21059.text: Daviess County is mostly dryland, and its notable trait is how much of the insurance money here has come from wet years rather than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of indemnities since 1989, while heat and drought was 53 percent in 1989-1999 and 19 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.55, and only 1 of 22 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $207 per acre, up 12.5 percent from 2016. The median county corn yield for 2008-2025 is 176.2 bushels per acre, with 2012 the worst year at 90.4.

21063.text: What stands out in Elliott County is the flood and wet-year claims. Excess moisture and flood made up 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1995 to 2022, which is the largest cause in the county. Heat and drought went from 71 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2000-2009, so the big dry-year losses were in the early period. Non-irrigated cash rent was $38 per acre in 2021, and the census put land and buildings at $2,304 per acre in 2022. Land value rose 42.3 percent from 2017 to 2022.

21065.text: Estill County's notable number is the crop insurance loss ratio of 1.29, which means claims have paid out more than the premiums collected over 1989-2025. Most of that comes from wet years, since excess moisture and flood account for 57 percent of indemnities, while heat and drought went from 79 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, down 35.3 percent from 2016, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Census land and buildings value is $3,319 per acre in 2022, up 38.1 percent from 2017. The July nightly low has averaged 66.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.2 F.

21069.text: Fleming County is a rainfed county, with no irrigated cropland in the 2022 census, so the weather that shows up in its claims is the weather it gets. Its crop insurance record leans toward too much water: excess moisture and flood account for 44 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for those closed years is 1.48, meaning claims have run well above premium. The recent stretch looks easier, with a 0.84 loss ratio for 2016-2025, but heat and drought were 67 percent of claims in 2020-2025, up from 23 percent in 2010-2019. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $132 per acre, and census land value is $3,780 per acre.

21073.text: Franklin County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Across the closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, insurance paid out $6.2 million, and the loss ratio was 1.13, which means claims ran above the premiums collected. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 43 percent. Heat and drought went from 59 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2020-2025, so heat is back in the picture after a quieter stretch. Rent is $70 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

21075.text: Fulton County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid $60.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and excess moisture and flood account for 56 percent of that, which is the largest cause by a wide margin. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, so it has stayed a steady share of the losses. The loss ratio is 0.85 over the full run, and 7 of 22 crop years paid out more than the premium. Cash rent is $191 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

21077.text: Gallatin County's notable pattern is in the insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 12 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 30 percent in 2010-2019 and 70 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 1.07, so claims paid out more than premiums came in. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2017 was $110 per acre. Census land and buildings value was $3,786 per acre in 2022, and land value rose 33.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July average nightly low for 2017-2026 was 68.3 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.8 F.

21079.text:
Garrard County's crop insurance record is the first thing to notice. Claims paid out $10.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.55, meaning the county has paid back more than it took in premiums. In the last ten closed years the ratio was 1.42. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 48 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 75 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry-year share has come back up after falling in the middle years.

Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, up 51.2 percent from 2016. Corn yields have a trend of 2.4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, with a median of 139 bushels.

21081.text: Grant County's corn has been hit more by too much water than by heat or drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 66 percent of crop insurance indemnities, and the loss ratio is 1.61, which means insurers have paid out more than the premiums collected over closed crop years 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $76 per acre in 2026, up 60.6 percent since 2014, and the 2022 census value of land and buildings is $5,003 per acre. No cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain falling at the right times.

21083.text: Graves County is dryland ground. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rent figure you're looking at, $170 per acre, is for non-irrigated ground. Heat and drought is the main source of claims here: it made up 50 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025, and its share went from 24 percent in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2010-2019 before coming down to 46 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields have still trended up, at 3.3 bushels per acre a year, but the worst year, 2012, was 49.5 bushels. Non-irrigated rent is up 23.2 percent since 2016, and the census land value of $5,523 per acre was 44.4 percent higher in 2022 than in 2017.

21085.text: Grayson County is not irrigated at all, and most of the claim money here has come from wet springs and floods rather than heat and drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 47 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for those closed years is 0.86, with insurance paying out more than the premium in 3 of 14 crop years. Heat and drought went from 77 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $110 per acre for 2026, up 25 percent from 2016, and the census land value was $3,703 per acre in 2022.

21087.text: Green County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums in 11 of the 12 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.86 over 1989-2025, and $23.29 paid per $100 of insured value over 2016-2025. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 50 percent. Heat and drought went from 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025. Rent is $142 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 8.4 percent since 2016, and no cropland is irrigated.

21089.text: Greenup County is mostly a wet-year county on the insurance side. Excess moisture and flood account for 54 percent of the indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over that whole stretch is 1.69, which means the claims have run well past the premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 64 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry side has gained weight lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings is $3,615 per acre in 2022.

21091.text: Hancock County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the insurance claims tell the story here. Excess moisture and flood caused 54 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.58 over those closed years, so claims have run below premium. Heat and drought was 59 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and 31 percent in 2020-2025. The county has had no weeks in severe drought since 2021. Cash rent on non-irrigated ground is $160 per acre for 2026, against a census land value of $4,217 per acre.

21093.text: Hardin County is a county where heat and drought has been the main reason for insurance payouts, though that has eased lately. Heat and drought made up 56 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, peaked at 70 percent in 2010-2019, and was 47 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record the county's loss ratio is 0.72, and five of 20 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Corn yield has been trending up 3.5 bushels per acre a year. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $142 per acre, up 2.2 percent since 2016.

21095.text: Harlan County's notable number is land value. The census put land and buildings at $2,816 per acre in 2022, and it rose 80.1 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 12.5 percent a year. That jump is what stands out here, since the county has no CRP acres and no wind or solar operating or proposed. July nights have run warm, with the 2017-2026 average low at 63.7 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 62.7 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.44 F per decade. Severe drought has been rare: 67 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with the worst year at 2007 and 29 weeks.

21097.text: Harrison County's cropland is mostly rainfed, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather risk falls on dry-land ground. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025 at 47 percent, and its share was 67 percent for 1989-1999 and 55 percent for 2020-2025. The loss ratio was 1.02 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 0.73 over 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $101 per acre for 2026, up 34.7 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $4,169 per acre in 2022.

21099.text: Hart County's loss ratio is the number that stands out: indemnities have run 1.47 times the premium paid across the closed crop years since 1989, and 1.49 over 2016-2025. Excess moisture and flood have been the largest cause of claims at 45 percent. Heat and drought share of indemnities went from 66 percent in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather picture here has shifted toward wet years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $148 per acre in 2026, up 51 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,110 per acre in 2022. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

21101.text: Henderson County is a dryland county. Only 5 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of the rest rides on rain. That shows in the claims: heat and drought paid 60 percent of the indemnities in 2010-2019, down to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have been paid out more than premium in 3 of the 22 closed crop years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.53. Non-irrigated rent is $236 per acre in 2026, up 31.8 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $6,088 per acre in 2022, so rent came to 3.6 percent of that.

21103.text: Henry County's corn has held up better than its weather record might suggest. The median yield across 2008-2025 is 149.3 bushels per acre, and the trend runs up 3.9 bushels a year, even with a bad 2012 at 77.5. Heat and drought claims are the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here at 47 percent of the total since 1989, and their share went from 73 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low averaged 67.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.4 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $95 per acre for 2026, up 28.4 percent since 2016.

21107.text: Hopkins County has no irrigated cropland, so every bushel here depends on the rain that falls. Heat and drought are the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 45 percent of all indemnities since 1989. That share went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, so the pressure has eased some, though 2010-2019 was 53 percent. Indemnities have paid out more than the premiums over the full span, with a loss ratio of 0.8. Non-irrigated cash rent is $160 per acre in 2026, up 23.1 percent since 2016.

21109.text: Jackson County's biggest story is the water, not the heat. Flood and excess moisture cause 48 percent of the crop insurance claims paid here since 1989, and the county's loss ratio is 1.92, meaning claims have run well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought used to drive most claims, falling from 63 percent in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2010-2019. The July nightly low has climbed to 66 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, down 33.8 percent from 2016.

21111.text: Heat and drought claims were a big share of this county's crop insurance payouts in the most recent years. They went from 27 percent in 2000-2009 to 56 percent in 2020-2025, while flood and excess moisture still led the overall total at 50 percent of indemnities from 1989-2025. The county's loss ratio is 0.87 across all closed years, so claims have run below what farmers paid in premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent was $52 per acre in 2025, and the census land value of $13,280 per acre was an operators' estimate. The July nightly low trend since 1976 is 0.33 F per decade, which is not a clear trend, and there is little land in CRP or wind and solar.

21113.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

21115.text: Johnson County's notable feature is how little of its cropland is irrigated: 3 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census. Most of the county's farm trouble has come from wet years, not dry ones. Excess moisture and flood made up 54 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2015, while heat and drought went from 65 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent was $30 per acre in 2022, against a census land and buildings value of $3,144 per acre. Weeks of severe drought across the county have been few, with 64 weeks from 2000-2025, and 12 of those came in 2021-2025.

21117.text: Kenton County's notable story is water, not heat. Floods and excess moisture have caused 57 percent of crop insurance claims since 1989, and the county has only 1 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated. Heat and drought claims went from 56 percent in 2000-2009 to 25 percent in 2010-2019, so that pressure has eased in the claims record. The non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre for 2026. Land and buildings were valued at $7,531 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale. Solar is 5.3 MW operating, with nothing wind.

21119.text: Knott County's notable number is the land itself. The census put land and buildings at $2,596 per acre in 2022, and that was up 103 percent from 2017, or 15.2 percent a year. That is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price, so it tells you how the market feels more than what a parcel would bring. The weather side is quieter. July nights averaged 65.3 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 64 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Drought has been modest: 67 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2007 the worst at 27 weeks.

21121.text: Knox County is mostly non-irrigated, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, so the rent and the yield history are the numbers to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2024, down 26.2 percent from 2013. The median corn yield over 2008-2023 was 123 bushels per acre, but the worst year, 2012, was 85.7. Heat and drought made up 31 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 2000-2009, while excess moisture and flood was the largest cause over 1989-2008 at 48 percent. The census puts land and buildings at $3,690 per acre in 2022, up 54.1 percent from 2017 to 2022.

21123.text: Heat and drought is the main reason claims get paid in Larue County. It accounts for 57 percent of the $34.9 million in indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025. Five of the 18 closed crop years paid out more than the premium, though the ten years from 2016-2025 ran at a loss ratio of 0.59. Corn yields show a trend of 5.2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2023, with a median of 154.6 and a bad year in 2012 at 62.7. Cash rent is $181 per acre, up 9.7 percent since 2016.

21125.text: Laurel County is mostly rain-fed ground, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the story here is wet springs more than dry summers. Crop insurance indemnities from 1989-2025 came to $2.0 million, and excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 67 percent. The loss ratio is 1.1, which means the county has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 61 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 7 percent in 2010-2019. The non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre, down 18.8 percent since 2016.

21127.text: Lawrence County is mostly non-irrigated, and the big story in its insurance record is wet weather, not heat. Flood and excess moisture made up 70 percent of the $511,989 in indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 to 2021. Heat and drought dropped from 61 percent of that in 1989-1999 to 12 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent was $44 per acre in 2025, and the census value of land and buildings was $2,800 per acre in 2022. Ground here has been wet more than it has been dry.

21131.text: Leslie County is mostly non-irrigated ground, with just 6 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022. The census put land and buildings at $1,450 per acre that year, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. What stands out for me is the drought record. The county logged 65 weeks with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse from 2000 through 2025, and 2007 alone had 28 of them. The last five years have been quieter, with 4 such weeks from 2021 through 2025. July nights have been warming slowly, with the average low at 65.5 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.2 F. There is no CRP acreage and no wind or solar operating here.

21133.text: Letcher County is mostly a dry-weather place where the notable thing is the land price. The census put land and buildings at $3,563 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 18.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 3.5 percent a year. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain. Drought has been present but not heavy: 61 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with the worst year being 2007 at 27 weeks. July nights have warmed slightly, with the 2017-2026 average low at 64.2 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.1 F. There are no solar or wind projects here.

21135.text: Lewis County is a non-irrigated county, and none of its harvested cropland has irrigation, so every crop here lives on rain. The insurance record shows the water risk moving. Heat and drought made up 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 21 percent in 2010-2019, then rose to 60 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.17 across all closed crop years since 1989, which means claims have paid out more than premiums came in over that span. Over the last ten closed years it is 0.85. Non-irrigated cash rent was $91 per acre in 2025, and the census put land and buildings at $2,517 per acre in 2022.

21137.text: Lincoln County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather years do most of the work here. Heat and drought claims are the largest cause of insurance payouts at 47 percent, and their share went from 57 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for the whole closed record is 0.93, meaning claims have run close to the premiums paid in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $97 per acre, down 3 percent from 2016, while the census land value is $3,852 per acre. Corn yields show a trend of 2.5 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 159.2 bushels and a worst year at 90 in 2012.

21139.text: Livingston County is a flood-and-rain county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the closed crop years add up to a loss ratio of 0.91, with 5 of the 18 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $168 per acre, up 40 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $4,592 per acre.

21141.text: Logan County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather and rain carry most of the risk here. Heat and drought has been the top cause of insurance claims, and its share went from 49 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.77, and 4 of 26 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $232 per acre, up 6.4 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $6,404 per acre in 2022.

21143.text: Rent here has climbed fast. Non-irrigated cash rent was $144 per acre in 2025, and it is up 73.5 percent from 2014. The more telling story is weather. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, at 53 percent of the $12.7 million paid, and its share went from 39 percent in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 64 percent in 2010-2019. The county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.62, and the census value of land and buildings was $4,987 per acre in 2022. July nights are warmer too, averaging 70.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.1 F.

21145.text: Heat and drought is the main thing in McCracken County's crop insurance record. It was 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 22 percent in 2000-2009, 55 percent in 2010-2019, and 39 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full 1989-2025 span it made up 47 percent of the $29.8 million paid out. The loss ratio of 0.85 means claims have run close to premiums, and 4 of 18 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $140 per acre for 2026, up 33.3 percent from 2016.

21149.text: Here in McLean County the thing that stands out is how much the weather has been on the claims side. Heat and drought went from 61 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is the largest cause over the whole record at 47 percent. The county's corn yield trend since 2008 is up 2.8 bushels per acre a year, and the median is 183.7 bushels, with a bad year in 2010 at 106.5. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground is living on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $191 per acre in 2026, up 36.4 percent since 2014.

21151.text: Madison County is dryland all the way through. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance record is the story here: indemnities have come to $7.1 million across the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.44, which means claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought drove 75 percent of those claims in 1989-1999, and that share fell to 32 percent in 2000-2009 before climbing back to 39 percent in 2020-2025. The county's July nights have warmed too, with the average low at 67.1 F across 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre, unchanged from 2016.

21155.text: Marion County's heat and drought claims are the story here. Heat and drought went from 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 61 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has no irrigated cropland at all, so every dry stretch lands on the crop. The county has paid out $26.5 million on closed crop years since 1989, with a loss ratio of 0.9, and five of fifteen crop years paid more than the premium. The July nightly low averaged 67.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 65.6 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent is $173 per acre in 2026, up 33.1 percent since 2016.

21157.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Marshall County. It was 42 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 56 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full closed run at 53 percent. The loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.81, and two of the 15 crop years paid out more than the premium brought in. None of the cropland is irrigated. The July average low has been 71.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.5 F. Cash rent is $131 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,272 per acre in 2022.

21161.text: Mason County's standout is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $26.4 million since 1989, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 48 percent. In 8 of the 14 closed crop years, payouts beat the premium, and the loss ratio over the full run is 1.06. The share of claims from heat and drought went from 61 percent in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025. The county has no irrigated cropland, so that exposure sits on dry ground every year. Non-irrigated cash rent is $90 per acre for 2026.

21163.text: Meade County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often the claims are heat and drought. Heat and drought went from 81 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025, and it is still the largest cause over the whole record at 71 percent. Indemnities paid $3.89 per $100 of insured value over the last ten closed crop years, while the loss ratio was 0.6 across 1989-2025, with 3 of 17 crop years paying out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $174 per acre, up 28.9 percent from 2016. The 2022 census value of land and buildings was $5,432 per acre, which puts the 2022 rent at 2.74 percent of it.

21165.text: Menifee County is a dryland county, and its claims history is the story. None of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so every acre depends on rain. Heat and drought made up 73 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, and that share fell to 27 percent in 2010-2019. Losses are still paid, though, at $1.6 million across closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought is still the largest cause at 48 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent was $41 per acre in 2023. The census put land and buildings at $2,876 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators themselves estimated.

21167.text: Mercer County is a dryland county with no irrigation at all, and the water risk shows up in the insurance claims. Heat and drought made up 69 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 57 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.01, so claims have run just past premiums over the whole record. The July nightly low has averaged 67.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.6 F, and the July average low reached 66 F first in the 2010s. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $79 per acre for 2026, down 36.8 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $5,326 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

21169.text: Metcalfe County is a dryland county with a loss ratio of 1.56 on crop insurance since 1989, which means claims have paid out more than farmers and the program put in. The biggest single cause of those claims was excess moisture and flood at 54 percent, not drought. Heat and drought share of claims went from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 24 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $180 per acre in 2026, up 26.8 percent since 2016. Census land value is $3,990 per acre in 2022, and the county has 55 MW of solar operating.

21171.text: Monroe County is a non-irrigated county, and the thing that stands out here is water coming in too much rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 1.98, with 11 of 14 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, so it has been a real share of claims, though not the main one. Non-irrigated cash rent is $150 per acre in 2026, up 17.2 percent since 2016.

21173.text: Montgomery County is a dryland county, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and its crop insurance record is shaped more by wet years than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 48 percent of indemnities paid over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for those closed years is 1.79, so claims have run well ahead of premiums over the long run. Heat and drought went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, which is the change to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, down 14.3 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,254 per acre.

21175.text: Morgan County is mostly a flood and wet-year county on the insurance side. Excess moisture and flood account for 61 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 2.14, so claims have run well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought used to lead the claims, at 77 percent in 1989-1999, but that share fell to 15 percent in 2020-2025. None of the cropland is irrigated. The 2026 non-irrigated cash rent is $25 per acre, down 16.7 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $2,458 per acre in 2022, up 26.2 percent from 2017.

21177.text: Muhlenberg County's notable number is water, not heat. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it collected in 4 of 17 closed crop years. The heat and drought share has held in a narrow band, 41 percent in 1989-1999 and 36 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields trend up 4.7 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2024, with a median of 158.6 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $148 per acre, up 29.8 percent since 2016. The Conservation Reserve Program holds 3662 acres, 6 percent of the cropland base, and 201 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

21179.text: Nelson County is dryland ground, with no irrigated acres in the 2022 census, so the county depends on rain for every bushel. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here, at 54 percent of the $28.8 million paid out over 1989-2025, and its share was 62 percent in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2020-2025. The crop insurance loss ratio is 0.73 over the closed years, and the payouts ran over the premium in 5 of 17 crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $180 per acre in 2026, up 23.3 percent from 2016.

21181.text: Nicholas County's notable number is the water side of the ledger. Excess moisture and flood carried the largest share of insurance claims, 46 percent, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.93, so claims have run well ahead of premiums over the long run. Heat and drought claims went from 64 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 25 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $120 per acre in 2025, up 51.9 percent since 2013. The county has had 1 week of severe drought or worse since 2021, against 40 weeks over 2000-2025.

21183.text: What stands out in Ohio County is the water, and it is wet water more than dry. Excess moisture and flood account for 68 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 6 of the 19 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's non-irrigated cash rent was $168 per acre in 2024, up 35.5 percent from 2014. The median corn yield is 180 bushels per acre, and the worst year, 2012, was 101.4.

21185.text: Oldham County is mostly ground that depends on rain, since only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Heat and drought has been the biggest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 58 percent of $3.1 million paid since 1989. It was 83 percent in 1989-1999 and 46 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has come down but is still the main cause. The loss ratio is 0.44 over 1989-2025 and 0.25 over the last ten closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $96 per acre for 2026, up 2.7 percent from 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $8,262 per acre in 2022.

21187.text: Owen County's crop insurance record leans toward too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.39, so claims have run above premiums. Heat and drought went from 69 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025, and that latest share is the one to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $86 per acre in 2024, and the census put land and buildings at $3,637 per acre in 2022.

21189.text: Owsley County is a dryland county. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $34 per acre in 2022. The bigger story in the insurance claims is water from above, not from below: excess moisture and flood account for 56 percent of indemnities paid over 1992-2021, while heat and drought went from 65 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2010-2019. The July nightly low has averaged 66.4 F over 2017-2026, up from a 1991-2020 normal of 64.8 F. Land and buildings were valued at $2,657 per acre in the 2022 census, and that figure is the operators' own estimate.

21191.text: Pendleton County's crop insurance record leans heavily toward wet years rather than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 54 percent of the $6.7 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for that whole stretch is 1.17, meaning more was paid out than was collected in premium. Heat and drought claimswas 59 percent in 1989-1999 and 51 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 25 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre for 2026, down 35.9 percent since 2016, while the census land value is $4,055 per acre for 2022.

21193.text: Perry County's notable number is the land. Census operators put land and buildings at $2,578 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 125 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 17.6 percent a year. Nightly lows in July have warmed a little, and the July average low for 2017-2026 is 65.7 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.4 F. Severe drought has been rare here: 67 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with 4 weeks in 2021-2025. Nothing in the county is generating power yet, though a 490 MW solar project has been proposed to EIA.

21199.text: Pulaski County's corn ground is all dryland, and the heat and drought claims are what stand out. Since 1989, insurers have paid $24.6 million on closed crop years, and heat and drought was the largest cause at 43 percent. That share went from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025, and the last ten closed years ran a loss ratio of 1.01. The county's land value was $4,741 per acre in 2022, and the 2026 non-irrigated rent is $105 per acre, which is a lot of money riding on each dry year.

21201.text: Robertson County's heat and drought claims stand out. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 62 percent in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the full span is 1.6, so the county has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premiums. None of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so a dry July lands straight on the crop. Non-irrigated cash rent was $74 per acre in 2025, up 86.2 percent since 2014. The census value of land and buildings is $3,643 per acre, which rose 66.6 percent between 2017 and 2022.

21203.text: Rockcastle County's corn ground is all dryland, and the notable thing here is wet springs more than dry summers. Excess moisture and flood account for 46 percent of the insurance payouts since 1989, and the county's loss ratio across 1989-2025 is 0.78. The last ten closed crop years have been much calmer, at 0.26. Heat and drought claims went from 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 66.6 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $72 per acre in 2026, up 30.9 percent since 2016.

21205.text: Rowan County is a non-irrigated county, and the thing that stands out is the insurance record. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.34, meaning claims have run above premium. Heat and drought went from 78 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is the largest cause overall at 54 percent. Cash rent is $42 per acre for 2024, down 45.9 percent since 2013.

21207.text: Russell County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn yield trend and the crop insurance record carry most of the story. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 46 percent, and its share went from 54 percent in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for closed years 1989-2025 is 0.96, and it was 0.62 over 2016-2025. Corn yields have trended up 4.8 bushels per acre a year over published years 2008-2024, with a worst year of 2012 at 63.3 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $92 per acre in 2026.

21209.text: Scott County's heat and drought exposure is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.88. Non-irrigated cash rent is $110 per acre for 2026, down 3.5 percent from 2016. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the July nightly low has climbed from 65.1 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 66.8 F over 2017-2026.

21213.text: Simpson County is a dryland county. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the corn crop lives or dies on rain. The county has paid out more in crop insurance claims than it collected in premium over the full record, with a loss ratio of 0.98, and 8 of 20 crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause of those claims at 49 percent, up from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $217 per acre, up 17.9 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $6,821 per acre in 2022.

21215.text: Spencer County is non-irrigated from end to end, with 0 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, so every dry spell lands on the crop. The heat and drought share of crop insurance indemnities went from 49 percent in 1989-1999 to 70 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.79 over 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $122 per acre for 2026, up 22 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $6,499 per acre in 2022, which was up 43.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. Corn yields have a trend of 3.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 169.7.

21217.text: Taylor County is a dry-land county, and the crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Since 1989 the closed crop years have paid out $33.6 million, and the loss ratio is 1.41, with 9 of 14 years paying more than the premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 49 percent, and its share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2020-2025. The July nights have also warmed, averaging 67.8 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $162 per acre, up 1.2 percent since 2016. The corn yield trend over 2008-2025 is 2.4 bushels per acre a year.

21219.text: Todd County is dryland corn and beans, and the drought record is what stands out. Heat and drought made up 57 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and the share rose from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out $74.4 million since 1989 against a loss ratio of 0.68, and the 2012 corn yield of 80.8 bushels per acre is the bad year to know. Rent is $200 per acre for non-irrigated ground, down 5.2 percent since 2016.

21221.text: Trigg County's heat and drought claims have been the biggest part of crop insurance payouts for as long as the records go, though their share has slipped from 57 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. The county's crop insurance loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.02, and 8 of 19 closed crop years paid out more than the premium collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $175 per acre for 2026, down 10.3 percent from 2014, and the county is only 5 percent irrigated. Land and buildings were valued at $5,078 per acre in 2022, up 23.6 percent since 2017, and CRP covers 8.9 percent of the cropland base, with 1565 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

21223.text: Trimble County is a rain county more than a dry one. Its crop insurance record is dominated by excess moisture and flood, which took 52 percent of indemnities, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.14, so claims have run ahead of premiums over that stretch. Heat and drought claims have shrunk, going from 59 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Nothing here is irrigated, and the county has had only 1 week of severe drought or worse since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $146 per acre, up 16.8 percent from 2014 to 2024.

21225.text: Union County is mostly dryland, and the water story here runs through the sky, not the pump. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 4 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims went from 14 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 52 percent in 2010-2019, then back to 14 percent in 2020-2025. The 2012 corn crop was 75.6 bushels per acre, far below the county's 183.9 median, and that one year is most of the drought story. Non-irrigated cash rent is $259 per acre for 2026, up 22.2 percent since 2016.

21227.text: Warren County's heat and drought claims have been the largest cause of crop insurance payouts for decades, but their share has eased. Heat and drought went from 61 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 47 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the full closed years is 0.9, and 8 of 20 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $200 per acre in 2026, up 17.6 percent since 2016. The county corn trend over 2008-2025 is up 3.8 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 177.3 bushels and a worst year at 65.4 in 2012.

21229.text: Washington County is dryland, and the numbers say the ground has been carrying more heat and drought claims lately. Heat and drought made up 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 80 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.94, so claims have run close to premiums over the long haul. Nightly July lows have warmed as well, averaging 67.1 F from 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $62 per acre, and land and buildings were valued at $4,727 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators themselves estimated.

21231.text: Heat and drought is the story in Wayne County. It was 43 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 79 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has no irrigated harvested cropland to fall back on. Non-irrigated cash rent is $130 per acre for 2026, up 11.1 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 67.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.3 F. Corn yields have trended up 2.9 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the worst year, 2012, was 90.3 bushels. The loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.62.

21233.text: Webster County is dryland all the way through. None of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so every bushel depends on rain falling at the right time. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 49 percent, and its share went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, though the 2010-2019 stretch hit 66 percent. The 2012 season was the worst year on record for corn, at 59.5 bushels per acre against a median of 172.1. Non-irrigated rent is $229 per acre for 2026, up 8.5 percent since 2016, and CRP holds 8.2 percent of the cropland base.

21235.text: Whitley County is a place where the notable thing is the water, or the lack of it. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. The insurance record backs that up: excess moisture and flood was the largest cause of losses from 1989-2007 at 37 percent, and heat and drought was 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999. The worst corn year in the 2008-2022 run was 2012, at 99.1 bushels per acre, against a median of 114. July nights have been warmer, averaging 65.9 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $17 per acre for 2026, down 38.2 percent from 2016.

21237.text: Wolfe County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here is dryland, and the rent reflects that. Non-irrigated cash rent is $54 per acre in 2026, and it was up 65.2 percent from 2016. The heat and drought share of crop insurance claims went from 72 percent in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2010-2019, while excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 47 percent of indemnities over the whole record. The July nightly low has averaged 65.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.4 F. Weeks in severe drought since 2021 are zero.

21239.text: Woodford County is a non-irrigated county with no irrigated harvested cropland in the 2022 census, so its corn lives or dies on rain. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.21, meaning indemnities have run above premiums over the full record, though the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 0.61. Heat and drought made up 57 percent of indemnities over the whole record, down from 73 percent in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $113 per acre for 2026, against a census land value of $8,841 per acre in 2022. The corn yield trend since 2008 is up 3.1 bushels per acre a year, with a worst year of 64.4 in 2012.

22001.text: Acadia Parish is a rice and irrigated ground county, and most of its harvested cropland is watered: 70 percent of it, with 70 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $88 per acre, against $54 for non-irrigated, and the non-irrigated rent is up 67.2 percent since 2016. The bigger risk here is too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood make up 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.72, with 6 of 18 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025.

22005.text: Ascension Parish has no irrigated cropland, and every drop of irrigation water comes from groundwater. What stands out here is the insurance record. Closed crop years from 1991-2025 paid out $4.6 million in claims, and wind was the largest cause at 65 percent. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 1.06, meaning claims ran above premium. Heat and drought claims were 6 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 and 7 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $46 per acre in 2010, and the census put land and buildings at $5,985 per acre in 2022.

22007.text: Assumption Parish is a county where the July nights have been getting warmer for a long time, and the average low has reached 70 F or higher in 124 Julys since 1900. The July average low was 75.1 F across 2017-2026, against a 73.8 F normal for 1991-2020. Still, the crop insurance picture leans on wind, not heat: wind caused 73 percent of the $11.5 million in indemnities paid over 2014-2024. Heat and drought claims fell from 35 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.86, and 40 percent of irrigation water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2022 was $44 per acre.

22009.text: Avoyelles Parish is mostly dryland, with only 18 percent of harvested cropland irrigated and most of that water coming from groundwater. The county's flood and excess moisture losses are the main thing the insurance record shows: 52 percent of indemnities since 1989 came from that cause. Heat and drought claims were 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 36 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years have been getting more expensive. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 1.18 over 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $115 per acre in 2026, up 45.6 percent since 2016, and the irrigated rent of $155 per acre is 1.35 times that.

22017.text: Caddo Parish is notable for the loss record more than for the rent. Crop insurance indemnities have paid out more than the premiums in 11 of 17 closed crop years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.64, with $14.24 paid per $100 of insured value. Excess moisture and flood caused the largest share of those losses at 40 percent. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 42 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $71 per acre in 2026, and irrigated is $130 per acre.

22019.text: Most of the ground in Calcasieu Parish is not irrigated, but the water claims are what stand out here. Crop insurance has paid $16.9 million on closed crop years since 1989, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 43 percent. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, up 46.4 percent from 2016. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.32, so claims have run above premiums.

22021.text: Caldwell Parish is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out here is the water coming in too fast. Excess moisture and flood make up 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.16, so claims have paid out more than premiums. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $48 per acre, down from 2016 after a long slide. Caldwell is a county where a wet year hurts more than a dry one, so plan the ground for drainage first.

22023.text: Cameron Parish is a flood county first. Excess moisture and flood make up 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over those closed years is 2.8, meaning claims have run well past premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025, and the last ten closed crop years show a loss ratio of 3.94. Non-irrigated rent is $12 per acre in 2024, down 50 percent from 2012, while irrigated rent is $84 per acre in 2026. Groundwater supplies 40 percent of irrigation water.

22025.text: Catahoula Parish is a dryland-rent county with a wet history. The county's worst corn year was 2009 at 128 bushels per acre, but the bigger story in the claims is excess moisture and flood, which made up 56 percent of the $135.9 million paid out since 1989. Heat and drought went from 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has come down. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $88 per acre, up 27.5 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground rented for $147 per acre in 2025, and there were 0 MW of solar or wind operating in the county.

22027.text: Claiborne is a dryland parish, with no irrigated harvested cropland in the 2022 census, so rain carries the whole crop. The county is hot at night in July: the average low for 2017-2026 was 72.8 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.1 F, and the July low has been warming at 0.61 F per decade since 1976. Drought is the bigger concern. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 163 of 1357 across 2000-2025, and 2011 alone logged 51 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent is $19 per acre for 2026, up 40.7 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,379 per acre.

22029.text: Concordia Parish is a non-irrigated ground county on paper, but the irrigated rent still is well above the dryland figure. Non-irrigated cash rent is $119 per acre in 2026, up 20.2 percent from 2016, and irrigated rent is $185. Only 24 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 78 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Corn yields trend up 4 bushels per acre a year on the published years 2008-2025, with a median of 169.5 and a worst year of 121 in 2009. Crop insurance has paid $112.8 million on closed years since 1989, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 49 percent of that.

22031.text: The loss ratio here is the first thing to look at. Crop insurance has paid out $3.8 million on closed crop years since 1989 against premiums that bring the loss ratio to 2.12, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 38 percent of that. Heat and drought claims went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 11 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. July nights have warmed, with the average low at 73.3 F for 2017-2026 against a 72.2 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre, up 5.4 percent since 2016.

22033.text: East Baton Rouge is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 40 percent of the $884,592 in crop insurance indemnities paid from 1990 to 2025, and heat and drought claims went from 14 percent in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, with none in 2010-2019. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre in 2026, up 56.5 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $8,027 per acre, down 2.7 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nights have warmed to an average low of 74 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.7 F.

22035.text: Most of the ground in East Carroll Parish is irrigated, 70 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and 82 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated ground rents for $183 per acre in 2026 against $130 for non-irrigated, and the gap has widened from 1.17 times in 2009 to 1.41 times now. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.98, and excess moisture and flood have been the largest cause, at 72 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025.

22037.text: East Feliciana is a rain county, not a heat county, and the claims show it. Excess moisture and flood make up 52 percent of the $1.4 million in indemnities paid over 2000-2025, and nothing here is irrigated. Heat and drought went from 41 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 48 percent in 2020-2025, with 4 percent in between, so the dry years have come back hard. Rent is $22 per acre, up 57.1 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings are valued at $4,244 per acre by operators, up 51.6 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nights now average 73.1 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.7 F. The county has 611 CRP acres, and none expire between fiscal 2027 and 2029.

22039.text: Evangeline Parish is a county where most of the cropland gets water, and that changes how the rent reads. Irrigated ground rents for $90 per acre, and irrigated cash rent was 1.49 times non-irrigated in 2009 and is 2.06 times now, so the gap has widened. Non-irrigated rent is $44, down 57.4 percent since 2016. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause at 61 percent. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio is 1.14, and claims have paid out more than premium in 6 of 17 years.

22041.text: Franklin Parish is mostly dryland ground, and the place where it stands out is water and wet years, not drought. Non-irrigated cash rent is $78 per acre in 2026, down 9.3 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $160. Floods and excess moisture are the largest cause of claims at 52 percent of indemnities, and the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 show a loss ratio of 0.97. Heat and drought made up 26 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and 20 percent in 2020-2025.

22043.text: Grant Parish is mostly dryland, and the county's loss history leans toward too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 44 percent of the $12.2 million in crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over those years is 1.34. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has grown more recently. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2025 is $78 per acre, up 10.7 percent since 2014. Only 13 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the July nightly low averaged 72.3 F in 2017-2026.

22045.text: Iberia Parish is a county where the ground is mostly dryland and the weather risk that shows up in the claims is wind, not drought. Wind accounts for 74 percent of the $14.0 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989. Heat and drought went from 10 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2010-2019, then 0 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $94 per acre, up 16 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has warmed 0.49 F per decade since 1976.

22047.text: Iberville Parish is a county where the crop insurance picture is the story. Wind caused 57 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1. Heat and drought claims went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 1 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre for 2026, down 11.3 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $2,562 per acre in 2022, up 42.7 percent from 2017. Groundwater supplied 60 percent of irrigation water in 2015, and July nightly lows averaged 74.5 F over 2017-2026.

22051.text: Jefferson Parish's most notable number is heat. The July average nightly low was 76 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 75.2 F, and July nights have run at or above 70 F in 127 Julys since 1900. The nightly low has been warming at 0.39 F per decade since 1976. Land and buildings were valued at $2,176 per acre in 2022, and that value fell 6.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. Drought has been present too, with 125 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year was 2000 with 42 weeks.

22053.text: Jefferson Davis Parish is an irrigated county, with 86 percent of harvested cropland watered, and 70 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Rent for irrigated ground is $70 per acre, against $18 for dryland, and the dryland rent is up 44 percent since 2016. The loss side has changed. Heat and drought was 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 25 percent in 2020-2025, and the ten closed years 2016-2025 paid out more than premium, at a loss ratio of 1.07. Over the full record, excess moisture and flood is the largest cause, at 52 percent.

22055.text: Lafayette Parish is a county where the water problem is too much rain, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 32 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, the largest single cause. Heat and drought share went from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years are claiming more ground than they used to, though the trend is still mostly a flood story here. Only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and groundwater supplies 80 percent of that water. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre in 2026, up 11.4 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $8,291 per acre in 2022.

22057.text: Lafourche Parish is a wind county, and the claims show it. Wind caused 73 percent of the $8.5 million in crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1990 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.86, up from 0.69 for the full 1990-2025 span. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $26 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $2,909 per acre. Heat and drought show up in the claims in some years: 11 percent in 2010-2019, and none in the other two periods. July nightly lows averaged 76.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 75.2 F.

22059.text: Flood is the story in La Salle Parish, not drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 60 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1990 to 2025, which came to $783,241 for closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 46 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent was $32 per acre in 2021, and census land and buildings value was $4,051 per acre in 2022.

22063.text: What stands out in Livingston Parish is the land price next to the rent. Operators put the value of land and buildings at $6,940 per acre in 2022, and that figure was up 29.7 percent from 2017, while non-irrigated cash rent was $15 per acre in 2010. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse ran 99 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, with 2000 the worst at 37 weeks. July nights are warming, with the average low at 73.8 F for 2017-2026 against a 72.6 F normal. There is no CRP, wind or solar on the books here.

22065.text: Madison Parish is an irrigated county more than most. Irrigated ground rents for $159 per acre, against $143 for dryland, and 52 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 86 percent of that water coming from groundwater. The thing that stands out is the insurance record. Crop years since 1989 have paid out $162.8 million, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.04, so claims have run past premium. Most of that comes from excess moisture and flood, 57 percent of the total. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The census puts land and buildings at $3,764 per acre, and CRP holds 10.7 percent of the cropland base.

22067.text: Morehouse Parish is a county where irrigation sets the rent. Irrigated ground is $150 per acre against $75 for non-irrigated, and irrigated rent was 1.25 times non-irrigated in 2009 and has moved up to 2.00 times in 2026. Most of the water comes from groundwater, 67 percent in 2015. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.32 over the closed years 1989-2025, and it is 1.47 over 2016-2025. Excess moisture and flood make up 65 percent of the indemnities. Heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025.

22069.text: Natchitoches Parish is a non-irrigated corn county where the crop insurance record is the story. Indemnities paid out more than premium in 11 of 16 closed crop years, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 2.04. Excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 61 percent of indemnities, and heat and drought went from 23 percent in 2000-2009 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $58 per acre, up 8.5 percent since 2016, and the county's median corn yield is 144.2 bushels per acre with a worst year of 117.1 in 2016.

22073.text: Ouachita Parish's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Over the ten closed crop years from 2016 to 2025, indemnities ran at 1.07 times the premium, and the parish paid out more than premium in 5 of 12 closed years since 1989. Excess moisture and flood account for 57 percent of all indemnities, so this is a wet-ground county more than a dry one. Heat and drought went from 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2010-2019, then 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $84 per acre, up 8.3 percent from 2016.

22075.text: Plaquemines Parish is one of the few counties in the Atlas where irrigation is a real part of the cropland picture, with 43 percent of harvested acres irrigated in the 2022 census. The land is valued at $2,130 per acre, and that value rose 51 percent between 2017 and 2022, or 8.6 percent a year. Drought is the piece to watch. The county had 142 weeks with at least 50 percent of the parish in severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, and 41 of those weeks came in 2021-2025 alone. The July nights have been warm too, averaging 77 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 76.3 F. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar operating here.

22077.text: Pointe Coupee is a county where the water is the story. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater, so the county is mostly dryland ground. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the ten closed crop years from 2016 to 2025, with a loss ratio of 1.05, and excess moisture and flood, not heat, has been the biggest cause of claims since 1989. Heat and drought went from 12 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $84 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground rents for $182 per acre.

22079.text: Rapides is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 54 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the county has paid out more than it took in premiums over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.14. Heat and drought claims rose from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is worth watching. Non-irrigated cash rent is $114 per acre in 2026, up 43.4 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $143. Only 32 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

22081.text: Red River Parish is a flood-and-rain county on paper, and the insurance record says so: excess moisture and flood account for 53 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.46, which means claims have run well above premiums. Heat and drought claims have fallen as a share, from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. July nights are warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, at an average low of 73.7 F for 2017-2026 against 72.1 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $78 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground is $125 per acre. Only 21 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 84 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

22085.text: Sabine Parish is a dryland county with no irrigation at all, so the water question here is rain, not pumps. The July nightly lows have run warmer lately, averaging 72.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.7 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.52 F per decade. Severe drought has been the bigger pressure. The county spent 154 weeks at or above that level between 2000 and 2025, with 52 of them in 2011 alone. Rent is $20 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and the census value of land and buildings is $3,692 per acre, down 2.3 percent from 2017 to 2022.

22089.text: St. Charles Parish has the nights to show for it. July's average low over 2017-2026 is 75.3 F, up from a 1991-2020 normal of 74.3 F, and the July nightly low trend since 1976 is warming at 0.43 F per decade. Julys with an average low at or above 70 F number 127 since 1900. The county also carries heavy drought history: 127 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 42 of those weeks in 2000 alone. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $26 per acre in 2023. Census land and buildings value was $4,463 per acre in 2022, up 27.8 percent from 2017 to 2022.

22091.text: St. Helena Parish's indemnity record points to wet years more than hot ones. Excess moisture and flood made up 63 percent of closed crop insurance claims from 2018 to 2024, and the parish paid $154,671 in that span. Heat and drought accounted for 24 percent of claims from 2020 to 2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre for 2026, up 71.4 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $4,232 per acre in 2022, and it rose only 1.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP holds 237 acres, and none of that expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

22093.text: St. James Parish is a county where wind does most of the damage to insured crops. Wind accounts for 70 percent of the $3.3 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1997. The loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.92, meaning claims came close to premiums, and the 1995-2025 ratio was 0.59. Non-irrigated cash rent is $62 per acre, while census land and buildings value was $4,097 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 33.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nightly lows averaged 74.8 F over 2017-2026, up from the 1991-2020 normal of 73.6 F. Heat and drought were 2 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 and 4 percent in 2020-2025.

22095.text: What stands out in St. John the Baptist Parish is the crop insurance record. Wind has caused 79 percent of the indemnities paid from 2006-2024, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.98, meaning claims came close to matching premiums. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 2 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low averaged 74.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 73.6 F. Census land and buildings were valued at $5,674 per acre in 2022.

22097.text: St. Landry is a flood county more than a drought one. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 42 percent, and the closed crop years since 1989 have paid out $124.5 million, a loss ratio of 1.02. The last ten closed years ran higher at 1.23, with $12.35 paid per $100 of insured value. Irrigated rent was $90 per acre in 2026 against $89 non-irrigated, and it was 1.56 times non-irrigated back in 2009. Heat and drought share of claims went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields trend up 2.9 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 167.4.

22099.text: St. Martin Parish is notable for its insurance record. Crop insurance paid $21.3 million in closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 1.24, meaning claims ran above premium. Heat and drought went from 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025, while wind is the largest single cause at 37 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $72 per acre, and only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

22101.text:
St. Mary Parish is notable for wind, not heat or water. Wind caused 74 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 2005-2025, out of $11.2 million paid in closed crop years. The loss ratio for closed crop years 1995-2025 is 0.62, and for the last ten closed years it is 0.77. No cropland is irrigated, and no acres are in CRP.

Heat and drought claims went from 14 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre in 2026, up 66 percent since 2014.

22103.text: St. Tammany's notable number is the July heat. The average nightly low for July in 2017-2026 was 73.9 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 72.7 F. July lows have hit 70 F or more in 120 Julys since 1900, and the July average low first reached 66 F in the 1900s. Crop insurance losses from 1997-2006 were mostly wind, at 52 percent, not drought. Non-irrigated cash rent is $14 per acre, and the census land and buildings value is $10,879 per acre, with 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated.

22105.text: Tangipahoa Parish is a county where heat and drought have carried most of the crop insurance claims, and the shift in that mix is the first thing to see. Heat and drought was 100 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 28 percent in 2020-2025, while the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.38, so claims have still paid out more than premiums came in. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre, up 60.9 percent from 2016 to 2026.

22107.text: Tensas Parish is a county where most of the cropland is non-irrigated, and the irrigated ground rents for $175 per acre against $104 for dryland.
