Irrigated rent has climbed from 1.03 times the dryland rent in 2009 to 1.68 times in 2026, while non-irrigated rent is down 1 percent since 2016. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.94. Heat and drought went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, and excess moisture and flood remain the largest single cause at 46 percent.

22109.text: Terrebonne Parish is a wind county. Of the $2.4 million in crop insurance indemnities paid from 2002 to 2024, wind caused 90 percent. Heat and drought accounted for none of the indemnities from 2020 to 2025, and only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The July nightly low averaged 76.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 75.4 F, and 127 Julys since 1900 have averaged a low at or above 70 F. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2017 was $70 per acre. The loss ratio for 1995-2025 was 0.65, and it was 0.83 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025.

22115.text: Vernon Parish is a dry-weather county more than a hot one. Drought has been the main pressure: 144 of the 1,357 weeks from 2000 through 2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2011 alone had 52 of them. The last five years already logged 28 such weeks. Irrigation is close to nonexistent, at 1 percent of harvested cropland, so the ground depends on rain. July nightly lows are warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, 72.7 F against 71.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026. The 2022 census put land and buildings at $5,108 per acre, up 37.9 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP acres are zero, and solar is 9.5 MW operating with nothing wind.

22117.text: Washington Parish is a county where the crop insurance record tells the story. Heat and drought claims made up 89 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 27 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather risk that drove most payouts in the early years has been a smaller share of losses since. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.31, meaning insurers paid out more than they took in premium. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground is mostly dependent on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 46.8 percent from 2016.

22119.text: Webster Parish is a non-irrigated county, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in the 2022 census, so the rain you get is the crop's water. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims in the closed years from 1991 to 2001, at 73 percent of $979,356 paid out, and its share fell from 81 percent in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2000-2009. The July nightly low averaged 73.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.8 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $22 per acre in 2025, up 209.9 percent since 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $4,320 per acre in the 2022 census, and there is no CRP or wind or solar in the county.

22121.text: West Baton Rouge is a county where the water problem has been too much water. Flood and excess moisture make up 55 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.47. Heat and drought claims went from 6 percent in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $66 per acre in 2023, up 6.4 percent since 2013, and the census value of land and buildings was $4,693 per acre in 2022, up 66.4 percent from 2017.

22123.text: Most of the ground in West Carroll Parish is not irrigated, and the bigger story here is wet years. Floods and excess moisture paid 66 percent of the crop insurance indemnities from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio for the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 1.12, which means claims ran past premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $98 per acre, up 47.7 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $176 per acre. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, so dry years have carried less of the claim load lately.

22125.text: Most of the trouble in West Feliciana Parish has come from too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 82 percent of the $10.8 million paid out on closed crop years since 1994, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.97. Heat and drought claims are small but rising, going from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. The county has no irrigated cropland, and cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $20 per acre in 2026, down 11.4 percent from 2016. Census land value was $3,197 per acre in 2022.

23001.text: The county's own story runs on cold rather than heat. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 31 percent of indemnities, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.19, which means claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in over that stretch. Heat and drought shares moved from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, with a lower share in between. July nights are a little warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, 59.9 F against 58.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre, up 42.6 percent since 2016. Solar is operating at 63.1 MW, with 29.8 MW more proposed.

23003.text: Aroostook is a county where the biggest insurance story is water in the wrong place. Excess moisture and flood account for 61 percent of the $148.7 million paid out on closed crop years since 1989, and indemnities for irrigation failure total only $19,115. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, with 8 percent in 2000-2009 in between. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $108 per acre, up 46.9 percent from 2016.

23005.text: Cumberland County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 5 percent irrigated in 2022, so rain decides most years here. The notable change is in the claims. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 22 weeks in severe drought or worse over 2021-2025. Freeze and frost still caused the largest share of losses over the full record, at 39 percent. The loss ratio of 0.63 means insurers have paid out less than premiums collected on closed crop years, so the account has mostly run in the farmers' favor. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, up 60.2 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings value was $9,968 per acre in 2022.

23011.text: Kennebec County is a non-irrigated county, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so the rain that falls is the rain the crop gets. The loss picture has shifted. Heat and drought went from 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood is the largest cause over the full 1990-2025 record at 30 percent. Rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 102.1 percent since 2016. The ten closed crop years from 2016 to 2025 show a loss ratio of 0.58.

23015.text: Lincoln County is one where the water question has been quieter than the land price. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has had 74 weeks at 50 percent or more in severe drought or worse since 2000, with 20 of those weeks in 2025 alone. Land and buildings were valued at $6,410 per acre in the 2022 census, and that value rose 38 percent from 2017 to 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2024 was $45 per acre. July nights have warmed a little, with the 2017-2026 average low at 60.4 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 58.6 F.

23017.text: Oxford County's most notable figure is the insurance record for heat and drought, which went from 22 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025, with 2000-2009 at 2 percent in between. Hail is the largest single cause over 1990-2025 at 31 percent, and the loss ratio for those closed years is 0.57, so claims have paid out more than the premiums taken in. Rent is $24 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, down 11.1 percent since 2014. The census value of land and buildings was $3,166 per acre in 2022, and the county had 20 weeks in severe drought or worse over 2021-2025, with 2025 the worst year at 18 weeks.

23019.text: Penobscot's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 5 percent irrigated, and the rent has moved a lot: non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre in 2026, up 52.2 percent from 2016. The county's biggest insurance claims have come from too much water rather than too little, with excess moisture and flood at 32 percent of indemnities since 1995. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, which is the shift to watch. The census put land and buildings at $3,836 per acre in 2022, and the July nightly low has been 57.5 F across 2017-2026 against a 56.2 F normal.

23023.text: Sagadahoc County is a small irrigated-free county where the notable thing is the land value. The 2022 census put land and buildings at $4,880 per acre, and that figure rose 18 percent between 2017 and 2022, or 3.4 percent a year. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is watered by rain alone. Drought is present but not heavy: 73 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year, 2002, had 19 of them. Julys are warming, with the 2017-2026 average nightly low at 60.7 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 59 F. Solar is the main new land use, with 10.6 MW operating and 17.2 MW proposed.

23025.text: What stands out in Somerset County is how little of the cropland is irrigated, 4 percent, and how much of the crop insurance money has come from hail, which is 39 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought claims went from 0 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 5 percent in 2020-2025, but that is a small share. The loss ratio is 0.55, meaning claims have paid out well below the premiums over 1990-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre in 2026, up 10.9 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $2,253 per acre in 2022, which rose 52.6 percent from 2017 to 2022.

23027.text: Waldo County's cropland rent is $28 per acre for 2026, up 31 percent since 2016. The bigger story in the numbers is the drought: 19 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2025 alone, and 19 across 2021-2025, which is most of the stretch since 2000 for a county that has spent only 66 of 1357 weeks that dry. Heat and drought account for 40 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid on closed claims since 2000, totaling $127,860. The July nightly low has averaged 59.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 57.8 F. Land and buildings were valued at $4,188 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 39.7 percent from 2017 to 2022.

23029.text:
Washington County's crop insurance record stands out more than its weather does. Indemnities have run well above premiums in the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.63 for 2016-2025 against 0.86 over 1997-2025. Most of the payouts over the full stretch came from area and index plans with no peril assigned, at 76 percent. Heat and drought claims were 11 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 and 12 percent in 2020-2025, so they are a small piece of the story.

The July nightly low has averaged 57.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 56.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $90 per acre in 2014. Census land and buildings value was $2,136 per acre in 2022, up 39.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

23031.text: York County's notable story is in the insurance claims and the rent. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, while freeze and frost is still the largest cause over the full record at 40 percent. Insurance has paid out $2.8 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.34, meaning claims have run above premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $58 per acre in 2026, up from the 2016 level by 110.9 percent. Solar is operating at 110.7 MW, and no CRP acres are enrolled.

24001.text: Heat and drought is the story in Allegany County. It was 18 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-1999, and it was 90 percent over 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.06, which means insurers paid out more than the premiums brought in. Corn yields have held up better in most years, with a median of 121.2 bushels per acre over 2008-2019 and a worst year at 87.5 in 2010. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 19.1 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $6,375 per acre in the 2022 census, and that figure is the operators' own estimate.

24003.text: Heat and drought is the story in Anne Arundel County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 48 percent in 2000-2009 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2020-2025 period also logged 24 weeks in severe drought or worse. The county's worst corn year was 2024 at 85.1 bushels per acre, against a median of 159.5. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre for 2026, and the land and buildings census value in 2022 was $12,289 per acre. The July nightly low has averaged 70.7 F over 2017-2026, up from 69.2 F across the 1991-2020 normal.

24005.text: Heat and drought is the story in Baltimore County. It caused 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1997-2025, and its share went from 98 percent in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2020-2025. Claims ran high through the 2000s, dropped to 47 percent in 2010-2019, then came back. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. The loss ratio over 1995-2025 is 0.43, and cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $156 per acre, up 108 percent since 2016.

24009.text: Calvert County is a county where heat and drought claims have been the story. Heat and drought made up 80 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, dropped to 62 percent in 2010-2019, and rose to 92 percent in 2020-2025. Over closed crop years since 1992 the loss ratio is 0.75, and indemnity paid was $8.84 per $100 of insured value in 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $68 per acre in 2026, up 5.4 percent from 2016, and none of the harvested cropland is irrigated. The census value of land and buildings was $11,544 per acre in 2022.

24011.text: Heat and drought are the story in Caroline County. They took 95 percent of crop insurance indemnity dollars in 1989-1999, and 68 percent in 2020-2025, which is still the largest cause in the county. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, indemnities totaled $45.6 million, and the loss ratio was 0.65, with 4 of 23 crop years paying out more than premium. The county corn yield trend is 2.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, against a median of 157.1 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $140 per acre and irrigated rent is $234, with census land and buildings at $9,891 per acre in 2022. The July nightly low has been warming, and it averaged 68.8 F over 2017-2026.

24013.text: Carroll County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $20.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 79 percent of that. The share went from 95 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 92 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2000-2009 and 2010-2019 periods sat lower in between. Three of the 20 closed crop years paid out more than the premium, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.44. Non-irrigated cash rent was $132 per acre in 2024, up 50 percent from 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $10,420 per acre in 2022.

24015.text: Cecil County's notable number is heat and drought in the claims. From 1989-1999 heat and drought made up 88 percent of indemnities, and in 2010-2019 it was 33 percent. In 2020-2025 it was back up to 69 percent. Only 3 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $131 per acre, up 39.4 percent since 2016. Crop insurance has paid out less than premium over the closed years, at a 0.33 loss ratio, and no single crop year has paid more than it took in. The July nightly lows have run warmer in recent years, with the 2017-2026 average at 69.1 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.1 F.

24017.text: The thing that stands out in Charles County is heat and drought, and it has been getting worse. Heat and drought made up 88 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 73 percent in 2020-2025. Over the whole record the county has paid $11.2 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.72, which means the claims have run well ahead of premium. The July nightly low has averaged 70.5 F since 2017, against a 68.6 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated rent is $44 per acre for 2026, up 12.8 percent since 2016.

24019.text: Dorchester County is a place where irrigation changes the rent picture. Irrigated ground rented for $270 per acre in 2025, and that was 2.48 times the non-irrigated rate, up from 1.32 times in 2011. Non-irrigated cash rent is $117 per acre in 2026, up 9.3 percent since 2016. Heat and drought went from 71 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the closed crop years is 0.54, so claims have paid out less than the premiums collected over the full period.

24021.text: Frederick County's ground is mostly dryland, and the weather risk that shows up in the claims is heat and drought. Heat and drought made up 94 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 90 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid out more than its premiums in 5 of 24 closed crop years. Summer nights are also warming: the July average low has reached 66.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.9 F. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $123 per acre in 2026, up 17.1 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $11,000 per acre.

24023.text: Garrett County is not irrigated at all, so every bushel here rides on rain, and the crop insurance record shows heat and drought doing more of the damage lately. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 70 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.17, meaning claims paid out more than the premiums that came in. The worst drought year on the record was 2024, with 21 weeks of severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre, up 36.9 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,541 per acre.

24025.text: What stands out in Harford County is the heat and drought claims. Over 1989-1999 heat and drought made up 85 percent of crop insurance indemnities, and over 2020-2025 it was 59 percent, after falling to 28 percent in 2010-2019. Corn yields have been trending up 2.3 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 165.9 and a bad year in 2010 at 129.7. Non-irrigated cash rent is $171 per acre for 2026, up 42.5 percent from 2016. The loss ratio of 0.19 over the last ten closed crop years is low, and the census value of $11,928 per acre is far above the rent.

24027.text: Howard County's crop insurance record leans on heat and drought more than most counties in this state. The share of indemnities from heat and drought went from 93 percent in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, with a dip to 41 percent in 2010-2019. Over the closed years 1995-2025 the loss ratio is 0.19, and the last ten closed crop years show 0.13. Land values are high next to the rent: the 2022 census value is $12,622 per acre against a 2017 non-irrigated cash rent of $72 per acre. Julys are running warmer at night, with the average low at 67.2 F for 2017-2026 against a 65.7 F normal.

24029.text: Kent County's corn has been trending up, not down, and the heat is the story to watch. Median yield over 2008-2025 was 164.1 bushels per acre, and the trend gained 3.8 bushels per acre a year, even with a worst year of 85.1 in 2011. Heat and drought was 86 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 81 percent in 2020-2025, and the July nightly low has been warming, averaging 70.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 68.3 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $191 per acre in 2026, up 69 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $282 per acre. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

24031.text: Montgomery County's cropland is small and mostly non-irrigated, and the rent there has climbed fast. Non-irrigated cash rent is $111 per acre in 2026, up 76.2 percent from 2016. Heat and drought is the main cause of claims, at 76 percent of indemnities since 1989. Its share went from 97 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 86 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 65 percent in 2010-2019. The July nightly low averaged 67.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.4 F. The county paid $7.2 million in indemnities over closed crop years 1989-2025.

24033.text: Prince George's County is a small irrigation county, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland watered in 2022, so most of the ground here lives or dies on rain. Heat and drought made up 90 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 70 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid $4.6 million on closed crop years since 1989. Its median corn yield for 2008-2023 was 91 bushels per acre, with the worst year, 2012, at 53.9. July nights have also warmed: the average low for 2017-2026 was 69.5 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.9 F. The county's non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $50 per acre.

24035.text: Queen Anne's is a county where irrigation changes the math. Irrigated ground rents for $259 per acre, against $177 for non-irrigated, and the gap has held in a narrow band rather than trending. Heat and drought made up 92 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 69 percent in 2020-2025, so that risk has stayed the main claim driver for decades. Groundwater supplies 81 percent of the irrigation water, which matters if you're counting on pumping through a dry July. July nightly lows have run warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, and insurance has paid out $40.7 million on closed crop years since 1989.

24037.text: St. Mary's is a county where heat and drought account for most of the crop insurance payouts, and the July nights are getting warmer. Heat and drought was 94 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and is 80 percent in 2020-2025. Heat and drought claims have stayed the largest cause for thirty-plus years, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.35, so payouts have come in well under premium. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre in 2026, down 3.7 percent from 2014.

24039.text: Somerset County is a dryland county, and the heat-and-drought pattern is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst year for drought weeks was 2002 with 31 weeks. Nightly July lows have also been running warmer, with 2017-2026 averaging 71.3 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.7 F. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.61, but over 2016-2025 it is 0.48, so the most recent decade has been easier on insurance claims. Non-irrigated cash rent is $102 per acre in 2026, up 15.3 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $7,951 per acre in 2022, and rent was 1.28 percent of that value.

24041.text: Talbot County is mostly ground that has to be watered to be worth much, and the heat is getting worse at night. July nightly lows averaged 70.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F, and July has reached an average low of 70 F or higher in 16 years since 1900. Heat and drought made up 95 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 71 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims still come from the same cause. The county's own corn yield trend is up 3.1 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, but the worst year, 2012, was 101.6 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $136 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $9,250 per acre in 2022.

24043.text: Washington County's most telling number is heat and drought. Their share of crop insurance payouts went from 77 percent in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst drought weeks came in 2002 with 16 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent is $128 per acre in 2026, up 70.7 percent from 2016. The corn yield trend is 1.6 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the worst year was 2010 at 65 bushels. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so dry years land hard on the ground you're renting.

24045.text: Wicomico County's cropland is mostly dryland, but a lot of the value sits in the 30 percent that is irrigated, and irrigated ground rents for $193 per acre against $114 for dryland. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here, at 67 percent of the $32.0 million paid across closed crop years 1989-2025, and its share went from 81 percent in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.7 over the full record, and only 4 of 21 crop years paid out more than premium. Dryland cash rent is up 39.9 percent from 2016 to 2026, and census land and buildings value is $7,641 per acre.

24047.text: Worcester County is mostly dryland, and the heat is showing up in the insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 79 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2020-2025, and they make up 62 percent of all indemnities since 1989. The county has been paying out more than premium in only 2 of 21 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.45. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $118 per acre, up 33.3 percent from 2016. The census land value of $8,232 per acre is far above the 2022 rent, which works out to 1.36 percent of value.

25001.text: Most of the cropland in Barnstable County is irrigated, 87 percent of it by the 2022 census, and the water comes mostly from groundwater, 83 percent in 2015. Irrigated ground rents for $433 per acre in 2026, against $38 for non-irrigated. Crop insurance has paid out $1.65 for every dollar of premium over 1989-2025, and the ten years 2016-2025 ran at 1.68. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. July nightly lows averaged 65.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 63.5 F normal for 1991-2020.

25003.text: Berkshire County is a dry-land county with a few notable things. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent is $58 per acre, up 96.6 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims went from 8 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 41 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.35, so insurers have paid out more than the premiums brought in. July nights are warmer than they were, with the average low at 59.3 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 57 F. Land and buildings were valued at $8,606 per acre in 2022.

25005.text: Bristol County's cropland is mostly rented on dry ground, and the water side is where the county stands apart. Irrigated rent was $273 per acre in 2025, and that was 2.46 times the $101 per acre non-irrigated rent in 2026, up from 1.97 times in 2009. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of insurance claims in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $1.8 million in closed years, more than the premiums paid in, with a loss ratio of 1.06.

25007.text: Dukes County is an island county, and the notable number here is the land value. The census put land and buildings at $8,824 per acre in 2022, down 22.8 percent from 2017, while non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $51 per acre. Irrigated ground rented for $86 per acre in 2021, so that is the only irrigated figure on the books. July nightly lows have averaged 65.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.9 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Drought has been rare here: 38 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2020 was the worst year with 13 weeks.

25009.text: Essex County is a small-acreage county where heat and drought claims have been the largest source of crop insurance payments, and that share has come back up in the latest years. Heat and drought was 44 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, dropped to 31 percent in 2010-2019, and was back at 46 percent in 2020-2025. Only 14 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $78 per acre, and irrigated ground rents for $345 per acre. The census puts land and buildings at $20,111 per acre, which was up 15.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

25011.text: Franklin County's cropland is mostly unirrigated, with only 9 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, yet the ground that is irrigated rents for $331 per acre against $141 for dryland. Crop insurance has paid out $28.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over those years is 1.76, meaning claims have run well above premiums. Heat and drought went from 39 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, with 2010-2019 at 27 percent. The 2026 non-irrigated rent is up 66.9 percent from 2016.

25013.text: Hampden County's cropland is mostly dryland, with 17 percent of harvested acres irrigated in 2022. The bigger story in the claims is wet weather: excess moisture and flood account for 45 percent of the $34.9 million in indemnities paid since 1991. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.12, so the payouts have run above premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $130 per acre, and irrigated ground rented for $265 per acre in 2023.

25015.text: Hampshire County is a small irrigated-ground county, with irrigation at 7 percent of harvested cropland in 2022. Irrigated rent is $268 per acre in 2026 against $129 for non-irrigated ground, a ratio of 2.08 that has not moved in a clear direction since 2009. Heat and drought claims were 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 9 percent in 2020-2025, while the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1. Census land and buildings value is $10,568 per acre in 2022, up 37.9 percent from 2017.

25017.text: Middlesex County is a small, mostly non-irrigated cropland county, and the one thing that stands out is the heat-and-drought share of crop claims. It went from 14 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2010-2019 and 31 percent in 2020-2025. Cropland is mostly not irrigated, with 15 percent irrigated in 2022, and non-irrigated cash rent is $64 per acre in 2026 against $122 per acre for irrigated ground. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.69, and freeze and frost is still the largest cause of claims at 47 percent. Land and buildings were valued at $22,138 per acre in 2022.

25027.text: Worcester County is a non-irrigated county, with only 6 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so most of the rent here is for ground that depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, up 132.7 percent since 2016. The crop insurance loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.11, meaning claims paid more than premium came in, and the share from heat and drought went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 13 percent in 2020-2025. Census land value is $15,447 per acre, and solar is the big land use here at 463 MW operating.

28001.text: Adams County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than the premiums over the full span, with a loss ratio of 1.17 for 1989-2025 and 1.5 for the last ten closed crop years. Excess moisture and flood caused 84 percent of the payouts. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, so that is the change to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2023 was $62 per acre, and the Census put land and buildings at $3,265 per acre in 2022, up 10.7 percent from 2017 to 2022.

28003.text: Alcorn County's crop insurance record leans toward too much water rather than too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 65 percent of the $18.2 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.96, close to even. Heat and drought claims went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 15 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, up 16.7 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $2,375 per acre in 2022.

28005.text: Amite County's crop insurance record is the story here. Heat and drought made up 94 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, and the loss ratio for closed crop years is 1.25, so claims have run ahead of premiums. The share fell to 45 percent in 2000-2009 and 2010-2019, then climbed back to 63 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $21 per acre in 2026, up 50 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings were valued at $3,315 per acre in 2022, rising 3.9 percent from 2017 to 2022. Enrollment in CRP covers 14.8 percent of the cropland base, and none of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

28007.text: Attala County is not an irrigated county: none of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop depends on rain. Its insurance record leans toward wet years, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause of indemnities at 57 percent. Heat and drought claims were 76 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 11 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $1.25 for every dollar of premium over the last ten closed crop years, against 0.88 across 1989-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $85 per acre in 2026, up 50.4 percent since 2016, and the census put land and buildings at $2,239 per acre in 2022.

28009.text: Benton County's rent is up 49.5 percent since 2016, to $77 per acre for non-irrigated ground, but the bigger story here is heat and drought. They took 77 percent of crop insurance indemnity dollars in 1989-1999 and 51 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 0.81. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the corn yield trend is 1.7 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2025, with a worst year of 116.1 in 2011. The land value of $2,707 per acre in 2022 was a rise of 40.6 percent from 2017, and CRP covers 2560 acres, with 325 of those expiring fiscal years 2027-2029.

28011.text: Bolivar County is a ground-water irrigation county, and that shapes most of what follows. Irrigated ground rents for $182 per acre in 2026 against $123 for non-irrigated, and the gap has widened since 2008, when the irrigated rent was 1.25 times the non-irrigated figure. Groundwater supplies 95 percent of the irrigation water. Insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.13 over the last ten closed crop years, and excess moisture and flood has been the largest cause of claims at 49 percent. Heat and drought went from 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025. Land is valued at $4,310 per acre in 2022, up 42.5 percent from 2017.

28013.text: Calhoun County is mostly dryland, and the water that matters here comes from the sky. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's corn yields have trended up 3.2 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 155.6 bushels. The loss side is where the story is. Excess moisture and flood account for 62 percent of indemnities since 1989, and heat and drought claims went from 26 percent in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, after peaking at 44 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $132 per acre in 2026, down 0.8 percent from 2016. The 13 percent of cropland in CRP is a fact you'll want in your planning, with 1582 acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

28015.text: Carroll County is a rain-fed corner of Mississippi where the irrigated ground is worth a lot more to rent than the dryland, and the gap has widened. Non-irrigated cash rent is $76 per acre in 2026, down 19.9 percent from 2016, while irrigated rent is $197 per acre. Losses have run ahead of premiums, with a loss ratio of 0.97 over 1989-2025 and 1.19 over 2016-2025. Excess moisture and flood account for 58 percent of indemnities, and heat and drought went from 62 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields have a trend of 2.7 bushels per acre a year, and 45 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

28017.text: Chickasaw County is mostly dryland, and the crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Insurance paid out $50.2 million on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, which works out to a loss ratio of 1.01, and claims paid more than premium in 4 of 18 closed years. Excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 50 percent. Heat and drought went from 46 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $88 per acre for 2026, down 24.4 percent from 2016, while irrigated ground rents at $165 per acre.

28019.text: Choctaw County's cropland is mostly under the Conservation Reserve Program: 3,607 acres in 2025, which is 46.3 percent of the cropland base, and 448 of those acres come out of contract in fiscal years 2027-2029. Crop insurance losses here have come mostly from too much water, with excess moisture and flood at 72 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought claims went from 32 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre for 2026, up 22 percent since 2016. The July nightly low averaged 71.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.7 F.

28021.text: Claiborne County's notable thing is the heat and drought claims. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still lead the whole record at 42 percent. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the crop rides on rain. The loss ratio of 0.68 over 2016-2025 says claims have been paid out at more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $102 per acre in 2026, up 48.9 percent since 2016, and the land and buildings were valued at $2,979 per acre in 2022.

28023.text: Clarke County's notable number is the heat. July nights now average a low of 72.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.5 F, and the county has had 53 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Crop insurance claims paid $645,327 over 1989-2025, and freeze and frost is the largest cause at 45 percent, while heat and drought was 3 percent in both 1989-1999 and 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $23 per acre for 2026, up 9.5 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $3,758 per acre in 2022, up 68 percent from 2017.

28025.text: Clay County is a dryland county with no irrigated cropland, and its insurance history leans toward too much water rather than too little. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025, with 13 percent in 2010-2019 in between. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, down 16.7 percent from 2016, and CRP holds 14.8 percent of the cropland base.

28027.text: Coahoma County is a county where irrigation sets the price of ground. Irrigated cash rent is $193 per acre against $155 for non-irrigated ground, and 72 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 95 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Heat and drought claims went from 53 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.2, so insurance has paid out more than it took in. Non-irrigated rent is up 25 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $3,910 per acre. Wind is the only power on the land, at 184.5 MW.

28029.text: Copiah County is a county where heat and drought have become the main source of claims. Heat and drought went from 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $72 per acre in 2026, up 222.2 percent from 2016.

Heat and drought share of indemnities went from 21 percent in 2010-2019 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. 28133.text: Sunflower County is mostly irrigated, with 69 percent of harvested cropland under water in 2022 and 95 percent of that water pulled from groundwater. The crop insurance record is the thing I'd look at first. Indemnities have paid out more than premium in 17 of 32 closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.16 over 1989-2025. Heat and drought claims were 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 43 percent again in 2020-2025, with a dip to 33 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $123 per acre in 2026, up 32.3 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $178 per acre.

28135.text: Tallahatchie is a county where the irrigated ground matters most. Irrigated acres make up 62 percent of harvested cropland, and 95 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Irrigated rent is $204 per acre against $147 for non-irrigated ground, and the crop insurance loss ratio is 0.91 over 1989-2025, with 10 of 31 crop years paying out more than premium. Most of the claim dollars have come from excess moisture and flood, at 60 percent. Heat and drought went from 44 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, and weeks of severe drought have clustered in recent years, with 67 in 2021-2025.

28137.text: Tate County is a rain county first. Only 4 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and the big claim dollars have come from excess moisture and flood, which took 48 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025. Heat and drought has been the cause that moved most, going from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings is $3,310 per acre, an estimate from the operators themselves. Corn yields have trended up 4.4 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 160.1 bushels.

28141.text: Tishomingo County is a wet-ground county more than a dry one. Crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025 went mostly to excess moisture and flood, at 68 percent, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.12, meaning claims have run past premiums. Heat and drought claims went from 33 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025, and the July average nightly low is 70.1 F for 2017-2026 against a 68.5 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026, up 77.8 percent since 2016, and the Census puts land and buildings at $2,290 per acre.

28145.text: Union County is a dry-year county more than a hot one, and the claims tell that story. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, while heat and drought went from 35 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.7, so claims have run ahead of premium. There's no irrigation on the cropland, and non-irrigated rent is $66 per acre, up 13.8 percent since 2016. Corn has held up at a median of 156.1 bushels per acre for 2012-2022, but the worst year, 2012, fell to 102.6.

28147.text: Heat and drought is the story in Walthall County. It was 99 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 40 percent in 2020-2025, but the county still paid out $2.7 million on closed crop years since 1994, with heat and drought the largest cause at 59 percent. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.94, so claims have run close to premiums over the whole period, and the 2016-2025 ratio is 0.76. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre for 2026, up 36.1 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $3,741 per acre in 2022. The July nightly low averaged 72.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 70.9 F normal for 1991-2020.

28149.text: Warren County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums over the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.09 across 1989-2025, and 1.24 across the ten closed years 2016-2025. Flood and excess moisture drive 83 percent of the claims, while heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $155 per acre in 2026, up 55 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents at $190 per acre. Groundwater supplies 95 percent of irrigation water, and CRP covers 13.9 percent of the cropland base.

28151.text: Washington County is a heavily irrigated county, and most of its cropland gets water from wells. The 2022 census put 73 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, and 95 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought went from 38 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are where the claims have been piling up. Non-irrigated cash rent is $172 per acre for 2026, and irrigated ground rents for $190 per acre. The insurance record is thin on the upside: the closed crop years from 1989 to 2025 paid out $151.7 million, with a loss ratio of 0.77.

28153.text: Wayne County's cash rent is the thing to look at first: $23 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, down 45.2 percent from 2016. That drop is steep, and it sits next to a crop insurance loss ratio of 1.27 over 1995-2025, meaning the county has paid out more in claims than it took in premiums. Freeze and frost caused the largest share of those claims at 39 percent. Heat and drought went from 40 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground runs on rain. The census puts land and buildings at $3,372 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated.

28155.text: The county's biggest story is water that is too much, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 55 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio for closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.57. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so this is ground that lives on rain. Heat and drought claims went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has had 22 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $125 per acre, up 40.4 percent since 2016. Over 2008-2023 the county corn yield trend is up 3.2 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 150 bushels per acre.

28157.text: Wilkinson County is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 94 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio over those closed crop years is 1.39, which means the county has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premiums. Heat and drought claims were 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 1 percent in 2010-2019, and 5 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $14 per acre. CRP covers 1011 acres, or 18.1 percent of the cropland base, and 267 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

28159.text: Winston County is mostly dryland, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so the weather shows up in the claims. Heat and drought made up 53 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and their share went from 20 percent in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over those closed crop years is 1.01, which means the insurance paid back what farmers put in. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $26 per acre in 2025, up 47.2 percent from 2014. The census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $2,658 per acre, and CRP covers 2070 acres, with 70 of those expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029.

28161.text: Yalobusha County is mostly dryland ground that floods more often than it dries out. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.84. Heat and drought claims were 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 24 percent in 2020-2025, with 43 percent in 2000-2009 in between. Non-irrigated cash rent is $104 per acre in 2026, up 67.7 percent since 2016.

28163.text: Yazoo County's cropland is a lot more irrigated than the county's history of wet years would suggest, and the groundwater is doing most of the work: 36 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 95 percent of that water comes from wells. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.21, and the largest cause is excess moisture and flood at 61 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought went from 71 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $152 per acre in 2026, and irrigated rent is $195.

30001.text: Beaverhead County is mostly irrigated ground: 91 percent of harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from wells. Irrigation failure is the largest single cause of crop insurance claims here, at 34 percent of the $7.5 million paid over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 29 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2010-2019, then 35 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated rent is $121 per acre and non-irrigated is $18, with non-irrigated up 23.3 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value is $1,883 per acre. Eighty megawatts of solar is operating, and 200 megawatts more is proposed.

30003.text: Big Horn County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the cash rent reflects that: $28 per acre non-irrigated against $102 per acre irrigated. Non-irrigated rent is up 37.5 percent from 2016 to 2026. The county's crop insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 0.89 over 1989-2025 and 9 of 28 closed crop years paying more than premium. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025, and hail is still the largest single cause at 29 percent. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 50 in 2021-2025.

30005.text: Heat and drought is the story in Blaine County. It caused 74 percent of crop insurance indemnity dollars in the 2020-2025 period, up from 28 percent in 1989-1999. Indemnities paid out more than premiums in 17 of the 37 closed crop years, and the ten years from 2016 to 2025 ran a loss ratio of 1.3. Only 14 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre for 2026, and the census land value of $849 per acre is well above that.

30007.text: Broadwater County is a county where a good share of the cropland sits under irrigation, and the non-irrigated ground has a lower rent than most of the state. Irrigated rent is $215 per acre for 2026, while non-irrigated rent in 2024 was $24 per acre, down 2 percent from 2013. The heat and drought share of crop insurance indemnities went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 82 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 0.91. Those claims are the main thing to watch on the dryland ground.

30009.text: Carbon County is mostly irrigated ground, with 76 percent of harvested cropland under water in the 2022 census, and every drop of it comes from surface sources. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims since 1989, at 41 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 22 percent in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated cash rent is $116 per acre against $32 for non-irrigated ground. Crop insurance has paid out $13.3 million on closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.88 over that span, though it was 0.42 across the last ten closed crop years. Wind is running at 239.8 MW, and no CRP acres expire through fiscal 2029.

30011.text: Carter County is a dryland place, and the insurance claims tell you where the trouble has been. Heat and drought went from 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, insurers paid $30.99 per $100 of insured value, and the loss ratio was 1.45. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2026, up 13.2 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $753 per acre in 2022. Irrigation is barely used here, with 2 percent of water from groundwater in 2015.

30013.text: Cascade County's heat and drought has cost more than anything else. Heat and drought was 52 percent of the $101.9 million paid out in closed crop years since 1989, and it went from 53 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025, with a dip to 30 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio is 0.79 over those years, and in the last ten closed years it was 0.88, so claims have run close to premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre, up 65.5 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground is $100 per acre, and only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

30015.text: Chouteau County is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is where the weather shows. Heat and drought make up 54 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the share went from 53 percent in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.82 over those closed years, with 9 of 37 crop years paying out more than premium. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is taking the weather as it comes. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre in 2026, up 17.7 percent since 2016.

30021.text: Dawson County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often heat and drought have cost growers money. Heat and drought went from 7 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.2, so insurers paid out more than premium in that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $36 per acre, and irrigated ground rented for $122 per acre in 2025. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

30025.text: Heat and drought is the story in Fallon County. It paid 73 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 20 percent in 1989-1999, and the county has paid out more than it took in premiums: a loss ratio of 1.04 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and 1.27 over the last ten. Weeks in severe drought or worse have run at 115 since 2021. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, up 43.2 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,043 per acre in 2022, a figure the operators themselves gave. Wind is the only power on the ground, 30 megawatts, and no CRP acres expire through 2029.

30027.text: Fergus County's dryland ground is the story here. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of insurance claims, and its share rose from 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, claims paid $1.08 for every dollar of premium. Non-irrigated rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 30.2 percent since 2016, while the census puts land and buildings at $1,279 per acre in 2022. Irrigated ground rents for $76 per acre in 2024, but only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

30029.text: Flathead ground is mostly dryland, and the irrigated acres carry a premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, up 19.7 percent from 2016, and irrigated rent is $71 per acre. The heat-and-drought share of crop insurance indemnities went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 51 percent in 2010-2019. Across the closed crop years 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.58, and there was a stretch of 42 weeks in severe drought in 2001 alone. Land and buildings were valued at $9,225 per acre in 2022, up 44.4 percent from 2017.

30031.text: Gallatin County is a tale of two kinds of ground. Irrigated cash rent is $173 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground now rents for 4.44 times the non-irrigated rate of $39 per acre, up from 2.51 times in 2016. Non-irrigated rent is up only 2.6 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $4,069 per acre in 2022, up 34.3 percent from 2017. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. The county has had 65 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021, and the July nightly low has averaged 48.5 F over 2017-2026.

30033.text: Garfield County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is the insurance record. Heat and drought was 20 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 46 percent in 2020-2025. The last ten closed crop years paid out $1.28 for every dollar of premium, and that is the number to look at if you're weighing ground here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre for 2026, up 87.1 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings were $672 per acre in 2022. July nightly lows averaged 58.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 56 F. CRP covers 15077 acres, and none of it expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

30035.text: Heat and drought is the story in Glacier County. It caused 48 percent of the $146.0 million paid out in closed crop insurance claims from 1989 through 2025, and its share went from 38 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025. Drought also took up a lot of the calendar: 89 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025 alone, against 343 of 1357 weeks across 2000-2025. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre in 2026, up 31.8 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,478 per acre in 2022.

30037.text: Golden Valley County's most notable number is that heat and drought drive most of the crop insurance payouts here. Heat and drought caused 57 percent of the $25.8 million paid out on closed crop years from 1989-2025, and its share went from 29 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2000-2009, then 46 percent in 2010-2019 and 48 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 0.81, and farmers got back $16.90 for every $100 insured. Only 17 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre, up 50 percent since 2016.

30039.text: Granite County is mostly irrigated ground: 88 percent of harvested cropland, and the irrigation water comes from surface sources, with none from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent was $15 per acre in 2023, while irrigated rent was $91 per acre in 2022, so the water is what the rent pays for. Drought is the thing to watch. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse went from 333 weeks across 2000-2025 with the worst years 2024 and 2025 at 44 weeks each, and 137 of those weeks fell in 2021-2025. July nights are a little warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, with a trend warming. Land and buildings were valued at $2,808 per acre in 2022, up 73.5 percent from 2017.

30041.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Hill County. It caused 60 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and its share was 53 percent in 1989-1999 and 68 percent in 2000-2009 and again in 2020-2025. Claims paid out more than premium in 10 of 37 closed crop years, and the loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.92. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated rent is $30 per acre for 2026, up 7 percent from 2016. Census land value was $1,066 per acre in 2022, and 30152 acres are in CRP.

30043.text: Jefferson County is mostly irrigated, and it is the heat-and-drought claims that stand out. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 96 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.96. Irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $98 per acre against $22 for non-irrigated ground, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,954 per acre. Groundwater supplies just 1 percent of irrigation water, so the ground depends on surface supply.

30045.text: Judith Basin is a dryland county. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rest lives on rain. The notable number is the insurance claims: heat and drought drove 63 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 64 percent in 2020-2025, against 30 percent in 1989-1999 and 27 percent in 2010-2019. Insurers have paid out more than they took in premiums, with a loss ratio of 0.85 across the closed years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre for 2026, up 23.6 percent since 2016. Census land value is $1,350 per acre, up 45.3 percent from 2017 to 2022, and that is what the operators say, not sale prices.

30047.text: Lake County's notable number is the irrigated ground: 74 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigated rent is $92 per acre against $42 for dryland. Insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 1.12 over 1989-2025 and 1.5 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 33 percent, and its share went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is up 60.4 percent since 2016, and 2026 is when that shows on the lease.

30051.text: Liberty County's drought record stands out more than its rent does. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of the $236.4 million in crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1989 through 2025, and the crop insurance loss ratio was 1.05 over that span, so claims ran past premium in 13 of 37 years. Over the last ten closed years the ratio was 1.19. Heat and drought share went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre, and irrigated is $60, with no groundwater in the irrigation mix.

30057.text: Most of Madison County's harvested cropland is irrigated, 80 percent in the 2022 census, and the county draws none of that water from groundwater. Heat and drought has been the biggest cause of crop insurance claims, and its share went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 72 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.78, and the 2016-2025 years run lower at 0.55. Irrigated cash rent in 2026 was $127 per acre, and land and buildings were valued at $2,757 per acre in 2022, a rise of 61.2 percent from 2017 to 2022.

30059.text: Meagher County's cropland is mostly watered, with 60 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, and the water comes from surface sources since none is pumped from groundwater. The place where the county stands out is heat and drought in the insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 10 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 0.71. Irrigated cash rent was $38 per acre in 2014 against $22 for non-irrigated ground, and census land and buildings were $1,316 per acre in 2022.

30063.text: Missoula County is mostly irrigated ground, 82 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and the water mostly comes from surface sources, with groundwater at 3 percent in 2015. Irrigated ground rents for $68 per acre in 2025 against $35 for non-irrigated, and non-irrigated rent is up 89.2 percent from 2014 to 2025. Heat and drought claims went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 83 percent in 2000-2009, and the county had 44 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2025. July nights are getting warmer, with the average low at 49.1 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 47.8 F.

30065.text: Musselshell's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, and the county's loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 1.19, meaning more was paid out than was collected in premium. Since then the share has come down, from 29 percent in 2010-2019 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. Dry ground is the common thread. The county was in severe drought or worse for 53 weeks in 2002, and 52 weeks in 2021-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $23 per acre, up 64.3 percent from 2016.

30067.text: Park County is mostly irrigated ground, 67 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and the water comes from surface sources, not wells. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 41 percent of indemnities since 1989, and its share went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 64 percent in 2000-2009 before settling at 49 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026, up 85.7 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $92 per acre. The census puts land and buildings at $2,000 per acre, and 25.4 percent of the cropland base is in CRP.

30069.text: Heat and drought is the thing that stands out in Petroleum County. It was 45 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 61 percent in 2000-2009, then 27 percent in 2010-2019 and 41 percent in 2020-2025. Closed years total $21.8 million paid out, and the loss ratio is 1.17 over the whole period, so claims have run past premiums. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation failure paid $722,015 in all. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre in 2025, down 5.3 percent from 2013, while land and buildings were valued at $1,059 per acre in 2022.

30071.text: Heat and drought is the story in Phillips County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 27 percent in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the ten closed crop years from 2016 to 2025 paid out $1.77 for every dollar of premium. Weeks in severe drought or worse reached 41 in 2021 and totaled 111 across 2021-2025. Only 14 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated rent is $30 per acre, up 32.6 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,124 per acre.

30073.text: Pondera County is a dryland county with a loss record worth a second look. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance loss ratio is 0.89 over the closed years 1989-2025, with 11 of 37 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 42 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre, up 23.9 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $86 per acre. Census land and buildings value is $1,751 per acre for 2022.

30075.text: Powder River County is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is what stands out. Heat and drought took 89 percent of indemnity dollars in 2020-2025, up from 30 percent in 1989-1999, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.14, with 0 of 10 crop years paying out less than premium. The 2016-2025 loss ratio is 0.96, so the recent stretch has run closer to even. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $18 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $957 per acre, an estimate from operators rather than a sale.

30079.text: Prairie County's notable number is heat and drought. It was 11 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and is 55 percent for 2020-2025. The ten closed crop years from 2016 through 2025 paid out 1.04 for every dollar of premium, and two of the eleven closed crop years paid more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre for 2026, up 51 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents at $153 per acre. Only 20 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most acres depend on rain. The July nightly low is warming, though it has not reached 70 F in any July since 1900.

30083.text: Richland County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often heat and drought have cost the growers here. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 70 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks follow the same path: 111 weeks of severe drought or worse came in 2021-2025 alone, and 2021 had 49 of them. Non-irrigated cash rent is $33 per acre in 2026, up 40.4 percent since 2016, while the census land value is $1,109 per acre.

30085.text: Roosevelt County is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how much the insurance claims have shifted toward heat and drought. That share went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $335.5 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 1.53, so claims have run well ahead of premium. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $30 per acre, up 9.1 percent since 2016. The county's census land value in 2022 was $1,108 per acre, and the 2022 rent came to 2.93 percent of that.

30087.text: Rosebud County is mostly dryland, and the heat and drought claims are where it stands out. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.98, close to paying out what farmers paid in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $25 per acre in 2026, up 47.1 percent since 2016, while the census value of land and buildings was $716 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves put on their ground. Wind is the other big thing here, with 568.3 MW operating and no solar yet.

30089.text: Sanders County is mostly dryland in what it pays on rent, but it leans on irrigation more than most of the state's ground. Irrigated land is 46 percent of the harvested cropland from the 2022 census, and a farmer pays $62 per acre to rent it against $22 for dry ground. Freeze and frost are the biggest cause of insurance claims here, at 50 percent of indemnities since 1989. Heat and drought claims went from 51 percent in 2000-2009 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigation failure has paid only $24,307 across all closed years.

30091.text: Heat and drought is the story in Sheridan County. Since 2000, it has been the largest reason for crop insurance payouts, at 62 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and its share went from 10 percent in 1989-1999 to 79 percent in 2020-2025. Indemnities have run above premiums in 11 of 36 closed crop years, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.28. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre for 2026, up 30.8 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $1,554 per acre in 2022, a 17.5 percent yearly gain from 2017. Irrigation is a small piece of the picture, and there is no wind or solar operating.

30095.text: Stillwater County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the thing that stands out is how often heat and drought have shown up in the claims. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 66 percent in 2000-2009, and it was still 43 percent in 2020-2025. Since 1989, insurers have paid $21.2 million on closed crop years, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.91, so payouts have run close to premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre in 2026, while irrigated ground rents at $103 per acre.

30097.text: Sweet Grass County is a county where the irrigated ground does most of the work. Irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre in 2026, against $15 for non-irrigated ground in 2019, and 53 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Crop insurance has paid out $4.6 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.21, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 57 percent, and its share went from 47 percent in 1989-1999 to 75 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $1,499 per acre in 2022, and CRP holds 43.5 percent of the cropland base.

30099.text: Teton County's notable thing is the heat and drought claims. Heat and drought made up 47 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 64 percent in 2000-2009, 33 percent in 2010-2019, and 62 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.98, so claims came close to premiums paid in. Irrigated ground rents for $108 per acre, against $42 for non-irrigated, and 26 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, all from surface water. The July nightly low averaged 50 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 48.5 F.

30101.text: Toole County is mostly dryland, and its insurance record is the story. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county has paid out $253.5 million in crop insurance indemnities since 1989, with heat and drought the largest cause at 59 percent. Its loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.38, so claims ran well past premium. Heat and drought went from 51 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 83 percent in 2000-2009, and then 57 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, up 5.2 percent since 2016.

30103.text: Treasure County is a county where most of the cropland is irrigated, 68 percent of harvested acres in the 2022 census, and the irrigated cash rent of $131 per acre for 2026 is what sets the tone here. Non-irrigated ground rents for $8 per acre in 2025, down 61.5 percent from 2014, so dryland is a very different business from the irrigated acres. The crop insurance loss ratio is 0.76 over 2016-2025, and heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Hail is still the largest single cause of claims, at 33 percent. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 44 in 2021-2025.

30105.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Valley County. It caused 70 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and its share went from 18 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 85 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.69, meaning claims paid out well more than premiums collected. Irrigation is small here at 5 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $27 per acre in 2026, with irrigated ground at $62 per acre.

30109.text: Heat and drought is the story in Wibaux County. It was 17 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 63 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the full record at 54 percent. The county has paid out more than it took in premium: a loss ratio of 1.07 across closed years, and 1.26 over 2016-2025. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre this year, up 35.4 percent from 2016. Census land value is $934 per acre, up 51.4 percent from 2017 to 2022.

30111.text: Yellowstone is a dryland county where the water question matters more than the heat question. Only 24 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026 and irrigated ground rents for $132 per acre, so the gap between the two is wide. Heat and drought claims went from 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out $60.1 million on closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.78 over 1989-2025. The land and buildings value is $1,216 per acre, and CRP covers 14.3 percent of the cropland base.

32013.text: Humboldt County is all irrigated cropland, and most of that water comes from the ground. Over the last ten closed crop years, insurance paid out $1.43 for every dollar of premium, and the loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 1.06, with five of ten crop years paying more than premium. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of claims at 38 percent, while heat and drought went from 46 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 14 percent in 2010-2019 and 25 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $1,164 per acre in 2022, up 31.2 percent since 2017. Nightly July lows have averaged 58.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 56 F.

32021.text: Mineral County is mostly a dry-weather story, and the ground is a big part of it. The county takes all of its irrigation water from groundwater, and it has spent a lot of weeks in severe drought: 520 of 1357 weeks between 2000 and 2025, with 2013 the worst at 53 weeks. In the 2021-2025 stretch alone there were 104 weeks in severe drought or worse. July nights are running warmer too, with the 2017-2026 average low at 58.8 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 56.6 F. Land value is $374 per acre on the census, and it was up 27.6 percent from 2017 to 2022, but that is the operators' own estimate, so weigh it with that in mind.

33001.text: Belknap County is mostly ground that depends on rain. Only 4 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, so the dry years show up directly in the crop. Drought got the county's attention most in 2002, when 20 weeks had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse. Across 2000-2025 that happened 76 of 1357 weeks, and 16 of those weeks fell in 2021-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 59.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 57.8 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.86 F per decade. Non-irrigated cash rent was $29 per acre in 2024, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,541 per acre in 2022.

33003.text: Carroll County is a small amount of ground, and the thing that stands out is the dry years. Drought weeks reached 57 of 1357 since 2000, and 2025 was the worst with 18 weeks in severe drought or worse. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the crop is growing on rain. The July nightly low is 57.4 F for 2017-2026, up from the 1991-2020 normal of 55.4 F, and it has warmed 0.82 F per decade since 1976. Non-irrigated cash rent was $28 per acre in 2021, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,885 per acre in 2022, up 49.8 percent from 2017 to 2022.

33005.text: What stands out in Cheshire County is how little of the cropland is irrigated, 2 percent in the 2022 census, so most of the ground depends on rain. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 39 percent, while heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 32 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $71 per acre in 2026. The census value of land and buildings was $7,375 per acre in 2022, up 94.5 percent from 2017. July nights have warmed too, with the average low at 59.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 57.5 F normal for 1991-2020.

33007.text: The county's notable features are its wet weather and its land values. Crop insurance claims over 1996-2025 total $223,076, and excess moisture and flood account for 75 percent of that. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain. Heat and drought are a smaller concern here: weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 37 of 1357 over 2000-2025, and the worst year was 2025 with 18 weeks. The land is worth $4,071 per acre by census, up 58.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, while non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $41 per acre. The county has 113.3 MW of wind operating and no solar.

33009.text: Heat and drought is the story in Grafton County. It was the largest cause of crop insurance claims over 1996-2025, and its share went from 7 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 58 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 18 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021-2025, and 18 of those weeks came in 2025 alone. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. The non-irrigated cash rent was $58 per acre in 2025, up 36.9 percent since 2014.

33011.text: Hillsborough County is a small cash-rent county where the notable thing is the crop insurance record.
