Freeze and frost are the largest cause of claims, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.16, which means insurers paid out more than farmers paid in premium. Heat and drought claims went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2010-2019 and 10 percent in 2020-2025. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $69 per acre. Land and buildings were valued at $10,594 per acre in 2022, up 36.3 percent since 2017.

33013.text: Merrimack County is a hail county first. Hail accounts for 47 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid out from 1996 to 2025, and the county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1995-2025 is 1.32, meaning claims have run above premiums. Heat and drought claims are the part that has grown. They went from 2 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 60.1 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 58 F. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the census put land and buildings at $7,512 per acre in 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $66 per acre.

33015.text: Rockingham County is mostly ground that gets its water from the sky. Only 3 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so a dry July lands on the crop straight away. Heat and drought went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025, and that's the number I'd watch. The loss ratio over 1995-2025 is 1.07, meaning the county has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premium. Freeze and frost still caused the most of the losses at 52 percent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $122 per acre for 2025, while the census puts land and buildings at $17,929 per acre.

33017.text: Strafford County's ground is mostly dry-land. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the crop insurance claims that have paid out since 1998 were driven by freeze and frost, which took 58 percent of the total. Heat and drought made up 7 percent of claims across 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 60.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 59.1 F, and the county has never had a July average low at or above 70 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $40 per acre in 2023. Land and buildings were valued at $10,359 per acre in 2022, up 59.5 percent from 2017.

33019.text: Freeze and frost is the cause that stands out in Sullivan County. It accounts for 46 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1999 through 2025, which came to $352,427 on closed crop years. Heat and drought show up at 0 percent for both 2010-2019 and 2020-2025, so that is not where the claims have come from here. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre for 2025, and the land and buildings are valued at $5,219 per acre in the 2022 census. The county has 24 MW of wind operating and no solar yet, with 4 MW of solar proposed.

34001.text: Atlantic County is an irrigated county, 77 percent of harvested cropland, and 95 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The heat stands out too. The July average low was 68.4 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.7 F, and the July average low first reached 66 F in the 1990s. Insurance has paid out $24.5 million since 1989, with a loss ratio of 1.39 over the full span and 2.48 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 2 percent in 2010-2019 and up to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Land is valued at $14,983 per acre in the 2022 census.

34005.text: Burlington County's heat-and-drought claims are what stand out. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 33 percent in 2000-2009 to 69 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 21 weeks of severe drought or worse from 2021 to 2025. The July nightly low averaged 67.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.2 F, and the trend since 1976 runs warming at 0.79 F per decade. Irrigation is limited to 26 percent of harvested cropland, and non-irrigated cash rent is $79 per acre against $160 for irrigated ground. The county's loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.88, and solar operates at 181.6 MW.

34011.text: Cumberland County is a county where heat and drought claims have stayed the largest share of crop insurance payouts. Heat and drought made up 74 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 73 percent in 2020-2025, and the county paid $12.2 million on closed crop years since 1989. The loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.65, which means claims ran well ahead of premiums in the recent stretch. Non-irrigated ground rents at $100 per acre are up 73 percent since 2016, and the irrigated premium is $159 per acre.

34019.text: Hunterdon County is mostly dry ground, and heat and drought is the main reason insurance has paid out here. Heat and drought was 92 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 85 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio for 2016-2025 was 0.97. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, up 27.2 percent since 2016. The worst corn year in the 2008-2016 window was 2012 at 113.2 bushels per acre, against a county median of 135.

34021.text: Mercer County is a small irrigated-ground county where heat and drought are now most of what the insurance company pays on. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, but heat and drought went from 99 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 90 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.01, meaning claims ran above premiums. July nights have been warming too, from 65.3 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 67 F over 2017-2026. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $54 per acre, against a census land value of $26,811 per acre.

34023.text: Middlesex is a small-acreage county where the heat is the story more than the ground. The July nightly low has averaged 67.8 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.6 F, and the average low has now reached 66 F or higher in every decade since the 2010s. Heat and drought made up 89 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019 and 86 percent in 2020-2025, so that is where the claims are. Non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings was $26,828 per acre in 2022, up 23.2 percent from 2017. The county has no CRP ground, and the solar on the books is 142.6 MW operating.

34025.text: Monmouth County's rent is mostly on the non-irrigated side, and the crop insurance record is the part to look at first. Heat and drought made up 96 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 84 percent in 1989-1999, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.97. Non-irrigated cash rent is $101 per acre for 2026, up 50.7 percent since 2014. July nights have warmed too: the 2017-2026 average low is 68.1 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66 F. Only 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground has no water to fall back on in a dry July.

34027.text: Morris County is a small cropland county where the water question shows up most in the insurance record. Heat and drought made up 73 percent of indemnities over 2010-2019 and 41 percent over 2020-2025, and the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 show a loss ratio of 0.34, so the claims have run well below premiums. Only 25 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent was $55 per acre in 2022 against $130 for irrigated ground in 2024. Land and buildings were valued at $30,022 per acre in 2022, up 40.1 percent from 2017.

34029.text: Heat and drought drive most of the crop insurance claims in Ocean County. They made up 75 percent of the $523,341 paid out on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and their share rose from 56 percent in 2010-2019 to 80 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 67.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.9 F. Land and buildings were valued at $23,893 per acre in the 2022 census, up 25.5 percent from 2017. The county has 76.5 MW of operating solar and no operating wind.

34031.text: Passaic County is a small piece of farmland, and the most notable thing here is how much of the cropland gets irrigated, 43 percent. That is a lot of water put on ground that would otherwise depend on the sky. Land and buildings were valued at $43,712 per acre in 2022, and that value climbed 36.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 6.5 percent a year. The July nightly low has averaged 65.4 F over 2017-2026, against 63 F for the 1991-2020 normal, and the trend since 1976 is 1.06 F per decade, which is warming. Solar is operating at 3.8 MW, with 2.5 MW more proposed.

34033.text: Salem County's heat and drought problem shows up most in the insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 74 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 86 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's closed crop years have paid out $20.3 million with a loss ratio of 0.61. The 2016-2025 loss ratio of 0.67 is the more recent picture. Only 25 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $89 per acre in 2026, up 30.9 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $10,421 per acre.

34035.text: Somerset County's heat and drought claims are the main thing to look at here. Heat and drought made up 92 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 82 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.27, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Only 5 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and July nights have warmed to an average low of 66.1 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.9 F. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $34 per acre in 2026.

34041.text: Warren County is a small cropland county where the ground is mostly dry-land, so the weather and the claims history tell most of the story. Heat and drought made up 98 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 87 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio for 2016-2025 is 1.02, meaning the county has paid out more in claims than it took in premium over those ten years. Non-irrigated cash rent is $129 per acre in 2026, up 68.6 percent since 2016. The July nightly low averaged 63.6 F over 2017-2026 against a 61.1 F normal for 1991-2020, and it has been trending warmer since 1976.

35005.text: Chaves County is an irrigated county first. Eighty-five percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 93 percent of that water comes from groundwater, so the aquifer is the thing to watch. Freeze and frost, not heat, has driven most of the crop insurance claims since 1989, at 61 percent of the $21.0 million paid. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, and the July nightly low averaged 66.5 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.4 F. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.66, which means claims have run well ahead of premiums.

35009.text: Curry County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the water that does get used comes entirely from the ground. Heat and drought has been the main cause of claims for a long time, and its share went from 46 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 82 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years from 2016 through 2025, indemnities ran 1.51 times premium, so the insurance has paid out more than it took in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground is $81, which tells you how much the water is worth here. Census land value was $763 per acre in 2022.

35011.text: Most of the ground in De Baca County is not in crops at all. CRP holds 90662 acres, which is 91.8 percent of the cropland base, and 530 of those acres come out of the program in fiscal years 2027-2029. Of the harvested cropland, 87 percent is irrigated, but only 21 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought went from 27 percent of crop insurance claims in 2010-2019 to 39 percent in 2020-2025. The census puts land and buildings at $385 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price.

35015.text: Eddy County is an irrigated place, with 95 percent of harvested cropland watered, and 58 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Nights in July have been warming, with the July average low at 68.8 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.3 F. Heat and drought claims are a small part of the insurance record, but they went from 0 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 11 percent in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost is the cause that matters most, at 66 percent of all indemnities since 1989. Land and buildings were valued at $907 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 53.5 percent from 2017 to 2022.

35023.text: Hidalgo County is a groundwater county. Ninety percent of the irrigation water came from wells in 2015, and that is the first thing I'd look at if you farm here. The July nightly low has risen from 64.8 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 65.9 F over 2017-2026, and the county has never had a July average low at or above 70 F in the record. Heat and drought claims were 20 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 and 0 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims picture is lumpy rather than steady. Crop insurance paid out less than the premiums over the long run, with a loss ratio of 0.46 across 1993-2025. CRP acres were 6985 in 2025, and the county has no wind or solar operating yet.

35025.text: Lea County has been hitting its heat and drought claims harder than most places in the Atlas. Heat and drought made up 31 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 59 percent in 2020-2025, and it is the largest cause over the whole record at 50 percent. The loss ratio is 1.83 across the closed years, with 15 of 18 crop years paying out more than premium. Eighty-two percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of the water comes from groundwater, so a dry stretch leaves little slack. In the wind and solar side, 307 MW of wind and 45.1 MW of solar are running now.

35029.text: Luna County's cropland has been hit hard by heat and drought in recent years. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 3.71, meaning insurers paid out well over what farmers paid in premiums. Drought was severe or worse across the county for 53 weeks in 2024, the worst year on record here, and the July average low has moved up from 66 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 67.6 F over 2017-2026. Groundwater supplies 42 percent of irrigation water, so that matters for any ground you rent or buy.

35033.text: Mora County's notable number is how much of its ground is in the Conservation Reserve Program: 22,631 acres, or 80.2 percent of the cropland base. That leaves little of the county in regular crop rotation. Most of what is still farmed is irrigated, 80 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and irrigation water has come entirely from surface sources, not wells, as of 2015. Irrigated ground rents for $85 per acre in 2025, against $15 for non-irrigated in 2022, and the census land and buildings value of $1,359 per acre is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. Weeks of severe drought ran 567 of 1357 from 2000 through 2025, with 2013 the worst at 53 weeks.

35035.text: Otero County is mostly irrigated, with 94 percent of harvested cropland watered, and 70 percent of that water comes from groundwater. The insurance picture is the one to look at. Indemnities have run past premiums over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 2.19, and in 2016-2025 the county paid $8.11 per $100 of insured value. Hail is the largest single cause over 1990-2025 at 39 percent. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 4 percent in 2010-2019 and 6 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 53 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2024, so the dry years are showing up in the weeks, even if they have not yet dominated the claims.

35037.text: Quay County is a dryland county where the rent has fallen, and the main thing to notice is how often the drought has cut the crop. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $11 per acre, and it was down 24.1 percent from 2014. Heat and drought made up 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2010-2019, and it was 26 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.39 over the closed years, with indemnities paid out more than premium in 15 of 23 crop years. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 86 in 2021-2025, and the worst year was 2013 with 53 weeks.

35041.text: Roosevelt County is a dryland-and-groundwater county, and the water question shows up most in the insurance claims. Crop insurance has paid out $151.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought went from 50 percent of that to 80 percent in the 2020-2025 period. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 2.07, so the claims have run well past the premiums. Irrigated ground rents for $122 per acre against $19 for non-irrigated, and all the irrigation water here comes from groundwater.

35047.text: San Miguel County's cropland is mostly irrigated, with 85 percent of harvested cropland watered in 2022, and none of that water comes from groundwater. The land is also largely out of production: CRP acres in 2025 were 20902, which is 84 percent of the cropland base. Drought is the thing to watch here. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 442 of 1357 from 2000-2025, or 32.6 percent, and 2021 had 52 of them, tied with 2012 for the worst year. The census put land and buildings at $836 per acre in 2022, a figure that rose 86.2 percent from 2017-2022. Solar is operating at 31.5 MW, and nothing wind-related is operating.

35051.text: Sierra County is mostly irrigated, with 73 percent of harvested cropland under water and 53 percent of that water coming from groundwater. Heat and drought took 44 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 0 percent in 2010-2019, and the county had 52 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2021. July nights have warmed too, with the 2017-2026 average low at 64.8 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 62.9 F. Census land and building value was $406 per acre in 2022, up 12.5 percent from 2017. Solar is 2.9 MW operating, and there is no wind or CRP ground here.

35057.text: Torrance County is a county where irrigation and the land itself stand out. Two-thirds of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance losses are small, with freeze and frost the largest cause, while heat and drought went from 5 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 0 percent in 2010-2019. Land and buildings were valued at $784 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 64.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP covers 97360 acres, or 89.9 percent of the cropland base.

35059.text: The loss ratio in Union County is the number to start with. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025 insurers paid out $46.1 million, and in the last ten closed years, 2016-2025, the indemnity came to 1.75 times the premium. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 36 percent of indemnities, and its share rose from 12 percent in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Groundwater supplies 97 percent of irrigation water, but irrigation failure paid only $322,738 across all closed years. Census land value was $852 per acre in 2022, up 106.3 percent from 2017.

36001.text: Albany County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent irrigated, and the bigger story is the crop insurance record. Claims paid out $3.1 million against premiums that produced a loss ratio of 1.91, so claims ran well ahead of what farmers paid in. Excess moisture and flood caused 45 percent of those claims. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of claims in 2000-2009 to 19 percent in 2020-2025, which is the shift to watch. July nights are also warmer now, averaging 61.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 59.7 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent was $48 per acre in 2024, up 174.3 percent since 2013, and census land value was $5,894 per acre in 2022.

36003.text: Allegany County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $1.13 for every dollar of premium since 1989, and over the last ten closed crop years that ratio climbed to 1.25. Heat and drought went from 23 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, so the claims have shifted toward dry years even as flooding remains the largest single cause. Rent is $85 per acre, up 39.3 percent since 2016, and the census value of $3,316 per acre is well above it.

36005.text:
Bronx County is a city county, and the notable thing here is the heat at night. July nightly lows averaged 70.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.4 F. Since 1976 the July low has been warming at 0.89 F per decade. Eleven Julys since 1900 averaged a low at or above 70 F, and the 1930s was the first decade the July average low reached 66 F.

Drought has been rare here. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 43 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, with 2002 the worst year at 25 weeks. Those weeks were 7 in 2021-2025.

There is no CRP ground, and no solar or wind operating or proposed to EIA.

36007.text: Broome County's notable feature is flood, not heat. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities at 35 percent, and heat and drought's share fell from 11 percent in 2000-2009 to 4 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, so the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre for 2026, up 101.5 percent from 2016. The county's corn yield trend is 2.4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the median is 153.2 bushels per acre. Crop insurance has paid out well below premium, with a loss ratio of 0.41 over 2016-2025.

36011.text: Cayuga County's biggest weather story in these numbers is wet springs and floods, not drought. Excess moisture and flood account for 72 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 0.76, with only 2 of 12 closed crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is growing, though it is still small next to the flood losses. Non-irrigated cash rent is $133 per acre in 2026, up 39.3 percent since 2016. Corn yields show a trend of 1.2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, against a median of 151 bushels.

36013.text: Chautauqua's notable number is the freeze. Freeze and frost cause 76 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1989, and the county has paid out more than its premiums in 4 of 17 closed crop years. Heat and drought have been a small share of claims, falling from 14 percent in 1989-1999 to 7 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the county's ground is mostly dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $96 per acre for 2026, up 20.9 percent from 2016.

36015.text: Chemung County is a rain county more than a heat county. Flood and excess moisture caused 49 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1992 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.58, which is well under 1. Heat and drought claims are a smaller part of the picture, though their sharewas 48 percent in 1989-1999 and 39 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $55 per acre for 2026, up 74.6 percent since 2016. Rent is only 1.06 percent of the 2022 census value of $3,542 per acre, so the land is priced high relative to what it rents for.

36017.text: Chenango County's heat and drought claims have climbed sharply. The share of indemnities from heat and drought went from 12 percent in 2000-2009 to 6 percent in 2010-2019 and then 49 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the money paid over the full record still came from excess moisture and flood, at 68 percent. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.7, and over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.55. Non-irrigated cash rent is $63 per acre for 2026, up 37 percent since 2016. Census land value was $2,434 per acre in 2022, so rent ran 1.77 percent of that value. Solar is operating at 23.3 MW and 103.2 MW of wind is proposed.

36019.text: Clinton County's notable number is the insurance record. Freeze and frost cause 44 percent of the indemnities paid since 1995, and the county's loss ratio over those closed crop years is 1.12, meaning claims have paid out more than premiums. Heat and drought went from 0 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry-year exposure has grown even though the county is only 1 percent irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $62 per acre in 2026, up 27.6 percent from 2016. The land value of $3,464 per acre in 2022 is a census figure.

36021.text: Columbia County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid $39.1 million across the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 1.13, which means payouts ran above premiums. Freeze and frost cause 46 percent of that. Heat and drought claims were 37 percent in 1989-1999 and 19 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry-year share has come back up after a quiet stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $54 per acre, up 4.9 percent from 2016.

36023.text: Cortland County's land is mostly rain-fed, and the notable thing here is that the crop insurance claims come from too much water, not too little. Excess moisture and flood account for 69 percent of indemnities paid in closed crop years 1998-2025, and heat and drought went from 16 percent in 2010-2019 to 18 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 0.71, and the county has had no weeks of severe drought since 2000. Non-irrigated cash rent is $76 per acre for 2026, up 24.8 percent from 2016.

36027.text: Dutchess County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the rent and yield numbers here are mostly rainfall numbers. Crop insurance has paid out $10.8 million on closed crop years since 1995, and loss ratio is 1.49, meaning claims have run ahead of premium. Freeze and frost cause 51 percent of that. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $54 per acre for 2026, up from 2016 by 77 percent. The median corn yield for 2008-2022 was 146.5 bushels per acre, and 2022 fell to 118.1.

36029.text: Erie County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premium over the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.01, and heat and drought went from 15 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood still lead the record at 45 percent. Irrigation is barely a factor, with 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated and irrigated rent at $90 per acre against $86 for non-irrigated ground. Non-irrigated cash rent is $86 per acre in 2026, up 43 percent from 2016. The corn yield trend is up 1.4 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 137.7 bushels. The land value on the census is $4,873 per acre.

36031.text: Essex County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Closed claims from 1989 through 2025 paid out $5.1 million, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 was 1.15, so claims ran past what farmers paid in premiums. Freeze and frost caused the largest share of losses at 39 percent. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 7 percent in 2010-2019, then back to 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is $45 per acre for 2026, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground here depends on rain.

36033.text: Franklin County is mostly a wet-year story. Flood and excess moisture account for 71 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here from 1995 to 2025, and the loss ratio over those years is 0.48, so the county has paid out less than it took in premiums. Heat and drought claims have been rising, though, from 6 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 35 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has risen from 55.4 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 56.5 F over 2017-2026. Non-irrigated cash rent is $64 per acre in 2026, up 17.4 percent since 2016.

36035.text: Fulton County is a rain county, not a dry one. Excess moisture and flood account for 63 percent of the indemnities paid since 1995, and none of its cropland is irrigated. Heat and drought claims have been a steady minority, going from 22 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 16 percent in 2010-2019 and back up to 24 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years the loss ratio is 0.77, well under the 1.27 it has run since 1993, so the recent decade has paid out less than it took in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre in 2026, up 70.7 percent since 2016.

36037.text: Genesee County is a wet-spring county more than a dry one. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid since 1989, and the county paid out more than it took in premium in 5 of 17 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 48 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is climbing. Non-irrigated cash rent is $131 per acre in 2026, up 79.5 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $4,099 per acre in 2022, a value the operators themselves estimated.

36041.text: Hamilton County is a land-value story more than a weather one. Census land and buildings were $4,967 per acre in 2022, and the value rose 48.7 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 8.3 percent a year. That is a fast climb for ground in the Adirondacks, and it is worth knowing before you set a rent. Irrigation is present on 29 percent of harvested cropland. July nights have warmed a little: the average low for 2017-2026 is 54.8 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.5 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.62 F per decade. There are no CRP acres here, and no wind or solar operating or proposed.

36043.text: Herkimer County is a dryland county, and the main thing to know is that it is a wet one. Excess moisture and flood account for 65 percent of the indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio for those years is 0.92, so the claims have run close to the premiums. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 40 percent in 2020-2025, which is worth watching on ground that has never had a severe drought week. Non-irrigated cash rent is $72 per acre for 2026, up 48 percent since 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $3,172 per acre in 2022.

36045.text: Heat and drought claims are the thing to watch in Jefferson County. Their share of indemnities went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 47 percent in 2020-2025, after sitting at 25 percent in 2010-2019. Excess moisture and flood is still the largest cause over the full record at 53 percent. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.98, meaning claims ran close to premium in that stretch. Non-irrigated rent is $49 per acre in 2026, up 12.6 percent from 2016, against a census land value of $2,496 per acre in 2022. Drought weeks have been rare, with 5 of 1357 weeks at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought since 2000.

36047.text: Kings County is a city county with no farmland to speak of in the Atlas: no CRP acres, no solar or wind on the ground, and no operating wind or solar capacity. What stands out is the heat. The July average low has been 70.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69 F, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.87 F per decade. There have been 16 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Land is priced at $588,578 per acre on the 2022 census, and it rose 32.7 percent over 2017-2022.

36051.text: Livingston County is a wet-spring ground county more than a dry one. Floods and excess moisture make up 66 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 6 of 19 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.74. Heat and drought went from 30 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $141 per acre in 2026, up 108.9 percent from 2016, and that has been the bigger move on the ground. The corn trend from 2008 to 2025 is 1.1 bushels per acre a year, and 2016 was the worst year at 122.8 bushels.

36053.text: Madison County's notable number is the insurance record: indemnities have paid out more than premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 1.19 since 1989, and the largest cause is excess moisture and flood at 73 percent. Heat and drought claims have been a smaller part of that, falling from 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $68 per acre, up 26.9 percent from 2016. The census land value of $3,841 per acre in 2022 was up 46.5 percent from 2017, so rent works out to a small share of that value.

36055.text: Monroe County's cropland is mostly watered by rain, and the flood claims are what stand out. Excess moisture and flood make up 58 percent of the indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the crop insurance loss ratio is 1.11, with 11 of 18 closed crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 29 percent in 2020-2025, so it is growing but still behind wet weather. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre in 2026, up 41.2 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings is $4,622 per acre in 2022.

36063.text: Niagara County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.06 across 1989-2025, and excess moisture and flood was the largest cause at 50 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 8 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025, so it is a smaller part of the story than water. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $74 per acre in 2026, up 65.6 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,796 per acre in 2022, and rent last year came to 1.51 percent of that value. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

36065.text: Oneida County is a rain-fed county, and the notable thing is how little of its cropland is irrigated. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in the 2022 census, so the county lives or dies on the sky. Corn has held up well over time, with a median yield of 149.5 bushels per acre from 2008 to 2025, though 2013 fell to 115.6. Flood and excess moisture is the largest cause of claims at 61 percent, and heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 29 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $73 per acre in 2026, up 37.7 percent from 2016.

36067.text: Onondaga County is mostly rain-fed ground, and the notable thing in its record is the insurance side. Heat and drought claims went from 7 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.02, so the county paid out more than it took in premium. Corn yields have a small upward trend at 0.9 bushels per acre a year, and the median was 147.1 with 2012 the worst year at 121.7. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre in 2026, up 24.8 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $3,467 per acre in 2022.

36071.text: What stands out in Orange County is the water and the claims. Heat and drought used to be the main reason claims got paid here, at 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, and that share has fallen to 21 percent in 2020-2025. Excess moisture and flood is now the largest cause at 45 percent over the full record. The loss ratio is 0.96 across 1989-2025, and 11 of 26 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $77 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $10,494 per acre in 2022, up 51.3 percent from 2017 to 2022.

36073.text: The thing that stands out in Orleans is the freeze. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here at 32 percent, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 8 of the 25 closed crop years. Heat and drought went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2000-2009, then came back down to 9 percent in 2020-2025. The non-irrigated cash rent is $128 per acre in 2026, and that rent was $70 per acre for irrigated ground in 2010. Corn yields have trended up 1.9 bushels per acre a year since 2008, with a median of 165.6 bushels per acre.

36075.text: Oswego County is a wet county more than a hot or dry one. Flood and excess moisture took 54 percent of the crop insurance payouts since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.89, which is high. Heat and drought claims fell from 10 percent in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025, and irrigation is barely used, at 2 percent of harvested cropland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre in 2026, up 122.2 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $2,848 per acre in 2022.

36077.text: Otsego County is mostly rain-fed ground, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather that matters here is water that falls or doesn't. The clearest change is in the claims. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still made up 73 percent of all indemnities since 1993. The loss ratio is 0.67 for both the full 1993-2025 run and the last ten closed years. Rent is $48 per acre for 2026, up 36.6 percent from 2016, against a census land value of $3,070 per acre.

36079.text: Putnam County's notable number is land value. The 2022 census put land and buildings at $11,485 per acre, and that figure is the operators' own estimate, up 91.4 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 13.9 percent a year. July nights have also warmed: the average low was 65.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 62.5 F, and the trend since 1976 is 1.14 F per decade. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 31 over 2021-2025, and the worst year on record here was 2002 with 17 weeks. Solar is the only renewable on the ground, at 2.3 MW.

36081.text: Queens County is a city county with a notable split. Forty-four percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and the census value of land and buildings reached $113,746 per acre in 2022, up 134.4 percent from 2017. Most of the stress shows up in the heat. The July average low was 70 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.3 F, and July lows have been warming. The county has also had 12 Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Drought has been rarer but sharp, with 44 weeks of severe drought over 2000-2025 and 2002 the worst year at 27 weeks.

36083.text: Heat and drought claims are the story in Rensselaer County. They went from 88 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 59 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.27, so insurers have paid out more than farmers paid in. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the median corn yield for 2008-2025 was 141.5 bushels per acre, with a worst year of 107.4 in 2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre, down 28.6 percent since 2016. Solar is the big land use here, with 77 MW operating and no wind.

36091.text: Saratoga County is mostly rain-fed, with only 2 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather that matters here is the weather that falls from the sky. Excess moisture and flood have been the largest cause of insurance claims since 1989, at 41 percent. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 23 percent in 2020-2025, which is the shift to watch. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities ran 0.97 of premium, a lot closer to even than the 1.22 for the full period. Non-irrigated cash rent is $65 per acre for 2026, up 41.3 percent since 2016.

36093.text: Schenectady County is mostly a county of rain problems rather than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood make up 64 percent of crop insurance indemnities since 1996, and the county has had no weeks in severe drought since 2000. Heat and drought claims went from 29 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is small but has held steady. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and July nights have warmed from a normal of 59.8 F to 61.7 F in 2017-2026. Cash rent on non-irrigated ground was $35 per acre in 2023, and the census value of land and buildings was $5,989 per acre in 2022.

36095.text: Schoharie County is a rain county more than a heat county. The biggest cause of crop insurance payouts here since 1990 is excess moisture and flood, at 49 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 4 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 22 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is the one to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $38 per acre, up 55.1 percent from 2016. The census land value was $3,551 per acre in 2022, and the land value change over 2017-2022 was 45.8 percent. The loss ratio over 2016-2025 was 0.55.

36097.text: Schuyler County's corn yields are not climbing much, and the loss ratio says insurance has paid out more than it took in. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities ran 1.04 times premium, and the median county corn yield for 2008-2025 was 150.6 bushels per acre, with 2022 the worst year at 107.7. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of claims since 1994, at 38 percent, and heat and drought held at 25 percent of claims in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $56 per acre, up 119.6 percent from 2016, while the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $3,972 per acre, so rent was 1.25 percent of that value.

36099.text: Seneca County's notable point is the weather pattern in the claims. Excess moisture and flood paid out 54 percent of the indemnities from 1989-2025, and the crop years from 2016-2025 paid $7.88 per $100 of insured value. Heat and drought held between 20 and 22 percent of claims in each of the three decades since 2000, so it has been steady, not climbing. The 2016 corn crop was 96.3 bushels per acre, far below the county median of 165.5. Non-irrigated cash rent is $90 per acre for 2026, up 34.6 percent since 2016, and the 2022 census value of $4,610 per acre puts rent at a small share of land value.

36101.text: The notable thing in Steuben is the insurance record. Closed crop years since 1989 have paid out $34.2 million, and the loss ratio is 1.17, so the claims have run ahead of premium. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 51 percent. Heat and drought went from 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 17 percent in 2000-2009, then back up to 43 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $58 per acre in 2026, up 64.3 percent since 2016. The corn yield trend over 2008-2025 is flat, at 0.4 bushels per acre a year, and the worst year in that span was 2016 at 102.5 bushels.

36107.text: What stands out in Tioga County is how little of the ground is irrigated and how the losses have come from wet years, not dry ones. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here is excess moisture and flood at 73 percent of the total. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 2 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $49 per acre in 2026, up 66.1 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings was $2,865 per acre in 2022.

36109.text: Tompkins County's most notable number is flooding, not drought. Excess moisture and flood made up 64 percent of the indemnities paid from 1996 to 2025, and the loss ratio for closed crop years 1993-2025 is 0.59, with 0.73 for the last ten. Heat and drought claims fell from 55 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 25 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $69 per acre, up 55.1 percent since 2016, against a census land value of $3,994 per acre, so rent is a small share of land value. Corn yields show a trend of 1 bushel per acre a year over 2008-2023, with 2018 the worst year at 110.8 bushels.

36111.text: Ulster County's cropland is mostly dry ground, and the heat and drought claims have been growing as a share of the total. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 9 percent in 2020-2025, which is lower, so I'd be careful reading that as a steady climb; the swings are the story. The loss ratio over the full 1989-2025 span is 1.05, and insurers paid out more than premium in 9 of 18 closed crop years. Non-irrigated rent is $104 per acre in 2026, up 65.1 percent from 2016, while census land value is $8,701 per acre. Freeze and frost, not drought, is the largest cause of claims here at 48 percent.

36113.text: Warren County's notable number is the nightly low in July. The 2017-2026 average is 57.8 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 56.3 F, and the trend since 1976 runs warm at 0.78 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, so the nights have stayed cool even as they warm. There have been no weeks in severe drought across 2000-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $6,662 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 59.6 percent from 2017 to 2022. The county has 6.9 MW of solar operating and no CRP acres in 2025.

36115.text:
What stands out in Washington County is the insurance record. Closed crop years since 1989 have paid out $8.9 million, and the loss ratio is 1.12, meaning claims have run above premiums over that stretch and 1.22 over the last ten closed years. Excess moisture and flood are the largest cause at 51 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2010-2019, then came back to 28 percent in 2020-2025.

Rent has moved a lot too. Non-irrigated cash rent is $88 per acre in 2026, up 107.1 percent since 2016. Census land value was $3,233 per acre in 2022, so rent was 1.84 percent of that value.

36117.text: Wayne County is mostly dryland, and what stands out is how much the insurance claims have been driven by freeze and frost rather than heat or water. Freeze and frost cause 44 percent of the indemnities since 1989, while heat and drought went from 12 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 5 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed years is 1.11, and insurers paid out more than premium in 8 of 24 crop years, so the ground has been a costly bet on the insurance side. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre in 2026, up 59.3 percent from 2016, against a census land value of $4,862 per acre in 2022.

36121.text: Wyoming County's corn ground is mostly rain-fed, and the insurance record shows wet springs and floods doing more damage than dry spells. Excess moisture and flood took 57 percent of the $20.1 million paid out on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025. The loss ratio is 0.68 over that stretch, and 3 of 17 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims were 47 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 47 percent again in 2020-2025, after a low of 17 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $126 per acre in 2026, up 31.2 percent since 2016. Wind is the big energy use here, with 433.4 MW operating.

36123.text: Yates County's notable thing is the insurance record, not the rent. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of claims at 36 percent, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.8, with 0.92 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought share of indemnities went from 28 percent in 1989-1999 to 26 percent in 2020-2025, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Non-irrigated cash rent is $111 per acre in 2026, up 22.7 percent from 2016.

37001.text: Alamance County's notable number is the loss ratio: crop insurance has paid out $1.32 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and $1.21 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought was the largest cause, at 45 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre in 2026, up 69.4 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $8,217 per acre in 2022, which is a lot higher than the rent.

37003.text: Alexander County is a dryland county, and its notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $21.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.55, meaning claims have run above premiums over the whole stretch. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 35 percent, and its share went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2000-2009, then down to 19 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 37 weeks of severe drought in 2008 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre for 2026, and the census value of land and buildings is $6,886 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate.

37005.text: Alleghany County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Closed claims since 1989 total $1.6 million, and the loss ratio is 1.07, so indemnities have run a little past premiums over the full period. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 61 percent of that, and its share went from 62 percent in 1989-1999 to 87 percent in 2010-2019 before falling back to 62 percent in 2020-2025. Only 12 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $99 per acre in 2026, up 1.5 percent from 2016.

37007.text: Anson County's notable number is the crop insurance record: the closed crop years have paid out $25.9 million, a loss ratio of 1.02, and in the last ten closed crop years the ratio was 1.11, with heat and drought at 48 percent of all indemnities. Heat and drought went from 46 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 65 percent in 2000-2009, and has come down to 42 percent in 2020-2025. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground runs on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $72 per acre for 2026, up 7.5 percent since 2016.

37009.text: Ashe County is a non-irrigated county, so the rent you see is the rent for dryland ground. It is $92 per acre in 2026, and that figure is only up 1.7 percent since 2016. The county's own history with heat and drought stands out more than the rent does. Heat and drought made up 48 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 64 percent in 2010-2019, and it was down to 1 percent in 2020-2025. The indemnities are large against premiums, with a loss ratio of 2.95 over the closed crop years. July nights have been running warmer, with the average low at 59.4 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 58.1 F.

37015.text: Bertie County is notable for how much of its ground still gets rained on. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's crop insurance has paid out more on flood and excess moisture (37 percent of indemnities) than on any other cause. Heat and drought claims went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 35 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has held steady. The non-irrigated cash rent is $133 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $4,072 per acre. Nightly July lows have warmed, with 26 Julys since 1900 averaging 70 F or higher.

37017.text: Bladen County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have run 1.45 times the premium over 1989-2025, and 17 of the 26 closed crop years paid out more than was collected. The last ten years are worse, at 1.68. Heat and drought made up 47 percent of claims in 2000-2009 and 33 percent in 2010-2019, then fell to 13 percent in 2020-2025. The county's corn trend is up 2.8 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 111.9 bushels, so the yield side is holding up better than the claims do. Only 16 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $82 per acre, down 7.3 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $136.

37019.text: Brunswick County is a dryland county where the water question shows up more in claims than in the yield trend. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought make up 30 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025. Those claims went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 43 percent in 2010-2019, then came back to 19 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.24, so insurers have paid out more than the premiums taken in over that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $78 per acre, up 14.7 percent since 2016.

37021.text: Buncombe County's cropland is mostly dry ground, and the one thing that stands out is the insurance record. Crop insurance has paid out $14.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and loss ratio is 2.24, so claims have run well ahead of premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 38 percent of that, but its share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $46 per acre, down 8 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground is only 3 percent of harvested cropland, and irrigated rent was $210 per acre in 2023.

37023.text: Burke County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the loss record is the thing to look at. Insurance indemnities have run above premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.07 across closed crop years 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. Corn yields show a small gain over 2008-2025, but 2024 was 62.1 bushels per acre against a median of 103.5. Non-irrigated rent is $43 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $6,651 per acre in 2022.

37025.text: Cabarrus is a county where heat and drought drive most of the crop insurance claims. Heat and drought was 91 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 55 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.05, so insurers have paid out more than they took in premium. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The median corn yield for 2008-2024 is 125.2 bushels per acre, but 2015 fell to 58.4. Non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre in 2026, up 25 percent since 2016. For a landowner, that rent is set against land the census puts at $9,055 per acre.

37027.text: Caldwell County's most notable shift is in insurance claims. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 76 percent in 2020-2025, so the recent years have been driven by the dry and hot weather more than anything else. The county's corn yield trend is up 4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2023, and the median was 144.9 bushels per acre, with 2013 the worst year at 91.8. Non-irrigated cash rent was $43 per acre in 2024, up 7.5 percent since 2014. The census put land and buildings at $5,873 per acre in 2022, up 29.4 percent from 2017.

37029.text: Camden County is a dryland county with a wet-side insurance story. No cropland is irrigated, and the largest share of crop insurance indemnities, 51 percent, came from excess moisture and flood rather than heat or drought. Heat and drought went from 68 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has grown in recent years. The loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 0.39, and no crop year has paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent was $120 per acre in 2025, against a census value of $4,007 per acre in 2022.

37031.text: Carteret County is a coastal county where the water problem is wet, not dry. Crop insurance has paid out $41.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 39 percent. The county has paid out more than it took in premium on 4 of 17 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.88 overall. Heat and drought claims were 13 percent of the total in 1989-1999 and 23 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $88 per acre in 2026, down 3.8 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $2,231 per acre in 2022.

37033.text: Caswell County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the county has paid out more in crop insurance than it took in premium. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, indemnities ran at 1.41 times premium, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years was 1.22. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 44 percent of indemnities, but its share fell from 49 percent in 2010-2019 to 37 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $92 per acre against $42 for non-irrigated, and only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Corn yields show a trend of 3.8 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2023, with a median of 84.3 bushels and a worst year at 40 in 2010.

37035.text: Catawba County has little irrigated ground, and the crop insurance record is the main story. The loss ratio over the closed years 1989-2025 is 0.97, and over the last ten closed crop years it was 1.03, so claims have run a little ahead of premiums. Heat and drought led the claims over the full period at 43 percent, but its share fell from 62 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2010-2019 before coming back to 43 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is $46 per acre, and the land value is $7,785 per acre.

37037.status: withheld: yield trend inside its 95% range

37039.text: Cherokee County is a dryland county, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so weather years decide the crop. The insurance record shows heat and drought at 36 percent of indemnities from 1995-2025, and that share rose to 48 percent in 2020-2025, which is the number to pay attention to. The 2008 corn crop was 130 bushels per acre, the worst year in the published record, against a median of 176.8. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $74 per acre. The census puts land and buildings at $6,855 per acre for 2022, an operator estimate and not a sale.

37041.text: Chowan County's heat is a slow climb, not a spike. The July nightly low has averaged 71.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.5 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.74 F per decade. Heat and drought made up 52 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 42 percent in 2020-2025, so the water side is worth watching. The county's corn yield trend, fitted over 2008-2025, is up 2.9 bushels per acre a year. Non-irrigated cash rent is $99 per acre for 2026, up 12.5 percent since 2016.

37043.text: Clay County is a non-irrigated county, with none of its harvested cropland under irrigation in the 2022 census, so the rent and the weather carry the farm's risk. The one number that stands out is drought: 204 of the 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year was 2008 with 53 weeks. The July nightly low averaged 62.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 61 F, and the Atlas shows no Julys since 1900 with an average low at or above 70 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $65 per acre in 2024. Census land and buildings were valued at $6,386 per acre in 2022, up 1.7 percent from 2017.

37045.text: Cleveland County is a dryland county, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the weather and the claims tell the story here. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities at 35 percent, and its share went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2010-2019 before settling at 35 percent in 2020-2025. The insured loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.14, meaning claims have paid out more than premiums came in, though the 2016-2025 stretch is closer to even at 0.96. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre for 2026, up 32.8 percent from 2016. Solar is the one energy use on the ground now, with 137.2 MW operating and no wind.

37049.text: Craven County is a county where heat and drought loss has become the main story. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.23, with 13 of 27 years paying out more than premium. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland. Non-irrigated rent is $92 per acre in 2026, up 28.5 percent from 2016. The worst drought year was 2011, with 13 weeks in severe drought or worse.

37051.text: Cumberland County's crop insurance record stands out: indemnities have paid out more than premiums in 18 of 23 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.49 since 1989. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 40 percent of claims, and its share went from 30 percent in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $105 per acre in 2026, up 59.1 percent since 2016. Operators put land and buildings at $5,708 per acre in 2022, so rent was 1.74 percent of that value.

37053.text: Currituck is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood account for 51 percent of the indemnities paid since 1994, and the loss ratio over the closed years is 0.44, so premiums have covered the claims. Heat and drought went from 47 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2020-2025, and the worst drought year in the record was 2002 at 19 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent is $98 per acre in 2026, down 2.5 percent since 2016. The county has 262.4 MW of solar operating and no wind.

37055.text: Dare County is a coastal county where the water is the story more than the dry weather. Two-thirds of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and crop insurance has paid out $2.1 million on closed crop years since 1999, with excess moisture and flood the largest cause at 60 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.8, so claims have run well ahead of premium. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, which is the trend worth watching here. July nights have warmed too: the 2017-2026 average low of 73.7 F is above the 1991-2020 normal of 72.4 F.

37057.text: Davidson County is mostly dryland, and its corn has carried a heavy insurance bill. Heat and drought account for 66 percent of the $16.7 million in indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.08 across those closed years and 1.2 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought went from 41 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 77 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 58 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre in 2026, up 40.8 percent from 2016. July nights have been warmer too, averaging 68.7 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.7 F.

37061.text: Duplin County's heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 39 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out $191.6 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 1.03, with payouts above premium in 17 of 31 years. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $88 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground rents for $131 per acre.

37063.text: Durham County is a small cropland county where the water story is in the claims. Heat and drought made up 49 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 35 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 1.27, so insurers have paid out more than farmers paid in premium. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The July nightly low has been running at 69.3 F over 2017-2026, against a 67.9 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent is $47 per acre, and census land and buildings value is $9,136 per acre, so the rent is a small slice of what the ground is valued at.

37065.text: Edgecombe County is a county where the big risk shows up in wet years more than dry ones. Excess moisture and flood account for 36 percent of the crop insurance payouts since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over closed crop years is 1, with 16 of 32 years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought claims went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 34 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $122 per acre for 2026, up 24.5 percent since 2016. Solar is the big change on the ground, with 281.5 MW operating and 75 MW proposed, and no wind yet.

37067.text: Forsyth County's heat is the story here. Heat and drought made up 27 percent of crop insurance claims in 1989-1999 and 53 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.46, so claims have paid out more than premiums came in. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which leaves most ground dependent on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $72 per acre, and irrigated ground rents for $103. The July nightly low has averaged 68.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.2 F. Land and buildings were valued at $9,658 per acre in the 2022 census.

37069.text: Franklin County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $67.5 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.24, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Heat and drought caused 43 percent of those payouts, and its share went from 33 percent in 1989-1999 to 44 percent in 2020-2025. Most of the cropland is not irrigated, at 4 percent, so the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, and irrigated ground rents for $90.

37071.text: Gaston County is a rain-fed county: only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop depends on what falls from the sky. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025 at 52 percent, and its share went from 41 percent in 2010-2019 to 64 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the closed years 1989-2025 is 0.77, with indemnity paid per $100 of insured value at $7.29 for 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, and that is up 27.3 percent from 2016.

37073.text: Gates County is a flood county more than a drought county. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here at 39 percent, and the county's loss ratio of 0.53 over 1989-2025 means claims have run well below premiums on average. Heat and drought claims are the second story: their share went from 66 percent in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 26 percent in 2010-2019. Corn yields have a trend of 3.3 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, and the worst year was 2011 at 62 bushels. Non-irrigated cash rent is $112 per acre in 2026, up 23.1 percent since 2016.

37077.text: Granville County's corn record is the first thing to look at. Insurance indemnities have paid out $46.4 million over 1989-2025, and heat and drought has been the largest single cause at 47 percent. Its share went from 43 percent in 1989-1999 to 63 percent in 2000-2009, and it has was 43 percent in each period since. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.31, so claims have run above premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $66 per acre in 2026, up 32 percent since 2016. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground here rides on rain. Irrigated rent was $81 per acre in 2023.

37079.text: Greene County is a county where the rain has to come on time. Heat and drought went from 18 percent of insurance payments in 1989-1999 to 42 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the closed crop years is 1.29, with payouts beating premiums in 18 of 28 years. The worst single year on record was 2008 at 43 bushels per acre against a median of 104.5. July nights are running a bit warmer, averaging 70.9 F across 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 70 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $136 per acre in 2026, up 43.2 percent since 2016. Solar is the only power project on the ground, at 21.9 MW.

37083.text: Halifax County's heat and drought story is the one to start with. Heat and drought made up 61 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 49 percent in 2020-2025, after dipping to 21 percent in 2010-2019. The county's corn yield trend has been climbing 4.4 bushels per acre a year across 2008-2023, though the worst year in that stretch was 2010 at 58 bushels. July nights have warmed too: the average low was 69.9 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $121 per acre for 2026, up 22.2 percent from 2016.

37085.text: Harnett County is mostly dryland, and the loss record is what stands out. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premium in 15 of 29 closed crop years, and heat and drought has been the largest cause at 38 percent of indemnities. Its share went from 25 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 49 percent in 2000-2009, then settled near 37 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $121 per acre, up 26 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground is only 2 percent of harvested cropland, and it rents for $200 per acre in 2023. The county's census land value is $6,229 per acre, so the 2022 non-irrigated rent is 1.75 percent of that figure.

37087.text: Haywood County is notable for how much its water-claim history has eased. Heat and drought made up 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 10 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.01, against 1.68 across all closed years. Irrigated ground rents at $240 per acre in 2024, 3.90 times non-irrigated rent, up from 1.57 times in 2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $68 per acre for 2026, down 20.8 percent since 2014. Census land and buildings value is $8,046 per acre in 2022.

37089.text: Henderson County is a land-value and freeze county more than a heat county. Freeze and frost are the largest cause of insurance claims at 55 percent, and crop insurance indemnities have paid out more than premium in 25 of 27 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.63. Heat and drought claims went from 4 percent in 1989-1999 to 1 percent in 2020-2025. Land and buildings were valued at $11,065 per acre in 2022, and non-irrigated cash rent is $117 per acre for 2026, up 33 percent since 2016.

37091.text: Hertford County's most notable pattern is the crop insurance record. Indemnities paid out more than premiums in 7 of 22 closed crop years, and heat and drought drove 38 percent of the $61.0 million paid since 1989. That share went from 41 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $115 per acre, up 16.2 percent from 2016. Corn yield has a trend of 3.2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2023, with a median of 120.2 and a worst year of 53.5 in 2010. Groundwater supplies 46 percent of irrigation water.

37093.text: Hoke County's heat story is the one to start with. Heat and drought made up 22 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 63 percent in 2000-2009, and it was still 50 percent in 2020-2025. The median corn yield over 2008-2022 was 103 bushels per acre, but 2009 was 67. July nights have been warmer too, averaging 71.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.9 F. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.69, so claims have run ahead of premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $61 per acre for 2025, up 10.9 percent since 2014.

37095.text: Hyde County is a flood county first. Excess moisture and flood make up 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 to 2025, and the county has paid out more than it took in premium in 7 of those 25 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.68. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 15 percent in 2020-2025, and the county had 52 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 13 of them in 2011. Non-irrigated cash rent is $182 per acre for 2026, up 23 percent from 2016. The census land value is $3,814 per acre for 2022.

37097.text: Iredell County's crop insurance losses have run heavier than premiums in recent years. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities came to $7.99 for every $100 of insured value, and the loss ratio was 0.92. Heat and drought was the largest cause over the full record at 58 percent, but its share fell from 70 percent in 1989-1999 to 50 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $86 per acre for 2026, up 52.7 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $7,124 per acre in 2022, a rent-to-value ratio of 0.99 percent.

37099.text: Jackson County's notable number is its flood history. Excess moisture and flood made up 52 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1995-2013, and that was the largest cause by a wide margin. Heat and drought was a smaller share, at 9 percent of indemnities over 2000-2009. Drought weeks have been fewer than in many places, with 193 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year was 2008 with 46 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent was $58 per acre in 2025. The census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $8,324 per acre, and that value rose 0.3 percent a year from 2017 to 2022.

37101.text: Johnston County's loss record is the first thing I'd look at. Crop insurance paid out $206.2 million on closed crop years from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio is 1.38, with 22 of 31 years paying more than the premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 35 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 39 percent in 2020-2025. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of this ground is rain-fed. Non-irrigated cash rent is $114 per acre in 2026, up 27.4 percent since 2016.

37103.text: Jones County's crop insurance record is the first thing to notice. Indemnities paid out $136.8 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.36, meaning claims ran above premium in 14 of 27 years. Heat and drought claims went from 19 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2000-2009, then 26 percent in 2010-2019 and 30 percent in 2020-2025. Cash rent was $91 per acre in 2025, and the census value of land and buildings was $3,602 per acre in 2022.

37105.text: Lee County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 7 percent irrigated in the 2022 census, so rain decides most years here. The loss ratio over the closed crop years is 1.6, and crop insurance has paid out more than premium in 9 of 14 years. Heat and drought was 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 31 percent in 2020-2025, with its peak of 52 percent in 2000-2009. The median corn yield since 2008 is 87.9 bushels per acre, but 2024 fell to 26.2. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre in 2026, and census land and buildings were $7,066 per acre in 2022.

37107.text: Lenoir County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Indemnities have paid out $185.4 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 1.16, with 17 of 31 crop years paying more than the premium taken in. Heat and drought was the largest cause, going from 25 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 37 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $126 per acre for 2026, up 48.2 percent from 2016, and only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

37109.text: Lincoln County's notable numbers are the insurance claims and the weather. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here, at 34 percent of the $10.3 million paid on closed crop years since 1989. Heat and drought's share went from 19 percent in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2010-2019 and 2020-2025. The insurance loss ratio over those closed years is 1.47, and over 2016-2025 it is 1.29, so claims have run above premiums. For renting, non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 42.6 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value was $8,442 per acre in 2022.

37111.text: McDowell County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Claims have paid out $3.0 million against a loss ratio of 1.84, meaning indemnities ran well past the premiums collected. Freeze and frost is the largest cause at 39 percent. Heat and drought went from 3 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, so that share is the one to watch. Cash rent is $67 per acre for non-irrigated ground, and the census puts land and buildings at $7,524 per acre in 2022.

37115.text: Madison County is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the crop insurance record matters more here than the rent does. Insurance indemnities paid $14.2 million on closed crop years from 1989 through 2023, and heat and drought was the largest cause at 44 percent. The loss ratio is 2.57, meaning claims paid out well more than the premiums collected. Heat and drought was 54 percent of claims in 1989-1999, 37 percent in 2000-2009, and 43 percent in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre for 2026, down 7.5 percent since 2014, and the census put land and buildings at $7,294 per acre in 2022.

37117.text: Martin County is a dryland county with a lot of wet-year pain. Not one acre of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and the largest single cause of crop insurance claims is excess moisture and flood at 34 percent. Insurance has paid out more than the premium in 8 of 31 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.95 over 1989-2025. Heat and drought went from 34 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 45 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are carrying more of the claims now. Non-irrigated cash rent is $116 per acre for 2026.

37119.text: Mecklenburg County is a county where heat and drought have shown up in the claims, though the dollars are small. Heat and drought made up 66 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, 60 percent in 2010-2019, and 55 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1994-2025 was 0.34, so premiums have run well ahead of claims. The July nightly low averaged 70 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.6 F. Census land value was $27,096 per acre in 2022.

37121.text: Mitchell County is a dryland county. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on what the sky gives it. The bigger story in the insurance record is water too much, not too little: excess moisture and flood made up 39 percent of indemnities over the closed crop years, and the loss ratio of 2.96 means claims paid out well above the premiums collected. Heat and drought claims were 45 percent of the total in 1989-1999 and 29 percent in 2010-2019, so they have been a big share of the claims, though not the only one. The 2026 non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre, against a census land and buildings value of $6,687 per acre.

37123.text: Montgomery County's crop insurance record is the first thing to notice. Indemnities paid out more than premiums collected over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for 1989-2025 is 1.17. Over the last ten closed crop years, 2016-2025, it reached 1.51, with farmers collecting $16.67 for every $100 of insured value. Excess moisture and flood was the largest single cause over the full record at 36 percent. Heat and drought claims went from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,267 per acre in 2022.
