37125.text: Moore County is a dry-ground county with a small irrigated corner. Only 11 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigated ground rents for $125 per acre against $58 for non-irrigated. Heat and drought made up 16 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 43 percent in 2020-2025, and it is still the largest cause over the whole record at 49 percent. The crop insurance loss ratio is 2.09 over the last ten closed crop years, so claims have been running well above premiums. Land and buildings were valued at $5,542 per acre in the 2022 census, which is the operators' own estimate. Solar is operating at 49.2 MW, and no wind is in the county.

37127.text: Nash County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Over the closed crop years 1989-2025, insurers paid out $118.0 million, and heat and drought was the largest cause at 40 percent. The loss ratio for those years is 0.98, and 15 of 30 crop years paid out more than the premium collected. Heat and drought went from 24 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2000-2009, and it was 39 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $126 per acre, up 23.5 percent since 2016. 37129.text: New Hanover County is mostly a heat-and-wind county for us, and the water story is different from the rest of the state. 37131.text: Northampton County is mostly rainfed ground, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent and the yields mostly reflect dry-land farming. Heat and drought claims are the main reason insurance has paid out here, at 57 percent of the $55.8 million in indemnities since 1989. The share fell from 82 percent in 1989-1999 to 40 percent in 2010-2019, then rose to 60 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $116 per acre, up 20.8 percent since 2016. 37133.text: Onslow County is mostly dryland, and the water it does rely on mostly comes from wells. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 79 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premium in 13 of 16 closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.59. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 36 percent. Heat and drought went from 9 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. 37135.text: Orange County is a small cropland county, and the most notable thing here is the insurance record. 37137.text: Pamlico County is mostly dryland, with just 7 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, and most of that water comes from groundwater. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 0.94, meaning claims paid out came close to premiums collected. Corn yields have a slight upward trend, and the worst year was 2022 at 91.1 bushels per acre. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $106 per acre, up 32.5 percent since 2016.

42121.text: Venango County's biggest story is claims, not heat. Excess moisture and flood made up 54 percent of the $7.1 million in indemnities paid on closed crop years since 1989. Heat and drought went from 6 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, so the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.46. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026, up 81.8 percent since 2016, while the census land value is $4,234 per acre. July nightly lows have warmed a little, from 58.5 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 60 F for 2017-2026, and the county has had no severe drought weeks since 2021. Solar is the only large new use at 20 MW operating.

42125.text: Washington County is a non-irrigated county, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rent and the yields are mostly a bet on rain. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 53 percent, and its share went from 27 percent in 2010-2019 to 62 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.45, meaning claims paid out more than premiums taken in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre for 2026, up 57.9 percent since 2016. The county corn median is 122 bushels per acre for 2010-2025, and the worst year, 2012, was 85.4.

42127.text: Wayne County's land is worth more than its rent suggests. Census operators put the value of land and buildings at $6,354 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 48 percent between 2017 and 2022, while non-irrigated cash rent is $15 per acre for 2026 and was down 31.8 percent from 2014. Crop insurance has paid $314,089 since 1997, and excess moisture and flood is the largest cause at 37 percent. Heat and drought took 38 percent of claims in 2000-2009 and 11 percent in 2010-2019. Wind is the energy use on the ground here, with 64.5 MW operating.

42131.text: Wyoming County's rent is cheap, but the crop insurance record is what stands out. Heat and drought made up 68 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999, fell to 17 percent in 2010-2019, and rose back to 61 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over 1989-2025 closed years is 0.93, and the worst corn year was 2022 at 71.8 bushels per acre against a median of 133.2. None of the cropland is irrigated, so the ground carries that weather risk on its own. Non-irrigated rent is $33 per acre in 2026, up 53.5 percent since 2014.

42133.text: Heat and drought are the story in York County. They made up 91 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2000-2009, and they were 58 percent in 2020-2025. The county's corn trend is up 2.5 bushels per acre a year, but the worst year, 2011, was 111 bushels. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $166 per acre, up 48.2 percent since 2016, and land and buildings were valued at $9,224 per acre in 2022.

44001.text: Bristol County is a small, mostly non-irrigated county, with just 3 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022. What stands out is the nights. The July average low was 66.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.8 F, and the first decade the July average low reached 66 F was the 2010s. Only one July since 1900 has averaged 70 F or higher on the low side, so warm nights are a recent pattern here. Drought has been less of a factor: 38 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with 2020 the worst year at 14 weeks. The census value of land and buildings was $49,530 per acre in 2022, up 9.9 percent from 2017.

44005.text: Newport County is a small place for farming, and the most notable thing here is the heat. The July average low reached 66 F in the 2017-2026 stretch, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.4 F, and the 2020s are the first decade the July average low got to 66 F. Heat and drought is still the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 41 percent of $716,225 in indemnities paid over 1996-2025. Its share was 43 percent in 2010-2019 and 42 percent in 2020-2025, so that part has held steady. Land and buildings were valued at $35,737 per acre in the 2022 census, up 46.4 percent from 2017.

44007.text: Heat and drought is the thing to watch in Providence County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 18 percent in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over closed crop years 1989-2025 is 1.43, meaning claims have paid out more than premiums came in. Summer nights are also running warmer, with July lows averaging 63.8 F in 2017-2026 against 62.2 F in the 1991-2020 normal. Land is priced at $18,606 per acre in 2022, up 30.5 percent from 2017, and the county has no CRP ground and no wind turbines running, with 130.9 MW of solar operating.

45003.text: Aiken County is a dryland county with a small irrigated share. Irrigated cash rent is $111 per acre against $40 for non-irrigated ground, and only 25 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, with 31 percent of that water from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in on premiums across 1989-2025, with a loss ratio of 0.9. Freeze and frost, not drought, drive most of those claims, at 57 percent. Heat and drought went from 15 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 8 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is up 76.1 percent since 2016.

45005.text: Allendale County is notable for how much its crop insurance claims have been driven by heat and drought, and for how the July nights have been running warm. Heat and drought was 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 53 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 25 percent in 2020-2025. The county's crop insurance loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.02, so insurers have paid out more than they took in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre in 2026, up 17.2 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $78 per acre in 2025. Census land value was $2,964 per acre in 2022.

45007.text: Anderson County is a dryland county, with only 7 percent of harvested cropland irrigated. That makes the weather the main story here. Crop insurance has paid out $7.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 70 percent of it. Their share went from 38 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 1.2, so claims have run ahead of premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre for 2026, up 23.1 percent from 2016.

45009.text: Bamberg County is one where the irrigated ground is worth a lot more to rent than the dryland. Irrigated rent is $147 per acre in 2026 against $38 for non-irrigated ground, and that gap has widened from 1.61 times in 2009 to 3.82 times now. Irrigation also covers 24 percent of harvested cropland, and 65 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Heat and drought claims have eased: they were 63 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 18 percent in 2020-2025, and 2 of 14 closed crop years paid out more than premium. The land itself has climbed too, with census value at $3,550 per acre in 2022, up 21.1 percent from 2017.

45011.text: Barnwell County's notable pattern is how much its crop claims have leaned on heat and drought, and how that has shifted. Heat and drought made up 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 12 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $72 per acre, against $44 for non-irrigated, and the loss ratio is 0.56 across closed crop years. Land and buildings were valued at $3,749 per acre in 2022, up 34.6 percent from 2017, and the county has 41 MW of solar operating with 124.9 MW proposed.

45015.text: Berkeley County's ground is mostly dryland, and the insurance record is where it shows. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities, at 39 percent of the $21.0 million paid over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 2.26, meaning claims ran well past premiums. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 31 percent in 2020-2025, so it has eased some, but the county still pays out more than it takes in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, up 8.2 percent since 2014. The median corn yield over 2008-2025 was 85.1 bushels per acre, with 2011 the worst year at 38.5.

45019.text: Charleston County is a county where the rain has done more damage than the heat. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities here at 32 percent, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.78, with a loss ratio of 0.46 across 1989-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2010-2019, then came down to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The county's non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $11,145 per acre. Corn yields show a trend of 0.7 bushels per acre a year over 2012-2024, with a median of 108 bushels.

45021.text: Cherokee County is mostly dryland, and freeze has done more damage to its crops than heat or drought. Freeze and frost make up 67 percent of the $5.6 million in insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, and the county's loss ratio over that stretch is 0.91, so claims have run close to premiums across the whole period. Heat and drought went from 2 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025, with the largest share, 18 percent, in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre for 2026, up 58.3 percent since 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,913 per acre in 2022.

45023.text: Chester County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at. Heat and drought was 68 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009, dropped to 28 percent in 2010-2019, and came back to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed years 2016-2025 the loss ratio was 1.1, so insurers paid out more than they took in premium. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county had 218 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 43 of those weeks in 2008. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre, up 22.2 percent since 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,702 per acre in 2022.

45025.text: Chesterfield County is a dryland corn county where the weather risk shows up in the insurance claims. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities over 1989-2025, at 42 percent, and it reached 57 percent in 2000-2009 before settling at 45 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, insurance paid out $15.22 per $100 of insured value, and the loss ratio was 1.02, so claims have run slightly ahead of premium. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $48 per acre.

45027.text: Clarendon County is a place where water is the big question. Irrigated ground rents for $150 per acre in 2023, against $54 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, and the ratio between them has climbed from 1.73 in 2013 to 2.97 in 2023. All of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums over the closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 0.94, and heat and drought were the largest cause at 41 percent of indemnities, down from 60 percent in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025.

45029.text: Colleton County is a dryland county with a loss record that is worth looking at. Crop insurance indemnities have run above premium, with a loss ratio of 1.45 over 1989-2025 and 1.53 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025. The largest cause of claims is excess moisture and flood at 40 percent, while heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, and the county has 7 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, all from groundwater.

45031.text: Darlington County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the water it does irrigate is pulled from the ground. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, and 68 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought made up 43 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and that share went from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio of 0.93 over closed crop years means claims have paid out close to what was collected in premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $47 per acre in 2026, against $2,794 per acre of census land value in 2022.

45033.text: Dillon County is a non-irrigated county, and the crop insurance record is the thing I'd look at first. Heat and drought was the largest cause of indemnities over 1989-2025, at 35 percent, but its share fell from 44 percent in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.96, meaning claims came close to premiums. Groundwater supplies all of the irrigation water, and 15 MW of solar is operating with 81 MW proposed. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre for 2026, up 19.8 percent since 2016.

45035.text: Dorchester County is a dryland county, with only 10 percent of harvested cropland irrigated and all of that water coming from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out $27.0 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought is the largest cause at 36 percent. Its share went from 41 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 27 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 0.87, so premiums have covered the claims there. Non-irrigated cash rent is $45 per acre in 2026, up 40.6 percent since 2016.

45037.text: Edgefield County's clearest story is the freeze. Freeze and frost make up 74 percent of the $150.7 million paid out in closed crop years since 1989, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.92, with 9 of 24 crop years paying out more than the premium collected. Heat and drought claims have shrunk from 6 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low averaged 71.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $26 per acre in 2025, down 10.3 percent from 2014.

45041.text: Florence County is a dryland county. Only 2 percent of its harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rest of the crop depends on rain. Heat and drought is the largest cause of insurance claims, at 38 percent since 1989, and the loss ratio of 1.1 means the county has paid out more than it took in premium over those years. The share of claims from heat and drought was 37 percent in 1989-1999 and 33 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $47 per acre in 2026, up 11.9 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 72.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 70.9 F.

45043.text: Georgetown County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $18.6 million since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.19 across those closed years, rising to 1.36 over 2016-2025. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 38 percent, and its share went from 33 percent in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 47 percent in 2000-2009. Irrigation is only 5 percent of harvested cropland, and non-irrigated cash rent is $39 per acre in 2026.

45045.text: Freeze and frost is the cause that shows up most in Greenville County's crop insurance claims, at 73 percent of the $3.5 million paid from 1989 through 2025. Heat and drought was 10 percent of claims in 1989-1999 and 15 percent in 2020-2025, so it is a bigger share now than it was early on. Only 12 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 19.1 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $12,103 per acre in 2022.

45047.text: Greenwood County's most notable number is the rent falling. Non-irrigated cash rent is $15 per acre in 2026, and it was down 16.7 percent from 2016 to 2026. Land and buildings were valued at $3,514 per acre in the 2022 census, which is the operators' own estimate and not a sale price, and that ground rose only 2.9 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low averaged 70.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.9 F. Drought has been a real factor here, with 264 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought or worse, and 50 of those weeks came in 2008 alone.

45049.text: Hampton County's most notable number is the heat and drought claim record. Heat and drought was 53 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 82 percent in 2000-2009, and 22 percent in 2020-2025, and it is still the largest cause over the full record at 41 percent. The county has paid $32.9 million in closed-year indemnities, against a loss ratio of 0.79. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre in 2026, up 102.1 percent since 2016, while irrigated ground rents for $105. Only 24 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of its irrigation water comes from groundwater.

45051.text: Horry County is a non-irrigated county, and that is the first thing a landowner should see. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and all of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $74 per acre in 2026, down 6.9 percent from 2016. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: the loss ratio is 1.57 across the closed years 1989-2025, and 28 of 32 crop years paid more than premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 37 percent, rising from 33 percent in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2010-2019 before falling to 25 percent in 2020-2025. Census land and buildings value is $4,912 per acre, up 8.9 percent from 2017 to 2022.

45053.text: The notable thing in Jasper County is the groundwater. Every acre of irrigation water here comes from wells, so a dry summer hits the aquifer as well as the crop. Heat and drought claims made up 63 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 79 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 28 percent in 2010-2019 and 27 percent in 2020-2025. Over 1989-2025 the loss ratio is 0.97, and the largest single cause of claims is excess moisture and flood at 39 percent. The census puts land and buildings at $4,579 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated.

45055.text: Kershaw County has run a heavy claims record. Crop insurance has paid out $5.6 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.11, meaning indemnities ran above the premiums paid in. Heat and drought was the largest cause at 43 percent of that total, but its share fell from 87 percent in 1989-1999 to 30 percent in 2010-2019 before rising to 41 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $30 per acre in 2020, up 33.3 percent from 2010. The July nightly low has averaged 71 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.8 F.

45057.text: Lancaster County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $1.04 for every dollar of premium over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the ten closed years 2016-2025 ran higher at 1.11. Heat and drought caused 55 percent of those claims overall, and their share was 99 percent in 2000-2009, 43 percent in 2010-2019, and 58 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, up 39.6 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $5,224 per acre in 2022, a 32.2 percent rise from 2017.

45059.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Laurens County. Its share of crop insurance indemnities went from 8 percent in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the closed years is 1.49, meaning claims paid out more than premiums taken in. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigation failure accounts for $228,592 in indemnities. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $20 per acre, up 29 percent from 2016.

45061.text:
Lee County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Claims paid out $72.8 million across the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.72, but 6 of the 27 crop years paid out more than the premium brought in. Heat and drought was the biggest cause at 35 percent. Its share went from 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025, so the weather picture has shifted toward other causes lately.

Most of the cropland here is non-irrigated, and rent for it is $52 per acre in 2026, up 25.3 percent since 2016. Irrigated ground rented for $135 per acre in 2021. Groundwater supplies 96 percent of the irrigation water.

45063.text: Lexington County's cropland is irrigated at 38 percent, and the irrigated rent is $120 per acre against $33 for non-irrigated ground. That gap has widened: the irrigated rent was 1.85 times the non-irrigated rent in 2009 and is 3.64 times now. Heat and drought went from 21 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1. Water comes mostly from groundwater, at 86 percent. Land and buildings were valued at $6,537 per acre in 2022.

45065.text: McCormick County has no irrigated cropland at all, and that shapes most of what a farmer here deals with. The rent is $15 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2021, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,216 per acre in 2022, up 60.5 percent from 2017. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse came to 282 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, and 2008 was the worst year with 50 weeks. July nightly lows have run at 71.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 70.2 F normal for 1991-2020. Nothing is enrolled in CRP and no wind or solar is operating here.

45067.text: Marion County's yield trend is the thing to look at first. Corn has added 2.5 bushels per acre a year over 2009-2025, from a median of 121.6 bushels, but the worst year, 2011, was 51. Heat and drought was the largest cause of insurance claims, at 34 percent over 1989-2025, and its share fell from 43 percent in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.13, so claims ran above premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $64 per acre in 2026, up 52.4 percent since 2016.

45069.text: Marlboro County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 49 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999, 72 percent in 2000-2009, and 33 percent in 2020-2025. Losses have paid out more than premium in 5 of 22 closed crop years, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.81. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 58 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre in 2026, up 17.6 percent from 2016. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 12 for 2021-2025, and the worst year was 2002 with 36 weeks.

45071.text: Newberry County is mostly dryland, and the water question shows up in the claims more than anywhere else. Heat and drought made up 98 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2020-2025, and that drop came partly as irrigation failure claims stayed tiny at $11,098 across all closed years. The loss ratio of 0.7 over 1989-2025 says the premiums have mostly come back to farmers in claims. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre for 2025, up 16.9 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $3,891 per acre in 2022, which is a lot higher than the rent, so the ground is worth more to buy than it pays to rent.

45073.text: The loss ratio of 1.36 stands out for Oconee County. Over 1989-2025, insurers paid out more than the premiums brought in, and that is driven by a shift toward heat and drought. Their share of indemnities went from 5 percent in 1989-1999 to 73 percent in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost are still the largest cause over the whole record at 50 percent. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $32 per acre, up 41.3 percent from 2016.

45079.text: Richland County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the weather risk shows up in the claims. Heat and drought made up 63 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 70 percent in 2000-2009, then fell to 37 percent in 2010-2019 and held at 37 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated rent is $42 per acre in 2026, up 31.2 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rented for $75 per acre in 2017. The county's closed-year loss ratio is 0.92, and the last ten years run 0.97, so the insurance has paid out close to what farmers put in. Julys have been warmer at night, with the average low at 71.9 F for 2017-2026.

45083.text: Spartanburg County's crop insurance record is the story here. Freeze and frost drove 63 percent of the $41.3 million paid out from 1989 to 2025, and the loss ratio over that stretch was 1.21, with claims paying more than premiums in 7 of 15 closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 9 percent in 2020-2025. Only 10 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre, up 35.9 percent since 2016. July nightly lows have averaged 69.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.7 F. The county has 37.7 MW of solar in operation and no wind.

45085.text: Sumter County's heat and drought claims have eased over time, even as irrigated rent has pulled ahead of dryland rent. Heat and drought made up 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 32 percent in 2020-2025. Still, the largest cause across all closed years is heat and drought at 41 percent. Only 21 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, but irrigated ground rented for $110 per acre in 2022 against $50 for non-irrigated in 2026, and the ratio was 2.34 in 2022 compared with 1.37 in 2009. Non-irrigated rent is up 35.6 percent since 2016.

45087.text: Heat and drought is the main thing the crop insurance claims show here. It accounts for 73 percent of the $106,169 paid out on closed crop years from 2015 through 2024, so this is a county where dry weather is what costs farmers money. The county has also had 242 of 1357 weeks since 2000 with at least 50 percent of the land in severe drought or worse, with 2008 the worst year at 50 weeks. Nightly July lows have warmed a little, to 69.9 F over 2017-2026 from a 69.2 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $15 per acre in 2026, down 11.8 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $3,814 per acre in 2022.

45089.text: Williamsburg County is a dryland county, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the loss record is the first thing to look at. Crop insurance has paid out $149.7 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio over that stretch is 1.09, meaning the county paid more in claims than it collected in premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause, but its share of indemnities went from 48 percent in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $40 per acre, up 23.1 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground rents for $56 per acre in 2025.

45091.text: Most of York County's cropland is dryland, with only 5 percent irrigated in the 2022 census, so rain decides the crop here. Heat and drought claims were 48 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 13 percent in 2020-2025, so the share has dropped a lot. The county's loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 0.98, close to paying out what it took in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $8,629 per acre in 2022. The July nightly low averaged 69.2 F over 2017-2026.

47001.text: Anderson County's notable number is the July nights. The average low has run 67.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.3 F, and the July nightly low trend since 1976 is warming at 0.42 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, so the county has not hit that mark yet. Drought has been a steady pressure in the 2000-2025 record: 103 of 1357 weeks had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, with the worst year, 2008, at 35 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $26 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $7,843 per acre.

47005.text: Heat and drought is the story in Benton County. It was 27 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 60 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.1, so claims have run past premiums. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which leaves most of the ground dependent on rain. The July nightly low has averaged 70.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.6 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $73 per acre in 2026, up 9 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value was $3,196 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 2207 acres, or 10.7 percent of the cropland base.

47007.text: Bledsoe County is mostly ground that depends on rain. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio is 1.59 over the closed crop years 1989-2025, meaning insurers have paid out more in claims than they took in premiums. Heat and drought is the largest cause of those claims at 38 percent, and its share went from 34 percent in 2000-2009 to 42 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $80 per acre in 2026, up 6 percent from 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 67.2 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.7 F.

47009.text: Blount County is mostly dryland ground, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the heat and drought weeks show up in the books. Crop insurance has paid out $3.5 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought made up 65 percent of that. The loss ratio is 1.47 over the last ten closed crop years, meaning claims have run ahead of premiums. Heat and drought was 62 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 64 percent in 2020-2025, so that share has held steady. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre in 2026, up 55.6 percent since 2016.

47011.text: Heat and drought are what stand out in Bradley County. They were 56 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 79 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.29, so claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and July nights have run warmer, averaging 69.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.7 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre for 2026, up 11.8 percent since 2016.

47013.text: Campbell County's cropland is all dryland, and the claims history is where the county's story shows up. Heat and drought made up 54 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, and drought weeks have been rare since 2021, with only 6 weeks at severe or worse since then. The July nightly low is 65.3 F for 2017-2026 against a 64.3 F normal, and the trend since 1976 is 0.38 F per decade, warming. Non-irrigated cash rent is $22 per acre in 2025 and has slipped 6.4 percent since 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $5,131 per acre in 2022, up 24 percent from 2017, though that is the operators' own estimate.

47015.text: Cannon County's heat-and-drought share of crop insurance claims has climbed steadily, from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, the loss ratio was 0.62, so insurers paid out less than the premiums collected. The county's corn yields show a trend of 2.2 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2024, and the worst year in that stretch was 2012 at 33 bushels. July nightly lows have warmed too, averaging 68 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre for 2026.

47017.text: Carroll County's notable number is the heat. Julys have been warming, with the average nightly low up to 70.4 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.9 F. Nineteen Julys since 1900 have averaged a low at or above 70 F. Heat and drought claims have climbed too, from 39 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 38 percent in 2020-2025, with a loss ratio of 0.52 over the closed crop years 1989-2025. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the crop rides on rain. Non-irrigated rent is $127 per acre for 2026, up 15.5 percent since 2016.

47019.text: Carter County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here rides on rain. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims from 1989 to 2011, at 42 percent of indemnities. Its share went from 46 percent in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2000-2009. The county's worst drought year was 2008, with 41 weeks in severe drought or worse. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, up 40 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $6,540 per acre in the 2022 census.

47021.text: Cheatham County's notable thing is the water, and it cuts both ways. Flood and excess moisture is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 44 percent, and the county's loss ratio of 1.13 over the 2016-2025 crop years means claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought claims went from 27 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, and the July nightly low has averaged 69.8 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 68 F. Non-irrigated cash rent was $94 per acre in 2024, up 14 percent from 2014, and land and buildings were valued at $6,673 per acre in 2022. Not much CRP ground remains, and there is no wind or solar on the books yet.

47023.text: Chester County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Excess moisture and flood account for 59 percent of the $8.8 million paid out on closed crop years since 1990, and the loss ratio has climbed from 0.63 over the full record to 0.78 across 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims went from 20 percent of indemnities in 2010-2019 to 36 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $92 per acre in 2026, up 22.7 percent since 2016, and only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

47025.text: Claiborne County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Since 1989, heat and drought has been the largest cause of indemnities, at 42 percent of the $5.9 million paid on closed crop years, though its share fell from 56 percent in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over all closed years is 1.63, but over the last ten closed crop years it is 0.57. Non-irrigated cash rent is $29 per acre in 2026, down 9.4 percent from 2016, and the census value of land and buildings was $4,395 per acre in 2022.

47027.text: Clay County is a dry-land county with very little irrigation, just 1 percent of harvested cropland. Its insurance record leans wet rather than dry: indemnities since 1989 have been led by excess moisture and flood at 59 percent, and the loss ratio over closed crop years is 1.4. Heat and drought claims were 56 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 34 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026, unchanged from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,793 per acre in 2022, up 13.8 percent from 2017.

47029.text: Cocke County has no irrigated acres in these figures, so the rent story is dryland rent: $75 per acre in 2026, up 41.5 percent since 2016. Heat is the thing to watch here. The July average nightly low went from 65.3 F over the 1991-2020 normal to 66.8 F across 2017-2026, and the warming trend since 1976 is 0.51 F per decade. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 45 percent of the $8.9 million paid since 1989, and its share went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 51 percent in 2020-2025, with a low of 29 percent in 2000-2009. Land and buildings were valued at $6,181 per acre in 2022, up 39.6 percent from 2017.

47033.text: Crockett County is mostly dryland. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent is $143 per acre in 2026, up 19.2 percent since 2016. Heat and drought claims made up 70 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 37 percent in 2020-2025, so dry weather has been the main thing paying out, even as its share has come down from the earliest decades. 47041.text: DeKalb County's crop insurance record is the thing to look at first. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $106 per acre for 2026, up 112 percent since 2016.

47043.text: Heat and drought is the story in Dickson County. It was 59 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, fell to 24 percent in 2010-2019, then climbed to 66 percent in 2020-2025. Claims paid out $3.7 million across closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 1.34 over the last ten closed years, meaning insurers paid out more than premiums collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $61 per acre, down 3.2 percent since 2016.

47047.text: Fayette County is a dryland county with a small irrigated share, and the bigger story is in the insurance claims. 47063.text: Hamblen County's crop insurance record has been steady rather than volatile. Solar is 10.1 MW in operation, and there is no wind or CRP ground here.

47069.text: Hardeman County is mostly dryland, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the rain each year carries the crop. Non-irrigated cash rent is $110 per acre in 2026, up 48.6 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings value was $2,804 per acre in 2022, and CRP covers 9.5 percent of the cropland base.

47071.text: Hardin County is a dry-land county with a wet-year problem. Only 8 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of the claims paid over the last four decades came from excess moisture and flood, at 49 percent of indemnities. 47073.text: Hawkins County is a rain-fed county where the crop insurance record stands out. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so that exposure is the one to plan around. The county non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2026, down 17.7 percent from 2016.

47075.text: Haywood County's notable thing is the heat and drought claims. They were 48 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 2000-2009, fell to 24 percent in 2010-2019, and came back to 43 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $205 per acre, but only 15 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Worst year for drought weeks was 2007 with 22 weeks.

The 2017-2026 July nightly low averaged 70.1 F, against 68.6 F for the 1991-2020 normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $92 per acre, up 26.7 percent since 2016, and census land and buildings value was $2,956 per acre in 2022.

47079.text: Heat and drought is the main reason crop insurance has paid out in Henry County. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and 17 weeks of severe drought came in 2021-2025 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $141 per acre in 2026, up 25.9 percent from 2016, and the county's 3735 CRP acres are 3.7 percent of the cropland base.

47081.text: Hickman County's heat and drought claims stand out. July nightly lows have averaged 69.9 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.2 F. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $64 per acre.

47085.text: Humphreys County is a rain-fed county with an unusually heavy insurance record. 47087.text: Jackson County's biggest insurance story is water, and too much of it. The county's July nightly lows have averaged 60.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 59.6 F.

47093.text: Knox County is a flood-and-rain county more than a heat or drought one. Non-irrigated cash rent is $36 per acre in 2026, and the census value of land and buildings is $12,302 per acre, an estimate from the operators.

47101.text: Lewis County is not irrigated at all, and that matters more than the rent here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $31 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $3,635 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated.

47103.text: Lincoln County is mostly dryland, with only 5 percent of harvested cropland irrigated and all of that water coming from groundwater. 47109.text: McNairy County's loss record is the first thing I'd look at. 47111.text: Macon County's crop insurance record leans toward wet years, not dry ones. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,749 per acre, a value the operators themselves estimated.

47125.text: Montgomery County's corn is mostly rain-fed, and the heat and drought side is where the story is. Heat and drought went from 41 percent of indemnity dollars in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's worst drought stretch was 2007 with 20 weeks. The county has paid out more than it took in premium over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.85 and 5 of 19 crop years paying more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $132 per acre in 2026, up 11.9 percent since 2016, and July nightly lows have averaged 70 F over 2017-2026 against a 68.3 F normal. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

47127.text: Moore County is a small place for ground, and the notable part is how much of the risk claims have come from heat and drought. Since 1991, heat and drought made up 74 percent of crop insurance indemnities, and in 2020-2025 that share was 76 percent. The county had 153 of 1357 weeks at or above 50 percent severe drought from 2000-2025, with 2007 the worst at 42 weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent is $55 per acre in 2026, down 14.1 percent from 2016, and census land and buildings value was $4,198 per acre in 2022.

47129.text: Morgan County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at here. Heat and drought made up 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 54 percent in 2020-2025, and it was the largest cause over the full 1991-2025 span at 53 percent of $1.2 million in closed claims. July nights are warming too: the 2017-2026 average low of 66 F is above the 1991-2020 normal of 64.6 F, and 2020s is the first decade the July average low reached 66 F. The county has no irrigated harvested cropland, so that heat and dry weather lands straight on the crop. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre in 2026, and the land and buildings census value of $4,274 per acre comes from operators' own estimates.

47133.text: Overton County's cash rent has gone up a lot. Non-irrigated ground is at $68 per acre for 2026, and it was up 80.3 percent from 2016. Heat and drought are the main reason insurance has paid out here: they were 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 82 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.41. The county's corn trend is up 3.6 bushels per acre a year, but the worst year, 2012, was 89.5 bushels. Land and buildings were valued at $4,036 per acre in 2022.

47135.text: Perry County is a non-irrigated county, with just 1 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, so the rain that falls on the ground is the crop's whole water supply. Heat and drought used to be a small part of what this county claimed on insurance, at 1 percent in 1989-1999, but that share was 83 percent in 2000-2009 and 34 percent in 2020-2025. Over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, indemnities ran 1.24 times premium, and the county paid $13.72 per $100 of insured value. Non-irrigated cash rent is $94 per acre, up from the 193.8 percent rise since 2016, while the census puts land and buildings at $3,130 per acre.

47139.text: Polk County's heat claims are the story here. Heat and drought went from 75 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 83 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.24, meaning claims have paid out more than the premiums brought in. Heat and drought weeks have been running well above the long-term pattern, and the July nightly low has climbed from 65.9 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 67.5 F across 2017-2026. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre for 2025, up 2.7 percent since 2014. The census value of land and buildings was $6,300 per acre in 2022, which the operators themselves estimated.

47141.text: Putnam County's crop insurance record is led by heat and drought, which made up 55 percent of indemnities over 1989-2025, and the share has moved around by decade: 51 percent in 1989-1999, 69 percent in 2000-2009, 60 percent in 2010-2019, and 52 percent in 2020-2025. The closed-year loss ratio of 0.93 is high, though the 2016-2025 ratio of 0.6 is lower. July nights have warmed too, with the average low at 67.1 F for 2017-2026 against a 65.9 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $75 per acre, up 38.9 percent from 2016, and census land value was $5,779 per acre in 2022.

47143.text: Rhea County has no irrigated cropland, so every acre here rides on rain. Heat and drought is the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 44 percent, and its share went from 50 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years, claims paid out more than premiums came in, with a loss ratio of 1.08. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $26 per acre in 2026, down 21.2 percent from 2014. The July nightly low has averaged 68.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 66.8 F.

47145.text: Roane County is a rain-fed county. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground lives or dies on the weather. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 132 of 1357 from 2000-2025, and the worst year was 2008 with 41 weeks. Since 2021-2025 alone, there have been 39 such weeks, so the dry years are still coming. Non-irrigated cash rent is $38 per acre for 2026, up 22.6 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $6,039 per acre in 2022, up 14.7 percent from 2017.

47147.text: The thing that stands out in Robertson County is the claims. Heat and drought went from 51 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio is 0.76 over the closed crop years, with six of the 21 years paying out more than premium. Corn still averages 172.4 bushels per acre at the median, but 2012 dropped to 69.5. Non-irrigated rent is $187 per acre for 2026, up 31.7 percent since 2016. Groundwater supplies all the irrigation water here, so the 2014 irrigated rent of $237 per acre is worth a look if you farm with a pivot. Hot July nights are running a little warmer than normal too.

47149.text: Rutherford County is a dryland county. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop lives or dies on rain, and heat and drought account for 69 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1989. The share ran 42 percent in 1989-1999 and 65 percent in 2020-2025, and the last ten closed years put the loss ratio at 0.84. Non-irrigated cash rent is $65 per acre for 2026, down 13.3 percent from 2016. The census value of land and buildings is $10,250 per acre, up 39.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low has averaged 69.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 67.9 F.

47151.text: Scott County is a dryland county, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. What stands out is the rent. The non-irrigated cash rent is $20 per acre for 2026, and it was down 34.4 percent from 2014. The census put the land and buildings at $3,689 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 38.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. Rent fell while the census value climbed, so most of the gap is in what operators are paying to work the ground. Weeks in severe drought or worse were 75 of 1357 between 2000 and 2025, and the worst year was 2007 with 30 weeks. Between 2021 and 2025 there were 10 such weeks.

47153.text: Sequatchie County has no irrigated cropland, so every bushel here depends on rain falling when the crop needs it. The loss ratio of 1.21 across 1995-2025 says insurance has paid out more than it took in, and the largest single cause is excess moisture and flood at 47 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought claims are a smaller share, but they rose from 1 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 19 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $48 per acre for 2025. The county has no CRP acres and no wind, with 1.3 MW of solar operating.

47155.text: Heat and drought is the main story in Sevier County. It caused 40 percent of crop insurance indemnities over the closed years from 1989 to 2015, and its share went from 51 percent in 1989-1999 to 14 percent in 2010-2019. The county has very little irrigation, at 1 percent of harvested cropland. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre in 2026, up 12.9 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings value is $7,730 per acre, which rose 26.4 percent from 2017 to 2022. July nightly lows have averaged 65.8 F over 2017-2026, against a 64.4 F normal for 1991-2020.

47157.text: Shelby County's notable number is its insurance record. Indemnities have paid out more than premiums over the closed years, with a loss ratio of 0.68 across 1989-2025 and 0.99 across 2016-2025, so the last decade ran close to even. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 18 percent in 2010-2019 and then 41 percent in 2020-2025, and the most recent period is the one to watch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $120 per acre in 2025, and none of the harvested cropland is irrigated. Land and buildings was $5,264 per acre in 2022, and the rent came to 1.78 percent of that.

47159.text: Smith County's biggest story in the claims is wet ground, not dry. Excess moisture and flood account for 52 percent of the $35.8 million in indemnities paid over the closed crop years 1989-2025, and the county's loss ratio over that stretch is 1.25, with 9 of 13 crop years paying out more than the premium. Heat and drought shares have moved around a lot, from 45 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2010-2019 and back up to 48 percent in 2020-2025. The non-irrigated rent is $130 per acre for 2026, up 52.9 percent from 2016, and the census land value was $5,358 per acre in 2022.

47161.text: Stewart County's notable number is the insurance record. Crop insurance has paid out $16.5 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.82, meaning claims ran well ahead of premiums. Heat and drought went from 35 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, so that is the cause to watch. Irrigation is 1 percent of harvested cropland, so most of the ground depends on rain. Rent is $64 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026, down 5.1 percent from 2016. The July nightly low averaged 70.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 68.7 F normal for 1991-2020.

47163.text: Sullivan County's loss ratio is 1.45, meaning crop insurance has paid out more in claims than farmers paid in premiums across the closed years 1989-2025, and heat and drought drove 55 percent of those indemnities. That share went from 61 percent in 1989-1999 to 67 percent in 2010-2019, with a dip to 40 percent in 2000-2009. The county's nightly July lows have warmed a little, and the corn trend over 2009-2023 is up 3.5 bushels per acre a year. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre for 2026, up 27.8 percent from 2016.

47165.text: Sumner County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Crop insurance has paid out $74.1 million on closed crop years since 1989, and in 11 of 15 years the payouts ran higher than the premiums. Over the last ten closed years the loss ratio is 2.5. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 44 percent of indemnities, and its share was 58 percent in 1989-1999 and 67 percent in 2000-2009 before it dropped to 40 percent in 2010-2019. Rent is $180 per acre for non-irrigated ground, up 19.2 percent since 2016.

47167.text: Tipton County's heat and drought claims have climbed sharply. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 57 percent in 2020-2025, while the county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 reached 0.59. Non-irrigated cash rent is $156 per acre in 2026, up 44.4 percent since 2016, and irrigated ground rents at $172. The corn yield trend since 2008 is up 2.7 bushels per acre a year, with a median of 152 bushels and a worst year of 112 in 2008.

47171.text: Unicoi County is a non-irrigated county, with only 9 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census, so the ground depends on rain. The loss pattern is different from the hot, dry counties. Excess moisture and flood made up the largest cause of indemnities in 1989-2004, at 39 percent, and heat and drought were 51 percent of claims in 1989-1999. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $58 per acre for 2026. The census value of land and buildings was $10,994 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 53.9 percent from 2017 to 2022.

47173.text: Union County's notable number is the rent. The non-irrigated cash rent is $25 per acre in 2026, and it has fallen 26.5 percent since 2016. The July nightly low has averaged 66.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 65.6 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance indemnities over 1991-2014, at 52 percent of $248,504. Census land and building value was $4,605 per acre in 2022, up 12.5 percent from 2017.

47175.text:
Van Buren County is a small, mostly unirrigated county, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022. That makes rainfall the main thing the ground depends on, and the claims record shows it. Heat and drought went from 20 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 41 percent in 2010-2019, then 35 percent in 2020-2025. The county's worst drought year was 2008, with 50 weeks of severe drought or worse.

Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $26 per acre in 2025, and it was down 38.8 percent from 2014. Census land and building value was $4,510 per acre in 2022, up 34.6 percent from 2017. July nights have also warmed, with the average low at 66.7 F for 2017-2026 against 65.4 F for the 1991-2020 normal.

47177.text: Warren County's crop insurance record is the story here: indemnities have paid out more than premiums, with a loss ratio of 1.28 over 1989-2025 and 6 of 22 closed crop years paying more than the premium. Freeze and frost is the largest cause at 26 percent of claims. Heat and drought went from 45 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $115 per acre in 2026, up 69.1 percent from 2016, and the county's own land value estimate for 2022 was $6,580 per acre. Most of the water used here comes from groundwater, at 85 percent in 2015.

47179.text: Washington County is mostly non-irrigated ground, with 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. That puts the county's corn in the weather's hands, and the crop insurance record shows it. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 64 percent, and its share went from 67 percent in 1989-1999 to 78 percent in 2010-2019 before dropping to 61 percent in 2020-2025. The median county corn yield for 2009-2025 was 153.7 bushels per acre, with the worst year 2024 at 100.5. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $64 per acre, up 24.5 percent from 2016.

47181.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Wayne County. It was 93 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009, fell to 50 percent in 2010-2019, and was 59 percent in 2020-2025. The county's loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.54, meaning claims paid out more than the premiums that came in. None of the county's cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $73 per acre for 2026, up 19.7 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $3,142 per acre in 2022.

47183.text: Weakley County's cropland has a lot of heat and drought in its claims record. Heat and drought went from 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 24 percent in 2000-2009, then back up to 65 percent in 2010-2019 and 42 percent in 2020-2025. Over closed crop years since 1989, the loss ratio is 0.78, and 5 of 25 crop years paid out more than premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $145 per acre for 2026, up 9.8 percent from 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $4,680 per acre, and CRP covers 5 percent of cropland.

47185.text: Heat and drought is the main thing to watch in White County. It made up 62 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, and the loss ratio for those closed years is 0.85, so claims have run ahead of premiums over the long stretch. Its share went from 59 percent in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025, but it was 70 percent in 2000-2009, so there's no clear trend in that share to lean on. The corn yield trend is up 4 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 165.8 bushels and a worst year of 73.3 in 2012. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre, up 20.2 percent since 2016.

47187.text: Williamson County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought made up 90 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 65 percent in 1989-1999, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.82. Corn yields have a trend of 2.9 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the worst year, 2012, was 33.3 bushels. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $53 per acre in 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $7,148 per acre.

47189.text: Wilson County's notable number is the claims record. Crop insurance has paid out more than the premiums taken in: a loss ratio of 1.31 across closed crop years 1989-2025, and 1.32 over the last ten. Heat and drought is the largest cause at 63 percent of indemnities, and its share went from 40 percent in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of that exposure is on dryland ground. Non-irrigated cash rent is $56 per acre in 2026, up 11 percent from 2016.

49005.text: Cache County is mostly irrigated: 70 percent of harvested cropland was under irrigation in the 2022 census, and most of the irrigation water still comes from surface sources, with groundwater at only 10 percent. Heat and drought is the biggest cause of crop insurance indemnities here, and its share has climbed from 12 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 41 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio for 2016-2025 was 1.2, meaning claims paid out more than premiums taken in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre and irrigated is $105 per acre.

49009.text: Daggett County is all irrigated. Every acre of harvested cropland in the 2022 census was irrigated, and only 1 percent of that water came from groundwater in 2015. That makes surface water the thing to watch here. Drought is the main pressure. The county was in severe drought or worse for 377 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, 27.8 percent of the time, and 2021 was the worst year with 52 weeks, tied with 2003 and 2004. The 2021-2025 span alone logged 124 weeks. Nights are warming slowly, with the July low averaging 51.8 F over 2017-2026 against 50.6 F in the 1991-2020 normal. Land and buildings were valued at $3,609 per acre in 2022, up 30 percent from 2017.

49035.text: Salt Lake County is a county where the water decides the rent. Two-thirds of the harvested cropland is irrigated, and irrigated ground rents for $121 per acre in 2026, against $41 for non-irrigated in 2023. Heat and drought accounted for 95 percent of crop insurance indemnities in closed crop years from 2004 to 2022, and 96 percent in 2000-2009. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse went from 2021 with 52 weeks to 117 weeks across 2021-2025. July nightly lows averaged 63.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 60.8 F. Groundwater supplies just 3 percent of the irrigation water.

49037.text: What stands out in San Juan County is how much of the insurance money has gone to heat and drought. Since 1989, the closed crop years have paid $15.1 million in indemnities, and heat and drought made up 67 percent of that. The share went from 38 percent in 1989-1999 to 74 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the full span is 1.15, so claims have run above premiums. Only 9 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent in 2010 was $34 per acre.

49039.text: Sanpete County is an irrigated county, with 89 percent of harvested cropland watered, and its insurance record is the story. Crop insurance has paid out $2.9 million against premiums across closed crop years 1989-2025, a loss ratio of 1.8, and irrigation failure accounts for 62 percent of those claims. Heat and drought claims went from 33 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $128 per acre in 2026, while non-irrigated ground rents $23 per acre in 2025, up 24.3 percent since 2014. The July nightly low is 54.4 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 52.7 F.

49043.text: Summit County is mostly irrigated ground, with 82 percent of harvested cropland watered in the 2022 census and none of that water pulled from groundwater. Irrigated rent for 2026 is $90 per acre, and the non-irrigated rent for 2025 is $31 per acre, which has gone up 260.5 percent since 2013. The land and buildings value from the 2022 census was $4,336 per acre, and it rose 32.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 358 of 1357 from 2000 to 2025, and 134 of those weeks fell in 2021-2025. July nights have warmed a little, with an average low of 48.8 F in 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 47 F.

49045.text: Tooele County is an irrigated county. Irrigation makes up 92 percent of harvested cropland, and 24 percent of that water comes from groundwater. When irrigation fails, it is the biggest cause of claims, at 40 percent of the $322,072 paid out on closed crop years from 1989-2022. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2010-2019. Dry weeks are the bigger story: 510 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2022 hit 52 of them. Non-irrigated ground rents for $26 per acre, while irrigated ground rents for $103 per acre. The census puts land and buildings at $3,447 per acre.

49057.text: Weber County is mostly irrigated ground, 86 percent of harvested cropland, and it has very little groundwater behind that water, only 2 percent. The notable thing here is how much heat and drought now shows up in the claims: they were 33 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost is still the largest cause of losses over the full run at 48 percent. Non-irrigated rent is $58 per acre in 2026, and irrigated rent is $163 per acre, so the water is what you are paying for. The census puts land and buildings at $18,674 per acre in 2022, which was up 100.4 percent from 2017.

50003.text: Bennington County's crop insurance story is hail, not heat. Hail is 58 percent of the $5.3 million paid out since 1993, and the loss ratio is 1.25 across the full record and 1.45 over the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 5 percent in 2010-2019 and 0 percent in 2020-2025. The county has 9 percent of its harvested cropland irrigated, and the July nightly low averaged 56.4 F over 2017-2026 against a 54.5 F normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $60 per acre, against a census value of $4,177 per acre for land and buildings, which is the operators' own estimate and not a sale price.

50005.text: Caledonia County is a rain county more than a dry one. Crop insurance has paid $310,624 in indemnities since 2000, and 92 percent of that came from excess moisture and flood. Heat and drought made up 0 percent of claims in 2010-2019 and 4 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years have shown up mostly in the last few seasons. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which makes non-irrigated ground the norm here. Non-irrigated cash rent is $52 per acre for 2026, up 52.9 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings were valued at $3,395 per acre in 2022.

50007.text: Chittenden County is a wet-weather county first. Flood and excess moisture account for 76 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1996 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.07, meaning claims paid ran above premiums in that stretch. Heat and drought claims are a smaller share, but they went from 13 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 21 percent in 2020-2025. The July nightly low has averaged 60.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 58.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $47 per acre for 2026, up 27 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $6,230 per acre in 2022.

50009.text: Essex County is the wet one here. Flood and excess moisture took 68 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid in this county from 2001 to 2024, and total closed claims for that stretch came to $578,773. Heat and drought claims were 3 percent of the total in 2000-2009 and 0 percent in 2010-2019, so that is not where the losses have been. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which fits a county that rarely needs it. The census puts land and buildings at $2,357 per acre in 2022, and that value went up 20.5 percent between 2017 and 2022. July nights have warmed too, with the 2017-2026 average low at 54.6 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.7 F.

50013.text: Grand Isle County is a flood-and-wet-spring county more than a heat county, and the insurance record shows it. Excess moisture and flood account for 67 percent of indemnities since 1995, and the closed-year loss ratio is 1.22, so claims have run ahead of premium over the long span. Heat and drought claims went from 5 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 28 percent in 2020-2025, which is the shift to watch. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. The July nightly low was 62.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 60.9 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $62 per acre.

50015.text: Lamoille County's cropland is mostly dryland, with only 4 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the main risk on these acres has been too much water rather than too little. Crop insurance indemnities from 1995 to 2024 total $998,047, and excess moisture and flood account for 98 percent of that. Heat and drought claims fell from 6 percent in 2000-2009 to 0 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent was $62 per acre in 2025, up 65.3 percent from 2013. The census value of land and buildings was $3,508 per acre in 2022.

50017.text: Orange County's notable number is the floods. Excess moisture and flood make up 60 percent of the crop insurance claims paid here, and the loss ratio is 0.44 on closed crop years from 1989-2025. Heat and drought claims were 3 percent in both 2000-2009 and 2010-2019, then rose to 19 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 17 weeks in severe drought or worse in 2021-2025, and the worst year was 2025 with 17 weeks alone. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and non-irrigated cash rent is $71 per acre in 2026.

50019.text: Orleans County's biggest story is weather that is too wet, not too hot. Excess moisture and flood account for 71 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years, and the county's loss ratio over 1995-2025 is 1.74, meaning claims have run well above premiums. Heat and drought claims are a smaller piece, but they went from 13 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 38 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $58 per acre for 2026, up 91.8 percent from 2016, and census land and buildings value was $3,763 per acre in 2022.

50021.text: Rutland County is a non-irrigated county, and that shapes most of what matters here. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the rent you see is for ground that lives or dies on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $58 per acre for 2026, up 71.6 percent from 2016. Crop insurance has paid out $2.1 million on closed crop years since 1995, and excess moisture and flood account for 81 percent of that. Heat and drought claims went from 11 percent in 2000-2009 to 21 percent in 2020-2025, so that side is picking up. The county has 20.4 MW of solar operating and no wind.

50023.text: Washington County's notable number is the water. Excess moisture and flood took 76 percent of the indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1996 to 2025, and the county's indemnities totaled $384,611 over that span. Heat and drought claims went from 8 percent in 2010-2019 to 14 percent in 2020-2025, so they are growing but still a small part of the picture. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the rent is $56 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2024, up 19.1 percent since 2014. Census land and buildings were valued at $5,057 per acre in 2022.

50025.text: Windham County is a small cropland county where frost and freeze, not heat or drought, have been the main cause of insurance claims. Freeze and frost make up 56 percent of indemnities since 2000, and heat and drought went from 0 percent of claims in 2000-2009 and 2010-2019 to 20 percent in 2020-2025. Only 4 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's loss ratio is 0.81 over the last ten closed crop years, so claims have run above premiums lately. Non-irrigated cash rent was $84 per acre in 2024, down 26.1 percent from 2014.

50027.text: Windsor County's biggest story is wet ground, not dry. Excess moisture and flood took 42 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1998-2025, and heat and drought went from 6 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 10 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated rent is $40 per acre in 2026, up 60 percent from 2016. Land values rose 25.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, and the county has no CRP acres expiring through 2029.

51001.text: Accomack County is a dryland county with a loss record that stands out. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.8 across 1989-2025, with 8 of 28 crop years paying out more than premium. Heat and drought claims were 65 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 54 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $112 per acre for 2026, up 33.3 percent from 2016. The corn yield trend is up 2.7 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, but the worst year, 2010, was 66.3 bushels per acre.

51003.text: Albemarle County's cropland is mostly dry ground. Only 3 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and none of the irrigation water comes from groundwater. Freeze and frost, not heat, is the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, at 35 percent of the $43.6 million paid out since 1989. Heat and drought share of claims went from 11 percent in 1989-1999 to 22 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 31 percent in 2000-2009. Non-irrigated cash rent is $33 per acre in 2026, up 40.4 percent from 2016. The county has had 0 Julys with an average low at or above 70 F since 1900, while the July average low reached 66 F first in the 2010s.

51005.text: Alleghany County has no irrigated cropland, and the drought record is the thing to look at here. Heat and drought went from 32 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 to 64 percent in 2010-2019, and it was the largest cause over 1995-2025 at 50 percent of the $359,473 paid on closed crop years. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $33 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $3,293 per acre. Only 5 weeks of severe drought or worse have shown up since 2021, after 16 weeks in 2002 alone.

51007.text: Amelia County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so the weather is the main risk here. Heat and drought has made up most of the crop insurance claims since 1989, at 74 percent of $17.0 million in indemnities, and its share was 60 percent in 1989-1999 and 77 percent in 2000-2009 and again in 2010-2019. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre in 2026, up 31.8 percent since 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $4,304 per acre in 2022, which rose 39.1 percent from 2017 to 2022. The county's corn yield trend has been rising 4.5 bushels per acre a year over 2008-2025, with a median of 126.7 bushels per acre.

51009.text: Amherst County's notable number is the loss ratio: indemnities have run 1.42 times premium over the closed crop years since 1989, and 1.45 over 2016-2025. Freeze and frost is the biggest cause of claims at 52 percent, while heat and drought went from 36 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 2 percent in 2020-2025. Nights are warmer, with the July average low at 66.5 F for 2017-2026 against a 64.7 F normal for 1991-2020. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre in 2026, up 8.3 percent from 2016, and the census puts land and buildings at $5,795 per acre in 2022.

51011.text: Heat and drought is the thing to look at in Appomattox County. It made up 62 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.89, so claims have run close to premiums across the whole record. Nothing here is irrigated, and the worst drought year was 2002, with 39 weeks of severe drought or worse across the county. Corn yields have trended up 5 bushels per acre a year over 2009-2025, with a median of 112.5 bushels and a worst year at 34 in 2010. The July nightly low has averaged 67.6 F over 2017-2026, against 65.8 F in the 1991-2020 normal. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026.

51017.text: Bath County's heat-and-drought history is the thing to look at first. Heat and drought made up 55 percent of crop insurance indemnities from 1998 to 2024, and the share was 74 percent in 2000-2009, 49 percent in 2010-2019, and 52 percent in 2020-2025. The county had 20 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025, and its worst year was 2002 with 14 weeks at that level. Non-irrigated cash rent is $45 per acre for 2026, up 91.5 percent since 2016. Census land and building value was $4,314 per acre in 2022, up 17.3 percent from 2017.

51019.text: Bedford County's loss ratio is the first thing to look at. Insurance has paid out $1.27 for every dollar of premium over 1989-2025, and the last ten closed crop years still was 1.01. Heat and drought was the largest cause of those claims at 56 percent overall, though its share fell from 62 percent in 2000-2009 to 42 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $28 per acre in 2026, up 33.3 percent since 2016.

51023.text: Botetourt County's notable number is the crop insurance record: the closed years since 1989 have paid out $10.2 million, a loss ratio of 1.35, and the last ten years run higher at 1.56. Freeze and frost is the largest cause at 48 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought went from 28 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre in 2026, and none of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the ground depends on rain.

51025.text: Brunswick County is mostly dryland ground, and heat and drought is what the crop insurance claims keep coming back to. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $30 per acre, down 9.1 percent from 2014, and the 2022 census put land and buildings at $2,749 per acre. July nightly lows averaged 69.5 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 68.2 F.

51029.text: Buckingham County has no irrigated cropland at all, so every acre here lives or dies on rain. The loss ratio over those years is 1.03, meaning claims paid more than the premiums collected. Non-irrigated cash rent is $30 per acre for 2026, and the census puts land and buildings at $4,400 per acre in 2022. The county also has 39.8 MW of solar in operation, with 224.4 MW proposed.

51031.text: Campbell County's corn has a lot of weather history behind it. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre in 2026, up 42.2 percent since 2016.

51033.text: Caroline County's cropland is mostly dryland. Only 5 percent of harvested cropland was irrigated in 2022, and heat and drought made up 78 percent of crop insurance indemnities over 1989-2025, with 93 percent in 1989-1999 and 75 percent in 2020-2025. The census puts land and buildings at $4,710 per acre in 2022, which means rent was 1.51 percent of value that year.

51035.text: Carroll County's biggest claim history is not heat or water. Freeze and frost cause the most crop insurance money here, at 38 percent of indemnities since 1989, and the county's loss ratio over that stretch is 1.65, meaning claims have run well above premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $44 per acre in 2026, up 20.3 percent from 2016.

51037.text: Charlotte County is mostly dryland, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022, so rain at the right time is what the crop depends on.
