Solar is the other big thing here, with 189.9 MW operating and none proposed for wind.

51119.text: Middlesex is a county where heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought went from 89 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 48 percent in 2000-2009, and back up to 89 percent in 2020-2025, so the recent years look a lot like the early ones. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 0.2, which says the claims have been light lately. Non-irrigated cash rent is $87 per acre for 2026, against a census land value of $4,041 per acre. The July nightly low has been running warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, at 71.4 F against 69.7 F.

They account for 77 percent of crop insurance indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1992 through 2025, and their share went from 69 percent in 2000-2009 to 80 percent in 2010-2019. The loss ratio over those years is 0.56, so claims have run well below premiums overall. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre for 2026, up 22.4 percent from 2016. The census puts land and buildings at $5,743 per acre in 2022, after a rise of 18.6 percent from 2017. The July nightly low averaged 63.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.7 F.

The nights are warming too: July's average low for 2017-2026 is 66.3 F, up from a 1991-2020 normal of 64.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026.

Heat and drought is the main cause of crop insurance claims, at 54 percent of the $69.1 million paid since 1989. That share went from 55 percent in 1989-1999 to 60 percent in 2020-2025. Insurance has paid out more than premium in 11 of 27 closed crop years, and the loss ratio is 0.89. Land and buildings are valued at $4,745 per acre, and the county has 38 CRP acres and 20 MW of solar.

The county's corn loss ratio was 0.51 over the full run, and 0.36 across 2016-2025. The worst year for corn was 2010, at 71.9 bushels per acre against a median of 142.3. Non-irrigated cash rent is $93 per acre, up 24 percent since 2016.

Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and heat and drought made up 84 percent of insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 78 percent in 2010-2019, and 78 percent again in 2020-2025. 51800.text: Suffolk City is a small cropland county, and only 1 percent of its harvested ground is irrigated, so the corn picture rests on rain. Heat and drought is the largest cause of insurance claims here at 52 percent of the $23.0 million paid since 1989, and its share went from 72 percent in 1989-1999 to 56 percent in 2020-2025. The crop insurance loss ratio over those years is 0.55, and five of the 18 closed crop years paid out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $103 per acre in 2026, up 33.8 percent since 2016. Census land and buildings were $4,816 per acre in 2022, so the rent was 1.76 percent of that value.

51810.text: Virginia Beach is not really a row-crop county anymore, and the numbers say so. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent of $62 per acre is down 15 percent since 2016. The loss ratio over 1995-2025 is 0.37, and the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.19, so the insurance has paid out a small share of premium. Most of the old claims were excess moisture and flood, at 48 percent of indemnities. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of claims in 2010-2019 to 58 percent in 2020-2025, which is the recent shift worth watching. The July nightly low has been running warm, with a 2017-2026 average of 72.9 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 71.6 F.

51830.text: Williamsburg City is a place where the nights have been getting warmer. The July average low was 71.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 69.5 F, and it has been warming at 0.72 F per decade since 1976. Julys with an average low at or above 70 F have happened 34 times since 1900. Drought has been light by comparison: 55 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year, 2002, had 36 of those weeks. None of the weeks in 2021-2025 reached that level. The county has no CRP acres and no wind or solar, operating or proposed.

51840.text: Winchester City is a small place for farm ground, with no CRP acres and no wind or solar in operation or proposed, so none of that enters the picture here. The notable part is the heat. July nights averaged 64.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.4 F, and the nightly low trend since 1976 runs warm at 0.68 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Severe drought has been less common, with 52 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent or more of the county in severe drought or worse. That's 3.8 percent, with 2002 and 2023 each at 14 weeks, and 29 weeks in 2021-2025 alone.

53001.text: Adams County is an irrigated county with a lot of dryland around it. Heat and drought is the biggest cause of insurance claims here, and the share has moved from 26 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 54 percent in 2020-2025. Over the closed crop years since 1989, indemnities have paid out $359.4 million, a loss ratio of 1.44, so the insurance has paid back more than the premiums collected. Irrigated ground rents for $467 per acre against $56 for dry ground, and 30 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Julys have been warming, from 54.2 F normal lows to 55.9 F over 2017-2026.

53003.text: Heat and drought is the story in Asotin County. It was 53 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 and 80 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's loss ratio of 1.23 across closed crop years means insurers have paid out more than farmers paid in premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $55 per acre for 2026, up 80.3 percent since 2014. July nightly lows have averaged 55.7 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 53.4 F. There are 89 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021, and 11,051 acres are in CRP, with 178 expiring over fiscal years 2027-2029.

53005.text: Benton County's cropland is mostly irrigated, 67 percent in the 2022 census, and the county's crop insurance has paid out more than it took in: a loss ratio of 1.22 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025. Heat and drought claims were 32 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 42 percent in 2020-2025, so that is the trend to watch. Non-irrigated ground rents at $45 per acre, while irrigated ground rents at $700 per acre. The census value of land and buildings is $4,153 per acre. July nightly lows have warmed to 60.3 F in 2017-2026 from the 1991-2020 normal of 58.6 F.

53011.text: Clark County's cropland is mostly dryland, and the rent shows it: $90 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2026. Irrigated ground rents for $418 per acre, though irrigation covers only 21 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and that ratio has not moved in a clear direction. Freeze and frost cause 63 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid here since 1996, while heat and drought make up 0 percent of claims for 2020-2025. The July nightly low averaged 54.8 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 54 F, and the county has had no July with an average low at or above 70 F since 1900. Non-irrigated rent is up 89.5 percent since 2014.

53013.text: Columbia County is a dryland county. Only 2 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop insurance record is the place to start. Heat and drought made up 81 percent of indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 54 percent in 1989-1999. The loss ratio is 1.63 over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025, meaning claims paid out more than premium in that stretch. Non-irrigated cash rent is $110 per acre for 2026, up 279.3 percent from 2014. The 2022 census land value is $2,280 per acre, and the 2022 rent was 3.51 percent of that. Between 2017 and 2022 land values rose 40 percent.

53017.text: Douglas County's cropland leans on irrigation. Irrigated ground rents for $285 per acre, against $53 for non-irrigated, and 18 percent of irrigation water came from groundwater in 2015. Heat and drought has been the top cause of claims, 42 percent of the $249.0 million paid since 1989, and its share went from 49 percent in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2000-2009 and 37 percent in 2020-2025. The county has paid out more in claims than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 1.45 over 1989-2025 and 1.79 over 2016-2025. Land is priced at $2,784 per acre on the census estimate, and the rent is 1.65 percent of that, so the ground is valued well above what it rents for.

53021.text: Franklin County is an irrigated county, and that shapes everything else here. Non-irrigated ground rents for $34 per acre in 2026, while irrigated ground rented for $553 per acre in 2025, so the water is where the money is. The loss ratio of 1.09 over 1989-2025 means the insurance has paid out more than the premiums taken in, and 13 of 29 closed crop years paid out more than premium. Heat and drought was the largest cause of claims at 40 percent, and its share went from 35 percent in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. Julys have been warmer at night, averaging 59.3 F lows from 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 57.5 F.

53023.text: Garfield County is a dryland county that has been paying out on bad years. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and crop insurance indemnities since 1989 total $49.8 million, with heat and drought behind 70 percent of that. The share from heat and drought went from 70 percent in 1989-1999 to 84 percent in 2020-2025. Over the last ten closed crop years, claims have run 1.14 times the premium paid in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $70 per acre in 2026, up 10.2 percent since 2016. The county also has 342.7 MW of wind operating and no solar yet.

53027.text: Grays Harbor is mostly a non-irrigated county, and what stands out is how little of the ground is watered. Only 26 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of that water comes from groundwater, 66 percent of it in 2015. Irrigated ground rents for $96 per acre in 2025, against $54 for non-irrigated, so the premium is real but the irrigated acreage is small. July nights have held close to the 1991-2020 normal, at 51.2 F against 51.1 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low of 70 F or higher. Drought weeks are few: 46 of 1357 since 2000, with 11 of them in 2021-2025. The census land value of $3,727 per acre was up 55.6 percent from 2017 to 2022.

53033.text: Irrigated ground is the thing to look at in King County. Irrigated cash rent is $460 per acre in 2026, against $164 for non-irrigated, and the irrigated share of harvested cropland is 23 percent. Most of the water comes from groundwater, 76 percent in 2015. Non-irrigated rent rose 31.2 percent from 2014 to 2026. Census land and buildings were valued at $38,716 per acre in 2022, up 9.8 percent from 2017. Drought weeks have been the thing to watch: 48 weeks of severe drought or worse from 2021-2025, and 2025 alone had 24 of them.

53039.text: Klickitat County is a dry-ground county where the heat and drought story stands out. Heat and drought went from 43 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 36 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.83, so insurers have been paying out more than they took in. Only 19 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre, while the census value of land and buildings was $2,482 per acre in 2022. Keep an eye on the 98 CRP acres expiring in fiscal years 2027-2029, since that ground will need a plan.

53041.text: Lewis County is a dryland county on the rent side, with irrigated ground renting for $103 per acre against $77 for non-irrigated. The gap has widened: irrigated rent was 1.09 times non-irrigated in 2010 and was 1.79 times in 2025. Non-irrigated rent is down 48.3 percent since 2014, so the ground that doesn't have water is where the drop is. Irrigation covers 19 percent of harvested cropland, and 45 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid out little here, with a loss ratio of 0.12 across the closed years since 1993.

53043.text: Lincoln County's notable number is the insurance record. Indemnities have paid out $291.4 million on closed crop years since 1989, and the loss ratio is 1.41, with 10 of the 34 closed crop years paying out more than the premium collected. Heat and drought caused 66 percent of those claims. That share went from 23 percent in 1989-1999 to 68 percent in 2020-2025, and the last ten closed years alone show the same 1.41 ratio. Only 6 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and most of the water comes from groundwater, so the dry years land on the ground that is not watered. Non-irrigated cash rent is $57 per acre for 2026, up 34.1 percent from 2016.

53047.text: Most of the cropland in Okanogan County is dryland, but the water that is there matters a lot. Irrigated ground rents for $253 per acre, while non-irrigated ground goes for $30. Freeze and frost were the largest cause of crop insurance claims, at 49 percent. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of claims in 1989-1999 to 11 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio for the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.84. The county has 5406 CRP acres, and none of that enrollment expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

53049.text: Pacific County is a county where freeze and frost is what has cost growers money, not heat or water. Crop insurance paid $284,052 on closed claims from 1997 to 2022, and freeze and frost made up 90 percent of that, while heat and drought made up 0 percent of indemnities from 2010 to 2019. Non-irrigated cash rent was $39 per acre in 2025, down 36.6 percent from 2014. Census land and buildings value was $5,238 per acre in 2022, up 51.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. Irrigation covers 48 percent of harvested cropland, and 37 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

53055.text: San Juan County is a small, mostly non-irrigated place, with only 6 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. The rent is $40 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2024. The land and buildings were valued at $12,320 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 30.3 percent between 2017 and 2022, or 5.4 percent a year. What stands out to me is the drought record: 27 weeks in severe drought or worse from 2021-2025, against 52 weeks across 2000-2025, with 2015 the worst year at 19 weeks. July nights are running a little warmer, with the average low at 52.7 F for 2017-2026 against a 52.3 F normal for 1991-2020.

53057.text:
Skagit County is a wet county, and the insurance record shows it. Excess moisture and flood is the largest cause of claims at 42 percent, and the loss ratio over 1989-2025 is 0.95. The part that stands out is heat and drought, which went from 7 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 53 percent in 2020-2025. July nightly lows have warmed a little, from a 1991-2020 normal of 50.4 F to 51.2 F over 2017-2026, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F.

Irrigated ground rents for $425 per acre in 2026, against $256 for non-irrigated. Most of the water comes from groundwater, 78 percent in 2015.

53061.text: Snohomish County is a wet county, and the claims show it. Excess moisture and flood make up 78 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1997 to 2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 0.29. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 to 7 percent in 2010-2019 and 0 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated ground rents for $402 per acre, close to three times the $140 non-irrigated rate, but that gap was 2.00 times in 2010, so the ratio moves around and is not a clear trend. The July nightly low is 51.6 F over 2017-2026, up from the 1991-2020 normal of 50.8 F. Only 42 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated.

53063.text: The loss record is what stands out here. Crop insurance has paid out $135.3 million on closed crop years since 1989, and heat and drought account for 68 percent of that. Their share of indemnities went from 38 percent in 1989-1999 to 81 percent in 2020-2025, and the 2016-2025 loss ratio is 1.72, so the policies have paid more than the premiums. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre for 2026, down 1 percent from 2016, and only 5 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground is dryland.

53065.text: Stevens County is a dry-land county where the heat and drought claims stand out. Heat and drought went from 22 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2010-2019 to 78 percent in 2020-2025, and the county's closed crop years have paid out $1.7 million in claims against a loss ratio of 1.52. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $50 per acre, up 35.6 percent from 2016. Irrigated ground is only 10 percent of harvested cropland, and its rent of $63 per acre in 2024 is well above the dry ground.

53069.text: Wahkiakum County is a small place with a quiet set of numbers. The July nights are close to normal, with the 2017-2026 average low at 51.6 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 51.4 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low of 70 F or higher. Severe drought has been rare: 34 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with the worst year in 2015 at 17 weeks. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground was $20 per acre in 2021. The census value of land and buildings was $6,630 per acre in 2022, up 38 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP holds 90 acres, and 11 of those expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

53071.text: Walla Walla County is mostly dryland, but a few numbers stand out. Heat and drought has been the largest cause of crop insurance claims here, and its share rose from 48 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 1.14 over closed crop years 1989-2025, and 11 of 31 crop years paid out more than the premium. The non-irrigated cash rent was $74 per acre in 2025, while irrigated ground rents at $297 per acre in 2026. Irrigation covers 27 percent of harvested cropland, and 43 percent of that water comes from groundwater.

53073.text: Whatcom County's irrigated ground is where the money is. Irrigated cash rent is $514 per acre in 2026, against $181 for non-irrigated, and 60 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Most of that water comes from groundwater, 89 percent in 2015. Heat and drought claims have grown as a share of indemnities, from 8 percent in 2000-2009 to 20 percent in 2010-2019 and 38 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio is 0.89 over the full closed record and 0.92 over the last ten crop years. Freeze and frost remain the largest cause of claims at 33 percent, and the census put land and buildings at $20,475 per acre in 2022.

53075.text: Heat and drought is the story in Whitman County. It was 52 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 29 percent in 2000-2009, 59 percent in 2010-2019, and 80 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full run of closed crop years, indemnities of $511.9 million have been paid against premiums, and the loss ratio is 1.33, with 9 of 33 crop years paying out more than the premium. Non-irrigated cash rent is $79 per acre for 2026, up 0.6 percent from 2016. The county is 1 percent irrigated, so most of this ground rides on rain. The census put land and buildings at $2,528 per acre in 2022, and rent that year was 3.38 percent of that value.

53077.text: Yakima County's cropland is mostly irrigated, and the water is the thing to watch. The irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $231 per acre, while the non-irrigated rent was $150 per acre in 2021, up 170.3 percent from 2011. Heat and drought went from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 1.26, so insurers have paid out more than they took in. Irrigation failure claims total only $3.8 million over all closed years.

54001.text:
Barbour County is a non-irrigated ground county, and most of the story is in the rent and the land price. Non-irrigated cash rent is $32 per acre for 2026, and it is down 1.6 percent from 2016. Census land and buildings were $2,673 per acre in 2022, up 14.5 percent from 2017 to 2022. That gap between a $32 rent and a $2,673 value is wide, and it is worth looking at before you set a lease.

Weather has been mild in July but not gentle in the dry weeks. The July nightly low averaged 62.5 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 60.9 F. There were 23 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2000-2025, and 2024 had 16 of them.

54003.text: Berkeley County's loss history is the first thing I'd look at. Freeze and frost cause 44 percent of the indemnities paid since 1989, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.59, meaning insurers paid out more than they took in. Heat and drought claims went from 20 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 19 percent in 2020-2025, with a peak of 87 percent in 2010-2019. The July nightly low is up from 63.4 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 64.4 F over 2017-2026. Non-irrigated cash rent is $46 per acre, up 24.3 percent since 2016, and the land value was $7,055 per acre in 2022.

54011.text: Cabell County is mostly a flood-and-wet-weather county on the insurance side. Excess moisture and flood made up 53 percent of the $446,816 paid out on closed claims from 1989-2009, and heat and drought went from 47 percent of those claims in 1989-1999 to 18 percent in 2000-2009. The county had 40 of 1357 weeks in 2000-2025 with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 24 of those weeks came in 2007 alone. Non-irrigated cash rent was $20 per acre in 2024, up 2.5 percent from 2014. Land and buildings were valued at $5,367 per acre in 2022, which is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price, and there is no wind or solar running here.

54013.text: Calhoun County is a small, unirrigated place, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, so the rent and land numbers mostly reflect ground that depends on the sky. Non-irrigated cash rent is $26 per acre for 2025, and it was down 8.6 percent from 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $1,800 per acre for 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. Drought has been rare here over the years, with 20 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county or more in severe drought or worse, and all 20 of those weeks fell in 2021-2025, with 2024 the worst at 20 weeks.

54019.text: Fayette County is a hills-and-hollows country with little flat ground to lose, and the numbers here point to a county where heat and water are not the main story. The July nightly low was 62.4 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.3 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Severe drought has been rare: 11 weeks out of 1357 from 2000 through 2025, with the worst year, 2024, at 6 weeks. Land values are the number to watch. The census put land and buildings at $4,123 per acre in 2022, and that figure rose 41.5 percent from 2017 to 2022. CRP is small at 155 acres, and 26 of those acres come out of the program in fiscal years 2027-2029.

54021.text: Gilmer County's notable number is the rent jump. Non-irrigated cash rent was $20 per acre in 2025, and it was up 95 percent from 2014 to 2025. Land and buildings were valued at $2,104 per acre in the 2022 census, and that value rose 59.8 percent from 2017 to 2022. The July nightly low averaged 64.5 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 62.9 F. Drought has been rare here: 20 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, and all 20 came in the 2024 season. Nothing is irrigated, and there is no CRP ground or wind and solar to speak of.

54023.text: Heat and drought is the main cause of crop insurance claims here, at 82 percent of indemnities since 1990, and its share rose from 84 percent in 1989-1999 to 89 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. The county has 1422 acres in CRP, which is 7.1 percent of the cropland base, and 17 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. Non-irrigated cash rent is $27 per acre in 2026, down 3.6 percent from 2016. The county has 367 MW of wind operating and no solar.

54025.text: Heat and drought is the main thing I'd look at in Greenbrier County. It caused 51 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2024, and its share went from 60 percent in 1989-1999 to 71 percent in 2010-2019 before falling to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $50 per acre in 2026. Census land and buildings are valued at $3,317 per acre, which is the operators' own estimate. CRP covers 15.1 percent of the cropland base, and 221 of those acres expire in fiscal years 2027-2029.

54027.text: Hampshire County's most notable number is the insurance record. Heat and drought went from 11 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 46 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.47, so claims have run above premiums. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, which puts most of the ground on rain alone. Non-irrigated cash rent is $42 per acre in 2026, up 123.7 percent from 2016. The census land and buildings value was $3,713 per acre in 2022, and weeks in severe drought or worse were 23 across 2021-2025.

54029.text: Hancock County's land value stands out more than its weather. The census put cropland and buildings at $4,294 per acre in 2022, and that figure fell 6.1 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 1.3 percent a year. That is a county where the land price has been sliding while the rest of the picture stays quiet. July nights have warmed some, with the 2017-2026 average low at 62.7 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.7 F. Severe drought has been rare, with 12 of 1357 weeks since 2000 at 50 percent of the county or more, though 2025 had 6 of those weeks. There is no CRP ground and no operating wind or solar yet, only 8.4 MW of solar proposed.

54031.text: Hardy County is a dryland place. None of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so the crop rides on rain. Heat and drought is the main cause of crop insurance claims, and its share went from 76 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 is 1.09, meaning claims paid out more than premiums taken in. Non-irrigated cash rent is $45 per acre in 2026, and census land and buildings value is $4,212 per acre in 2022.

54035.text: Jackson County's biggest story in the numbers is the claims. Heat and drought went from 16 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2000-2009 to 50 percent in 2020-2025, while excess moisture and flood still account for 54 percent of all closed claims since 1989. Rent for non-irrigated ground is $25 per acre in 2026, down 39.8 percent from 2016. The census put land and buildings at $2,620 per acre in 2022, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale price. July nights have warmed a little, with the 2017-2026 average low at 64.9 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.5 F. Solar is the one energy use here, with 113.1 MW operating and nothing wind.

54037.text: Jefferson County is a small corn county where heat and drought is the main thing that costs farmers money. Heat and drought went from 58 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 77 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.81. Non-irrigated cash rent is $55 per acre in 2026, down 26.7 percent from 2016. The July nightly low averaged 65.6 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.1 F, and the county has seen 35 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021.

54041.text: Lewis County is a non-irrigated county, with only 1 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation, so the land depends on rain. The dry-weeks record is light: 23 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, and the worst year, 2024, had 20 of them. That is most of the county's drought in one season, and the 2021-2025 stretch alone logged 22 weeks. Nightly July lows have warmed a little, from 62.3 F normal to 64 F over 2017-2026. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre, up 56.7 percent since 2014.

54043.text: Lincoln County's notable number is the crop insurance record. Indemnities paid out more than premiums collected, with a loss ratio of 2.78 across the closed crop years 1990-2009, and the 2000-2009 ratio was 2.95. Excess moisture and flood were the largest cause at 65 percent of claims in 1990-2009. Heat and drought claims were 54 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 and 16 percent in 2000-2009, so that share has fallen. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the county's ground depends on rain. Nights are warming too: the July average low was 66.3 F in 2017-2026, up from 64.7 F in the 1991-2020 normal.

54047.text: McDowell County is a quiet one on most measures. Its July nights have warmed a little, with the average low up from 61.9 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 62.8 F over 2017-2026, and the trend since 1976 is warming at 0.42 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low of 70 F or higher. Drought has been rare here, with 43 of 1357 weeks since 2000 seeing at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and the worst year was 2007 with 17 weeks. The land is valued at $4,027 per acre, and there are only 2 CRP acres, none of them with wind or solar on the ground.

54049.text: What stands out in Marion County is the rent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 252.2 percent since 2016, so the ground that rented cheap a decade ago now costs a good deal more to lease. Land and buildings were valued at $3,858 per acre in the 2022 census, and that is the operators' own estimate, not a sale. The county has 2 percent of its harvested cropland under irrigation, so most of the crop rides on rain. Summer nights have been warmer, with July lows averaging 62.9 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.6 F. Drought weeks have been few overall, 15 of 1357 since 2000, but 2024 alone had 15.

54051.text: Marshall County is quiet on most counts, and the notable one is land value. Operators put land and buildings at $3,668 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 41.8 percent from 2017 to 2022, or 7.2 percent a year. Nights are running a little warmer than the 1991-2020 normal, with July lows averaging 63.2 F over 2017-2026 against 62 F in the normal. Drought is the other thing to watch: the county had 24 weeks of severe drought or worse from 2000 through 2025, and 17 of those came in 2024. No CRP acres are in the county now, and only 1 acre expires over fiscal years 2027-2029. There is no solar or wind operating, and none proposed.

54053.text: Heat and drought is the story in Mason County. It was 63 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, down to 14 percent in 2010-2019, and back up to 77 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the last ten closed crop years is 0.81, and the county paid out $7.11 per $100 of insured value over 2016-2025. Non-irrigated cash rent is $103 per acre for 2026, up 24.1 percent since 2014. The census puts land and buildings at $2,972 per acre in 2022, and only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated. Median corn yield for 2008-2016 was 138 bushels per acre, with 2012 the worst year at 123.3.

54057.text: Heat and drought is the story in Mineral County. It made up 80 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 2020-2025, up from 44 percent in 2010-2019, and it was the largest cause over the full 1989-2025 record at 67 percent. The worst single year for drought was 2024, with 24 weeks at severe drought or worse across the county. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most ground depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent is $27 per acre in 2026, up 3.8 percent since 2016.

54059.text: Mingo County is notable for its warm summer nights more than anything else. The July average low has been 65.7 F over 2017-2026, up from the 1991-2020 normal of 64.5 F, and the 2020s are the first decade the July average low reached 66 F. The nightly low trend since 1976 is warming at 0.49 F per decade. Severe drought has been rare here: 36 of 1357 weeks since 2000, with 2 weeks in 2021-2025. Census land and buildings were valued at $1,361 per acre in 2022, up 22 percent from 2017. There is no CRP, no operating wind or solar, and none proposed.

54061.text: Monongalia County's notable number is the rent rise. Non-irrigated cash rent is $18 per acre in 2026, and it was up 63.6 percent from 2014. That's a big move for ground that isn't irrigated, so I'd want to know what's behind it before deciding anything. The July nightly low has climbed too, from 61.4 F in the 1991-2020 normal to 62.7 F over 2017-2026, and the warming trend since 1976 is 0.54 F per decade. Drought has been quiet by comparison: 15 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with 15 of those weeks all in 2024. Solar is running at 18.9 MW, and there's no wind or CRP acres on the books here.

54063.text: Monroe County is mostly dryland, and the notable thing in the insurance record is that heat and drought claims have come back in a big way. Their share of indemnities was 54 percent in 1989-1999, fell to 16 percent in 2000-2009, and was 45 percent in 2020-2025. Freeze and frost is still the largest cause over the full record at 48 percent, and total indemnities of $2.3 million against premiums have a loss ratio of 1.39, so claims have run ahead of premium overall. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre for 2026, up 5.7 percent since 2016, and the census value of land and buildings is $3,501 per acre for 2022.

54065.text: Morgan County's notable number is hail. It accounts for 41 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989 through 2025, which came to $998,644 across the closed crop years. Heat and drought have been a smaller part of the claims, though their share went from 4 percent in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2000-2009 and then 6 percent in 2010-2019. Only 1 percent of the harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground here depends on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $21 per acre, and the census value of land and buildings in 2022 was $5,715 per acre.

54071.text: Pendleton County's cropland is all dryland, and heat and drought account for most of what it has paid out. Crop insurance indemnities have run $2.0 million over the closed crop years 1989-2025, with heat and drought at 81 percent of that, and the loss ratio is 0.88. The share held steady across periods, at 85 percent in 1989-1999 and 83 percent in 2020-2025, so this is a county where dry years have been the main claim all along. July nights have warmed too, from a 1991-2020 normal of 58.2 F to 59.7 F over 2017-2026. Cash rent for non-irrigated ground is $34 per acre, up 19 percent since 2016.

54073.text: Pleasants County is mostly dryland ground, with only 3 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in 2022. The land and buildings were valued at $3,209 per acre in the 2022 census, and that value was up 39 percent from 2017, or 6.8 percent a year. Drought is the main thing to watch here. The county had 16 weeks with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, and all 16 came in 2024. Nightly July lows have warmed too, averaging 64.3 F over 2017-2026 against 62.6 F in the 1991-2020 normal. No wind or solar is operating or proposed here, and the CRP acres that expire in fiscal years 2027-2029 are zero.

54075.text: Pocahontas County has no irrigated acres at all, so every bushel here rides on rain. The loss record shows it. Heat and drought was the largest cause of crop insurance claims at 39 percent, out of $127,656 in indemnities for closed crop years from 1989-2018. The county has also had 18 weeks in severe drought or worse since 2021, and 2024 alone logged 11 of those weeks. July nights are warming, with the average low up from the 1991-2020 normal of 56.9 F to 58.3 F over 2017-2026. Non-irrigated cash rent is $37 per acre in 2026, down 10.8 percent from 2016. Land and buildings were valued at $3,089 per acre in 2022, up 64.7 percent from 2017.

54077.text: Preston County's loss record is the thing to look at first. Insurance indemnities have run above premium over the last ten closed crop years, with a loss ratio of 1.06, and the 2016-2025 payout came to $14.36 for every $100 insured. Heat and drought used to be a small share of those claims, 3 percent in 2010-2019, and jumped to 50 percent in 2020-2025. Over the full record since 1993, excess moisture and flood have been the biggest cause at 52 percent. July nights have been warmer too, averaging 61.2 F over 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 59.5 F. Rent is $27 an acre for non-irrigated ground, up 25.6 percent since 2016.

54079.text: Heat and drought is what stands out in Putnam County. It caused 45 percent of the crop insurance indemnities paid from 1989-2025, and its share went from 58 percent in 1989-1999 to 83 percent in 2020-2025. Ground that is dry in July is hard on a crop here, and the claims show it. Non-irrigated cash rent was $44 per acre in 2024, down 42.8 percent from 2012. The July average nightly low has risen to 65.9 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.3 F, and 2020s was the first decade the July average low reached 66 F.

54083.text: Randolph County's notable number is the rent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $34 per acre for 2026, and it has climbed 47.8 percent since 2016, with no irrigated ground at all to lift the average. The land itself is priced at $2,785 per acre by the census, and that value rose 14.8 percent between 2017 and 2022. Heat is not the story here: the July nightly low is 59 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 57.5 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged 70 F or higher. Drought weeks are few, 37 of 1357 since 2000, with 2024 the worst year at 19 weeks. CRP holds 1294 acres, 8.1 percent of cropland, and 3 of those acres expire over fiscal years 2027-2029.

54085.text: Ritchie County is a quiet one on most measures. Its July nights have warmed a little, with the average low up to 64.3 F from a 1991-2020 normal of 62.6 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.58 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Drought has been rare here: 20 weeks of severe drought or worse in 2000-2025, and all 20 came in 2024, so the 2021-2025 span carries no other such weeks. Non-irrigated cash rent was $14 per acre in 2024, and the census put land and buildings at $2,306 per acre in 2022, up 27.8 percent from 2017, which is 5 percent a year. There are 64 CRP acres and no wind or solar operating.

54087.text: Roane County's land is the one thing here that stands out for a reason other than rent. Non-irrigated cash rent is $16 per acre in 2026, up 45.5 percent from 2016, and the operators' own estimate for land and buildings in 2022 was $2,057 per acre, up 6.6 percent from 2017. Drought has been the rarer problem: 19 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with the worst year being 2024 at 19 weeks. Nights have warmed a little. The July average low for 2017-2026 is 64.6 F against a 1991-2020 normal of 63.1 F, and no July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. There is no CRP and no wind or solar in the county.

54089.text: Summers County's most notable number is the crop insurance record. Heat and drought made up 44 percent of the $187,351 in indemnities paid on closed crop years from 1992 to 2003, and the share was 55 percent for 1989-1999. Nights are warming too: the July average low for 2017-2026 is 62.2 F, against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.3 F. Rent is $24 per acre, up 56.7 percent from 2013 to 2023. None of the cropland is irrigated, and 11.3 percent of the cropland base sits in CRP.

54091.text: Taylor County's rent is low and rising fast. Non-irrigated cash rent is $24 per acre in 2026, and it has gone up 84.6 percent since 2014. Nothing here is irrigated, so the ground runs entirely on rain. The county has had 15 weeks of severe drought or worse since 2021, and 2024 was the worst year at 15 weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $4,194 per acre in the 2022 census, up 36.4 percent from 2017. Nightly July lows have averaged 63 F across 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.7 F.

54093.text: What stands out in Tucker County is the July heat and the wind. The July nightly low has averaged 59 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 57.3 F, and the trend has run warm at 0.51 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F, so the heat is real but the nights stay cool. Drought has been light by comparison: 39 weeks in severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, with the worst year, 2024, at 21 weeks. The county has 66 MW of operating wind and 86 acres in CRP, with none of that CRP expiring in fiscal 2027-2029. Non-irrigated cash rent is $35 per acre for 2026.

54097.text: Upshur County is mostly dryland ground, with 1 percent of harvested cropland irrigated in the 2022 census. Nights in July have been warming: the July average low was 62.5 F for 2017-2026 against a 1991-2020 normal of 61 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.53 F per decade. Drought has been rare here over the full run, with 33 weeks of severe drought or worse across 2000-2025, but the worst year, 2024, had 20 of them. Non-irrigated cash rent was $25 per acre in 2019, while the census land and buildings value was $3,215 per acre in 2022, up 21.6 percent from 2017.

54099.text: Wayne County is mostly dryland, with only 2 percent of harvested cropland irrigated, so the water picture runs through the weather more than through a well. Drought has been the thing to watch here. The county spent 34 of 1357 weeks since 2000 with at least 50 percent of its area in severe drought or worse, and 24 of those weeks came in 2007 alone. Heat is creeping up too: the July average nightly low was 66.2 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 64.5 F. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $31 per acre. The census put land and buildings at $2,644 per acre in 2022, up 31.6 percent from 2017.

54101.text: Webster County is a place where the water has mostly held. Only 1 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and the county had 34 weeks of severe drought or worse from 2000-2025, with the worst year being 2024 at 19 weeks. The July nightly low is running 60.7 F for 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 59.5 F, and the trend since 1976 is 0.42 F per decade, warming. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Census land and buildings were $1,960 per acre in 2022. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar operating or proposed here.

54103.text: Wetzel County has warmed a little, and the change shows up in the nights more than the days. July nightly lows averaged 63.1 F over 2017-2026, against a 1991-2020 normal of 61.7 F, and the long record since 1976 trends warmer at 0.55 F per decade. No July since 1900 has averaged a low at or above 70 F. Drought has been rare here. Only 20 of 1357 weeks since 2000 had at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse, and 2024 was the worst year at 15 weeks. Census land and buildings were valued at $2,290 per acre in 2022, up 18.8 percent from 2017.

56001.text: Albany County is mostly irrigated ground, 81 percent of harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from groundwater, so the pumping and the wells are not the story here. The drought weeks are the thing to watch. Weeks with at least 50 percent of the county in severe drought or worse were 238 of 1357 across 2000-2025, with 2002 the worst year at 46 weeks. Land and buildings were valued at $1,040 per acre in 2022, and that value rose 42.3 percent from 2017-2022. Wind is the big new use, with 487.1 MW operating and 504 MW proposed.

56003.text: Big Horn County is an irrigated county. Eighty-two percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, and only 1 percent of the water comes from groundwater, so most of the supply is surface water. Non-irrigated ground rented for $23 per acre in 2020, and irrigated ground rented for $106 per acre in 2026. Freeze and frost is the largest cause of claims over 1989-2025, but heat and drought went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 23 percent in 2020-2025. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in premium, with a loss ratio of 1.12 across closed years.

56005.text: Heat and drought is the story in Campbell County. It was 19 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999, 53 percent in 2000-2009, 67 percent in 2010-2019, and 81 percent in 2020-2025. The loss ratio over the ten closed crop years 2016-2025 was 1.25, so claims have run above premiums. Only 7 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most of the ground rides on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent was $10 per acre in 2019, and CRP covers 49.4 percent of the cropland base.

56007.text: Carbon County is mostly irrigated ground, 96 percent of harvested cropland, and none of that water comes from wells. The bigger story on the paper is wind. There are 1754.6 MW of wind operating in the county, with another 3556.6 MW proposed, and no solar either way. Land and buildings were valued at $971 per acre in the 2022 census, up 76.5 percent from 2017, while irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $24 per acre. Non-irrigated rent in 2022 was $17 per acre. CRP takes up 23.2 percent of the cropland base, and 81 acres of it expire in fiscal years 2027-2029. Weeks of severe drought ran 24.1 percent of the time from 2000-2025, with 2003 the worst at 52 weeks.

56011.text: Crook County's heat and drought claims are the thing to look at. Heat and drought went from 26 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 80 percent in 2020-2025, and the county has paid $20.0 million on closed crop years since 1989. Its loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.05, so the premiums there have not covered the claims. The July nightly low has warmed to 56.4 F in 2017-2026 from 55.1 F in the 1991-2020 normal. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $14 per acre, and the census land value was $1,776 per acre in 2022.

56013.text: Fremont County is an irrigated county. Irrigated land is 94 percent of harvested cropland, and the water comes from surface sources, not groundwater. The rent that matters most here is the irrigated rate of $78 per acre for 2026, against $15 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2025. Crop insurance has paid out $9.3 million on closed years since 1989, with irrigation failure the largest single cause at 27 percent. Heat and drought claims have moved from 13 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 16 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the last ten closed years is 0.25.

56015.text: Goshen County is mostly irrigated ground. The census put 66 percent of harvested cropland under irrigation in 2022, and the irrigated cash rent for 2026 is $170 per acre, against $20 for non-irrigated ground in 2025. Non-irrigated rent is up 57.7 percent since 2014. Heat and drought claims went from 4 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 33 percent in 2020-2025. The county's crop insurance loss ratio is 0.89 over 1989-2025, so claims have paid out more than premiums over the full record. Land and buildings were valued at $1,871 per acre in 2022.

56021.text: Laramie County is mostly dryland ground, and the thing that stands out is how the losses have been landing. Heat and drought went from 5 percent of crop insurance indemnities in 1989-1999 to 52 percent in 2020-2025, and the loss ratio over the ten closed years 2016-2025 is 1.03, so the county has paid out a bit more than the premium it took in. Irrigated ground rents for $112 per acre against $28 for the dryland, and the census puts land and buildings at $2,003 per acre, up 136.2 percent from 2017 to 2022. Non-irrigated cash rent is up 37.5 percent since 2016.

56025.text: Natrona County is mostly irrigated ground, 93 percent of harvested cropland in the 2022 census, and all of its irrigation water comes from surface sources. Crop insurance has paid out more than it took in, with a loss ratio of 1.39 across closed crop years 1990-2025. Heat and drought was the largest cause of those claims, though its share fell from 76 percent in 1989-1999 to 6 percent in 2020-2025. Irrigated cash rent in 2026 is $89 per acre, against $12 per acre for non-irrigated ground in 2012. The census value of land and buildings was $825 per acre in 2022.

56027.text: Niobrara County is notable for heat and drought claims. Their share of crop insurance indemnities went from 3 percent in 1989-1999 to 55 percent in 2020-2025, and 85 weeks of severe drought or worse have been logged since 2021. The county's loss ratio is 1.39 across the closed crop years 1989-2025, though it was 0.28 over 2016-2025. Irrigation is 35 percent of harvested cropland, and 91 percent of that water comes from groundwater. Non-irrigated cash rent in 2025 was $14 per acre, with irrigated at $135 per acre for 2026.

56029.text: Most of Park County's harvested cropland is irrigated, 89 percent in the 2022 census, and the irrigation water comes from surface sources, not groundwater. Irrigated cash rent was $110 per acre in 2026 against $30 for non-irrigated ground in 2021. Heat and drought claims went from 3 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 25 percent in 2020-2025, and freeze and frost is still the largest cause at 55 percent of the $29.3 million paid since 1989. The county has 49714 acres in CRP, which is 35.8 percent of the cropland base, and none of it expires in fiscal years 2027-2029.

56031.text: Platte County is a county where irrigation sets the rent. Irrigated ground rents for $120 per acre in 2025, while non-irrigated ground goes for $22, and 60 percent of harvested cropland is under irrigation. Heat and drought claims went from 1 percent of indemnities in 1989-1999 to 32 percent in 2020-2025, so the dry years are showing up on claims. Hail is still the largest single cause at 26 percent. Losses have run close to premiums over time, with a loss ratio of 0.88 across 1989-2025.

56039.text: Teton County is mostly irrigated ground, with 67 percent of harvested cropland watered in 2022, and the water doesn't come from wells. Drought is the number to watch here. The county was in severe drought or worse for 375 of 1357 weeks from 2000 to 2025, 27.6 percent of the time, and 2003 alone had 52 such weeks. The last five years logged 131 weeks in that condition. Non-irrigated cash rent is $40 per acre for 2026, up 158.1 percent from 2016, and irrigated ground rents for $45 per acre. The census value of land and buildings is $11,792 per acre. July nights have held close to the 1991-2020 normal, and no July since 1900 averaged a low at or above 70 F.

56043.text: Washakie County is mostly irrigated: 91 percent of harvested cropland was watered in the 2022 census, and only 3 percent of that water came from groundwater. Crop insurance has paid $2.3 million in indemnities since 1989, and the loss ratio is 0.34 over the full record but just 0.12 across the last ten closed crop years. Heat and drought claims were 25 percent of indemnities in 2000-2009 and 1 percent in 2020-2025. Drought weeks were heavy in 2002, with 53 weeks, and the census puts land and buildings at $1,623 per acre. There is no CRP ground and no wind or solar on the books here.

56045.text: Heat and drought is the story in Weston County. It paid 43 percent of the closed crop insurance indemnities from 1989 to 2025, and it was 29 percent of the claims in 2000-2009 and 74 percent in 2010-2019. Losses have run heavier than premiums: the loss ratio is 1.32 over the full record and 1.19 over the last ten closed crop years. Only 29 percent of harvested cropland is irrigated, so most acres depend on rain. Non-irrigated cash rent was $17 per acre in 2023, up 25.9 percent from 2012. Census land and buildings value was $953 per acre in 2022, up 42.5 percent since 2017.
